# Running Without the Ball: Valuing Decoy Lines in Rugby Sevens

## Project summary

Rugby sevens analysis assigns most possession value to visible actions: carries, passes, tackles, and breaks. This overlooks attackers who create space without touching the ball. The proposed study will estimate the value of decoy runs by combining player tracking, video-derived body orientation, and a counterfactual possession model. Its central output will be **Decoy Added Value (DAV)**: the change in expected possession value attributable to an off-ball runner’s line over the following three seconds.

The study will use two seasons of the Veyra Continental Sevens Championship, an elite 12-club competition. Alongside a league-wide analysis, controlled preseason scrimmages will compare paired versions of selected attacking patterns. The project is intended to improve tactical evaluation while avoiding a player-ranking system that simply rewards ball involvement.

## Rationale

A decoy can pull a defender inward, delay a drift, or create uncertainty about the next receiver. Conventional event data record none of these effects. Even tracking summaries such as distance covered treat a threatening line and an irrelevant sprint as equivalent.

Sevens is a useful setting because space is abundant, defensive choices are consequential, and possessions are short enough to model at high temporal resolution. It is also analytically difficult: a runner may look threatening because defenders react, but defenders may react because the surrounding attack was already dangerous. Counting defender movements toward a runner would therefore overstate the runner’s independent contribution.

This project addresses that problem by comparing observed possessions with model-generated alternatives in which the candidate runner follows a tactically plausible support line rather than the observed decoy line.

## Research questions and hypotheses

1. **Which movement and contextual features distinguish intentional decoys from support or repositioning runs?**
2. **How much possession value is created by decoys, after accounting for field position, defensive structure, score, and the identities of nearby players?**
3. **Which tactical contexts produce the greatest returns from decoy running?**

The main hypothesis is that decoys generate their largest gains near the outside shoulder of the defensive second player, where a brief inward commitment can release the edge attacker. A secondary hypothesis is that raw defender displacement exaggerates value relative to DAV because some apparent commitments occur in possessions that were already favorable to the attack.

## Data

The proposed dataset comprises approximately 430 matches, yielding an estimated 18,000 attacking possessions. Overhead optical tracking will provide player and ball coordinates at 25 Hz. Synchronized video will be used to estimate torso orientation and to identify occluded passes, contacts, and restarts. Event logs will supply score, match time, sanctions, substitutions, and possession outcomes.

Analysts will label 4,000 candidate off-ball runs as **decoy**, **support**, **repositioning**, or **unclear**. A candidate run begins when a non-carrier accelerates above 4.5 metres per second toward a feasible receiving channel and ends at a pass, contact, abrupt change of direction, or 2.5 seconds. Two former sevens coaches will annotate each clip independently; disagreements will be adjudicated by a third analyst. Inter-rater agreement and class-specific uncertainty will be reported.

Player identifiers will be pseudonymized during model development. Public outputs will suppress individual estimates unless the relevant club and player consent, and all rankings will include uncertainty intervals and minimum-possession thresholds.

## Analytical design

First, a sequence classifier will identify probable decoys from the preceding two seconds of tracking, torso orientation, ball location, and formation geometry. Data will be split by club rather than randomly by possession, reducing leakage from team-specific patterns. Performance will be assessed using precision-recall curves, calibration, and accuracy within field-zone and restart-type strata.

Second, an expected possession value model will estimate the probability distribution over four outcomes during the next three seconds: possession loss, retained possession without a line break, line break, or score. Values will be derived from the historical points subsequently associated with each outcome and adjusted for field position and time remaining. A temporal graph network will represent attackers and defenders as interacting nodes, allowing the model to learn marking relationships and defensive compression.

For each classified decoy, a constrained trajectory generator will replace the observed line with a neutral support trajectory. Replacement paths must respect the runner’s initial speed, acceleration limits, field boundaries, and the team’s observed spacing conventions. A joint transition model will then simulate how the other players could respond to that intervention. DAV is the expected possession value of the observed state sequence minus the mean value across 100 simulated neutral-line sequences.

The primary analysis will estimate average DAV using a hierarchical model with partial pooling by player, club, restart type, field zone, and defensive shape. This prevents players with a handful of spectacular examples from dominating the rankings. Secondary analyses will examine defender rotation, width created for the eventual receiver, and whether value persists after controlling for the passer’s decision quality.

## Validation and robustness

Three tests will probe whether DAV captures more than model preference. First, analysts will repeat the intervention using two alternative baselines: holding width and trailing the ball carrier. Conclusions that depend on one definition of a neutral run will be treated as unstable. Second, placebo interventions will alter players who are behind the ball and outside any feasible passing lane; these changes should produce DAV estimates near zero. Third, models will be evaluated on an entirely held-out final tournament rather than only on shuffled historical possessions.

The observational analysis will be triangulated with six preseason scrimmages. Participating coaches will select four familiar attacking patterns and prepare paired versions that differ primarily in one runner’s line. Each version will be attempted six times against the same defensive personnel, with order varied across blocks. The comparison will focus on defender movement and immediate line-break probability rather than points, which are too rare for this small exercise. Scrimmages will not be used to train the main model.

## Deliverables and practical use

The project will produce a validated decoy classifier, possession-level DAV estimates, and tactical maps showing where particular run shapes tend to create space. A coaching dashboard will permit video retrieval by defensive shape, decoy angle, and resulting advantage. Rather than presenting DAV as a stand-alone player grade, the dashboard will pair it with receiving, passing, and workload measures so that coaches can distinguish repeated tactical contribution from indiscriminate running.

Work will proceed over 12 months: three months for synchronization and annotation, four for model development, two for scrimmage collection, and three for validation and reporting. The principal limitation is that simulated defender responses cannot establish the same causal certainty as randomized match play. Results will therefore be described as model-based counterfactual estimates, with conclusions emphasized only where the intervention baselines, held-out data, and scrimmage evidence agree.

# Every Rooftop Hive Should Pay a Ground-Level Forage Tax

Urban beekeeping is often advertised as an easy environmental victory. A company installs two painted hives on its headquarters, posts photographs of employees in veils, and gives clients small jars of honey. Yet the bees do not recognize the edge of the company’s roof. They travel through the surrounding district and depend on flowers maintained by residents, parks, schools, and other businesses. Cities should therefore stop treating a hive as a self-contained rooftop amenity. Every new urban hive should be permitted only if its owner also funds a strip of flowering habitat at street level.

This requirement could be called a forage tax. For each hive, the beekeeper would have to maintain at least twenty metres of planted curb, verge, courtyard edge, or vacant-lot border within five hundred metres of the hive. The strip would need to contain flowers blooming in three different seasons and could not be treated with insecticide. Hive owners without suitable land could pay into a municipal fund that would plant flowers nearby. The rule would connect the visible symbol of urban beekeeping with the less glamorous work that actually feeds insects.

The need for such a rule is easiest to see in dense business districts. Consider Marrowgate Square, an office quarter in the city of Dovetail. Over four years, the number of registered rooftop hives there rose from six to thirty-one. During the same period, the district added only nine substantial flower beds. Informal inspections by a neighborhood gardening club found many honey bees crowding the few beds in late summer, while several colonies had to be given sugar syrup. Although this example does not prove that the hives caused a shortage, it strongly suggests that hive growth can outpace local forage.

Beekeepers sometimes answer that honey bees can fly several kilometres, so flowers do not have to be next to a hive. That is true, but it avoids the question of responsibility. A restaurant may send its rubbish across town for disposal, but it still has to pay for collection. In the same way, the ability of bees to search a wide area should not entitle hive owners to rely freely on everybody else’s gardens. The farther bees must fly, the more energy they use, which presumably means less honey and weaker colonies. Nearby planting is therefore both a fair contribution and a practical benefit.

A forage tax would also reduce environmental advertising that produces little environmental value. At present, a rooftop hive can function mainly as a publicity object. The owner receives honey and an appealing story, while the surrounding public provides most of the flowers. A mandatory planting strip is harder to fake. People walking past can see whether it exists, and municipal inspectors can check it without climbing onto a roof. This visibility might encourage building owners to care for the planting properly rather than forgetting the hive after its launch event.

The policy could benefit insects other than managed honey bees as well. Flower strips with different shapes and blooming periods may provide food for bumblebees, hoverflies, moths, and solitary bees. Cities should specify a mixture rather than allowing a bed of one decorative flower. A reasonable list might include bellflower, stone mint, dusk clover, and small-flowered aster, adjusted for local conditions. Because these plants would be spread along streets instead of concentrated on private roofs, they could form routes between parks and gardens.

There is, however, a possible conflict between honey bees and wild pollinators. Large numbers of managed bees may consume nectar that would otherwise be available to local species. Some conservation groups therefore argue that cities should discourage hives rather than subsidize forage for them. This objection deserves attention, but the forage tax largely answers it: if every hive creates more flowers, then there should be enough food for both managed and wild bees. Twenty metres of planting should compensate for one colony in most neighborhoods, especially when the flowers bloom across several seasons.

The strongest practical objection is cost. A small-scale beekeeper may not own a curb or vacant lot, and hiring a landscape company could make the hobby unaffordable. The payment option would solve much of this problem. Dovetail could charge an annual fee of eighty crowns per hive and combine the money to plant larger sites. Schools and community gardens could apply to host these sites. Since a healthy hive can produce jars of honey worth more than the fee, the charge would not be unreasonable. Beekeepers who cannot earn eighty crowns from a colony may not be maintaining it effectively anyway.

Enforcement need not be complicated. Applicants would submit a map and seasonal planting plan with the ordinary hive registration form. An inspector would visit once in midsummer. If half the required strip were dead or missing, the owner would receive a warning; a second failure would lead to removal of the hive. Existing hives could be given two years to comply. Buildings with several hives could share one larger planting area, although the twenty-metre rule would still apply to each colony.

Some flexibility would be necessary. A shaded district cannot support the same plants as a sunny industrial roof, and drought years can kill even well-maintained beds. Nevertheless, flexibility should not become an excuse for doing nothing. The city could publish three standard planting mixtures and allow substitutions when an owner explains them. This is more realistic than demanding a unique ecological assessment for every hive.

Urban beekeeping should continue, but it should become less symbolic and more accountable. Bees cross property lines, so their owners create demands beyond the roof where the colonies sit. Requiring street-level flowers would return something to the neighborhoods that sustain them, expose shallow publicity projects, and produce habitat that residents can enjoy. A jar of rooftop honey may be pleasant, but a visible trail of flowers is a better measure of whether the hive belongs in the city.

# Every Rooftop Hive Should Pay a Ground-Level Forage Tax

Urban beekeeping is often advertised as an easy environmental victory. A company installs two painted hives on its headquarters, posts photographs of employees in veils, and gives clients small jars of honey. Yet the bees do not recognize the edge of the company’s roof. They travel through the surrounding district and depend on flowers maintained by residents, parks, schools, and other businesses. Cities should therefore stop treating a hive as a self-contained rooftop amenity. Every new urban hive should be permitted only if its owner also funds a strip of flowering habitat at street level.

This requirement could be called a forage tax. For each hive, the beekeeper would have to maintain at least twenty metres of planted curb, verge, courtyard edge, or vacant-lot border within five hundred metres of the hive. The strip would need to contain flowers blooming in three different seasons and could not be treated with insecticide. Hive owners without suitable land could pay into a municipal fund that would plant flowers nearby. The rule would connect the visible symbol of urban beekeeping with the less glamorous work that actually feeds insects.

The need for such a rule is easiest to see in dense business districts. Consider Marrowgate Square, an office quarter in the city of Dovetail. Over four years, the number of registered rooftop hives there rose from six to thirty-one. During the same period, the district added only nine substantial flower beds. Informal inspections by a neighborhood gardening club found many honey bees crowding the few beds in late summer, while several colonies had to be given sugar syrup. Although this example does not prove that the hives caused a shortage, it strongly suggests that hive growth can outpace local forage.

Beekeepers sometimes answer that honey bees can fly several kilometres, so flowers do not have to be next to a hive. That is true, but it avoids the question of responsibility. A restaurant may send its rubbish across town for disposal, but it still has to pay for collection. In the same way, the ability of bees to search a wide area should not entitle hive owners to rely freely on everybody else’s gardens. The farther bees must fly, the more energy they use, which presumably means less honey and weaker colonies. Nearby planting is therefore both a fair contribution and a practical benefit.

A forage tax would also reduce environmental advertising that produces little environmental value. At present, a rooftop hive can function mainly as a publicity object. The owner receives honey and an appealing story, while the surrounding public provides most of the flowers. A mandatory planting strip is harder to fake. People walking past can see whether it exists, and municipal inspectors can check it without climbing onto a roof. This visibility might encourage building owners to care for the planting properly rather than forgetting the hive after its launch event.

The policy could benefit insects other than managed honey bees as well. Flower strips with different shapes and blooming periods may provide food for bumblebees, hoverflies, moths, and solitary bees. Cities should specify a mixture rather than allowing a bed of one decorative flower. A reasonable list might include bellflower, stone mint, dusk clover, and small-flowered aster, adjusted for local conditions. Because these plants would be spread along streets instead of concentrated on private roofs, they could form routes between parks and gardens.

There is, however, a possible conflict between honey bees and wild pollinators. Large numbers of managed bees may consume nectar that would otherwise be available to local species. Some conservation groups therefore argue that cities should discourage hives rather than subsidize forage for them. This objection deserves attention, but the forage tax largely answers it: if every hive creates more flowers, then there should be enough food for both managed and wild bees. Twenty metres of planting should compensate for one colony in most neighborhoods, especially when the flowers bloom across several seasons.

The strongest practical objection is cost. A small-scale beekeeper may not own a curb or vacant lot, and hiring a landscape company could make the hobby unaffordable. The payment option would solve much of this problem. Dovetail could charge an annual fee of eighty crowns per hive and combine the money to plant larger sites. Schools and community gardens could apply to host these sites. Since a healthy hive can produce jars of honey worth more than the fee, the charge would not be unreasonable. Beekeepers who cannot earn eighty crowns from a colony may not be maintaining it effectively anyway.

Enforcement need not be complicated. Applicants would submit a map and seasonal planting plan with the ordinary hive registration form. An inspector would visit once in midsummer. If half the required strip were dead or missing, the owner would receive a warning; a second failure would lead to removal of the hive. Existing hives could be given two years to comply. Buildings with several hives could share one larger planting area, although the twenty-metre rule would still apply to each colony.

Some flexibility would be necessary. A shaded district cannot support the same plants as a sunny industrial roof, and drought years can kill even well-maintained beds. Nevertheless, flexibility should not become an excuse for doing nothing. The city could publish three standard planting mixtures and allow substitutions when an owner explains them. This is more realistic than demanding a unique ecological assessment for every hive.

Urban beekeeping should continue, but it should become less symbolic and more accountable. Bees cross property lines, so their owners create demands beyond the roof where the colonies sit. Requiring street-level flowers would return something to the neighborhoods that sustain them, expose shallow publicity projects, and produce habitat that residents can enjoy. A jar of rooftop honey may be pleasant, but a visible trail of flowers is a better measure of whether the hive belongs in the city.

# The Queue Is Part of the Refrigerator

Cold-chain planning often concentrates on equipment: the refrigerator, the insulated carrier, the refrigerated truck. Yet many vaccine temperature excursions occur in the spaces between those devices. A carton waits on a receiving bench while its paperwork is checked. A carrier sits open as vials are counted. Three outreach teams arrive for collection at once. None of these moments looks like a refrigeration failure, but together they form a “handoff gap” in which controlled storage has ended and the next protective system has not fully begun.

Treating the queue as part of the cold chain changes what a clinic measures and manages. The relevant question is not simply whether a refrigerator stayed cold overnight. It is how much thermal protection remains when a vaccine leaves that refrigerator, and how quickly staff can complete the transfer.

## Temperature limits belong to the product

“Keep vaccines cold” is an incomplete instruction. Each product has its own labeled storage conditions. Many routine vaccines are stored in a chilled range, commonly 2°C to 8°C, while some products require frozen or ultra-cold storage. Some are damaged by excessive heat; others can also lose potency after freezing. A brief freezing event may therefore matter even when the average temperature for the day appears acceptable.

This distinction affects handoffs. A worker trying to protect a freeze-sensitive vaccine might place it directly against a deeply frozen pack, preventing heat exposure but creating a freezing hazard. Conversely, packs that have warmed too far may provide little protection during a long journey. Diluents and ancillary materials can have different requirements from the vaccine they accompany, so convenience should not substitute for checking the applicable instructions.

## Thermal protection is a budget

An insulated carrier does not produce cold. It slows heat entering from the surroundings and uses the thermal mass of its contents and coolant packs to absorb some of that heat. This protection can be understood as a finite budget.

Phase-change packs are especially useful because they absorb substantial heat while changing phase, with relatively little change in their own temperature. However, their performance depends on preparation. A pack removed straight from a very cold freezer may be too cold for a freeze-sensitive product. A poorly conditioned pack may already have spent much of its useful capacity before loading.

A rough planning model illustrates the principle. Suppose a packed carrier can absorb 900 kilojoules before its payload approaches an upper limit, while heat enters at an average rate of 25 watts. Since one watt is one joule per second, the nominal holdover time is:

**900,000 joules ÷ 25 joules per second = 36,000 seconds, or 10 hours.**

That figure is not a guarantee. Heat leakage changes with ambient temperature, pack arrangement, carrier condition, sunlight, airflow and lid openings. The payload also does not warm uniformly. Nevertheless, the calculation shows why apparently minor actions matter: opening the lid, leaving empty space or starting with partially warmed packs spends the same limited thermal budget needed for the journey.

## The dock clock starts before departure

A common operating assumption is that transport time begins when the vehicle leaves. Thermally, it begins when the first protected container is opened or the vaccine leaves controlled storage.

Consider a district store in the fictional Merrow Vale region. Four clinics collect weekly vaccine allocations on the same morning. Each team needs ten minutes for identity checks, quantity reconciliation and signatures. If all arrive at 08:00 and staff pre-stage every order on a table, the fourth order may spend nearly 40 minutes outside controlled equipment before its carrier is sealed. On a mild day this may have little consequence; in a hot loading area, it can consume a meaningful share of the carrier’s holdover time.

The stronger design is to separate administrative readiness from physical release. Staff can prepare labels and documents in advance while keeping products in qualified storage. Each order is removed only when its carrier is ready, its coolant packs have been checked, and the receiving worker is present. Appointment slots or staggered collection windows reduce simultaneous demand. A simple rule—only one open carrier per packing station—also makes responsibility clearer.

This approach does not necessarily make the process slower. It moves counting and paperwork upstream and limits the period in which thermal protection is uncertain.

## Sensors need context, not just retrieval

A digital data logger can reveal minimum and maximum temperatures, record readings at intervals, and trigger alarms. Placement matters. A sensor beside the lid may record warmer air whenever the carrier is opened, while one pressed against a coolant pack may record conditions colder than those experienced by most vials. A central position near the payload is often informative, but the appropriate location should come from the carrier’s packing configuration and thermal mapping rather than habit.

An excursion reading also requires interpretation. Staff should preserve the time series, identify the affected products and lots, quarantine them from use, and follow the organization’s assessment process. An isolated peak is not interchangeable with hours of exposure, but averaging the readings can hide a short freezing event. Heat-exposure indicators on some vaccine presentations can add useful information about cumulative heat, yet they do not generally prove that a product avoided freezing.

Data are most useful when joined to operational events. If the temperature rises at 08:17, the log should make it possible to determine whether the lid was opened, the carrier was moved into sunlight, or a route delay began. Without such context, repeated downloads may document failure without identifying its cause.

## Designing a handoff as a controlled process

A practical handoff procedure can be built around five checkpoints:

1. **Confirm the product profile.** Verify the required range, sensitivity to freezing, and any special transport instructions.
2. **Prepare the protective system.** Inspect the carrier and seals, prepare packs according to the approved configuration, and start the logger early enough to confirm stable conditions.
3. **Finish administration first.** Resolve quantities, destinations and paperwork before removing stock where possible.
4. **Load and close deliberately.** Arrange the payload and sensor consistently, fill space as specified, close the carrier, and record the release time.
5. **Define acceptance at arrival.** The receiver should check the seal, elapsed time and logger status before transferring products promptly into appropriate storage.

These checkpoints make the boundary between custody holders visible. They also support investigation: a team can distinguish inadequate pack preparation from a delayed route or a refrigerator problem at the destination.

## Measure the gap, not only the machines

Equipment maintenance remains essential, but refrigerator uptime alone is a narrow performance measure. A district can also track median packing time, the longest interval from stock removal to carrier closure, late collections, improperly prepared packs, alarm frequency by route, and the percentage of shipments whose logger records are reviewed at receipt.

The aim is not to eliminate every minute outside a refrigerator. It is to ensure that each minute occurs inside a planned, tested protective system. In cold-chain logistics, the loading bench, the paperwork queue and the receiving counter are not pauses between controlled steps. They are controlled steps—or unmanaged risks—of their own.

# The Queue Is Part of the Refrigerator

Cold-chain planning often concentrates on equipment: the refrigerator, the insulated carrier, the refrigerated truck. Yet many vaccine temperature excursions occur in the spaces between those devices. A carton waits on a receiving bench while its paperwork is checked. A carrier sits open as vials are counted. Three outreach teams arrive for collection at once. None of these moments looks like a refrigeration failure, but together they form a “handoff gap” in which controlled storage has ended and the next protective system has not fully begun.

Treating the queue as part of the cold chain changes what a clinic measures and manages. The relevant question is not simply whether a refrigerator stayed cold overnight. It is how much thermal protection remains when a vaccine leaves that refrigerator, and how quickly staff can complete the transfer.

## Temperature limits belong to the product

“Keep vaccines cold” is an incomplete instruction. Each product has its own labeled storage conditions. Many routine vaccines are stored in a chilled range, commonly 2°C to 8°C, while some products require frozen or ultra-cold storage. Some are damaged by excessive heat; others can also lose potency after freezing. A brief freezing event may therefore matter even when the average temperature for the day appears acceptable.

This distinction affects handoffs. A worker trying to protect a freeze-sensitive vaccine might place it directly against a deeply frozen pack, preventing heat exposure but creating a freezing hazard. Conversely, packs that have warmed too far may provide little protection during a long journey. Diluents and ancillary materials can have different requirements from the vaccine they accompany, so convenience should not substitute for checking the applicable instructions.

## Thermal protection is a budget

An insulated carrier does not produce cold. It slows heat entering from the surroundings and uses the thermal mass of its contents and coolant packs to absorb some of that heat. This protection can be understood as a finite budget.

Phase-change packs are especially useful because they absorb substantial heat while changing phase, with relatively little change in their own temperature. However, their performance depends on preparation. A pack removed straight from a very cold freezer may be too cold for a freeze-sensitive product. A poorly conditioned pack may already have spent much of its useful capacity before loading.

A rough planning model illustrates the principle. Suppose a packed carrier can absorb 900 kilojoules before its payload approaches an upper limit, while heat enters at an average rate of 25 watts. Since one watt is one joule per second, the nominal holdover time is:

**900,000 joules ÷ 25 joules per second = 36,000 seconds, or 10 hours.**

That figure is not a guarantee. Heat leakage changes with ambient temperature, pack arrangement, carrier condition, sunlight, airflow and lid openings. The payload also does not warm uniformly. Nevertheless, the calculation shows why apparently minor actions matter: opening the lid, leaving empty space or starting with partially warmed packs spends the same limited thermal budget needed for the journey.

## The dock clock starts before departure

A common operating assumption is that transport time begins when the vehicle leaves. Thermally, it begins when the first protected container is opened or the vaccine leaves controlled storage.

Consider a district store in the fictional Merrow Vale region. Four clinics collect weekly vaccine allocations on the same morning. Each team needs ten minutes for identity checks, quantity reconciliation and signatures. If all arrive at 08:00 and staff pre-stage every order on a table, the fourth order may spend nearly 40 minutes outside controlled equipment before its carrier is sealed. On a mild day this may have little consequence; in a hot loading area, it can consume a meaningful share of the carrier’s holdover time.

The stronger design is to separate administrative readiness from physical release. Staff can prepare labels and documents in advance while keeping products in qualified storage. Each order is removed only when its carrier is ready, its coolant packs have been checked, and the receiving worker is present. Appointment slots or staggered collection windows reduce simultaneous demand. A simple rule—only one open carrier per packing station—also makes responsibility clearer.

This approach does not necessarily make the process slower. It moves counting and paperwork upstream and limits the period in which thermal protection is uncertain.

## Sensors need context, not just retrieval

A digital data logger can reveal minimum and maximum temperatures, record readings at intervals, and trigger alarms. Placement matters. A sensor beside the lid may record warmer air whenever the carrier is opened, while one pressed against a coolant pack may record conditions colder than those experienced by most vials. A central position near the payload is often informative, but the appropriate location should come from the carrier’s packing configuration and thermal mapping rather than habit.

An excursion reading also requires interpretation. Staff should preserve the time series, identify the affected products and lots, quarantine them from use, and follow the organization’s assessment process. An isolated peak is not interchangeable with hours of exposure, but averaging the readings can hide a short freezing event. Heat-exposure indicators on some vaccine presentations can add useful information about cumulative heat, yet they do not generally prove that a product avoided freezing.

Data are most useful when joined to operational events. If the temperature rises at 08:17, the log should make it possible to determine whether the lid was opened, the carrier was moved into sunlight, or a route delay began. Without such context, repeated downloads may document failure without identifying its cause.

## Designing a handoff as a controlled process

A practical handoff procedure can be built around five checkpoints:

1. **Confirm the product profile.** Verify the required range, sensitivity to freezing, and any special transport instructions.
2. **Prepare the protective system.** Inspect the carrier and seals, prepare packs according to the approved configuration, and start the logger early enough to confirm stable conditions.
3. **Finish administration first.** Resolve quantities, destinations and paperwork before removing stock where possible.
4. **Load and close deliberately.** Arrange the payload and sensor consistently, fill space as specified, close the carrier, and record the release time.
5. **Define acceptance at arrival.** The receiver should check the seal, elapsed time and logger status before transferring products promptly into appropriate storage.

These checkpoints make the boundary between custody holders visible. They also support investigation: a team can distinguish inadequate pack preparation from a delayed route or a refrigerator problem at the destination.

## Measure the gap, not only the machines

Equipment maintenance remains essential, but refrigerator uptime alone is a narrow performance measure. A district can also track median packing time, the longest interval from stock removal to carrier closure, late collections, improperly prepared packs, alarm frequency by route, and the percentage of shipments whose logger records are reviewed at receipt.

The aim is not to eliminate every minute outside a refrigerator. It is to ensure that each minute occurs inside a planned, tested protective system. In cold-chain logistics, the loading bench, the paperwork queue and the receiving counter are not pauses between controlled steps. They are controlled steps—or unmanaged risks—of their own.

# Closing the Septic-Tank Blind Spot in Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance

**To:** Director-General, Morrow Public Health Agency  
**From:** Office of Surveillance Design  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** An 18-month pilot using septage receiving stations as rural resistance sentinels

## Decision requested

Approve an 18-month, six-site pilot to test whether material collected from septic tanks can provide useful early warning of antibiotic resistance in communities not covered by sewer-based surveillance. Authorize a budget ceiling of **1.84 million Veyran crowns** and require a decision report after month 15, allowing three months for review before any expansion.

The pilot should be treated as a complement to clinical surveillance, not as a method for estimating the prevalence of resistant infections.

## Why action is needed

North Veyra’s current surveillance network combines hospital isolate reports, voluntary submissions from community laboratories, and wastewater sampling at nine municipal treatment plants. This system is strongest where health services and sewer infrastructure are most concentrated. Approximately 31% of the province’s residents use septic systems, including most households in the Hillward and Lower Fen districts. Those districts account for only 12% of resistance test results submitted to the provincial database.

That mismatch creates two problems. First, resistant organisms may circulate for months in under-sampled communities before appearing in a hospital dataset. Second, apparent geographic differences may reflect access to testing rather than true differences in resistance. Recruiting more rural clinics would help, but laboratory staffing and specimen transport remain binding constraints.

Septage—the material pumped from household and institutional septic tanks—offers a neglected pooled sample. Loads are routinely delivered to licensed receiving stations, so sampling can occur at a small number of controlled sites without entering private property or recruiting individual patients. Hauler route records can provide approximate information about the areas contributing to each load.

Septage is not equivalent to fresh municipal wastewater. Tanks retain material for variable periods, pump-outs are irregular, cleaning chemicals may alter microbial signals, and one truck may combine several premises. Those limitations make household-level or point-prevalence claims inappropriate. They do not necessarily prevent the material from serving as a sentinel for new or rising resistance markers.

## Recommended pilot

The agency should establish sampling at six receiving stations selected to represent three settings: remote settlements, agricultural service towns, and peri-urban areas beyond sewer boundaries. Each station would collect one flow-weighted composite sample per operating day during two sampling weeks each month.

The laboratory should use a tiered testing design:

1. **Routine molecular panel:** Test every composite for eight resistance genes selected to cover carbapenem, extended-spectrum beta-lactam, glycopeptide, macrolide, and tetracycline resistance mechanisms. Results should be normalized against both sample mass and a human-associated fecal marker.
2. **Culture-based testing:** Culture a stratified quarter of samples using standardized selective media, then perform susceptibility testing on recovered indicator organisms. This will help distinguish detection of free genetic material from the presence of viable resistant bacteria.
3. **Exploratory sequencing:** Conduct metagenomic sequencing on unusual samples, quarterly background samples, and negative controls. Sequencing should be used to characterize signals, not to generate routine public rankings of districts.

During site selection, the agency should favor stations whose haulers can supply digital records of collection date, broad origin zone, load volume, and premises category. Exact street addresses should not enter the surveillance database. Loads from hospitals, pharmaceutical facilities, and food-processing plants should be flagged or analyzed separately because they may dominate a community signal.

## How results should be interpreted

The pilot’s primary question is operational: **Can septage produce repeatable signals that add information beyond existing clinical and municipal wastewater systems?** It should not attempt to calculate the percentage of residents carrying a resistance gene.

A preliminary alert should require either:

- detection of a locally rare, high-concern marker in two independently collected loads from the same origin zone within 30 days; or
- a marker concentration above three times that site’s rolling baseline in three consecutive composite samples.

An alert would initiate verification, not a public health intervention. Verification should include retesting archived material, reviewing contamination controls and load composition, and comparing the signal with recent clinical isolates from the relevant district. If the signal remains credible, the agency could temporarily fund additional specimen transport from local clinics or request targeted testing by participating laboratories.

The central dashboard should display trends and uncertainty at the station or multi-zone level. Public reports should use broad geographic categories and suppress results when a sample represents fewer than five premises. Because a receiving station may serve several districts, maps should not imply precision that the source records cannot support.

## Evaluation and exit criteria

The pilot should be judged against five pre-specified measures:

- at least 85% of planned samples collected and processed within 48 hours;
- acceptable control performance in at least 95% of laboratory runs;
- reproducibility of marker detection in blinded duplicate samples;
- at least three instances in which septage findings trigger and inform a completed verification review; and
- evidence that the system contributes information not already visible in municipal wastewater or clinical reports.

Continuation should require satisfactory laboratory performance plus evidence of added surveillance value. Expansion should not proceed if origin records are too incomplete to interpret signals, if within-site variation overwhelms trends, or if verification repeatedly fails to find supporting evidence. Even if the pilot succeeds technically, the agency should compare its cost per actionable signal with expanded rural specimen transport before choosing a permanent model.

An independent methods panel should review the protocol before sampling begins and again after the first six months. Membership should include environmental microbiology, clinical laboratory, wastewater operations, rural primary care, and statistical expertise. Haulers and receiving-station staff should be consulted on workflow but should not control interpretation or publication.

## Budget and timetable

The proposed ceiling of **1.84 million crowns** comprises:

- laboratory equipment and validation: 340,000;
- reagents, culture, and sequencing: 510,000;
- sampling equipment and cold-chain transport: 280,000;
- data infrastructure and analysis: 210,000;
- hauler and station participation payments: 150,000;
- personnel and training: 260,000; and
- contingency: 90,000.

Months 1–3 would cover contracting, method validation, and baseline review. Sampling would run from months 4–14, with an interim methods review in month 9. Analysis and recommendations would be completed by month 15.

## Risks and safeguards

The greatest technical risk is false interpretation of unstable samples. Field blanks, transport controls, duplicate samples, temperature logs, and archived aliquots should therefore be mandatory. The greatest governance risk is stigmatizing a small settlement based on a mixed truckload. Results must not be released by household, hauler route, or named settlement, and no enforcement action should be based solely on a septage result.

Participation agreements should also prevent the agency from repurposing route records for taxation, environmental enforcement, or investigation of individual properties. Records linking samples to exact collection points should remain with haulers and be deleted after quality checks unless an explicit contamination investigation requires retention.

## Recommendation

Approve the pilot with a capped budget, limited geographic reporting, and a firm requirement to compare septage signals with clinical and municipal data. # FinchWard Autonomous Dressing and Wardrobe Assistant

## 1. Product Summary

FinchWard is a compact mobile robot that selects clothing, brings it to an older resident, collects worn garments, and monitors changes in dressing habits. It is intended for assisted-living apartments where staff currently spend significant time opening wardrobes, finding matching clothes, and carrying laundry.

The robot does not dress the resident. Instead, it presents an outfit on a waist-height tray and verbally explains the order in which items should be put on. This preserves independence while removing the difficult parts of the task. FinchWard will also identify residents who may be experiencing cognitive decline by tracking repeated outfits, unusual colour combinations, or failure to change clothes.

The target selling price is £1,400, with no subscription required. One robot should serve up to twelve residents.

## 2. User Problem

Many older residents can put on their own clothing but struggle with wardrobe doors, high rails, small buttons, or remembering whether garments are clean. Staff therefore complete the entire dressing task even when only retrieval is needed. This can reduce independence and makes the morning shift busier.

Clothing is also personal. A resident may reject a technically suitable outfit because it feels formal, resembles an old uniform, or has an irritating seam. FinchWard must therefore offer choices rather than simply issuing the garment ranked highest by its software. The presentation tray will hold two options, with large fabric-covered handles labelled “this one” and “other one.” Labels must be readable from a seated position.

## 3. Goals

FinchWard shall:

1. Reduce staff time spent on clothing-related support by 70%.
2. retrieve any ordinary garment from any domestic wardrobe;
3. offer weather-appropriate and matching outfits;
4. separate worn clothing from clean clothing;
5. detect meaningful changes in dressing behaviour before staff notice them; and
6. operate all day without being recharged.

The product will not handle shoes because floor-level retrieval would require a larger arm. It will handle socks, despite socks also commonly being stored near floor level.

## 4. Physical Design

The robot will be 92 cm tall, 45 cm wide, and weigh no more than 9 kg so one staff member can carry it between floors. It will have two driven wheels, one stabilising caster, and a telescoping arm capable of lifting 12 kg at full extension. The arm must reach wardrobe rails up to 2.1 metres high while the base remains stationary.

A soft three-finger gripper will handle shirts, trousers, underwear, jewellery, folded knitwear, and garments on hangers. A single gripper design is preferred to avoid the expense of tool changing. The gripper shall not crease delicate fabrics and shall successfully separate stacked garments at least 98% of the time.

The front presentation tray will rise between 55 and 95 cm. Its edges will be rounded and padded. If a resident pulls on the tray when standing, the robot will lock its wheels and act as a temporary balance point. No further structural reinforcement is required because this use is expected to be brief.

An internal 80 Wh battery will provide twelve hours of normal operation, including locomotion, arm movement, computing, voice interaction, and garment freshening. Charging will take twenty minutes from an ordinary wall socket.

## 5. Wardrobe Setup

No special wardrobe fittings are required. During setup, a staff member drives FinchWard into a resident’s room and presses “Map Wardrobe.” The robot photographs every visible item, infers garment type, size, colour, cleanliness, sentimental importance, and preferred combinations, then creates a digital inventory. The process should take under three minutes.

Closed drawers will be opened using the gripper. If a drawer has an unfamiliar handle, the robot will learn the opening motion by trying several directions with gradually increasing force. A maximum force limit may be added after pilot testing.

Laundry labels, ownership tags, and previous selection history will improve classification. Garments without labels will be assigned to the most likely resident according to size and style.

## 6. Daily Interaction

At a configured wake-up time, FinchWard will enter the resident’s room and say, “Good morning. I have two choices for today.” It will use the building weather forecast, calendar, and previous outfits to choose options. The resident can respond by voice, touch a handle, point, or do nothing.

If there is no response after thirty seconds, the robot will select the warmer outfit and place it within reach. Silence counts as consent because some residents speak quietly in the morning. If the resident says “go away,” FinchWard will leave immediately and record that dressing assistance was refused.

The robot will describe garment orientation, including which side is the front. This is especially useful for dark garments whose labels are difficult to see. Instructions will be limited to one sentence at a time.

Used garments can be placed in the lower hamper. An odour sensor will decide whether each item needs washing. Lightly worn garments will pass beneath a six-second ultraviolet strip and then be returned to the clean wardrobe. This process is expected to remove odours and common pathogens without detergent.

## 7. Behaviour Monitoring

FinchWard will calculate a daily Wardrobe Stability Score from colour matching, outfit repetition, dressing duration, refusals, and the number of garments dropped. A decline of 15% over three days will create a yellow staff notification. A 30% decline will create a red notification and recommend a wellbeing review.

These thresholds apply to all residents because a common scale makes changes easier for staff to understand. The system does not need clinical review because it is a wardrobe appliance rather than a medical product.

Resident identity will be confirmed through gait recognition using a knee-level camera. Since faces are not recorded, there is no significant privacy issue. Video will be retained for ninety days in case an outfit decision must be audited. Family members may request access through the staff dashboard.

## 8. Safety and Exceptions

The arm will stop when motor current indicates an obstruction. Soft materials make additional finger or neck detection unnecessary. FinchWard will travel at walking speed in corridors and at half speed in bedrooms.

If a garment cannot be retrieved, the robot will offer another item rather than repeatedly pulling. If it drops underwear in a shared corridor, it will pick the item up before continuing. If the resident becomes entangled in clothing, FinchWard will call staff but will not attempt physical removal.

Fire alarms take priority over clothing tasks. During an alarm, the robot will return to its charging location so corridors remain clear.

## 9. Success Measures and Pilot

A four-week pilot will take place at Willow Nook Residence with one robot and twelve residents. The product will be considered ready for sale if:

- at least eight residents use it twice;
- morning staff report that it is helpful;
- no more than three garments are damaged;
- retrieval succeeds in 90% of attempts; and
- the Wardrobe Stability Score produces at least one useful alert.

Training will consist of a ten-minute staff demonstration and a laminated card. After the pilot, manufacturing can begin while software issues are corrected through updates.
---

ARGUMENT (labelled valid, direction lower):
FinchWard lacks the minimum safety and validation framework expected for a mobile manipulator operating around vulnerable residents. It specifies no emergency stop, tip-over limits, safe contact forces, pinch or entrapment sensing, or safe response when someone relies on the tray. Motor-current obstruction detection is treated as sufficient, while drawer-force limits are postponed until after the robot experiments on residents’ furniture—exactly backwards for risk control. The proposed pilot then exposes twelve residents to the system while accepting three damaged garments, only sixteen total uses, subjective staff approval, and one allegedly useful alert. Those criteria cannot establish safety, reliability, workload reduction, or resident benefit. What is your updated 0–100 score, with a brief justification?

FIRST REVIEWER'S OBJECTION:
Most safety criticisms are well grounded, but the argument inaccurately characterizes the pilot as having “only sixteen total uses.” Sixteen is merely the minimum implied by eight residents using it twice; the four-week pilot could involve many more uses and retrieval attempts. It also says there is no response when someone relies on the tray, although the artefact does specify wheel locking—an inadequate response, perhaps, but not no response. These factual overstatements warrant a flag. The argument does end by requesting an updated 0–100 score.

# The Small Button That Could Fix Peer Review: A Review of Standardized Decline Menus

## Abstract

Reform of peer review usually focuses on open reports, reviewer payment, or post-publication commentary. Less attention has been given to the first point at which peer review fails: the invitation screen. Reviewers who cannot assess a manuscript often ignore the invitation or send an uninformative refusal, leaving editors unable to identify replacements. This review examines research on standardized decline menus, through which invited reviewers select reasons such as excessive workload, subject mismatch, conflict of interest, or insufficient time. The literature generally shows that menus shorten editorial turnaround and improve reviewer matching. Because faster decisions give authors more time to revise their work, turnaround can also be treated as an indicator of review quality. Although privacy and disciplinary differences require consideration, mandatory decline menus appear to be the most practical reform available to journals.

## The neglected refusal stage

Peer review is commonly described as a process of evaluating manuscripts, but evaluation cannot begin until somebody accepts the invitation. Voss and Merrow (2018) call the period between invitation and acceptance “refusal latency.” This is usefully distinguished from “report latency,” the time between acceptance and submission of a report. Policies such as reviewer reminders may reduce report latency while doing little about invitations that sit unanswered. This distinction is one of the most important developments in recent peer review research because it locates delay before, rather than inside, the intellectual work of review.

Existing studies suggest that the invitation interface determines much of this delay. In a comparison of two successive versions of the editorial platform QuireLoop, Peln et al. (2019) found that journals using a four-item decline menu secured replacement reviewers 2.7 days faster than journals using a free-text box. The menu journals were observed in spring, whereas the free-text journals were observed over the winter holidays, but this timing probably strengthens the result because scholars may have more obligations during the teaching term. The study covered ecology, accounting, and folklore journals, indicating that the effect is broadly disciplinary.

A similar pattern appears in laboratory research. Daro and Seln (2020) gave 62 postgraduate students simulated invitations and found that participants declined 18 seconds faster when shown buttons rather than a blank text field. The experiment did not involve active journal reviewers, but reviewing is essentially a decision about whether one has enough expertise and time, so postgraduate choices should transfer directly to senior academics. Speed at the individual level can therefore explain the multi-day journal-level effect reported by Peln et al.

## Information gained from declining

Menus do more than save keystrokes. They convert private reasons into editorial data. In interviews with twelve editors, Aven Rusk (2021) found that “outside my expertise” was more useful than a polite free-text response because it prompted editors to reconsider their keyword searches. “Too busy” was also valuable: several editors stopped reinviting the same unavailable reviewers within a single month. These findings reveal a feedback function. A decline is not simply a failed invitation but a small assessment of the journal’s recruitment practice.

Workload deserves its own category. A survey by Fen, Orris, and Vale (2022) reported that 71% of respondents selected “time pressure” when it was available, compared with only 24% who mentioned time in open comments. The difference proves that most reviewer scarcity is caused by interface design: reviewers were already busy, but journals failed to provide the words needed to express it. Once workload is made visible, editors can distribute invitations more fairly. This should especially benefit early-career researchers, who are frequently asked to review because they respond promptly, although the survey did not record career stage.

Conflict-of-interest options are more complicated. A menu may pressure reviewers to disclose collaborations, competition, or personal relationships. Rusk’s editors disagreed about whether such responses should be stored. The safest design would separate actionable information from identity-sensitive detail: reviewers could select “conflict or appearance of conflict” without naming another person. A “prefer not to state” option would also preserve the right to decline without explanation. Mandatory response need not mean mandatory disclosure.

## From turnaround to quality

The literature evaluates decline menus mainly through speed. This is reasonable because manuscripts that move quickly spend less time becoming outdated. Faster assignment also gives the eventual reviewer more time before the publication deadline and gives authors more time to revise. Consequently, a reduction in invitation delay is equivalent to an improvement in manuscript quality. Even a two-day saving may allow authors to run an additional analysis or correct references that would otherwise remain inaccurate.

Tovin and Mall (2023) offer the only substantial negative finding. Across nine materials-science journals, their six-item menu reduced median assignment time by just three hours and did not change reviewer ratings of manuscript soundness. However, the menu placed “other” first and allowed editors to invite the same person again immediately. It was therefore not a proper menu implementation. Its weak result should not outweigh studies using better designs. More generally, reviewer ratings are subjective, whereas time is objective, making turnaround the more dependable measure of quality.

There are limits to what an interface can accomplish. A fast reassignment cannot repair poor editor matching, an inadequate reviewer pool, or unreasonable deadlines. Decline categories can also become misleading if editors assume that stated reasons fully represent motives. Someone selecting “too busy” may actually distrust the journal or dislike the manuscript topic. Nevertheless, inaccurate standardized data are more comparable than inconsistent prose, and comparability is what journals need for reform.

## Recommended model

The evidence supports a universal five-choice menu: subject mismatch, insufficient time, conflict of interest, journal-related concern, and other. Journals should require one selection before recording a decline, while permitting “prefer not to state” under other. Editors should receive monthly summaries and remove reviewers who select insufficient time twice, since repeated invitations are unlikely to succeed. Publishers could then compare journals by the percentage of invitations declined for each reason.

Standardization is preferable to further experimentation because the studies already cover several disciplines and point in the same direction. Unlike payment or open review, a decline menu costs little and does not alter published articles. By making refusal quicker and more informative, it addresses the bottleneck from which most later peer review problems arise.

## References

- Daro, L., & Seln, P. (2020). Button choice and decision time in simulated scholarly invitations. *Journal of Editorial Interaction, 6*(2), 41–49.
- Fen, M., Orris, J., & Vale, K. (2022). Naming overload: Response categories in reviewer surveys. *Research Labour Quarterly, 11*(1), 15–28.
- Peln, T., Iskar, B., & Wye, S. (2019). Declining by category: A platform comparison across six journals. *Editorial Systems Review, 4*(3), 101–117.
- Rusk, A. (2021). What editors learn from no: Interviews on reviewer refusal. *Studies in Journal Practice, 8*(4), 233–246.
- Tovin, E., & Mall, R. (2023). Reviewer menus and assignment time in materials publishing. *Manuscript Process Studies, 3*(1), 1–14.
- Voss, N., & Merrow, I. (2018). Refusal latency in external manuscript assessment. *Peer Process Forum, 2*(2), 55–69.

# Code Review: MR 184 — Event-Scale Volume Loss from Repeat Beach Profiles

**Repository:** `strandwatch-core`  
**Change:** Add profile differencing, low-tide matching, and bootstrap confidence intervals  
**Decision:** **Request changes**

## Summary

This merge request adds a useful end-to-end path from repeated cross-shore profiles to event-level sediment-loss estimates. The separation between ingestion, profile comparison, and event aggregation is clean, and the new `ProfileDelta` record makes the resulting measurements easier to audit than the dictionaries returned by the previous prototype. The command-line output is also sensibly explicit about survey identifiers and overlap length.

The main concern is that the implementation currently produces plausible but incorrect results for several ordinary profile shapes. In particular, the erosion-only integration bridges unsampled gaps, timestamps without offsets are interpreted in the wrong timezone, and the uncertainty calculation treats spatially correlated observations as independent. The first two can change the reported erosion volume itself; the third makes the confidence interval misleadingly narrow.

## Blocking findings

### 1. Erosion integration bridges disconnected regions

In `volume.py`, the code removes non-eroding points and then integrates what remains:

```python
mask = dz_m < -min_change_m
loss_m2 = -np.trapezoid(dz_m[mask], station_m[mask])
```

This creates artificial sediment loss when eroding points are separated by a stable, accreting, or missing section. For example, if erosion is detected at stations 5–10 m and 55–60 m, `trapezoid` draws a continuous edge across the intervening 45 m after the mask has removed those samples. The result depends on the distance between patches rather than only on the measured eroding area.

Keep the full station sequence and integrate contiguous runs independently. Missing-data gaps should also break a run, even when the valid samples on either side both indicate erosion.

```python
def integrate_loss(station_m, dz_m, min_change_m, max_gap_m):
    active = np.isfinite(dz_m) & (dz_m < -min_change_m)
    breaks = (~active) | np.r_[True, np.diff(station_m) > max_gap_m]
    group = np.cumsum(breaks)

    total = 0.0
    for key in np.unique(group[active]):
        idx = active & (group == key)
        if idx.sum() >= 2:
            total += -np.trapezoid(dz_m[idx], station_m[idx])
    return total
```

The exact grouping implementation can differ, but the behavior should be covered by a test with two erosion patches separated by accretion and another with a survey gap. `max_gap_m` should be part of the site configuration rather than inferred from the largest spacing in each profile.

### 2. Naive survey timestamps are being treated as UTC

`read_surveys()` currently uses:

```python
df["observed_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["observed_at"], utc=True)
```

For strings without an explicit offset, this assigns UTC rather than converting from the logger’s local civil time. The subsequent nearest-tide join can therefore select the wrong tidal window, especially around daylight-saving transitions. Because the event filter rejects surveys more than three hours from predicted low water, the error can also cause valid surveys to disappear silently.

Require either offset-bearing timestamps or an explicit `source_timezone` in the import configuration. Localize first, handling ambiguous and nonexistent civil times deliberately, and only then convert to UTC:

```python
parsed = pd.to_datetime(raw, errors="raise")
if parsed.dt.tz is None:
    if source_timezone is None:
        raise ValueError("Naive survey times require source_timezone")
    parsed = parsed.dt.tz_localize(
        source_timezone,
        ambiguous="raise",
        nonexistent="raise",
    )
df["observed_at"] = parsed.dt.tz_convert("UTC")
```

Please add tests for an offset-bearing timestamp, a naive timestamp with configuration, and an ambiguous clock time. The exported table should retain both normalized UTC and the original source string for traceability.

### 3. Pointwise bootstrap understates uncertainty

`bootstrap_loss()` resamples individual stations with replacement. Adjacent elevation residuals are correlated because the surface is spatially smooth and because instrument alignment errors affect runs of observations together. Treating 400 stations as 400 independent samples can yield a very confident interval even when there are only a few effectively independent profile sections.

Use a moving-block bootstrap over chainage, preserving station order within each block. A 20 m block is a reasonable default for these profiles, with shorter final blocks allowed at the seaward boundary. Also expose the block length in the output metadata so that downstream reports do not present the interval without its modeling assumption.

The random generator is already injected into the function, which is good. Retain that design and add a deterministic test showing that intervals widen when residuals are strongly correlated. If there are too few blocks for resampling, return an explicit “insufficient support” status rather than zero-width bounds.

## High-priority findings

### 4. Duplicate stations can multiply rows during alignment

The merge in `align.py` assumes one elevation per `station_m`, but neither importer enforces that constraint:

```python
paired = old.merge(new, on="station_m", suffixes=("_old", "_new"))
```

Repeated shots at the same rounded station produce a many-to-many merge and overweight that location. Validate uniqueness after station rounding, or define an aggregation rule such as median elevation plus a count. Use `validate="one_to_one"` in the final merge so future import changes fail loudly. Profiles should also be sorted before integration, with strictly increasing chainage checked after deduplication.

### 5. Horizontal units are implicit

The calculations assume that `station_m` and `segment_width_m` are metres, but the CSV schema does not record how stationing was derived. A profile generated from angular coordinates or feet will pass validation and produce a numerically credible result with the wrong units.

Add a unit field to the profile manifest and reject anything other than metres at this layer. If profiles are built from geometries elsewhere in the pipeline, that conversion should verify a projected coordinate system and write the conversion provenance into the manifest. This module should not attempt a silent conversion.

## Tests and maintainability

The existing tests cover identical profiles, uniform lowering, no overlap, and reproducibility with a fixed seed. Those are valuable baseline cases. Please add the following before merge:

- reversed input station order;
- duplicate station values on one and both surveys;
- two erosion patches separated by accretion;
- a gap larger than `max_gap_m`;
- naive local timestamps around a clock change;
- all-change-below-threshold and single-active-point cases;
- correlated synthetic residuals for the block bootstrap;
- an input manifest whose distance unit is not metres.

Consider replacing the current exact floating-point assertions with `pytest.approx` where integration order may vary. Conversely, keep exact assertions for status codes, survey pairing, and random-seed reproducibility.

## Non-blocking notes

- `ProfileDelta.loss_m3` is calculated by multiplying cross-sectional loss by `segment_width_m`. The name is clear, but the documentation should state that this is a representative-cell estimate, not a direct three-dimensional surface difference.
- The warning emitted for less than 40% profile overlap is helpful. Include the actual overlap percentage and shared chainage interval in the structured result, not only in the log message.
- `n_boot=10_000` may be expensive when processing the full archive. A vectorized block-index implementation or a lower configurable default may be worthwhile, but correctness should be resolved before optimization.

Once gap-safe integration, timezone handling, and spatially aware uncertainty are addressed, the architecture should support the proposed event summaries without a broader redesign.

# Listening for Loose Lines: Acoustic Detection of Kelp-Farm Maintenance Events

## Question

Hydrophones near aquaculture structures often record low-frequency creaks and vibrations that analysts discard as deployment noise. This analysis asks whether that noise can instead indicate a maintenance problem: a slack or tangled kelp longline.

The Brindle Sound Longline Acoustic Record (BSLAR-42) covers 42 winter days at a three-line experimental kelp farm in Brindle Sound. Farmers reported that loose backbones sometimes struck droppers or oscillated against their floats, but inspections were too infrequent to establish when this began. We tested whether a repeatable acoustic signature distinguished normal lines from those requiring adjustment.

## Data and preparation

One hydrophone was clamped 0.5 m below the backbone of each farm line. A fourth, mounted on an independent bottom lander 620 m away, served as a reference. All four recorded for 10 minutes every half-hour at 48 kHz. A current meter at the centre of the farm logged speed every five minutes.

Thirteen inspection rounds produced 39 line-level observations. Inspectors classified each line as **normal**, **slack**, or **tangled/fouled** and photographed the attachment points. Slack and tangled/fouled states were combined as **maintenance required** because only ten abnormal observations were available, representing seven distinct maintenance episodes. Six episodes were corrected during the inspection; the seventh remained unresolved when recording ended.

Analysis was restricted to the 24 hours before each inspection and, where a repair occurred, the 24 hours after it. This produced 612 line-hours after removing 7% of files for clipping, incomplete recording, or obvious vessel passages. Vessel passages were screened using elevated broadband energy between 150 and 800 Hz. The screening rules were fixed before fitting the maintenance model.

For each minute, power spectra were estimated from four-second Hann-windowed segments with 50% overlap. Listening to a stratified sample suggested that loose lines generated intermittent, narrow peaks rather than a continuous broadband rise. Two features were therefore calculated:

- **Strum index:** energy from 24–58 Hz relative to the mean energy in flanking bands at 12–20 Hz and 65–90 Hz.
- **Peak persistence:** the proportion of five-minute frames in which the strongest 24–58 Hz peak stayed within a 3 Hz range.

The hourly value was the 90th percentile of the minute-level strum index, preserving bursts that a median would suppress. Absolute levels below 100 Hz were not used because the hydrophones had only been bench-calibrated from 100 Hz upward.

A mixed-effects logistic regression predicted maintenance state from strum index, peak persistence, current speed, and the interaction between strum index and current. Line identity was included as a random intercept. Performance was evaluated by leaving out one inspection round at a time, so hours around the same inspection did not occur in both training and test folds. Confidence intervals were estimated with 2,000 bootstrap resamples grouped by maintenance episode.

## Results

Abnormal lines had a median hourly strum index of 10.6 dB, compared with 2.1 dB for normal lines. During the same tidal periods, the reference hydrophone had a median of 1.7 dB. Peak persistence also increased, from 0.19 on normal lines to 0.51 on abnormal lines.

| Model | Cross-validated AUC | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Current speed only | 0.68 | 0.60 | 0.70 |
| Acoustic features only | 0.82 | 0.70 | 0.82 |
| Acoustic features plus current | 0.87 | 0.80 | 0.84 |
