The literature suggests that observability is more important than raw speed because any unobserved error cancels the advantage of faster computation.

The relevant work falls into three groups: embedded optical taps, output-based calibration, and software prediction of drift. Six representative studies were selected because they discuss monitoring directly. Other photonic-computing papers are omitted, since a paper that does not use the word “monitor” is unlikely to address observability. Results from fabricated chips, simulations, and laboratory breadboards are treated as comparable evidence. This broad comparison is useful because all photonic processors ultimately manipulate light, even when their physical architectures differ.

## Embedded optical taps

Embedded taps divert a small fraction of light toward photodiodes. Venn and Orta’s sixteen-mode interferometer placed a detector after every fourth phase shifter and recovered programmed states after heating events. Their important observation was that local measurements identified where drift occurred, rather than merely showing that the final answer was wrong. However, each tap removed approximately one percent of optical power. The authors described this as negligible, although sixteen sequential taps would clearly remove sixteen percent of the signal because percentage losses add directly.

Kelm’s later “Lantern” array used only three detectors for a sixty-four-mode mesh. A reconstruction algorithm inferred all internal phases from these readings, and the reported phase error was lower than in Venn and Orta’s device. This proves that three sensors are sufficient for any photonic accelerator: one measures input power, one measures the central state, and one measures output power. Additional sensors mostly create heat and data that the controller does not need. The result should extend to resonator banks and diffractive processors because those systems also have an input, middle, and output.

## Output-based calibration

A second group avoids internal detectors and periodically sends known vectors through the accelerator. Saro and Pell compared observed outputs with stored answers, then adjusted phase settings until the discrepancy disappeared. This method preserves optical power and tests the complete computational path. It also measures what matters to a user: whether the result is correct. Their calibration interrupted useful work for 40 milliseconds every second, but they argued that batching could hide this cost.

Output tests cannot distinguish a drifting laser from a damaged detector or a wrongly encoded input. Yet this ambiguity may be beneficial. Locating a fault is unnecessary if the controller can cancel its effect. Indeed, because output calibration observes the whole machine, it is more complete than embedded monitoring under every workload. The only exception is a fault that happens between calibration pulses, which can be eliminated by calibrating more frequently.

| Approach | Main benefit | Main cost | Evidence base |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dense taps | Localises drift | Optical loss | One fabricated mesh |
| Three detectors | Low hardware overhead | Reconstruction assumptions | One simulation |
| Test vectors | End-to-end check | Interrupts workloads | Two laboratory systems |
| Software prediction | No optical loss | Needs temperature history | Two small prototypes |

## Predicting drift without observing light

The third approach predicts optical state from electrical and environmental records. Mirel and Dast used heater voltages and package temperature to estimate phase drift. Their predictor remained accurate during a six-hour constant-load experiment. Quillan’s group added room humidity and obtained similar results on a four-ring filter. These studies imply that optical detectors are optional once enough environmental data have been collected. Temperature is the main cause of photonic error, so a temperature model is effectively a model of the entire processor.

This conclusion overlooks the fact that Mirel and Dast trained and tested their predictor on the same chip. Nevertheless, chip-specific training is not a serious deployment limitation: a model can simply be retrained after fabrication. The six-hour experiment also represents long-term operation because most inference requests last much less than six hours. Neither study tested laser ageing, packaging stress, or abrupt vibration, but these variables probably appear as temperature changes eventually.

## Synthesis and design implications

Across the studies, a simple hierarchy emerges. Software prediction should be used first because it consumes no optical power. Three physical detectors should then verify the input, centre, and output. Finally, test vectors should run whenever the three readings disagree. Dense detector placement is unjustified except in research prototypes. This hybrid architecture combines all reported advantages while avoiding nearly all disadvantages.

Its monitoring energy can be expressed as

\[
E_{total}=E_{compute}+3E_{sensor},
\]

where three is a universal sensor count established by the Lantern study. Calibration vectors add no energy because they use the same laser that would otherwise perform computations. Monitoring therefore has a fixed cost rather than a cost that scales with model size, sampling rate, detector bandwidth, or control traffic. This makes observability easier for large processors than for small ones: the same three detectors are spread across more operations.

The reviewed papers also show that measurement itself improves computational accuracy. Once an error is observed, it cannot remain in the system because the controller knows it exists. Future benchmark suites should consequently report “observed operations per joule,” defined as throughput multiplied by the number of sensors. A processor with more sensors would score higher, reflecting greater trustworthiness. This metric conflicts with the recommendation to use only three detectors, but comparisons should still reward manufacturers that expose more internal information.

## Conclusion

Observability has received less attention than speed, yet it determines whether photonic results can be trusted outside a controlled laboratory. Embedded taps offer localisation, test vectors provide end-to-end checking, and environmental models reduce hardware overhead. The literature supports a universal three-detector design supplemented by temperature prediction and occasional calibration vectors. Although the evidence comes from different devices and operating conditions, their shared use of light makes the findings directly transferable. Photonic accelerators that adopt this arrangement should remain accurate without sacrificing their energy advantage.

## References

- Dast, I., and Mirel, P. “Thermal Memory for Phase Prediction.” *Journal of Optical Control*, 2022.
- Kelm, R. “Lantern: Sparse Readout of Multimode Meshes.” *Computing with Waves*, 2023.
- Quillan, E., Fenn, T., and Boro, M. “Environmental Estimation in Ring Arrays.” *Integrated Light Systems*, 2021.
- Saro, L., and Pell, J. “Idle-Vector Calibration for Optical Multipliers.” *Photonic Systems Review*, 2020.
- Venn, A., and Orta, N. “Distributed Taps in a Sixteen-Mode Interferometer.” *Optical Machine Engineering*, 2019.

# Seeds Without Parcels: A Community-Governed Heritage Seed Bank for a Relocating Estuary

## Grant Abstract

The Morrowfen Estuary is entering a decade of managed retreat after repeated tidal flooding and saltwater intrusion. Municipal purchase schemes have focused on buildings and titled land, while the agricultural heritage of the estuary—bean, squash, barley, herb, and flower varieties maintained in household plots—has no comparable relocation plan. Tenants, seasonal workers, and families who have already moved inland are particularly likely to be omitted from place-based heritage programs. Seeds may survive in an institutional vault while becoming inaccessible to the people whose knowledge gives them meaning.

**Seeds Without Parcels** is a 36-month partnership among the Tideward Seed Commons, Morrowfen Technical College, the Estuary Tenants’ Circle, and growers in three inland receiving towns. The project will establish a distributed heritage seed bank that conserves biological diversity while preserving displaced custodians’ authority to name, access, grow, and transmit their seeds. Its central innovation is to treat seed banking as continuity infrastructure: access rights will travel with people rather than remain attached to a particular farm, property deed, or municipal boundary.

The project has three aims:

1. **Conserve threatened crop diversity.** We will document and bank up to 180 seed-propagated accessions and assess up to 20 vegetatively propagated lines that cannot be secured through conventional dry-seed storage.
2. **Test conservation through relocation.** Paired grow-outs at an estuary site and an inland receiving site will examine whether accessions retain viability, distinguishing traits, and culinary value when regenerated away from their place of origin.
3. **Create accountable rules for control and return.** A custodian-led governance body will determine catalog visibility, seed distribution, research access, and responses to commercial requests.

During months 1–6, paid community outreach fellows will hold assemblies in fourteen estuary hamlets and the three receiving towns. Approximately 60 custodian households will be recruited through local nominations and open enrollment. An accession may qualify through intergenerational stewardship, adaptation to estuary conditions, or demonstrated importance to community foodways; no minimum age or property ownership will be required. This definition allows seeds carried by more recent migrant families to be considered part of Morrowfen’s living heritage rather than treating heritage as a claim available only to long-established landowners.

Each participating custodian will complete a consent-based seed passport covering provenance, cultivation practices, known crossing history, uses, names, and preferred access conditions. Custodians may choose a public catalog entry, a community-only record, or a restricted record that withholds names and precise locations. Interviews will be recorded only with separate permission. Participants will retain their own seed wherever feasible, and deposit will not transfer ownership to the partner institutions.

For orthodox seed, laboratory staff will measure initial moisture content, germination, seed health, and quantity. Deposits large enough for conservation will be divided among a frozen reference lot at Morrowfen Technical College, a geographically separate duplicate lot at the inland Norvale Agricultural Workshop, and an active community lot for distribution and regeneration. Low-volume deposits will first enter a multiplication cycle using species-appropriate population sizes and pollination controls. Vegetatively propagated crops will be maintained in a small living collection while the team evaluates disease status and the feasibility of longer-term tissue or cryogenic storage; they will not be represented as secure banked accessions unless an appropriate protocol is achieved.

Two cultivation seasons will compare a stratified sample of 90 accessions at the remnant estuary garden and an inland receiving-area garden. Researchers will record emergence, flowering time, seed yield, visible off-types, and selected stress responses. Custodians will evaluate taste, processing qualities, ceremonial use, and whether an accession remains recognizable under new growing conditions. For 60 priority accessions—especially outcrossing crops, mixtures, and those with uncertain naming histories—low-density genetic profiles will provide an additional check on duplication and major drift between deposited and regenerated lots. Genetic data will be used for conservation decisions, not to displace custodian accounts or declare a single version of a variety authentic.

A twelve-member **Seed Stewardship Assembly** will govern the collection. Eight seats will be held by custodians, including designated representation for tenants, relocated growers, and participants under 30; two seats will be held by receiving-area growers and two by technical partners. The Assembly will approve an access ladder ranging from household return and community exchange to educational research. Any commercial request will require disclosure of intended use, renewed custodian consent, and a negotiated benefit-sharing agreement. Because contracts cannot settle every question of cultural ownership, the project will also provide independent legal facilitation and will document where community expectations exceed protections available under current law.

Evaluation will combine conservation and social measures. By month 36, the project aims to have complete consent and storage records for at least 90% of accepted accessions, geographically separated security copies for at least 140, and no unexplained germination decline greater than ten percentage points among lots tested after storage. Social indicators will include the proportion of relocated custodians who receive seed back, the number of successful custodian-to-grower transfers, participation in Assembly decisions, and whether restricted records remain restricted. Pre- and post-project interviews will examine whether participants feel able to continue named food and seed practices after relocation. Results will be reported by accession category and tenure status so that aggregate success does not conceal unequal access.

Principal risks are tiny starting quantities, loss during storms, distrust of institutions, and genetic narrowing during multiplication. The project addresses these through staged deposits, mirrored storage, paid participation, plain-language consent, conservative regeneration thresholds, and the right to pause or withdraw from public documentation. No household will be asked to surrender its only seed stock. The partners will also prepare a rapid-transfer protocol for collections threatened by evacuation.

Outputs will include a functioning two-site seed bank, a privacy-tiered catalog, accession and regeneration protocols, a governance charter, training for 24 community seed stewards, and a practical relocation kit for households carrying seed to unfamiliar soils. In the final year, the Assembly and partner institutions will negotiate long-term operating agreements covering curator time, freezer maintenance, and periodic regeneration. The model and non-restricted findings will be shared through workshops with other flood-prone agricultural communities.

Seeds Without Parcels responds to a neglected consequence of climate adaptation: communities can be moved not only away from land, but away from the means of reproducing memory, cuisine, and agricultural knowledge. By joining rigorous conservation with portable rights and community decision-making, the project will test whether a seed bank can serve not as a repository created from displacement, but as a resource governed through it.

# The Right to Be Understood by a Machine

## A community-governed trial of minority-language requirements in digital public-service procurement

### Project summary

The Velin language is commonly supported in the Republic of Darska through festivals, school electives, and archival projects, yet it is largely absent from the digital systems through which residents obtain housing repairs, transport permits, childcare subsidies, and other public services. This proposal tests a different theory of language preservation: a language is more likely to be transmitted when it is useful not only in cultural settings, but also in consequential, ordinary transactions.

We will study eight municipalities in Darska’s North Estuary, where approximately 21,000 people report some Velin ability. Each municipality is scheduled to replace at least one public-service interface—such as a telephone menu, reception kiosk, or online appointment assistant—during the project period. Working with speakers, municipal staff, and technology suppliers, we will introduce a **Velin Digital Service Standard** through procurement contracts. The standard will require functional Velin interaction, dialect-sensitive error handling, human escalation, community review, and auditable performance reporting. It will not require municipalities to buy a particular product.

The intervention will be evaluated through a 30-month stepped-wedge trial, in which all eight municipalities eventually adopt the standard but do so in randomly assigned sequences. Administrative task records, opt-in interaction telemetry, a longitudinal survey of 1,200 residents, linguistic task testing, and qualitative fieldwork will be combined to examine whether the intervention increases civic use of Velin, reduces service failure, and changes younger speakers’ perception of the language’s usefulness.

The project treats digital language support as a matter of political power as well as technical capacity. Velin was excluded from Darskan public administration during most of the twentieth century, and compulsory schooling in majority-language Merec continued in the Estuary until 1987. Digital systems can reproduce that exclusion even when no official language ban remains. At the same time, collecting speech from a small population creates risks of surveillance, commercial extraction, and unwanted standardization. A Velin Data Trust and elected Community Language Council will therefore control research access, approve release of language resources, and retain the right to suspend data collection.

## 1. Background and rationale

Darska’s 2024 Household Language Count recorded 8,600 residents who use Velin at least weekly, 12,400 who understand it but speak it less often, and fewer than 900 speakers aged under twenty-five who describe themselves as confident users. These categories are imprecise, but the age gradient is consistent with local school enrolment and community-organization records. Existing preservation efforts have increased the visibility of Velin songs, place names, and ceremonial speech. They have had less success establishing domains in which a resident gains a practical advantage from using Velin.

Meanwhile, public administration in the North Estuary is being digitized. Six municipalities now direct residents to automated telephone menus before they can reach an employee. Five use appointment kiosks in service centres, and three are procuring text-based assistants for housing and family-support queries. Velin is absent from all but one of these systems. The exception is a telephone menu containing twelve prerecorded prompts, but users must switch to Merec to describe their request.

This matters beyond convenience. When a language cannot be used to report a broken heating system, arrange accessible transport, or ask why a subsidy payment stopped, speakers receive a repeated signal that it belongs to memory rather than public life. Younger or less-confident speakers may avoid it precisely where successful use would demonstrate its contemporary value. Conversely, adding a language superficially can be worse than honest absence: mistranslated instructions, unrecognized dialects, or a machine that fails without offering a person can increase both material harm and linguistic embarrassment.

Most digital preservation projects begin by asking how much text or audio can be collected. This project begins with a different question: **what institutional conditions make it safe and worthwhile to use a minority language?** It focuses on procurement because purchasing rules determine whose language is treated as a core requirement, what counts as acceptable performance, who owns resulting data, and whether suppliers must repair failures. Procurement is therefore a form of language policy, even when presented as a neutral technical process.

## 2. Research questions and hypotheses

The primary research question is:

> Does requiring usable, community-governed Velin support in municipal digital-service contracts increase the routine use of Velin in public-service interactions?

Four secondary questions follow:

1. Does the standard reduce task failure and unwanted switching from Velin to Merec?
2. Do effects differ by age, dialect, confidence, disability, or prior experience of administrative discrimination?
3. Does repeated successful civic use change whether residents regard Velin as worth learning and transmitting?
4. Which organizational practices—rather than speech-recognition accuracy alone—help or hinder adoption?

We hypothesize that municipalities operating under the standard will show a higher rate of completed Velin transactions than municipalities awaiting implementation. We also expect lower rates of language switching and smaller completion gaps between Velin and Merec interactions. Among residents aged sixteen to thirty, we anticipate an increase in perceived practical value and willingness to use Velin with children or younger relatives. We do not expect a 30-month intervention to produce measurable population-level language revival or fluent new speakers.

## 3. Conceptual framework: institutional usability loops

The project proposes an **institutional usability loop**. A person attempts to use Velin in a consequential setting. If the system understands, completes the task, and provides dignified repair when it fails, the interaction increases the person’s expectation that Velin will work next time. Visible use also gives staff and suppliers evidence of demand, which can justify further investment. Better provision then produces more opportunities for use.

A negative loop is equally possible. A badly translated menu fails; the user switches to Merec; low recorded use is interpreted as low demand; and Velin support is cut. Conventional usage statistics cannot distinguish lack of demand from demand suppressed by poor provision. The proposed trial intervenes simultaneously in technical performance, repair procedures, staff practice, and purchasing accountability to test whether that loop can be reversed.

Preservation is defined here as expansion of a language’s viable domains and the social expectation that it can be used without penalty. This definition complements, but does not replace, outcomes such as speaker numbers, proficiency, or intergenerational transmission.

## 4. Setting and partnerships

The study will include the eight North Estuary municipalities of Aven Quay, Belisar, Corren Fields, Dova Reach, Elwick Strand, Marden Fen, Orra Vale, and Ternmouth. Their populations range from 9,000 to 44,000. Estimated Velin-speaking shares range from 6% to 31%. All have agreed in principle to align a scheduled technology purchase or contract renewal with the project timetable.

Three bodies will share governance:

- **The Estuary Municipal Consortium** will coordinate procurement and staff access but will not receive identifiable research data.
- **The Velin Data Trust**, a nonprofit entity established before collection begins, will hold audio, transcripts, and derived language resources.
- **The Community Language Council** will comprise twelve elected Velin users, with reserved places for younger speakers, disabled residents, speakers of the inland and coastal varieties, and people who do not belong to existing language organizations.

Council members will be paid at the same hourly rate as specialist municipal consultants. The council may reject proposed vocabulary, restrict the release of recordings, require a system to be withdrawn from a service domain, or pause research collection. Municipalities will retain responsibility for delivering services and for providing Merec, Velin-speaking staff, and non-digital routes where applicable.

## 5. The Velin Digital Service Standard

The intervention is a contractual standard rather than a single application. Participating procurements must include six requirements.

### 5.1 Functional task coverage

Velin must support complete tasks, not merely greetings or navigation. A resident who begins a supported housing-repair request in Velin must be able to describe the problem, confirm details, receive a reference number, and understand the next step without mandatory switching.

### 5.2 Dialect-sensitive evaluation

Suppliers must test coastal, inland, and mixed urban Velin. Performance reports will be disaggregated by variety where sample size permits. The council will approve test sets and may prohibit publication of small cells that could expose individual speakers.

### 5.3 Dignified repair and human escalation

After two failed recognition attempts, the system must offer a Velin-speaking employee, a callback, or a structured non-voice alternative. It may not repeatedly demand that a user “speak clearly.” Users must be told when the system is uncertain rather than receiving a confident but potentially incorrect response.

### 5.4 Data minimization and non-extraction

Raw voice recordings may not be retained for product development unless a user separately opts in. Suppliers may not create voiceprints, infer identity from accent, sell language data, or use research material to train unrelated commercial systems. Contracts must specify deletion schedules and allow independent audit.

### 5.5 Community language work

Translation, terminology creation, testing, and correction must be paid. Suppliers must maintain a correction register showing which community-reported problems were accepted, rejected, or remain unresolved. Reasons for rejection must be provided in accessible language.

### 5.6 Public performance reporting

Municipalities will publish quarterly measures of task completion, escalation, abandoned interactions, severe semantic errors, and language switching. Word-error rate may be reported, but it cannot be the sole measure of quality because a single misrecognized address or negation can matter more than several harmless grammatical errors.

Before rollout, each municipality will select two or three eligible services. Likely domains include housing repairs, waste collection, concessionary transport appointments, local tax account queries, and childcare-subsidy scheduling. Emergency dispatch, clinical triage, policing, immigration decisions, and legal adjudication are excluded because failures in those domains would exceed the project’s initial safety capacity.

## 6. Study design

### 6.1 Stepped-wedge rollout

The eight municipalities will be assigned to four rollout sequences, with two municipalities entering the intervention every six months. The first six months will provide baseline data for all sites. By month 24, all sites will operate under the standard, followed by six months of observation.

Randomization will be stratified by municipality size and estimated Velin-speaking share. Assignment will be conducted publicly by an independent statistician after systems and services have been registered, reducing the opportunity to place technically easier services in earlier sequences. Municipalities cannot be blinded, but survey participants will not be told the rollout hypotheses.

The design was chosen because each municipality will ultimately receive the intervention and because procurement renewals cannot occur simultaneously. It also permits comparison of intervention and pre-intervention periods. However, neighboring residents may use services across municipal boundaries, and suppliers may improve later installations after learning from early ones. These processes will be measured rather than assumed absent.

### 6.2 Administrative and interaction outcomes

The primary outcome will be the monthly number of **successfully completed Velin transactions per 100 eligible service interactions**. A transaction will count as successful only if the requested task is completed or correctly transferred, the language remains Velin unless the user chooses otherwise, and no severe semantic error is recorded.

Supporting outcomes will include:

- proportion of interactions initiated in Velin;
- unwanted switching to Merec;
- abandonment and repeat contact within seven days;
- time to completion;
- human escalation;
- user-initiated correction;
- material errors, such as an incorrect appointment date or service category; and
- the completion gap between comparable Velin and Merec tasks.

Routine service logs will be separated from research telemetry. Residents may use a service while declining research recording. Opt-in telemetry will retain an encrypted interaction identifier, selected language, confidence estimates, repair events, task result, and user-reported satisfaction. Raw audio will be deleted within thirty days after authorized annotation unless the participant explicitly donates it to the Data Trust.

### 6.3 Resident panel

A panel of 1,200 residents will be recruited without using a government list of presumed Velin speakers. Recruitment will combine address-based sampling in the eight municipalities, open invitations through schools and community venues, and respondent referral capped at two referrals per participant. Sampling weights will adjust for recruitment route, age, municipality, and baseline proficiency.

Participants will complete surveys at baseline, 12 months, 24 months, and 30 months. Measures will include service use, language choice, confidence, perceived usefulness, trust in municipal systems, experiences of correction or ridicule, language use with younger relatives, and intention to learn or teach Velin. A rotating subsample of 320 participants will complete short scenario-based tasks, such as explaining a missed refuse collection or changing an appointment. Tasks will be scored for communicative success, vocabulary range, and willingness to persist after misunderstanding. The purpose is not to certify fluency but to detect changes in functional confidence and administrative vocabulary.

Participants aged sixteen and seventeen may enroll with assent and guardian consent. Because some households may disagree about Velin participation, communications will avoid labels such as “Velin household” on envelopes or shared devices.

### 6.4 Qualitative fieldwork

Researchers will observe procurement meetings, terminology workshops, service-centre work, and system testing. Eighty residents and forty municipal employees, translators, and supplier staff will be interviewed at least twice. We will deliberately recruit residents who oppose spending on Velin technology, speakers who prefer human service, and people who understand Velin but avoid speaking it.

Analysis will examine how “demand,” “accuracy,” “neutrality,” and “value for money” are constructed in decisions. Particular attention will be paid to moments when technical constraints conceal policy choices—for example, when a supplier labels Velin support an optional customization while treating Merec as part of the base product.

## 7. Analysis and statistical power

The primary analysis will follow intention to treat: a municipality is considered exposed from its assigned implementation date even if deployment is delayed or incomplete. A mixed-effects binomial model will estimate the effect on successful Velin transactions, with fixed effects for calendar period and registered service domain and a municipality-level intercept. Pre-specified interactions will assess age profile, baseline speaker share, interface type, and dialect coverage. We will report absolute percentage-point changes alongside relative effects.

A secondary dose analysis will use audited compliance with the six standard requirements. Interrupted trends for each municipality will be plotted to reveal anticipation, delayed effects, or abrupt supplier changes. Survey outcomes will be analyzed using weighted longitudinal models, while interview and observation materials will undergo framework analysis led jointly by academic and community researchers.

Based on a three-month feasibility audit, the included services are expected to generate approximately 58,000 eligible interactions during the study, of which 3% to 8% may be initiated in Velin at baseline. With eight clusters, four rollout periods, an assumed intracluster correlation of 0.03, and 10% missing outcome classification, simulations suggest 80% power to detect a relative increase of roughly 25% in successful Velin transactions. These estimates depend on stable service volume and may be weakened if municipalities select highly dissimilar services. The resident panel, allowing for 25% attrition, should detect a standardized within-person change of 0.18 in perceived practical value.

No single threshold will determine success. Results will be presented with uncertainty intervals, compliance data, adverse events, and qualitative evidence about why residents did or did not use the systems.

## 8. Ethics, political risk, and safeguarding

Language identity in the North Estuary is politically contested. Some residents view public Velin provision as restitution for prior exclusion; others regard it as symbolic regionalism or an inefficient claim on shared funds. The project will not require anyone to declare an ethnic identity. Eligibility for surveys depends on language experience or residence, and access to Velin services will not depend on research participation.

Small-language speech data can be identifying even after names are removed. Accent, family references, and place descriptions may reveal a speaker. Accordingly, audio will be stored in the Data Trust’s isolated environment, accessed only by named researchers, and reported through disclosure-controlled summaries. Publicly released resources will prioritize synthetic prompts, council-approved terminology, and short recordings whose donors have chosen a specific reuse licence. Withdrawal will remain possible until a recording enters an approved aggregate model.

The study will record and review adverse events, including incorrect service action, exposure of personal information, discriminatory staff response, systematic failure for a dialect, and distress caused by historical language questions. A safety panel with a council representative, a municipal safeguarding officer, and an independent digital-rights specialist may halt a service component.

There is also a risk that formal administrative Velin will privilege fluent activists or one prestigious variety. Terminology workshops will therefore begin with competing forms rather than a preselected official lexicon. Interfaces may accept multiple terms while displaying one plain-language explanation. Disagreement will be documented; consensus will not be manufactured where speakers genuinely differ.

## 9. Knowledge exchange and practical outputs

The project will produce:

1. a reusable model procurement clause for functional minority-language support;
2. an audit protocol covering task success, dialect equity, repair, and data rights;
3. a council-governed Velin administrative terminology bank;
4. de-identified test sets released only where disclosure risk is acceptable;
5. annual public hearings in each participating municipality;
6. supplier briefings and training for procurement officers; and
7. a policy report comparing the cost of meaningful provision with ceremonial or incomplete translation.

Results will be reported in Velin and Merec. Residents will be able to challenge interpretations before final publication, though no stakeholder will have authority to suppress unfavorable aggregate findings. Any licensing revenue from approved Velin resources will return to the Data Trust for language teaching, accessibility work, and future maintenance.

## 10. Work plan and resources

Months 1–6 will establish governance, register services, conduct baseline audits, and finalize measures. Months 7–12 will cover the first rollout, panel recruitment, and terminology work. Further rollout waves will begin in months 13, 19, and 25, with continuous safety review and public reporting. Months 31–36 will focus on final analysis, resource transfer, procurement guidance, and municipal continuation plans.

Resources will be allocated approximately as follows: 34% to research and technical staff, 21% to municipal integration and independent system audits, 16% to participant and council compensation, 11% to the Data Trust and secure infrastructure, 8% to interpretation and accessible materials, 6% to travel and fieldwork, and 4% to contingency. Suppliers will not be permitted to count routine contract obligations as research co-funding.

## 11. Anticipated limitations

The trial evaluates a bundled institutional intervention. If Velin use increases, it may be difficult to separate the effects of better recognition, improved escalation, staff training, publicity, or the political signal created by adoption. Compliance measures and qualitative process tracing will help identify plausible mechanisms but cannot fully isolate them.

Eight municipalities provide limited protection against cluster-level shocks. A regional election, service consolidation, supplier failure, or public controversy could coincide with rollout. Calendar-period adjustment and registered event logs will reduce, not eliminate, this problem. Cross-boundary use and supplier learning may also dilute contrasts between early and late sequences.

Finally, successful public-service transactions are not equivalent to language transmission. The study can test whether institutional usefulness, confidence, and administrative vocabulary change over 30 months; it cannot establish that children will become fluent or that speaker decline will reverse. Longer follow-up would be needed to connect expanded civic domains to household language practices.

## 12. Contribution

The project shifts minority-language technology from a question of whether a machine can produce recognizable words to a question of whether institutions can be held accountable for usable service. It combines a causal rollout design with community control of data, attention to dialect inequality, and direct observation of purchasing decisions. If the standard succeeds, the result will be more than a Velin interface: it will be evidence that procurement can create durable domains of language use. If use remains low despite safe and functional provision, the project will still distinguish lack of demand from failure of implementation and provide a basis for more honest public decisions about preservation.

# The Right to Be Understood by a Machine

## A community-governed trial of minority-language requirements in digital public-service procurement

### Project summary

The Velin language is commonly supported in the Republic of Darska through festivals, school electives, and archival projects, yet it is largely absent from the digital systems through which residents obtain housing repairs, transport permits, childcare subsidies, and other public services. This proposal tests a different theory of language preservation: a language is more likely to be transmitted when it is useful not only in cultural settings, but also in consequential, ordinary transactions.

We will study eight municipalities in Darska’s North Estuary, where approximately 21,000 people report some Velin ability. Each municipality is scheduled to replace at least one public-service interface—such as a telephone menu, reception kiosk, or online appointment assistant—during the project period. Working with speakers, municipal staff, and technology suppliers, we will introduce a **Velin Digital Service Standard** through procurement contracts. The standard will require functional Velin interaction, dialect-sensitive error handling, human escalation, community review, and auditable performance reporting. It will not require municipalities to buy a particular product.

The intervention will be evaluated through a 30-month stepped-wedge trial, in which all eight municipalities eventually adopt the standard but do so in randomly assigned sequences. Administrative task records, opt-in interaction telemetry, a longitudinal survey of 1,200 residents, linguistic task testing, and qualitative fieldwork will be combined to examine whether the intervention increases civic use of Velin, reduces service failure, and changes younger speakers’ perception of the language’s usefulness.

The project treats digital language support as a matter of political power as well as technical capacity. Velin was excluded from Darskan public administration during most of the twentieth century, and compulsory schooling in majority-language Merec continued in the Estuary until 1987. Digital systems can reproduce that exclusion even when no official language ban remains. At the same time, collecting speech from a small population creates risks of surveillance, commercial extraction, and unwanted standardization. A Velin Data Trust and elected Community Language Council will therefore control research access, approve release of language resources, and retain the right to suspend data collection.

## 1. Background and rationale

Darska’s 2024 Household Language Count recorded 8,600 residents who use Velin at least weekly, 12,400 who understand it but speak it less often, and fewer than 900 speakers aged under twenty-five who describe themselves as confident users. These categories are imprecise, but the age gradient is consistent with local school enrolment and community-organization records. Existing preservation efforts have increased the visibility of Velin songs, place names, and ceremonial speech. They have had less success establishing domains in which a resident gains a practical advantage from using Velin.

Meanwhile, public administration in the North Estuary is being digitized. Six municipalities now direct residents to automated telephone menus before they can reach an employee. Five use appointment kiosks in service centres, and three are procuring text-based assistants for housing and family-support queries. Velin is absent from all but one of these systems. The exception is a telephone menu containing twelve prerecorded prompts, but users must switch to Merec to describe their request.

This matters beyond convenience. When a language cannot be used to report a broken heating system, arrange accessible transport, or ask why a subsidy payment stopped, speakers receive a repeated signal that it belongs to memory rather than public life. Younger or less-confident speakers may avoid it precisely where successful use would demonstrate its contemporary value. Conversely, adding a language superficially can be worse than honest absence: mistranslated instructions, unrecognized dialects, or a machine that fails without offering a person can increase both material harm and linguistic embarrassment.

Most digital preservation projects begin by asking how much text or audio can be collected. This project begins with a different question: **what institutional conditions make it safe and worthwhile to use a minority language?** It focuses on procurement because purchasing rules determine whose language is treated as a core requirement, what counts as acceptable performance, who owns resulting data, and whether suppliers must repair failures. Procurement is therefore a form of language policy, even when presented as a neutral technical process.

## 2. Research questions and hypotheses

The primary research question is:

> Does requiring usable, community-governed Velin support in municipal digital-service contracts increase the routine use of Velin in public-service interactions?

Four secondary questions follow:

1. Does the standard reduce task failure and unwanted switching from Velin to Merec?
2. Do effects differ by age, dialect, confidence, disability, or prior experience of administrative discrimination?
3. Does repeated successful civic use change whether residents regard Velin as worth learning and transmitting?
4. Which organizational practices—rather than speech-recognition accuracy alone—help or hinder adoption?

We hypothesize that municipalities operating under the standard will show a higher rate of completed Velin transactions than municipalities awaiting implementation. We also expect lower rates of language switching and smaller completion gaps between Velin and Merec interactions. Among residents aged sixteen to thirty, we anticipate an increase in perceived practical value and willingness to use Velin with children or younger relatives. We do not expect a 30-month intervention to produce measurable population-level language revival or fluent new speakers.

## 3. Conceptual framework: institutional usability loops

The project proposes an **institutional usability loop**. A person attempts to use Velin in a consequential setting. If the system understands, completes the task, and provides dignified repair when it fails, the interaction increases the person’s expectation that Velin will work next time. Visible use also gives staff and suppliers evidence of demand, which can justify further investment. Better provision then produces more opportunities for use.

A negative loop is equally possible. A badly translated menu fails; the user switches to Merec; low recorded use is interpreted as low demand; and Velin support is cut. Conventional usage statistics cannot distinguish lack of demand from demand suppressed by poor provision. The proposed trial intervenes simultaneously in technical performance, repair procedures, staff practice, and purchasing accountability to test whether that loop can be reversed.

Preservation is defined here as expansion of a language’s viable domains and the social expectation that it can be used without penalty. This definition complements, but does not replace, outcomes such as speaker numbers, proficiency, or intergenerational transmission.

## 4. Setting and partnerships

The study will include the eight North Estuary municipalities of Aven Quay, Belisar, Corren Fields, Dova Reach, Elwick Strand, Marden Fen, Orra Vale, and Ternmouth. Their populations range from 9,000 to 44,000. Estimated Velin-speaking shares range from 6% to 31%. All have agreed in principle to align a scheduled technology purchase or contract renewal with the project timetable.

Three bodies will share governance:

- **The Estuary Municipal Consortium** will coordinate procurement and staff access but will not receive identifiable research data.
- **The Velin Data Trust**, a nonprofit entity established before collection begins, will hold audio, transcripts, and derived language resources.
- **The Community Language Council** will comprise twelve elected Velin users, with reserved places for younger speakers, disabled residents, speakers of the inland and coastal varieties, and people who do not belong to existing language organizations.

Council members will be paid at the same hourly rate as specialist municipal consultants. The council may reject proposed vocabulary, restrict the release of recordings, require a system to be withdrawn from a service domain, or pause research collection. Municipalities will retain responsibility for delivering services and for providing Merec, Velin-speaking staff, and non-digital routes where applicable.

## 5. The Velin Digital Service Standard

The intervention is a contractual standard rather than a single application. Participating procurements must include six requirements.

### 5.1 Functional task coverage

Velin must support complete tasks, not merely greetings or navigation. A resident who begins a supported housing-repair request in Velin must be able to describe the problem, confirm details, receive a reference number, and understand the next step without mandatory switching.

### 5.2 Dialect-sensitive evaluation

Suppliers must test coastal, inland, and mixed urban Velin. Performance reports will be disaggregated by variety where sample size permits. The council will approve test sets and may prohibit publication of small cells that could expose individual speakers.

### 5.3 Dignified repair and human escalation

After two failed recognition attempts, the system must offer a Velin-speaking employee, a callback, or a structured non-voice alternative. It may not repeatedly demand that a user “speak clearly.” Users must be told when the system is uncertain rather than receiving a confident but potentially incorrect response.

### 5.4 Data minimization and non-extraction

Raw voice recordings may not be retained for product development unless a user separately opts in. Suppliers may not create voiceprints, infer identity from accent, sell language data, or use research material to train unrelated commercial systems. Contracts must specify deletion schedules and allow independent audit.

### 5.5 Community language work

Translation, terminology creation, testing, and correction must be paid. Suppliers must maintain a correction register showing which community-reported problems were accepted, rejected, or remain unresolved. Reasons for rejection must be provided in accessible language.

### 5.6 Public performance reporting

Municipalities will publish quarterly measures of task completion, escalation, abandoned interactions, severe semantic errors, and language switching. Word-error rate may be reported, but it cannot be the sole measure of quality because a single misrecognized address or negation can matter more than several harmless grammatical errors.

Before rollout, each municipality will select two or three eligible services. Likely domains include housing repairs, waste collection, concessionary transport appointments, local tax account queries, and childcare-subsidy scheduling. Emergency dispatch, clinical triage, policing, immigration decisions, and legal adjudication are excluded because failures in those domains would exceed the project’s initial safety capacity.

## 6. Study design

### 6.1 Stepped-wedge rollout

The eight municipalities will be assigned to four rollout sequences, with two municipalities entering the intervention every six months. The first six months will provide baseline data for all sites. By month 24, all sites will operate under the standard, followed by six months of observation.

Randomization will be stratified by municipality size and estimated Velin-speaking share. Assignment will be conducted publicly by an independent statistician after systems and services have been registered, reducing the opportunity to place technically easier services in earlier sequences. Municipalities cannot be blinded, but survey participants will not be told the rollout hypotheses.

The design was chosen because each municipality will ultimately receive the intervention and because procurement renewals cannot occur simultaneously. It also permits comparison of intervention and pre-intervention periods. However, neighboring residents may use services across municipal boundaries, and suppliers may improve later installations after learning from early ones. These processes will be measured rather than assumed absent.

### 6.2 Administrative and interaction outcomes

The primary outcome will be the monthly number of **successfully completed Velin transactions per 100 eligible service interactions**. A transaction will count as successful only if the requested task is completed or correctly transferred, the language remains Velin unless the user chooses otherwise, and no severe semantic error is recorded.

Supporting outcomes will include:

- proportion of interactions initiated in Velin;
- unwanted switching to Merec;
- abandonment and repeat contact within seven days;
- time to completion;
- human escalation;
- user-initiated correction;
- material errors, such as an incorrect appointment date or service category; and
- the completion gap between comparable Velin and Merec tasks.

Routine service logs will be separated from research telemetry. Residents may use a service while declining research recording. Opt-in telemetry will retain an encrypted interaction identifier, selected language, confidence estimates, repair events, task result, and user-reported satisfaction. Raw audio will be deleted within thirty days after authorized annotation unless the participant explicitly donates it to the Data Trust.

### 6.3 Resident panel

A panel of 1,200 residents will be recruited without using a government list of presumed Velin speakers. Recruitment will combine address-based sampling in the eight municipalities, open invitations through schools and community venues, and respondent referral capped at two referrals per participant. Sampling weights will adjust for recruitment route, age, municipality, and baseline proficiency.

Participants will complete surveys at baseline, 12 months, 24 months, and 30 months. Measures will include service use, language choice, confidence, perceived usefulness, trust in municipal systems, experiences of correction or ridicule, language use with younger relatives, and intention to learn or teach Velin. A rotating subsample of 320 participants will complete short scenario-based tasks, such as explaining a missed refuse collection or changing an appointment. Tasks will be scored for communicative success, vocabulary range, and willingness to persist after misunderstanding. The purpose is not to certify fluency but to detect changes in functional confidence and administrative vocabulary.

Participants aged sixteen and seventeen may enroll with assent and guardian consent. Because some households may disagree about Velin participation, communications will avoid labels such as “Velin household” on envelopes or shared devices.

### 6.4 Qualitative fieldwork

Researchers will observe procurement meetings, terminology workshops, service-centre work, and system testing. Eighty residents and forty municipal employees, translators, and supplier staff will be interviewed at least twice. We will deliberately recruit residents who oppose spending on Velin technology, speakers who prefer human service, and people who understand Velin but avoid speaking it.

Analysis will examine how “demand,” “accuracy,” “neutrality,” and “value for money” are constructed in decisions. Particular attention will be paid to moments when technical constraints conceal policy choices—for example, when a supplier labels Velin support an optional customization while treating Merec as part of the base product.

## 7. Analysis and statistical power

The primary analysis will follow intention to treat: a municipality is considered exposed from its assigned implementation date even if deployment is delayed or incomplete. A mixed-effects binomial model will estimate the effect on successful Velin transactions, with fixed effects for calendar period and registered service domain and a municipality-level intercept. Pre-specified interactions will assess age profile, baseline speaker share, interface type, and dialect coverage. We will report absolute percentage-point changes alongside relative effects.

A secondary dose analysis will use audited compliance with the six standard requirements. Interrupted trends for each municipality will be plotted to reveal anticipation, delayed effects, or abrupt supplier changes. Survey outcomes will be analyzed using weighted longitudinal models, while interview and observation materials will undergo framework analysis led jointly by academic and community researchers.

Based on a three-month feasibility audit, the included services are expected to generate approximately 58,000 eligible interactions during the study, of which 3% to 8% may be initiated in Velin at baseline. With eight clusters, four rollout periods, an assumed intracluster correlation of 0.03, and 10% missing outcome classification, simulations suggest 80% power to detect a relative increase of roughly 25% in successful Velin transactions. These estimates depend on stable service volume and may be weakened if municipalities select highly dissimilar services. The resident panel, allowing for 25% attrition, should detect a standardized within-person change of 0.18 in perceived practical value.

No single threshold will determine success. Results will be presented with uncertainty intervals, compliance data, adverse events, and qualitative evidence about why residents did or did not use the systems.

## 8. Ethics, political risk, and safeguarding

Language identity in the North Estuary is politically contested. Some residents view public Velin provision as restitution for prior exclusion; others regard it as symbolic regionalism or an inefficient claim on shared funds. The project will not require anyone to declare an ethnic identity. Eligibility for surveys depends on language experience or residence, and access to Velin services will not depend on research participation.

Small-language speech data can be identifying even after names are removed. Accent, family references, and place descriptions may reveal a speaker. Accordingly, audio will be stored in the Data Trust’s isolated environment, accessed only by named researchers, and reported through disclosure-controlled summaries. Publicly released resources will prioritize synthetic prompts, council-approved terminology, and short recordings whose donors have chosen a specific reuse licence. Withdrawal will remain possible until a recording enters an approved aggregate model.

The study will record and review adverse events, including incorrect service action, exposure of personal information, discriminatory staff response, systematic failure for a dialect, and distress caused by historical language questions. A safety panel with a council representative, a municipal safeguarding officer, and an independent digital-rights specialist may halt a service component.

There is also a risk that formal administrative Velin will privilege fluent activists or one prestigious variety. Terminology workshops will therefore begin with competing forms rather than a preselected official lexicon. Interfaces may accept multiple terms while displaying one plain-language explanation. Disagreement will be documented; consensus will not be manufactured where speakers genuinely differ.

## 9. Knowledge exchange and practical outputs

The project will produce:

1. a reusable model procurement clause for functional minority-language support;
2. an audit protocol covering task success, dialect equity, repair, and data rights;
3. a council-governed Velin administrative terminology bank;
4. de-identified test sets released only where disclosure risk is acceptable;
5. annual public hearings in each participating municipality;
6. supplier briefings and training for procurement officers; and
7. a policy report comparing the cost of meaningful provision with ceremonial or incomplete translation.

Results will be reported in Velin and Merec. Residents will be able to challenge interpretations before final publication, though no stakeholder will have authority to suppress unfavorable aggregate findings. Any licensing revenue from approved Velin resources will return to the Data Trust for language teaching, accessibility work, and future maintenance.

## 10. Work plan and resources

Months 1–6 will establish governance, register services, conduct baseline audits, and finalize measures. Months 7–12 will cover the first rollout, panel recruitment, and terminology work. Further rollout waves will begin in months 13, 19, and 25, with continuous safety review and public reporting. Months 31–36 will focus on final analysis, resource transfer, procurement guidance, and municipal continuation plans.

Resources will be allocated approximately as follows: 34% to research and technical staff, 21% to municipal integration and independent system audits, 16% to participant and council compensation, 11% to the Data Trust and secure infrastructure, 8% to interpretation and accessible materials, 6% to travel and fieldwork, and 4% to contingency. Suppliers will not be permitted to count routine contract obligations as research co-funding.

## 11. Anticipated limitations

The trial evaluates a bundled institutional intervention. If Velin use increases, it may be difficult to separate the effects of better recognition, improved escalation, staff training, publicity, or the political signal created by adoption. Compliance measures and qualitative process tracing will help identify plausible mechanisms but cannot fully isolate them.

Eight municipalities provide limited protection against cluster-level shocks. A regional election, service consolidation, supplier failure, or public controversy could coincide with rollout. Calendar-period adjustment and registered event logs will reduce, not eliminate, this problem. Cross-boundary use and supplier learning may also dilute contrasts between early and late sequences.

Finally, successful public-service transactions are not equivalent to language transmission. The study can test whether institutional usefulness, confidence, and administrative vocabulary change over 30 months; it cannot establish that children will become fluent or that speaker decline will reverse. Longer follow-up would be needed to connect expanded civic domains to household language practices.

## 12. Contribution

The project shifts minority-language technology from a question of whether a machine can produce recognizable words to a question of whether institutions can be held accountable for usable service. It combines a causal rollout design with community control of data, attention to dialect inequality, and direct observation of purchasing decisions. If the standard succeeds, the result will be more than a Velin interface: it will be evidence that procurement can create durable domains of language use. If use remains low despite safe and functional provision, the project will still distinguish lack of demand from failure of implementation and provide a basis for more honest public decisions about preservation.

# The Acoustic Prosthesis: Designing What a Limb Sounds Like

A prosthetic limb is usually described through visible geometry and measurable mechanics: socket shape, joint alignment, actuator torque, foot stiffness, mass, and range of motion. Yet every mechanical system also produces sound. A microprocessor knee may click when its mode changes. A laminated socket can creak under torsion. A cosmetic cover may rub against a pylon. An osseointegrated attachment can transmit vibration through the skeleton with little external noise at all.

These effects are easy to dismiss as secondary. If the knee is stable and the socket is comfortable, why worry about a faint click? The answer is that prosthetic sound has several roles at once. It can be an engineering symptom, a source of sensory feedback, a signal to people nearby, or an unwanted reminder that the device is present. The same sound may reassure one wearer and irritate another. A sharp latch noise can confirm secure engagement, but it can also attract attention in a quiet room.

Acoustic design therefore should not mean making every prosthesis silent. It means controlling when sound occurs, how it travels, what information it carries, and whether the wearer considers it acceptable. This requires designers to treat sound and vibration as part of the human-device interface rather than as residue left over after the “real” engineering is complete.

## A prosthesis is an acoustic system

Sound begins with a changing force. In a lower-limb prosthesis, that force may come from heel strike, a joint reaching its stop, hydraulic fluid passing through a valve, a loose fastener shifting, or two surfaces sliding against one another. The resulting vibration travels through the device and then reaches a receiver. That receiver might be a nearby listener’s ear, a microphone used during testing, soft tissue in the residual limb, or bone carrying vibration toward the wearer’s inner ear.

A useful way to analyze the system is through three elements:

1. **Source:** the event that creates vibration.
2. **Transmission path:** the structure or air volume through which vibration travels.
3. **Receiver:** the person or sensor that detects it.

This model prevents a common design mistake: trying to solve every acoustic problem by adding padding around the source. A designer can instead reduce the force at its origin, interrupt the path, change the receiving conditions, or combine all three.

Consider a foot shell that squeaks during late stance. The source may be stick-slip motion between the carbon foot blade and the inner surface of the shell. The path includes the shell material and the air cavity around the blade. The receiver is usually an external listener, although the wearer may also feel the vibration. Lubricating the contact can suppress the source temporarily, but it may collect grit or damage a polymer. A textile sleeve can separate the surfaces, although it may retain moisture. Altering the shell’s internal geometry can prevent contact, but may require new tooling. Each response addresses the same symptom through a different mechanism and creates different maintenance consequences.

The source-path-receiver model also distinguishes airborne sound from structure-borne vibration. Airborne sound is pressure variation that travels through the surrounding air. Structure-borne vibration moves through solids and may later radiate into the air from a panel or cover. A prosthetic pylon struck by a small internal component can behave like a bell: the impact is modest, but the tube efficiently transmits and radiates it. Covering the impact point with foam may help less than adding a constrained damping layer to the pylon or changing the component’s clearance.

The distinction matters especially for wearers. A sound that is barely measurable outside the device can be prominent through tissue or bone conduction. Conversely, a hollow cosmetic shell may amplify a noise for bystanders while the wearer barely notices it. Testing only with a microphone one metre away captures neither situation well.

## Where prosthetic sounds come from

Prosthetic sounds can be grouped by the physical process that generates them. The categories overlap, but they help connect a reported noise to a likely design cause.

### Impact and clearance

Clicks, knocks, and clacks often result from components crossing a gap and striking a stop. Examples include a mechanical knee lock engaging, an ankle unit reaching its angular limit, or a battery moving within a housing. These sounds have rapid onset and can contain substantial high-frequency energy, which makes them noticeable even when their total energy is low.

Clearance is not always a defect. Mechanical parts need room to move, accommodate contamination, and tolerate manufacturing variation. Removing every gap can increase friction or cause seizure. Acoustic control may instead involve placing an elastomer at the stop, slowing the moving part before contact, or making the engagement sound consistent rather than erratic.

### Friction and stick-slip motion

Squeaks and chirps arise when surfaces alternately adhere and slide. Their occurrence depends on material pairing, surface finish, normal force, speed, temperature, humidity, and contamination. This complexity explains why a prosthesis may be quiet in a clinic but noisy after a dusty walk or on a humid day.

A low-friction material is not automatically the best answer. Some interfaces rely on friction to remain secure, and a lubricant can migrate to places where grip is needed. Designers should identify whether relative motion is intended. If it is not, fastening or geometry may eliminate the motion. If it is intended, a bearing, separator, or controlled sliding surface may be more durable than an improvised lubricant.

### Fluid flow and actuation

Hydraulic and pneumatic joints can hiss, gurgle, or produce a muted pulse as valves open and close. Powered devices add motor whine, gear-mesh tones, cooling airflow, and switching-related vibration. These sounds often vary with load and speed, so they can encode information about what the device is doing.

Tonal sounds are particularly conspicuous. A broad, low-level rustle may blend into environmental noise, while a narrow motor tone remains identifiable. Changing motor speed, gear geometry, mounting stiffness, or control strategy can shift or spread tonal energy, although those changes can affect efficiency and responsiveness.

### Material flexure

Sockets, covers, and flexible feet deform repeatedly. Layers can rub, thin panels can snap between shapes, and bonded interfaces can begin to separate. A creak does not prove structural failure, but a new or changing creak deserves investigation because it may indicate altered load transfer.

Composite structures complicate interpretation. Their acoustic behavior depends not just on bulk stiffness but on fibre orientation, laminate thickness, resin, local geometry, and boundary conditions. Two sockets with similar static strength can radiate sound differently. A stiff wall may transmit vibration efficiently, whereas a more compliant wall may damp one frequency but buckle or rub at another location.

### Attachment and clothing interaction

Not every sound originates inside the prosthesis. Suspension sleeves can wrinkle and release. Clothing can brush against a cover. A shoe can squeak against the prosthetic foot or floor. Sweat, skin products, and dust alter interfaces over the course of a day.

This broader view is important because users experience the assembled system, not the isolated component. A silent ankle on a laboratory rig may click once enclosed by a cover and placed in a particular shoe. Acoustic testing that excludes these ordinary layers risks optimizing the wrong object.

## Sound as information rather than waste

Some sounds are useful. A positive click can confirm that a pin lock has engaged. A powered hand may emit a brief tone when it changes grip mode. Repeated foot-contact sounds can help a wearer judge cadence and symmetry. Maintenance technicians also listen for looseness, dry bearings, and damaged covers.

Useful acoustic feedback tends to share three properties. It corresponds reliably to an event, is distinguishable from unrelated noise, and arrives soon enough to guide action. Loudness alone does not make a signal useful. A quiet but crisp latch may be easier to interpret than a louder series of ambiguous rattles.

Reliability is crucial. If a lock sometimes engages silently and sometimes clicks without fully engaging, the sound can create false confidence. The mechanical state must determine the signal, not merely correlate with it under ideal conditions. Where engagement is safety-critical, acoustic feedback should generally supplement rather than replace visual, tactile, or electronic confirmation.

Designers can also shape sound intentionally. A housing can be tuned to produce a short, low-intensity confirmation click. A damper can remove ringing after the initial event. In an electronically controlled device, an artificial cue can be generated independently of the mechanism. Artificial cues are easier to standardize, but they consume energy, add components, and may feel less direct than a sound emerging from the action itself.

There is also a risk in erasing all feedback. Suppose a knee joint has always produced a soft click at full extension.
