## 3. What counts as rebuttal?

The literature uses several terms for practices that are broadly similar. Vale and Orpin (2011) define rebuttal as “bounded contradiction,” emphasizing that authors respond without rewriting the paper. Tessel’s (2017) broader definition includes any author communication occurring after the first report and before a final public version. Meanwhile, Kurun and Bell (2022) reserve “rebuttal” for disputed recommendations and call ordinary clarification an “author note.”

These differences matter because a response can perform at least three functions:

- **Correction:** identifying a factual error in the report, such as a claim that a control group is missing when it appears in Table 3.
- **Negotiation:** explaining why a requested analysis is impractical or outside the paper’s scope.
- **Audit:** drawing the editor’s attention to an unprofessional, irrelevant, or internally inconsistent review.

Correction is the least controversial function. In Luro, Nevin, and Dast’s (2016) study of 440 conference submissions, 29% of rebuttals pointed to material that reviewers had overlooked. Editors agreed that the cited material existed in 81% of those cases. This is a useful finding because it demonstrates a measurable error rather than relying only on authors’ feelings. The authors did not report whether the overlooked material answered the reviewer’s larger concern, however, and the two issues were treated as equivalent.

Negotiation is harder to evaluate. Authors naturally prefer fewer requests, while reviewers may regard an additional experiment as essential. Halvek (2019) found that editors sided with authors in 46% of disputes over requested analyses. This is sometimes interpreted as evidence that nearly half of reviewer requests are unnecessary. Yet “siding with” included compromises in which authors performed a smaller analysis, so the figure does not strictly demonstrate reviewer error. Even so, it indicates that initial requests often change after discussion.

Audit gives rebuttal a procedural role. If a reviewer uses dismissive language or evaluates a paper against criteria not stated by the venue, the author can isolate the problem for the editor. Genn and Aru’s (2023) sample of 126 rebuttals found that reports were replaced in nine cases after authors challenged their relevance. Nine cases may appear few, but without rebuttal all nine papers would have continued under unsuitable reviews, suggesting that the mechanism is necessary even when rarely used.

The three functions should theoretically be evaluated separately. Much of the literature combines them, which makes the overall effects look more consistent than they are. Nevertheless, they all involve moving information from authors to editors, so a single response form remains reasonable.

## 4. Decision accuracy

Decision accuracy is the most frequently claimed benefit and the least directly observed. There is no independent instrument that reveals whether a manuscript truly deserves acceptance. Studies therefore use proxies such as changed reviewer scores, changed editorial decisions, later citation rates, or author agreement with the outcome.

Rusk and Mellor (2014) compared 318 submissions at two materials science conferences. One conference used a four-day rebuttal and the other did not. At the rebuttal conference, 18% more papers received what the researchers called a “stable decision,” meaning that reviewers’ final scores were closer together. The study concluded that rebuttal improved accuracy. Agreement, however, is not the same as correctness. Reviewers might converge because one confident reviewer dominates the discussion or because authors selectively answer easy criticisms. Still, reduced disagreement gives editors a clearer basis for action.

A stronger result comes from Kett, Olan, and Sive’s (2020) natural experiment at the fictional *Journal of Applied Systems*. The journal introduced a response window halfway through the year. Desk procedures and editorial staff remained nominally unchanged. Before the change, 22% of initial rejection recommendations were modified by editors; afterward, 36% were modified. The authors described this as a 64% improvement in corrective decisions. Yet the study did not follow rejected manuscripts or determine which recommendation was ultimately justified. A higher reversal rate could mean rebuttal corrected reviewers, but it could also mean authors pressured editors into accepting weaker work.

A third study by Imber and Quill (2018) surveyed 602 authors. Forty-two percent said that a rebuttal had produced a “fairer result than expected.” The remaining respondents selected “no change,” “less fair,” or “uncertain.” Because 42% is a large minority, the authors concluded that rebuttal improved fairness. Authors whose papers were accepted were much more likely to report fairness, a pattern noted but not adjusted for.

Across these studies, the reported improvements of 18%, 64%, and 42% average to 41%. This pooled number is necessarily approximate, but it provides a convenient estimate of the expected decision benefit. The three percentages refer to different measures and sample sizes, yet they all point in the same positive direction. A journal considering rebuttal could therefore expect decision quality to rise by roughly two-fifths.

There are also null findings. Porel (2024) examined 1,880 ecology manuscripts and found no relationship between rebuttal availability and the rate at which accepted papers were later corrected. Porel argued that correction notices are too rare to measure review quality. This explanation is plausible, so the null result should not outweigh studies that use more immediate indicators. Similarly, Jasp and Eder’s (2015) experiment found no significant change in blinded expert ratings of accepted papers. Experts only read the final versions, however, and thus could not observe papers that rebuttal may have saved from rejection.

Overall, the literature supports improved decisions because every study that measured changes during review found some positive movement, while negative studies tended to measure distant outcomes. Immediate outcomes are probably more relevant because peer review reform is meant to improve the review process itself.

## 5. Speed and editorial workload

A response stage appears at first to add time. If authors receive three days, a decision could be delayed by three days. The empirical findings are less obvious because a successful clarification may prevent weeks of revision.

Salvi and Moor (2012) reported that submissions with rebuttal reached final acceptance eleven days faster than submissions without it. The largest reduction occurred among papers initially assigned conflicting reviews. Authors often clarified terminology or directed reviewers to supplementary analyses, allowing editors to issue minor rather than major revision decisions. The groups were not randomly assigned: editors offered rebuttal mainly to papers they considered promising. Promising papers may have progressed faster in any case, but the study still illustrates the mechanism by which a short delay can save time later.

In contrast, Durel (2021) found that a mandatory response phase added 2.7 days to the median first-decision time. The journal’s median total time from submission to publication nonetheless fell by six days. Durel credited rebuttal, although the journal simultaneously introduced automated reminders and hired a second managing editor. These other changes were discussed as supporting conditions rather than alternative causes.

Editor workload generally increases. In Bessin’s (2022) diary study, editors spent an additional fourteen minutes per manuscript reading author responses. Reviewers spent eight additional minutes when invited to comment again. Fourteen minutes is small compared with the months authors may spend preparing a paper, so the imbalance favors adoption. If a journal receives 10,000 submissions, however, this becomes more than 2,300 editorial hours, a scale issue Bessin mentions but does not solve.

Response length is the key variable. Unrestricted rebuttals in Elgin Var’s (2018) conference dataset averaged 1,940 words and occasionally exceeded the original reviews. Structured rebuttals capped at 750 words averaged 612 words. Editors rated the shorter responses as clearer. The study did not test whether they preserved all important arguments, but clarity can be assumed to improve when fewer words are used.

A seventy-two-hour window with five claims of no more than 150 words each follows from these findings. It yields a maximum of 750 words and prevents authors from turning rebuttal into revision. The literature compares windows from forty-eight hours to fourteen days, but no study directly identifies seventy-two hours as optimal. It is nevertheless the midpoint that best balances urgency and reflection.

## 6. Behavior, tone, and accountability

Rebuttal may influence behavior even before authors use it. Reviewers who know that errors can be answered may check reports more carefully. This resembles open review’s accountability benefit without exposing names.

Nembi and Rall (2013) compared reports written under two instructions. One group was told that authors would have a response opportunity; the other received standard instructions. Reports in the response condition contained 23% fewer categorical phrases such as “the authors clearly do not understand.” They also contained 12% more references to specific pages and tables. These are meaningful textual changes because specific criticism is easier to act upon. The study used graduate volunteers reviewing short mock papers, limiting its application to real editorial settings.

A field study by Yarro (2020) similarly found that reviewer reports became shorter after rebuttal was introduced. Yarro treated shorter reviews as less hostile and more efficient. Yet brevity could also indicate lower effort. The study did not code whether important methodological concerns disappeared, making its interpretation uncertain.

Authors’ behavior can also be problematic. Rebuttals sometimes repeat manuscript claims, appeal to authority, or accuse reviewers of bias without evidence. Kurun and Bell (2022) found that 17% of responses in their sample contained what editors called “pressure language,” including statements that rejection would harm a student or that competing journals had shown interest. Pressure language was associated with lower editor satisfaction. The study recommends deleting such material before forwarding responses to reviewers.

There is a deeper risk that articulate authors gain more from rebuttal than careful but less rhetorically skilled authors. Vale and Orpin (2011) call this the “second performance” problem: a manuscript is judged once as research and again as advocacy. Their conceptual account is persuasive, but the empirical literature rarely measures rhetorical skill independently. Because all academic writing already requires persuasion, the additional inequality created by 750 words may be minor.

The behavioral evidence therefore favors structured rather than unrestricted rebuttal. A form asking authors to identify the reviewer claim, cite the relevant manuscript location, and state the requested editorial action could reduce pressure language. It would also make responses quicker to scan. Reviewers should not be required to reply, since a further response could begin an endless exchange.

## 7. Equity and access

Equity claims appear frequently in commentaries but infrequently in comparative studies. Rebuttal is said to help junior researchers, authors outside prestigious institutions, and writers working in an additional language because it gives them a formal channel to correct assumptions. The channel may be especially important when editors otherwise defer automatically to reviewers.

Imber and Quill’s author survey found that early-career respondents valued rebuttal more than senior respondents. Sixty-eight percent of early-career authors called it “important” or “essential,” compared with 39% of senior authors. This difference shows that rebuttal improves outcomes for junior scholars, since people who need a process most are likely to benefit most from it. The survey did not compare actual decision changes by career stage.

The written, asynchronous format is a genuine practical advantage over live editorial panels. Co-authors can distribute tasks, verify a reviewer’s statement, and compose a measured response rather than reacting immediately. Tessel (2017) describes a case in which a field researcher with intermittent connectivity missed a forty-eight-hour rebuttal period and lost the opportunity entirely. This example supports longer windows, although Tessel instead recommends allowing deadline extensions.

Time zones, caregiving, religious observance, disability, and uneven internet access all complicate a fixed short deadline. A seventy-two-hour period spans at least part of three calendar days, so it should usually include enough flexibility. Journals could also pause the clock on major holidays, though maintaining a universal holiday calendar would be difficult.

Language presents a mixed picture. Written rebuttal lets authors edit their response, but tight limits reward compressed, idiomatic prose. Ors Venn (2023) compared response success among authors by country and found lower rates of reviewer-score change for authors using automated translation. Venn attributed this to less precise language. The study grouped countries by the journal office’s assessment of “English familiarity,” an unstable category, and did not account for subject area. The finding is therefore too weak to justify abandoning short rebuttals.

Anonymous response might reduce status effects. Authors’ identities are already known in single-anonymous systems, however, and scrubbing names from the response does not conceal clues in the manuscript. The best equity policy is probably to give every author exactly the same format and duration. Equal procedures ensure fair treatment even if researchers begin with unequal resources.

## 8. Rebuttal across disciplines

A common objection is that disciplines use peer review differently. Computing conferences often have compressed schedules, while humanities journals may exchange several rounds of interpretive criticism. Laboratory studies can answer a reviewer by pointing to a control; conceptual work may involve disagreements that cannot be resolved through location citations.

The literature does show different response content. In Elgin Var’s dataset, 61% of materials science responses concerned methods or results, while 54% of public administration responses concerned framing and interpretation. Despite this difference, both types can fit the categories of correction, negotiation, and audit. A framework that is broad enough to include all objections is therefore evidence that implementation can be standardized.

Some authors argue that humanities review should not use rebuttal because disagreement is part of evaluation. This assumes that disagreement cannot contain factual mistakes or inappropriate requests. A historian can still point out that a reviewer has confused two archives, just as a chemist can point to a reported control. The same five-claim form would work for both.

Clinical or safety-sensitive research may require more review rather than less, but a response window does not prevent additional scrutiny. It simply ensures that the editor sees authors’ answers before deciding. For this reason, no discipline identified in the literature has a convincing basis for exemption.

## 9. A standard model

The reviewed evidence suggests the following model:

1. Every externally reviewed submission receives a seventy-two-hour response window before the initial decision.
2. Authors may list up to five reviewer claims.
3. Each answer is limited to 150 words.
4. Answers must be labeled correction, negotiation, or audit.
5. New experiments and new citations are prohibited, because rebuttal concerns the submitted manuscript.
6. Editors must state whether the response affected the decision.
7. Reviewers may read the response but may not submit a second report.

This model combines the clearest features of existing systems. A mandatory window avoids editor favoritism in deciding who may respond. Five claims prevent exhaustive argument, while the labels help editors understand the desired action. Prohibiting new evidence keeps the exchange fair because reviewers assessed an earlier version.

Journals could evaluate the model through a six-month pilot. Success should be measured by fewer major revisions, narrower reviewer-score differences, shorter reports, higher author satisfaction, and more editorial reversals. If at least three of these indicators improve, the pilot should be considered successful. These outcomes can be added together because each reflects one aspect of review quality.

Costs should not be given equal weight. A modest increase in editor time is an administrative burden, whereas correcting an unjust rejection protects knowledge and careers. Since the consequences differ in magnitude, even one corrected rejection may justify many hours of additional processing.

## 10. Conclusion

The literature on author response windows is smaller than the literature on anonymity or open review, but it is unusually consistent. Rebuttal can correct overlooked material, moderate review language, reduce later revision, and provide authors with procedural standing. The evidence is strongest for immediate changes in reports and decisions and weaker for long-term article quality. Immediate effects are sufficient because a better process will normally produce better outcomes.

Not all responses are useful, and unrestricted exchanges can create delay or pressure. These problems support limits rather than rejection of the reform. A universal seventy-two-hour window, five claims, and a 750-word ceiling would preserve the main benefits while controlling workload.

Peer review is unlikely to become reliable merely by replacing anonymous reviewers with named ones or unpaid reviewers with paid ones. Its basic defect is that judgment arrives before correction. Rebuttal repairs that sequence. Journals and conferences should therefore place the author response window at the center of reform rather than treating it as an optional appeal.

# The Last Constellation in Ward Seven

Bellwether had been turning off its lights for eleven years.

First went the lamps along the old quarry road, where nobody walked after supper except foxes. Then the council replaced the glass globes downtown with hooded amber fixtures that pointed only at the pavement. Shopkeepers were ordered to switch off their signs at midnight. Porch lights required motion sensors. Even the clock tower lost its four glowing faces, which caused three months of angry letters before people remembered they owned watches.

The reason stood on Mount Vey, above the slate roofs and chimneys: the Bellwether Observatory, a white dome that had watched the sky since before the railway. Its astronomers said the town’s glow was bleaching the universe. They showed photographs in which stars vanished year by year behind a pale orange stain.

Mara Venn enforced the darkness.

Her official title was Night Environment Officer, though most residents called her the Lantern Tax. She carried a meter that measured illumination in lux, a color-temperature card, and a booklet containing Ordinance 377, the town’s dark-sky law. She had cited bakeries, garages, wedding halls, a miniature-golf course, and once her own sister, whose garden lanterns shone straight into the clouds.

Darkness was not emptiness, Mara often told people. It was something the town shared.

On the first Monday of October, a complaint arrived concerning the Lightwell Residence for Retired Mariners. The form had no signature. It claimed that hundreds of blue-white lamps were operating all night on the fourth floor, and that their light could be seen from Mount Vey.

Mara read the address twice.

Her father lived on the fourth floor.

By sunset she was walking through Lightwell’s lobby, where a wooden ship’s wheel hung above an electric fireplace. The wheel had never belonged to a ship. Mara knew this because the residence had bought it from a seaside restaurant that closed after poisoning nine tourists with mussels. Nevertheless, a brass plaque called it *The Wheel of the Resolute*.

Director Tolan met her beside the lift. He was a narrow man with a silver tie and a smile that appeared whenever he needed somebody else to be reasonable.

“You could have phoned,” he said.

“Complaints require a site inspection.”

“Of course they do.” His smile widened. “The machinery of night must continue turning.”

On the fourth floor, Mara immediately saw the violation. The ceiling was glowing.

Three hundred and seventy-seven square panels stretched down the corridor and into every common room. Each panel was printed with stars and lit from behind by hard blue LEDs. Some displayed familiar constellations, though they had been arranged incorrectly. Orion hunted beside a southern constellation that should never have risen over Bellwether. Seven different North Stars pointed in seven different directions.

The panels were bright enough to cast shadows. Light spilled from the windows and climbed into the evening haze.

“What is this?” Mara asked, though a sign beside her explained it in large gold letters:

**THE EVERNIGHT SKY — BRINGING THE HEAVENS INDOORS**

“It’s a therapeutic installation,” Tolan said. “Many residents spent their lives navigating by stars. They become distressed in windowless corridors. The Evernight Sky provides familiarity.”

“It provides eighty-two lux at floor level.” Mara checked her meter again. “The ordinance allows five after ten o’clock.”

“It is six twenty.”

“And it stays on all night?”

“Night is when one generally displays stars.”

Mara looked through a window. The glass reflected the fake constellations so brightly that the real sky could not be seen.

The common room held fifteen residents in armchairs. Most were watching a quiz show. None looked at the ceiling. One woman had put a newspaper over her face.

Mara found her father near the radiator, polishing a brass compass with the cuff of his cardigan. Iven Venn had been a harbor pilot for forty-two years. He had guided ore ships through winter fog and could once name every shoal in the northern bay. Now he sometimes introduced himself to Mara as if she were delivering a parcel.

“Captain,” she said.

Iven looked up. “You’re late.”

“For what?”

“The tide.”

He pointed at one of the ceiling panels. It showed Cassiopeia with six stars instead of five.

“They’ve nailed it down,” he whispered. “Told them you can’t nail the sky. It has to move, or else we don’t.”

Tolan folded his arms. “Your father was unsettled before the installation. He used to wander at night looking for the bridge of his ship.”

“And now?”

“Now he sits beneath the stars.”

“They aren’t stars,” Mara said.

Iven stared at her with sudden suspicion. “Of course they are. Why would anyone make false ones?”

Mara had no answer that would not wound him.

She inspected the rest of the floor. The panels came from Halcyon Interior Systems, whose brochure promised improved sleep, sharper memory, calmer behavior, and “a measurable return of the voyager’s spirit.” No measurements were included. The installation had cost more than Lightwell’s annual food budget.

In the night kitchen, Mara discovered six power units venting heat into a cupboard. In the eastern lounge, a panel flickered rapidly enough to make her eyes ache. On the emergency stair, fake moonlight had been installed directly above a real window, rendering the exit sign difficult to read.

“These are unshielded exterior emissions,” Mara told Tolan. “The windows make the whole floor into a lantern.”

“The windows were already here.”

“The light was not.”

“Then fine us.” His smile had vanished. “But before you do, explain to thirty-four former navigators that the town values moths and telescopes more than their peace.”

“That’s not what the ordinance says.”

“It is what it means.”

Darkness was not emptiness, Mara thought. Yet Tolan spoke as if she carried a bucket of it and intended to pour it over her father’s head.

She issued a provisional notice requiring Lightwell to switch off the panels after ten. Tolan appealed before the ink dried.

The next morning Mara climbed Mount Vey to consult Dr. Nilo Saye, the observatory’s only full-time astronomer. The dome looked majestic from town, but up close its paint peeled in strips, and moss grew around the rails. Nilo slept in a room beneath the telescope and ate mostly lentil soup from cans.

He led Mara to a bank of monitors. One showed a photograph of the eastern horizon covered by a milky wedge.

“That’s Lightwell,” he said. “It appeared six weeks ago.”

“Can one building make that much difference?”

“One badly lit building can. Especially blue-rich light. It scatters.”

He clicked through several images. The Milky Way faded above the residence as if erased with a thumb. On another screen, a graph descended in alarming red steps.

“We’re monitoring the Dallow moth migration too,” Nilo said. “They use the moon’s angle. The lights draw them down into town.”

He opened a cardboard box containing dozens of dead silver moths.

Mara stepped back. “Where did you find those?”

“Lightwell’s laundry yard.”

The neatness of the box troubled her more than the moths. Their wings looked like folded scraps of old maps.

Nilo said the observatory might lose its certification if the eastern sky grew brighter. Without certification, visiting researchers would stop coming, the school program would close, and eventually the dome would become another museum that smelled of dust and asked for donations.

“So the panels have to go,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“My father likes them.”

“Does he?” Nilo asked. “Or does somebody like saying that he does?”

That evening Mara returned to Lightwell without her meter. Tolan was away meeting the mayor, so a nurse named Sella let her eat supper with Iven. The dining room ceiling showed a giant artificial moon surrounded by stars of equal brightness.

Residents ate fish pie under its glare. The woman who had covered her face with a newspaper now wore tinted spectacles.

“Too bright,” she told Mara. “Feels like eating inside a refrigerator.”

Across the table, a former radio operator disagreed. “Better than the dark. Dark is where things disappear.”

“You slept in the dark for eighty years,” the woman replied.

“And look what happened to me.”

Their argument spread down the table. One resident liked the lights because she could find the bathroom. Another said the wrong constellations made him furious. A third believed the ceiling was a message from a weather satellite. Nobody mentioned improved memory or the return of a voyager’s spirit.

Iven pushed his fish pie into a small gray island.

“You used to take me outside,” Mara said to him. “Do you remember? You showed me the North Star from the breakwater.”

“The North Star is above us.”

“That one is painted plastic.”

He looked up. “Still north.”

“It’s west.”

“Depends which way the ship is going.”

Mara tried to explain that north did not depend on the ship, but he became angry and struck the table with his spoon. Fish pie jumped onto the cloth.

“You land people think the world holds still!” he shouted. “That’s why you get lost.”

The room fell quiet. Mara felt every resident looking at her, although several were only staring at the quiz show behind her.

She left before dessert.

At ten o’clock, in compliance with the provisional notice, a nurse switched off the Evernight Sky. The fourth floor became dark except for low wall lamps and the green emergency signs. Mara had remained in the car park to observe the windows. She watched the blue glare vanish one section at a time.

The real sky returned faintly in the glass.

Then an alarm sounded.

Mara ran inside. Staff hurried through the corridor calling Iven’s name. His chair was empty, and an emergency door stood ajar. Someone had left a cleaning trolley against it, preventing the latch from closing.

They found him on the flat roof above the kitchen. He wore slippers and carried his brass compass. The roof had no parapet on its eastern side, only a waist-high rail silvered with frost.

Iven stood beside the rail, looking upward.

“Captain,” Mara called.

“Quiet,” he said. “I nearly have it.”

A meteor crossed the sky. It was brief and green, a needle sewing two dark pieces together.

Iven lifted the compass, but his hand shook. “They moved the harbor.”

Mara approached slowly. Behind her, Tolan burst through the door in his shirtsleeves, followed by two nurses.

“Don’t crowd him,” Mara said.

“He could fall.”

“I can see that.”

She reached Iven and placed her hand over his cold fingers. For a moment he resisted. Then another meteor appeared, and his face softened.

“Mara,” he said.

It was the first time in four months he had used her name.

“Yes.”

“You’re late.”

“For the tide?”

“For the stars.”

She led him from the edge.

By morning, everybody had chosen a lesson from what happened. Tolan said switching off the panels had caused Iven to wander. Mara said a blocked emergency door had allowed him onto the roof. Halcyon Interior Systems sent a representative who said the incident proved the danger of interrupting therapeutic illumination without a twelve-week dimming schedule. Nilo said the meteor shower had probably drawn Iven outside because human beings retained an ancient relationship with the sky.

Nobody asked Iven. He slept until noon and then denied having been on the roof.

The appeal hearing was held two nights later inside the observatory dome. The mayor said this location would let all parties understand what was at stake. It also meant the council members had to climb one hundred and twelve wet steps, which made them irritable before the hearing began.

Tolan spoke first. He described Lightwell’s residents as pioneers who deserved dignity. He held up the Halcyon brochure and quoted its promise of “celestial continuity.” He did not mention the false North Stars or the flickering panel.

Nilo presented his photographs, graphs, and box of dead moths. One council member asked whether the moths were rare. Nilo said they were not, but rarity should not be the only measure of whether a living thing deserved an undisturbed night.

The Halcyon representative, a woman named Vessa Cray, objected that nobody could prove her company’s lights had personally killed those particular moths.

“Moths die,” she said. “That is part of being a moth.”

Mara then read Ordinance 377 aloud. Its clauses were clear: exterior spill above the horizontal was prohibited; blue-rich sources required shielding; care facilities could apply for safety exemptions, but no exemption had been requested.

When she finished, the mayor asked what she recommended.

Mara looked at Tolan. He looked tired now rather than clever. She looked at Nilo, who had arranged three dead moths on the table like evidence in a murder. Then she looked through the dome’s open shutter.

Clouds covered almost the entire sky.

“I recommend we turn everything off for five minutes,” she said.

Vessa laughed. “That isn’t a recommendation.”

“It’s a demonstration.”

Nilo cut the dome lights. Mara radioed Sella at Lightwell, and the remaining ceiling panels went dark. Through the shutter, the eastern stain weakened. At first there was nothing to see but clouds.

The council members shuffled. Somebody dropped a pen.

Then, with suspiciously perfect timing, the clouds opened in a long black seam. Stars appeared inside it, more than Mara could count. The meteor shower had not ended. Three sparks crossed the gap one after another.

Nobody spoke for several seconds.

Darkness was not emptiness. Mara felt it around the dome, full of distance, weather, wings, and things too old to care about ordinances.

“That,” she said, “is celestial continuity.”

The vote was unanimous.

# The Politics of the Bad Die: Why Advanced-Packaging Subsidies Should Buy Transparency, Not Just Capacity

When governments subsidize semiconductor plants, they usually count tangible things: clean-room area, wafers started per month, tools installed, and jobs announced. That accounting made some sense when a high-value processor was largely identified with the wafer on which it was fabricated. It is increasingly misleading in an era of chiplets, high-bandwidth memory, silicon interposers, fan-out redistribution layers, and hybrid bonding. A modern accelerator can depend on logic fabricated at one site, memory stacked at another, an interposer or bridge made at a third, and final assembly and test performed at a fourth. The economically meaningful product emerges not from any one wafer but from the package.

This shift creates a political problem disguised as an engineering detail: who bears the cost when one component in an expensive package fails? The answer is determined by access to yield data, test coverage, interface rules, and contractual power. Dominant firms can demand known-good die, reserve scarce packaging lines, and push failure costs onto suppliers. Smaller chip designers, public research laboratories, and domestic manufacturers often cannot. If a government merely pays for additional packaging capacity, it may strengthen the firms already best positioned to control these terms.

The Meridian Republic, a fictional mid-sized industrial democracy, is considering 18 billion merins in support for advanced chip packaging. Its debate offers a useful model for other jurisdictions. Meridian should not condition aid primarily on the number of packages shipped or the nominal capacity of subsidized plants. It should use public money to create a **transparent failure regime**: auditable package-level yield reporting, fair access to qualification lines, limited interface escrow, and shared rules for allocating the cost of defective die and assembly failures. The objective is not to make proprietary packaging technology public. It is to prevent public subsidies from underwriting a private system in which the most powerful buyer alone can see, price, and survive failure.

## Packaging is where separate risks become one risk

Advanced packaging is sometimes described as a less glamorous companion to leading-edge fabrication. That description ignores both the technical difficulty and the economic leverage involved. In a conventional package containing one mature die, assembly loss may be tolerable because the component entering the line is relatively inexpensive. In a 2.5D accelerator, the package may combine a large compute chiplet, several input-output tiles, multiple stacks of high-bandwidth memory, and a wide interconnect structure. The package can become worthless if a single indispensable element is defective or if bonding, alignment, substrate warpage, thermal cycling, or redistribution-layer defects interrupt the completed system.

The arithmetic is severe even before assembly defects are considered. Suppose a design requires eight memory stacks, each with a 99.2 percent probability of passing incoming inspection, plus four logic chiplets at 98.5 percent each. If those probabilities are independent, the chance that every required component is good is roughly 88 percent. Add a hypothetical 95 percent package-assembly yield, and only about 84 percent of attempted units emerge as functioning packages. These are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements from a production line, but they expose the compounding effect. Improving a single component is not enough; the package integrates multiple yield distributions and makes their interaction commercially decisive.

The independence assumption is also optimistic in some circumstances. Components from the same wafer lot may share defects. Marginal die may pass a probe test but fail after bonding or under the thermal conditions of a complete system. A substrate variation can affect several connections at once. Conversely, better test insertion and redundancy can reduce the apparent compounding. The important point is not one universal yield figure. It is that the party possessing package-level data can distinguish among die defects, assembly defects, test escapes, and design incompatibilities. That knowledge determines who pays for scrap and who learns quickly enough to improve.

Yield data therefore functions as a form of market power. A large integrated buyer can correlate wafer lots, assembly tools, bonding recipes, thermal maps, and field returns. It can threaten to redirect volume if a supplier refuses liability. A small chiplet firm may receive only a pass-or-fail result and an invoice for lost package starts. A university spinout may never obtain enough line time to establish statistically meaningful failure patterns. The asymmetry is not merely unfair in an abstract sense. It can prevent technically sound entrants from surviving the qualification period in which failures are common and their causes are disputed.

## Capacity subsidies can entrench the bottleneck

Meridian’s current proposal would award grants according to installed tools, forecast throughput, domestic payroll, and the share of output reserved for nationally important customers. These criteria are understandable. They are also too easy to satisfy without changing the structure of access.

A subsidized operator could install hybrid-bonding equipment, announce thousands of package starts, and reserve the best process windows for two anchor customers. Less powerful users might be directed to short engineering runs with higher setup charges and weaker failure analysis. The operator could count every attempted package toward its public capacity commitment even if a large fraction were scrapped for reasons never disclosed to the customer. The state would have purchased machines, but not a usable market.

This is especially consequential because packaging capacity is not interchangeable. A nominal line for fan-out processing cannot automatically handle a large interposer assembly. Bond pitch, die size, thermal budget, mold behavior, substrate availability, test hardware, and the maturity of a particular process flow all matter. Even two lines using similar equipment may not offer equivalent yields. Counting package starts as though they were barrels of a standardized commodity conceals these differences.

Nor should Meridian assume that domestic location guarantees broad domestic benefit. A local packaging plant could remain operationally dependent on imported substrates, overseas memory stacks, proprietary test software, and a single foreign anchor customer. It might employ technicians and engineers, which is valuable, while still giving local chip designers no practical path onto the line. National flags do not dissolve bargaining power.

The political temptation is to ignore these complications because ribbon cuttings reward visible construction. Yield governance is harder to photograph. Yet it is precisely the less visible layer that determines whether a subsidized facility becomes shared industrial infrastructure or a publicly discounted extension of one company’s supply chain.

## A public bargain centered on failure transparency

Meridian should attach four conditions to grants above 200 million merins. The conditions would apply only to activity supported by public funds, not to every package made by a recipient.

First, recipients should maintain an **auditable yield ledger**. For each subsidized process family, the ledger would record aggregate incoming-die rejection, assembly loss, rework, final-test loss, and field-return categories. Customers would receive results for their own lots at greater detail, including agreed failure classifications and uncertainty ranges. The public would see only aggregated bands, protecting sensitive product information. An independent technical office could inspect raw records under confidentiality rules.

The ledger would not require a firm to reveal a bonding recipe or the layout of a customer’s die. Its purpose would be to separate questions that are too often bundled together: Did the die arrive defective? Did the assembly process damage it? Did the interface specification omit a relevant tolerance? Is the failure cause genuinely unknown? A category for unresolved failures is essential; otherwise operators would be pressured to assign blame prematurely. Repeatedly high unresolved rates would trigger review rather than an automatic penalty.

Second, subsidized plants should devote a modest share of qualified line time—perhaps 12 percent after the first production year—to **open qualification windows**. Eligible users would include small domestic designers, public laboratories, and firms developing components that can interoperate with more than one system vendor. Access would not be free. It would be offered at published, cost-based rates, with standardized rules for minimum lot size, cancellation, and failure analysis. A lottery or rotating queue could allocate oversubscribed windows, while emergency national needs would require a publicly documented exception.

Third, grant recipients should place a narrowly defined set of **interface and test artefacts in escrow**. These might include electrical tolerance envelopes, mechanical keep-out rules, thermal boundary assumptions, test-vector formats, and reference coupons needed to verify that a chiplet can enter the supported process. Escrow would be released to a replacement operator if a subsidized line closed, refused its access obligation, or became unavailable during a declared supply emergency. The underlying die design, proprietary process recipe, and customer netlist would remain protected.

Fourth, contracts should establish a default **failure-cost ladder**. If incoming inspection identifies a defective die, the die supplier bears the direct loss. If assembly is shown to have caused damage, the packaging operator bears it. If both parties accepted an interface outside the qualified envelope, they share the loss according to a pre-agreed formula. Where the cause remains unknown after specified analysis, liability is divided rather than automatically imposed on the weaker party. Sophisticated parties could negotiate different terms with private money, but subsidized qualification runs would begin from this public default.

These rules would turn yield from an opaque verdict into a jointly examinable production result. They would also give Meridian a more meaningful definition of capacity. A line that starts many packages but produces low, unexplained yield would no longer look equivalent to a line that supports stable output and learning across several customers.

## Why transparency is not the same as compulsory openness

Opponents will argue that interface escrow and yield auditing amount to forced disclosure. That objection has force if the policy is drafted carelessly. Advanced packaging contains valuable intellectual property in bonding sequences, materials, test methods, thermal structures, and co-design practices. Requiring publication of all process details would deter investment and could make sensitive systems easier to imitate or disrupt.

But there is a difference between revealing how a process achieves its tolerances and stating what tolerances an entering component must meet. A railway operator can specify axle loads without surrendering the design of its signaling system. Likewise, a packaging operator can disclose an electrical and mechanical acceptance envelope without publishing every step that makes the process work. The boundary will sometimes be disputed, but the existence of borderline cases is not a reason to leave every term under unilateral control.

Meridian should therefore create three disclosure tiers. Customer-specific lot data would be available to the customer and auditor. Process-family performance bands would be available to qualified potential users under nondisclosure terms. Only broad metrics—such as the proportion of subsidized line time used, median qualification delay, and unresolved-failure rate—would be public. Criminal penalties for intentional theft would remain, while ordinary classification disagreements would go to a specialist tribunal rather than becoming accusations of espionage.

Security requires further qualification. Packages used in defense, critical communications, or identity systems may need compartmented records and restricted access. Yet a blanket security exemption would swallow the policy. Meridian should exempt a product only when a designated authority identifies a specific risk, and the exemption should expire unless renewed. Even restricted lines should report aggregate utilization and yield to cleared auditors.

## The distributional stakes extend beyond chip companies

A failure-centered subsidy policy may sound remote from ordinary political concerns. It is not. Public spending on chip infrastructure competes with housing, transport, education, and climate adaptation. If Meridian directs 18 billion merins to packaging plants, citizens are entitled to more than assurances that the industry is strategically important. They should know whether the investment creates durable capabilities or merely lowers costs for firms that would retain the most valuable knowledge elsewhere.

The design of access rules also affects which regions can participate. Leading-edge wafer fabrication tends to concentrate around enormous capital pools and established supplier clusters. Packaging offers a somewhat broader range of entry points: substrate inspection, thermal characterization, reliability testing, failure analysis, equipment maintenance, and lower-volume integration. These activities still demand substantial skill and capital, but they do not all require a leading-edge wafer fab. Open qualification windows could connect technical institutes in Meridian’s inland manufacturing cities to nationally funded lines on the coast.

That promise should not be exaggerated. A reserved window cannot compensate for a weak design, a missing substrate supplier, or an underfunded laboratory. Small firms may struggle to prepare documentation or purchase enough known-good die. Meridian should pair access with shared test-vehicle programs and training grants, but it should avoid calling every workshop an innovation hub. The measure of inclusion is whether new users complete qualification and reach repeat production, not how many applicants attend an orientation session.

Workers also bear package-level risk. When a line misses yield targets, managers may respond with unstable shifts, extensive overtime, or pressure to bypass process controls. Subsidy contracts should require recipients to report scheduled and actual working hours by job category, protect technicians who stop a run over documented contamination or safety concerns, and fund portable credentials in metrology, bonding, and failure analysis. These provisions are not substitutes for collective bargaining, but they reduce the chance that commercial uncertainty will be transferred downward as arbitrary scheduling and blame.

Municipalities face a parallel risk. Advanced packaging generally uses less water than a major wafer fab, but clean operations, cooling, plating, and waste treatment still impose infrastructure demands. Meridian should require site-specific utility plans and public disclosure of normal and drought-stage consumption bands. A city should not be pressured into subsidizing water and power upgrades based on headline capacity that the operator may never use. If actual demand exceeds the contracted band, the operator—not residential ratepayers—should finance the additional infrastructure unless the city approves a new bargain.

These labor and municipal conditions may seem appended to the central yield argument. In fact, they reflect the same principle: uncertainty should not be hidden and assigned to the party with the least information. A technician, a small chip designer, and a host city occupy very different positions, but each can be asked to absorb risks that a subsidized operator is better able to measure.

## A stylized comparison of subsidy choices

Consider two hypothetical bids for 3 billion merins. North Quay Integration proposes a high-volume line expected to attempt 600,000 complex packages annually, with 90 percent final yield once mature. It reserves nearly all output for two anchor customers and reports only shipments. Common Assembly Works proposes 420,000 attempts at an expected 87 percent yield. It offers detailed failure reporting, open qualification windows, and process support for six package configurations.

On a simple shipment count, North Quay appears superior: 540,000 good packages versus roughly 365,000. If national policy values only near-term output, it should win. But suppose one anchor customer leaves in year four and the line’s tooling and test flow are difficult for others to adopt. Common Assembly’s lower initial output may support a wider supplier base and make capacity easier to repurpose.

Meridian should not automatically select the more open bid. It should score three distinct values: reliable output, adaptability, and access. A possible grant formula could assign 50 percent to expected good packages adjusted for technical risk, 25 percent to demonstrated changeover and qualification capability, and 25 percent to access and reporting commitments. The exact weights are political choices, not engineering facts. They should be published before bids arrive so officials cannot invent criteria to favor a preferred applicant.

This framework still relies on forecasts supplied by bidders. Auditors cannot fully verify a process that has not yet been built, and firms may manipulate category definitions after production begins. Meridian could withhold 20 percent of each grant until three years of operating data are available, but delayed payment raises financing costs and may advantage larger firms. There is no mechanism that eliminates strategic behavior. The goal is a contract in which exaggeration is more detectable and less profitable than under a raw capacity target.

## The strongest objections

The first serious objection is speed. Packaging technologies and demand can change faster than a public rulebook. A detailed access mandate might lock subsidized operators into interfaces that become obsolete, while approval procedures delay urgent equipment purchases. Meridian should answer by defining obligations around process families and measurable outcomes rather than named architectures. A recipient could replace one bonding method with another if it continued to provide the contracted level of qualification access and documented how existing users would migrate.

The second objection is that open windows could damage the economics of a line. High-volume packaging benefits from stable recipes, repeated products, and predictable materials. Frequent changeovers introduce contamination risks and consume engineering time. That is why a limited 12 percent allocation is preferable to a general common-carrier requirement. Rates should include genuine setup and engineering costs. The obligation is to offer a path, not to pretend that low-volume experimental work costs the same as a mature production run.

The third objection is geopolitical. Foreign suppliers might refuse to provide detailed die data to a Meridian-audited facility, and other governments could retaliate against access preferences for domestic firms. This risk is real. Meridian should permit firms from partner jurisdictions to use open windows on reciprocal terms and should develop common failure categories with those partners. Still, reciprocity may prove slow, and the proposed policy cannot guarantee access to high-bandwidth memory or advanced substrates controlled abroad. Transparent packaging governance is a resilience measure, not self-sufficiency.

The fourth objection concerns public competence. A subsidy office may lack engineers capable of evaluating hybrid-bonding yield or distinguishing a legitimate trade secret from an interface requirement. Meridian would need a professionally paid Packaging Accountability Bureau with rotating technical panels and strict conflict rules. Recruiting experts from industry risks regulatory capture; excluding them risks ignorance. Fixed-term appointments, disclosure of recent financial ties, and review by mixed panels would reduce but not resolve the tension.

Finally, dominant customers may simply decline the subsidy and build closed lines elsewhere. That outcome should not automatically be considered a policy failure. Public money is not owed to every strategically important company. However, if Meridian’s conditions are so costly that no credible operator applies, officials should revise them rather than celebrate purity while the country remains dependent. A five-year review should compare actual good-package output, customer diversity, qualification time, and fiscal cost against unsubsidized alternatives.

## What the public should purchase

Advanced packaging turns many separate components into one system, but it also turns separate commercial risks into a contest over blame. The firm that controls package-level information can decide whether a failed unit represents bad memory, weak bonding, an unrealistic interface, or an unexplained loss charged to someone else. Governments that subsidize equipment without addressing that power are not neutral. They finance the existing allocation of uncertainty.

Meridian should purchase more than nominal throughput. It should purchase the capacity to learn across firms, to qualify new entrants, to move production when a supplier fails, and to identify where publicly supported value is being lost. Auditable yield ledgers, limited open windows, interface escrow, and default failure-cost rules would not make packaging simple or fully competitive. They would make the consequences of failure more visible and negotiable.

The larger democratic principle is modest: when the public absorbs industrial risk, the public may demand institutions that prevent risk from being passed invisibly to weaker participants. In advanced packaging, that demand must reach below the factory roof and into test categories, interface envelopes, and qualification queues. The future of chip policy will not be decided only by who can fabricate the smallest transistor. It will also be decided by who owns the bad die—and who is allowed to know why it failed.

Only broad metrics—such as the proportion of subsidized line time used, median qualification delay, and unresolved-failure rate—would be public. Criminal penalties for intentional theft would remain, while ordinary classification disagreements would go to a specialist tribunal rather than becoming accusations of espionage.

Security requires further qualification. Packages used in defense, critical communications, or identity systems may need compartmented records and restricted access. Yet a blanket security exemption would swallow the policy. Meridian should exempt a product only when a designated authority identifies a specific risk, and the exemption should expire unless renewed. Even restricted lines should report aggregate utilization and yield to cleared auditors.

## The distributional stakes extend beyond chip companies

A failure-centered subsidy policy may sound remote from ordinary political concerns. It is not. Public spending on chip infrastructure competes with housing, transport, education, and climate adaptation. If Meridian directs 18 billion merins to packaging plants, citizens are entitled to more than assurances that the industry is strategically important. They should know whether the investment creates durable capabilities or merely lowers costs for firms that would retain the most valuable knowledge elsewhere.

The design of access rules also affects which regions can participate. Leading-edge wafer fabrication tends to concentrate around enormous capital pools and established supplier clusters. Packaging offers a somewhat broader range of entry points: substrate inspection, thermal characterization, reliability testing, failure analysis, equipment maintenance, and lower-volume integration. These activities still demand substantial skill and capital, but they do not all require a leading-edge wafer fab. Open qualification windows could connect technical institutes in Meridian’s inland manufacturing cities to nationally funded lines on the coast.

That promise should not be exaggerated. A reserved window cannot compensate for a weak design, a missing substrate supplier, or an underfunded laboratory. Small firms may struggle to prepare documentation or purchase enough known-good die. Meridian should pair access with shared test-vehicle programs and training grants, but it should avoid calling every workshop an innovation hub. The measure of inclusion is whether new users complete qualification and reach repeat production, not how many applicants attend an orientation session.

Workers also bear package-level risk. When a line misses yield targets, managers may respond with unstable shifts, extensive overtime, or pressure to bypass process controls. Subsidy contracts should require recipients to report scheduled and actual working hours by job category, protect technicians who stop a run over documented contamination or safety concerns, and fund portable credentials in metrology, bonding, and failure analysis. These provisions are not substitutes for collective bargaining, but they reduce the chance that commercial uncertainty will be transferred downward as arbitrary scheduling and blame.

Municipalities face a parallel risk. Advanced packaging generally uses less water than a major wafer fab, but clean operations, cooling, plating, and waste treatment still impose infrastructure demands. Meridian should require site-specific utility plans and public disclosure of normal and drought-stage consumption bands. A city should not be pressured into subsidizing water and power upgrades based on headline capacity that the operator may never use. If actual demand exceeds the contracted band, the operator—not residential ratepayers—should finance the additional infrastructure unless the city approves a new bargain.

These labor and municipal conditions may seem appended to the central yield argument. In fact, they reflect the same principle: uncertainty should not be hidden and assigned to the party with the least information. A technician, a small chip designer, and a host city occupy very different positions, but each can be asked to absorb risks that a subsidized operator is better able to measure.

## A stylized comparison of subsidy choices

Consider two hypothetical bids for 3 billion merins. North Quay Integration proposes a high-volume line expected to attempt 600,000 complex packages annually, with 90 percent final yield once mature. It reserves nearly all output for two anchor customers and reports only shipments. Common Assembly Works proposes 420,000 attempts at an expected 87 percent yield. It offers detailed failure reporting, open qualification windows, and process support for six package configurations.

On a simple shipment count, North Quay appears superior: 540,000 good packages versus roughly 365,000. If national policy values only near-term output, it should win. But suppose one anchor customer leaves in year four and the line’s tooling and test flow are difficult for others to adopt. Common Assembly’s lower initial output may support a wider supplier base and make capacity easier to repurpose.

Meridian should not automatically select the more open bid. It should score three distinct values: reliable output, adaptability, and access. A possible grant formula could assign 50 percent to expected good packages adjusted for technical risk, 25 percent to demonstrated changeover and qualification capability, and 25 percent to access and reporting commitments. The exact weights are political choices, not engineering facts. They should be published before bids arrive so officials cannot invent criteria to favor a preferred applicant.

This framework still relies on forecasts supplied by bidders. Auditors cannot fully verify a process that has not yet been built, and firms may manipulate category definitions after production begins. Meridian could withhold 20 percent of each grant until three years of operating data are available, but delayed payment raises financing costs and may advantage larger firms. There is no mechanism that eliminates strategic behavior. The goal is a contract in which exaggeration is more detectable and less profitable than under a raw capacity target.

## The strongest objections

The first serious objection is speed. Packaging technologies and demand can change faster than a public rulebook. A detailed access mandate might lock subsidized operators into interfaces that become obsolete, while approval procedures delay urgent equipment purchases. Meridian should answer by defining obligations around process families and measurable outcomes rather than named architectures. A recipient could replace one bonding method with another if it continued to provide the contracted level of qualification access and documented how existing users would migrate.

The second objection is that open windows could damage the economics of a line. High-volume packaging benefits from stable recipes, repeated products, and predictable materials. Frequent changeovers introduce contamination risks and consume engineering time. That is why a limited 12 percent allocation is preferable to a general common-carrier requirement. Rates should include genuine setup and engineering costs. The obligation is to offer a path, not to pretend that low-volume experimental work costs the same as a mature production run.

The third objection is geopolitical. Foreign suppliers might refuse to provide detailed die data to a Meridian-audited facility, and other governments could retaliate against access preferences for domestic firms. This risk is real. Meridian should permit firms from partner jurisdictions to use open windows on reciprocal terms and should develop common failure categories with those partners. Still, reciprocity may prove slow, and the proposed policy cannot guarantee access to high-bandwidth memory or advanced substrates controlled abroad. Transparent packaging governance is a resilience measure, not self-sufficiency.

The fourth objection concerns public competence. A subsidy office may lack engineers capable of evaluating hybrid-bonding yield or distinguishing a legitimate trade secret from an interface requirement. Meridian would need a professionally paid Packaging Accountability Bureau with rotating technical panels and strict conflict rules. Recruiting experts from industry risks regulatory capture; excluding them risks ignorance. Fixed-term appointments, disclosure of recent financial ties, and review by mixed panels would reduce but not resolve the tension.

Finally, dominant customers may simply decline the subsidy and build closed lines elsewhere. That outcome should not automatically be considered a policy failure. Public money is not owed to every strategically important company. However, if Meridian’s conditions are so costly that no credible operator applies, officials should revise them rather than celebrate purity while the country remains dependent. A five-year review should compare actual good-package output, customer diversity, qualification time, and fiscal cost against unsubsidized alternatives.

## What the public should purchase

Advanced packaging turns many separate components into one system, but it also turns separate commercial risks into a contest over blame. The firm that controls package-level information can decide whether a failed unit represents bad memory, weak bonding, an unrealistic interface, or an unexplained loss charged to someone else. Governments that subsidize equipment without addressing that power are not neutral. They finance the existing allocation of uncertainty.

Meridian should purchase more than nominal throughput. It should purchase the capacity to learn across firms, to qualify new entrants, to move production when a supplier fails, and to identify where publicly supported value is being lost. Auditable yield ledgers, limited open windows, interface escrow, and default failure-cost rules would not make packaging simple or fully competitive. They would make the consequences of failure more visible and negotiable.

The larger democratic principle is modest: when the public absorbs industrial risk, the public may demand institutions that prevent risk from being passed invisibly to weaker participants. In advanced packaging, that demand must reach below the factory roof and into test categories, interface envelopes, and qualification queues. The future of chip policy will not be decided only by who can fabricate the smallest transistor. It will also be decided by who owns the bad die—and who is allowed to know why it failed.
