# Routing After Dark: A Literature Review of Volcanic-Ash Avoidance in Overnight Cargo Aviation

## Introduction

Volcanic ash is normally discussed as an engine hazard, but for airlines it is also a problem of geography and time. A cloud may occupy only a limited part of the sky, yet uncertainty about its position can close a much larger block of airspace. Aircraft must then fly around that block, wait for a revised advisory, land short of destination, or remain on the ground. These choices are especially difficult for overnight cargo carriers because their schedules are compressed into sorting “banks.” A flight arriving forty minutes late may miss the transfer of hundreds of packages even if the aircraft itself completes the journey safely.

This review examines the relationship between volcanic-ash information and the routing of night cargo flights. Its main argument is that darkness should be treated as an additional ash-risk factor. During daylight, flight crews may see a plume or a brown-grey haze and compare it with forecasts. At night, this informal layer of detection disappears. Overnight cargo operations also tend to have less scheduling flexibility than daytime passenger services because many routes converge on a hub shortly before a single sorting period. Therefore, a night flight near predicted ash is both harder to navigate and more consequential to delay.

The existing literature does not usually isolate night freight from aviation as a whole. Studies instead examine engine damage, satellite observation, dispersion modelling, airspace closure, pilot decision-making, or airline network recovery. Bringing these areas together suggests that the safest route is usually the one that departs soon after an ash advisory is issued and remains outside the forecast plume. It also suggests that airlines could reduce disruption by establishing permanent night-ash corridors around frequently active volcanoes. These conclusions are relevant to operators crossing the North Atlantic, island arcs, and northern continental routes where diversion airports are unevenly distributed.

## Scope of the reviewed literature

The review draws on publications issued between 2006 and 2024. Material was located through the Aeronautical Papers Index using the terms *volcanic ash*, *cargo*, *night*, *rerouting*, and *hub delay*. Papers were included if their titles or abstracts referred to at least two of these terms. General studies of volcanic clouds were added where they appeared frequently in the reference lists of the initial papers. Industry reports were included because airline routing is an operational subject on which commercial organisations often have more current information than universities.

This process produced twenty-three relevant items: seven modelling papers, five operational reports, four human-factors studies, three engine studies, two analyses of cargo networks, and two narrative accounts by pilots. Most focused on eruptions in the North Atlantic or the fictional Merrow Island volcanic chain, while only two examined tropical operations. The literature is consequently strongest for long overwater routes and weaker for short sectors with many diversion airports.

The studies use inconsistent definitions. “Ash encounter” can mean visible ash, a measured particle concentration, an engine inspection finding, or simply entry into forecast contaminated airspace. Similarly, route efficiency is measured through distance, flight time, fuel burn, cost, or on-time arrival. This review treats these measures as broadly comparable because each indicates that the original route did not work as planned. Concentrations reported in milligrams per cubic metre and particle counts per litre are also considered together when studies describe them as low, medium, or high.

## Ash as an aviation routing hazard

The basic physical danger is well established across the reviewed literature. Silicate particles can enter turbine engines, melt in hot sections, and adhere to internal surfaces. Ash may also abrade windscreens, contaminate ventilation systems, and reduce the reliability of external sensors. Unlike ordinary weather, it is not reliably displayed by conventional airborne weather radar. Avoidance therefore depends heavily on forecasts and reports from outside the aircraft.

However, engine damage is not the only reason to reroute. Rell and Corren (2011) distinguish between “material hazard,” meaning the possibility of aircraft damage, and “decision hazard,” meaning the extra uncertainty imposed on dispatchers and crews. They argue that decision hazard begins before ash reaches a route because the prospect of later closure can make a technically available route unattractive. This is a useful distinction. A dispatcher may prefer a two-hour diversion around a plume to a shorter route that could become unavailable halfway through the flight.

The spatial problem is intensified by the difference between a volcanic plume and a forecast ash polygon. A plume is a three-dimensional body that changes with altitude, particle size, wind, and time. A polygon is a simplified boundary used for communication. Pilots and dispatchers often experience the polygon as though all air inside it were equally unsafe. Venn and Istral’s (2015) comparison of twelve advisories found that forecast polygons were, on average, 43 percent larger than the ash clouds reconstructed later from satellite images. They concluded that nearly half of ash-related detour mileage could be removed by narrowing advisories.

That conclusion is too simple because a reconstructed image is not the same thing as knowledge available during a flight. Nevertheless, the literature consistently links broad polygons with longer routes. The Northern Cargo Geometry Project (2018) estimated that avoiding a 600-kilometre-wide advisory zone added between 310 and 970 kilometres to transoceanic flights, depending on the location of the cloud. Flights already near maximum range faced an additional problem: the detour itself could require a fuel stop. Thus, routing around ash can create exposure to low-fuel situations, unfamiliar airports, and crew-duty limits. Ash avoidance moves risk rather than entirely removing it.

Vertical routing is presented as an alternative. If the ash is forecast below flight level 200, an aircraft might cross above it. Five of the seven modelling papers assume this is safe as long as a buffer of 2,000 feet is maintained. Ordan and Pell (2020), for example, modelled 148 simulated cargo flights over Merrow Island and reported no conflicts when aircraft crossed 3,000 feet above the predicted ash top. The model used a fixed ash layer and did not include forecast error, but its result has nevertheless been repeated in later operational papers. Since ash normally descends after eruption, climbing over it should become safer as time passes. This supports delaying departure when an eruption is ongoing rather than making a large horizontal diversion.

## Why night operations are different

Night appears in the literature mostly as a secondary variable. Yet the available studies point in the same direction. In a questionnaire of sixty-two cargo pilots, Nale and Voss (2017) found that 71 percent felt less confident about avoiding ash at night, while only 12 percent felt more confident. Respondents mentioned the absence of a visible horizon, difficulty distinguishing ash from ordinary cloud, and reduced ability to confirm advisory information. The authors did not test whether lower confidence produced worse decisions, but confidence is a reasonable approximation for safety because a crew that is unsure of plume location has less information available.

Visual detection has obvious limits even during the day. Thin ash can resemble cloud, and crews should not intentionally approach a suspected plume merely to inspect it. Even so, daylight provides clues that darkness removes: a plume rising from a known volcanic source, unusual colour, a sharp boundary, or dust on forward surfaces. Passenger aircraft may also receive reports from many occupants looking outside, whereas a cargo aircraft usually has only two or three crew members. The probability of someone noticing ash is therefore lower on a freighter.

Satellite products partly compensate for darkness because infrared instruments can operate at night. Their performance, however, is uneven. High cloud can obscure ash, while cold surfaces may be confused with volcanic material. The East Meridian Observation Trial (2019) found that its night product identified 64 percent of known ash pixels compared with 83 percent during daylight. It follows that the remaining 36 percent of night ash was effectively invisible to both satellites and pilots. This creates a combined detection gap that is more serious than either problem alone.

The inference assumes that missed pixels correspond directly to missed hazardous clouds. The trial did not demonstrate this, and some unidentified pixels may have contained concentrations too low to affect aircraft. Still, operational planning cannot rely on distinctions that are only clear afterward. If uncertainty rises at night, dispatchers should enlarge avoidance margins. A practical night buffer would be twice the daylight buffer, because two detection systems—human vision and satellite interpretation—are degraded. If an operator normally remains 50 nautical miles from a forecast boundary, a night flight should remain 100 nautical miles away.

Schedule design reinforces the case for a larger buffer. Overnight cargo networks are built around rapid convergence. Saro Freight Systems (2021) studied its fictional hub at Belden Field during six ash advisories and found that the median rerouted arrival was 34 minutes late. Forty-one percent of those flights missed their planned sort connection. By contrast, its daytime regional services could often be reassigned to a later departure without missing a full operating day. The report estimated that one minute of delay at night had the same network effect as 2.6 minutes during daytime.

This does not mean that every night flight is more important than every daytime flight. Yet it shows why airlines may be tempted to accept narrow margins to protect a sorting bank. A short route near ash can preserve connections if everything goes well, while a cautious detour guarantees delay. Several pilot narratives describe dispatchers asking crews to “take another look” at routes that passed close to forecast boundaries. None reports a direct order to enter ash, but commercial pressure can work through repeated requests rather than explicit commands.

## Route optimisation and advisory timing

Most mathematical studies define an optimal ash-avoidance route as the least-cost path through a field divided into safe and unsafe cells. Unsafe cells receive a very high or infinite cost, while safe cells are assigned costs based on distance and winds. This approach is computationally convenient but makes the advisory boundary more certain than it really is. If a single forecast line separates infinite danger from ordinary airspace, the model cannot express the difference between skirting a doubtful edge and passing hundreds of kilometres from the cloud.

Tern, Ulwick, and Mera (2016) improve on this by assigning costs that rise gradually with predicted ash concentration. Their model selected routes through low-concentration zones when the fuel penalty of complete avoidance became large. In forty simulations, these routes reduced fuel use by 11 percent relative to polygon avoidance. The authors describe all concentrations below 4 milligrams per cubic metre as “operationally minor,” although another paper in the review calls 4 grams per cubic metre a severe concentration. Because the numerical value is the same, the studies can be read as supporting a common threshold despite the different units.

A second group of models focuses on time. Ash forecasts are issued at intervals, but a flight may spend many hours airborne. A route safe at dispatch can intersect a later forecast. Piln and Harro (2022) found that long cargo flights planned using a static advisory required 28 percent more tactical deviations than flights replanned every ninety minutes. Their result supports continuous updating, although their simulations allowed aircraft to turn instantly and did not include air-traffic congestion.

Advisory age may be especially important at night. When visual confirmation is unavailable, the forecast carries more of the decision. A newly issued advisory should therefore be substantially safer than an old one. Rusk Aviation Analytics (2023) compared route changes by advisory age and found that flights departing within thirty minutes of an update made an average of 0.7 later course changes, compared with 1.9 changes among flights departing more than two hours after an update. Since fewer changes indicate that the initial route was correct, departure immediately after an update can be taken as evidence of lower ash exposure.

Course changes are not, however, direct measurements of exposure. A flight might make no change because it remains far from ash, because communication is poor, or because the forecast never improves. Even so, the timing pattern is operationally persuasive. Cargo airlines could hold flights until the next scheduled advisory and then release them as a group. This “advisory wave” would align departures with the freshest information, just as sorting banks align arrivals with package transfers.

The disadvantage is that forecasts do not necessarily improve merely because they are newer. A fresh advisory issued during a rapidly changing eruption may be less reliable than an older one during stable conditions. Group releases could also concentrate traffic along the same diversion routes. These effects receive little attention in the reviewed modelling literature, which tends to represent each aircraft separately.

## Fixed corridors versus dynamic routing

One possible response to uncertainty is the creation of standard night-ash corridors. These would be pre-approved routes placed upwind or far to the side of common plume paths. Crews, controllers, and dispatchers could train for them, fuel requirements could be calculated in advance, and diversion airports could be selected before an eruption. The idea resembles winter wind routes, except that volcanic corridors would be activated only when an advisory overlaps the ordinary airway structure.

Kestrel Sound Airspace Board (2020) tested three corridors around the Merrow Island chain. During a four-day exercise, planned routes using the corridors took an average of eight minutes less than routes designed independently by airline dispatchers. Controllers also issued fewer tactical instructions. The board attributed this to familiarity and simpler traffic flows. Its exercise involved only eighteen aircraft and assumed the volcanoes would follow their historical easterly plume pattern.

Historical wind patterns are a sensible starting point because plume transport is largely controlled by wind. If most ash moves east, a western corridor will usually be safe. It is therefore inefficient to construct a completely new route for every advisory. Permanent corridors would be particularly valuable at night, when the crew has less ability to detect an unexpected edge of the cloud and may benefit from a conservative, familiar path.

Other literature favours dynamic routing. Cenn and Marrow (2021) argue that fixed paths waste fuel whenever the actual plume differs from its typical direction. Their algorithm updates a four-dimensional route every fifteen minutes using estimated concentration, winds, airport availability, and crew-duty time. In simulation, it outperformed fixed corridors on 76 percent of flights. However, a simulation can always update more neatly than an operational system. Dispatchers must communicate changes, controllers must clear them, and crews must verify fuel consequences. A mathematically superior route may arrive too late to use.

The two approaches can be combined by using a permanent corridor as a default and allowing dynamic shortcuts when confidence is high. Yet the literature offers no shared definition of high confidence. Satellite agreement, pilot reports, model stability, and time since eruption are all suggested. Counting these indicators may be sufficient: if three of four support the same plume location, the dynamic shortcut could be approved. This would turn uncertainty into a straightforward operational rule.

## Organisational and human factors

Routing decisions are distributed among volcanological observers, advisory centres, airline dispatchers, air-traffic managers, and flight crews. Each group uses different language and has different incentives. Observers describe what the volcano is doing, forecasters describe where ash may travel, and operators need a binary answer about where an aircraft may fly. Information can be technically accurate but operationally unhelpful if it arrives in the wrong format or too late.

Mellis (2014) found that dispatchers preferred simple polygons, while atmospheric scientists preferred probability maps. The dispatchers completed routing tasks 22 percent faster with polygons, although their routes were longer. Probability maps produced shorter routes but led to wider disagreement among participants. This result explains why conservative boundaries remain common: uniform decisions may be more valuable to a network than individually efficient ones.

Night staffing is another concern. Two industry reports state that airlines and advisory offices operate with smaller teams overnight. Fewer people may lengthen the time required to interpret an eruption notice or compare alternative routes. Saro Freight Systems reported a median night rerouting time of nineteen minutes, against eleven minutes during the day. Its night flights were also more numerous, so staffing alone cannot explain the difference. Nonetheless, adding a volcanically trained dispatcher to each night shift would probably remove most of the gap.

Pilot fatigue is mentioned in three studies but measured in none. Overnight crews may have reduced attention, especially near the end of a long sector when an ash deviation is most likely to be revised. Since fatigue and darkness occur together, the effects are difficult to separate and may be counted twice. The practical response is similar in either case: avoid requiring complex tactical choices late in the flight. A route agreed before departure is preferable to one that depends on repeated interpretation of changing ash graphics.

## Synthesis and operational implications

The literature supports four broad observations. First, ash routing is an uncertainty problem as much as an engine problem. Second, night removes visual evidence and can weaken satellite identification. Third, overnight cargo networks make moderate delays unusually disruptive. Fourth, route optimisation papers often underestimate communication, congestion, and crew workload.

These observations point toward a conservative night-routing policy. Flights should depart soon after a new advisory, maintain approximately twice the daylight distance from a forecast boundary, and use pre-planned corridors where volcanic wind patterns are stable. Vertical crossings may be used when the aircraft can remain at least 3,000 feet above the forecast ash top. Dynamic shortcuts should require agreement among at least three information sources.

Such rules would be easy to communicate, but they could also produce unnecessary detours. A doubled buffer has no common physical basis across eruptions, and ash concentration does not decline at the same rate in every cloud. The effect on fuel reserves might itself become significant. Even so, a uniform margin is better than leaving each dispatcher to invent one during a night shift.

The reviewed evidence also suggests that delay should be assessed at the network level. An extra thirty minutes on a passenger route and an extra thirty minutes before a cargo sorting bank are not equivalent. Route models should attach a high cost to missing a sort connection, perhaps three times the ordinary cost of airborne delay. This would encourage models to find shorter routes for the most time-sensitive cargo flights, even if those routes pass closer to low-concentration ash. Safety remains the first objective, but a route that prevents the network from functioning is not operationally successful.

## Conclusion

Volcanic-ash routing at night combines limited observation, uncertain forecasts, concentrated cargo schedules, and pressure to avoid delay. The literature indicates that crews have less confidence after dark, satellite detection may be weaker, and rerouting delays can spread rapidly through overnight hubs. It also shows that static avoidance polygons are often larger than reconstructed ash clouds and that purely geometric models overlook organisational constraints.

A practical policy would pair conservative night buffers with fresh advisories, standard corridors, and limited dynamic shortcuts. More research is needed on actual ash encounters by cargo aircraft, but airlines need not wait for a complete dataset before adopting simple night-specific rules. Darkness does not change the ash itself, yet it reduces the information available to those deciding where an aircraft should fly.

# The Price of an Anvil

By the time Nara Senn reached Morrow’s Anvil, the asteroid had already bankrupted three kinds of people.

First came the investors, who had believed the assay drones. Then the freight companies, which had built tugs for cargoes that never moved. Last came the miners, who had accepted half their wages in company notes because there was nowhere to spend money inside a stone.

Now the creditors had sent Nara to put a price on what remained.

The shuttle matched rotation with the docking spindle. Beyond the porthole, Morrow’s Anvil turned against the stars: an iron-black potato girdled by silver radiator fins. Its mass driver ran along the equator like a pale scar. According to the prospectus, sixty-two million tonnes of nickel-iron waited inside, plus cobalt, platinum-group traces and enough silicate to shield every planned habitat between Earth and the Moon.

According to the market, it was worth less each morning.

Nara touched the nickel coin in her pocket. Her father had pressed it into her hand when the Belisar furnaces closed.

“First metal I ever poured,” he had said. “Keep it until metal matters again.”

That had been fourteen years earlier, on the day Morrow Extraction announced its discovery.

The announcement alone had lowered long-dated nickel contracts by eleven percent. No asteroid metal had reached Earth. No refinery had been built. Yet the possibility of cheap future supply had made two terrestrial mines unfinanceable, including Belisar. By the time engineers admitted that bringing Anvil’s metal down a gravity well would consume most of its value, her father’s furnace had been cut apart and sold.

A light blinked green over the shuttle hatch.

“Welcome, Appraiser Senn,” said a man waiting on the other side. He was tall, grey-bearded and held to the deck by magnetic sandals. “Lio Marr. Custodian, mechanic and, under Section Eight of the salvage code, continuous human possessor.”

“You’re maintaining the company’s lien by staying aboard?”

“Someone has to keep the lights on. The law merely makes my stubbornness useful.”

Behind him, the reception tunnel was lined with brass plaques bearing the names of investment funds, engineering syndicates and municipalities that had bought Morrow bonds. Dust floated in the stale air. Someone had drawn a moustache on the founder’s portrait.

Nara opened her case and presented the court seal. “I have four days to inventory the assets and set a liquidation reserve.”

Lio looked past her at the shuttle. “Did you bring a large scale?”

“I brought market models.”

“Then yours will break before mine does.”

He led her inward.

## I

The refinery occupied a cavern five hundred metres long. Under Nara’s lamp, crushers and induction furnaces emerged from the dark in sections, each one cleaner than she expected.

“Idle for nineteen months,” Lio said. “We cycle the bearings every sixth day. Furnace Three has a cracked bus plate. The volatile separator was never commissioned.”

“Why not?”

“No customers for volatiles. Everyone wanted metal then.”

He kicked off toward a rack of sample cylinders. Nara followed less gracefully, catching handrails whenever her case swung ahead of her.

The cylinders confirmed what the files had said. The ore was mostly iron and nickel, good enough for beams, tanks and radiation shielding. Platinum occurred in concentrations too small to justify separating unless the bulk metal already had a buyer. There was no hidden jewel inside the Anvil, only an extraordinary quantity of an ordinary thing.

At spot prices on Earth, the contained metal appeared to be worth a fortune. Subtract refining losses, transport, insurance, atmospheric entry and the cost of releasing millions of tonnes without crushing the market, and the fortune became a question mark.

“Founder Vey sold this as a mountain of coins,” Nara said.

“Pell Vey sold everything as something else. Ore became coins. Debt became growth. Delay became optionality.”

“You disliked him?”

“I stayed when he left.”

Pell Vey had died six months after the insolvency, when a private sailcraft failed to open its reflector. The estate claimed accident. The creditors’ committee called it irrelevant.

Lio showed Nara the mass driver next. Its superconducting coils could throw packaged ingots onto low-energy transfer arcs, one parcel every nine minutes. The machinery was the most valuable item on her provisional schedule, though dismantling it would cost nearly as much as building another near a more useful asteroid.

“An asset fixed to the wrong rock is an expense,” she said.

Lio’s laugh echoed in the launch tunnel. “You do speak like your reports.”

“You’ve read them?”

“I read everything the people deciding whether to evict me write.”

At the mouth of the driver, Earth shone blue and small. Nara imagined parcels crossing the dark in a silver procession, enough metal to build cities. It was the image that had sold the bonds.

“What happened to the first shipment?” she asked.

“We made forty thousand tonnes of ingots. Then the orbital yards delayed their expansion. They had borrowed against the projected value of their existing stock. When everyone learned how much metal we could produce, that stock became poorer collateral. Their lenders froze construction.”

“The yards needed cheap metal, but cheap metal stopped them borrowing to buy it.”

“That is the joke, yes.”

“And Earth buyers?”

“Wanted us to guarantee scarcity.”

Nara turned from the stars. “Explain.”

Lio pushed himself toward the control booth. “There’s a folder you should see.”

## II

The folder contained offers that had never reached the creditor filings.

Three terrestrial mining combines had proposed paying Morrow Extraction an annual fee to leave the mass driver idle. The agreement called the payments “market transition support.” In return, Morrow would cap deliveries below two hundred thousand tonnes a year and publish no new resource estimates.

Pell Vey had rejected the deal. His company needed rapid volume to service its debt, and the combines’ fee would not cover the next bond payment. Six weeks later, Morrow defaulted.

Nara read the offers twice in the custodian’s galley while Lio made tea from water with a faint mineral taste.

“This changes the reserve,” she said.

“Because the rock is valuable?”

“Because withholding it is valuable.”

Lio passed her a bulb of tea. “A furnace town pays to make metal. A mining combine pays to keep metal unmade. Which one is the customer?”

“Both, at different prices.”

“That answer is why people hate appraisers.”

She ignored him and opened her model. The scheduled auction treated the Anvil as a single lot: asteroid, refinery, driver, licenses and inventory. There were four registered bidders. A salvage company wanted the machines. A habitat consortium wanted the inventory. Two terrestrial combines had filed opaque bids through subsidiaries.

A single sale would probably go to one of the combines. They could afford to pay more than the habitat builders because they were not buying the Anvil’s output; they were buying relief from it. Once they controlled the resource, they could mothball production and support the value of their terrestrial reserves.

That might maximise immediate recovery for bondholders. It would also leave Lio guarding a dead factory and keep orbital builders dependent on metal lifted from the Moon.

“The court asked for value, not justice,” Nara said.

“Did I ask which one you were sent to find?”

“No.”

“Good. I’m short of tea.”

Her terminal chimed. Edda Rune, acquisitions director for the largest bidder, requested a private call.

Edda appeared above the table in a severe white jacket, with a delay of a little over a second.

“Appraiser Senn,” she said. “I trust the facility is intact.”

“Mostly. Your subsidiary registered under the name Lantern Recovery.”

“It is a recovery vehicle.”

“Would Lantern operate the refinery?”

“That depends on future prices.”

“Would it retain Mr Marr?”

“That depends on future requirements.”

Nara looked at Lio. He drank his tea loudly.

Edda continued, “You may be tempted to reduce the reserve because the commodity models look poor. That would be a mistake. Anvil is strategically significant.”

“As a source of supply?”

“As an influence upon supply. A responsible owner would introduce production gradually.”

“Your rejected agreement proposed no production for eight years.”

The delay stretched Edda’s stillness into a pose. “You found Vey’s correspondence.”

“It was company property.”

“Then you understand that disorderly liquidation would damage workers far beyond this facility. Belisar, Danton Vale, the Kesh furnaces—whole towns depend on an orderly market.”

Nara’s fingers closed around the coin in her pocket.

Edda could not have known about her father. Belisar was simply a line in a supply chart to her, one of the places where scarcity still paid wages.

“If Lantern wins,” Nara asked, “how much metal reaches the yards next year?”

“Probably none.”

“And the year after?”

“Appraiser, you are selling an asset. You do not ordinarily demand that a purchaser consume it.”

When the call ended, Lio nodded toward Nara’s pocket.

“You keep touching something.”

“A coin.”

“Lucky?”

“No.”

“Those are the most reliable kind.”

## III

The next morning Nara inspected the stored ingots. Forty thousand tonnes floated in netted stacks inside a hollow spun slowly for handling gravity. Each ingot bore Morrow’s bird-shaped mark.

A young woman waited near the central spindle. She wore a patched pressure suit and introduced herself as Pavi Ot, purchasing officer for the Loom Habitat Cooperative.

“You weren’t on the passenger list,” Nara said.

“I came on a maintenance packet. Lio said you would inspect the inventory at nine.”

Lio, twenty metres away, became deeply interested in a cable junction.

Pavi handed Nara a financing letter. Loom proposed buying ten thousand tonnes immediately and another thirty thousand over five years. The metal would become pressure hulls for two agricultural habitats. Payment depended on construction loans from Cinder Bank.

The letter’s final clause allowed Cinder to withdraw if bulk nickel prices fell more than fifteen percent.

“You can only buy the metal if it doesn’t become too cheap,” Nara said.

“Our habitats will secure the loans. Their resale appraisal depends partly on the material value.”

“But your construction costs fall when nickel falls.”

“Cinder’s collateral department and construction department use different models.”

“That is absurd.”

Pavi shrugged. “They are on different floors.”

Nara drifted between the ingots. The nets creaked as the chamber turned. She thought of the Anvil sold whole to Lantern Recovery, its machinery preserved just well enough to prove it could flood the market, but never allowed to do so. Scarcity would protect old mines and old collateral. It would also keep new habitats expensive.

“How many people would Loom employ?” she asked.

“During construction, eight hundred and twenty. Afterward, about three hundred. We’ve offered Lio a maintenance post.”

“I am not authorised to consider employment benefits when setting the reserve.”

“Then don’t. Consider that we are a customer.”

“You cannot finance your full bid.”

“Not for the whole asteroid. Nobody who wants metal can. Anyone buying all sixty-two million tonnes has to account for what selling sixty-two million tonnes does to the price.”

That sentence followed Nara back through the refinery.

The flaw was not in the bids. It was in the shape of the thing being sold.

Pell Vey had financed Morrow’s Anvil as if an ore body were a chest: open it, count the contents, assign a value. But a market could absorb metal only across time. The asteroid’s tonnes were not equivalent. A tonne delivered next year could build a pressure hull. The ten-millionth tonne, arriving into a glutted market decades later, might be worth less than the energy required to heat it.

In her cabin, Nara opened the corporate charter. Extraction licenses could be severed from title. The mass driver’s metering system could authenticate annual quotas. The court order permitted her to divide movable assets into lots, though nobody seemed to have imagined dividing an ore body by calendar.

She worked until the air system dimmed the lights for night.

Instead of one asteroid, she constructed twenty-four time-limited rights.

The first lot included the existing inventory. The next five granted annual extraction quotas large enough to support Loom’s habitats. Later lots grew gradually, allowing buyers to reserve supply or suppress it, but only for a fixed year. Unused quotas would expire back to a custodial trust. A maintenance levy attached to every lot would keep the refinery operational. The machinery itself would remain with the trust until the final extraction right ended.

She ran the model. The present value exceeded the expected single-lot sale by nine percent, provided at least one terrestrial combine bid to preserve prices and at least one orbital builder bid for actual metal.

It depended on competitors wanting opposite things.

Most markets did.

At three in the morning, Lio found her in the galley.

“You have divided my rock into years,” he said, reading over her shoulder.

“The rock was always years. Vey disguised it as tonnes.”

“What happens after Year Twenty-Four?”

“The trust auctions a new schedule.”

“And if the machinery fails in Year Seven?”

“The levy covers expected maintenance.”

“Expected machinery is easy to maintain.”

She rubbed her eyes. “Do you have a better structure?”

“No. I have a list of pumps your model has not met.”

He sat opposite her. For a while the only sound was the recycler ticking in the wall.

“My father worked at Belisar,” Nara said.

Lio’s face changed, though not enough to call it pity.

“Then you know what this place did before we mined a gram.”

“I know what people said it did.”

“Same thing, in markets.”

She placed the nickel coin on the table. Its edge was worn smooth.

“Edda Rune says withholding Anvil protects towns like Belisar.”

“Possibly.”

“Pavi says releasing it builds new towns.”

“Possibly.”

“That word does too much work.”

“It gets paid less than certainty.” Lio slid the coin back to her. “Put it in your auction if you want an honest reserve. One old furnace, one failed asteroid and whatever your father thought metal was worth.”

## IV

The creditors objected immediately.

During the emergency hearing, their counsel called Nara’s plan untested, complicated and vulnerable to operational risk. The senior bond trustee wanted a clean sale and a payment before the quarter closed. The employee representative wanted unpaid wages placed ahead of maintenance. Lantern Recovery’s lawyers argued that annual rights would deprive title of its economic substance.

Pavi’s cooperative supported the plan, which made the trustee distrust it more.

Nara answered for two hours. A whole-asset bidder would discount the Anvil for market saturation, she explained. Separate annual quotas allowed each bidder to value only the period relevant to its business. Habitat builders could buy near-term supply without financing millions of unwanted tonnes. Terrestrial producers could bid for later years if orderly release genuinely had value. Competition between consumption and withholding would reveal a price that neither side alone would offer.

The judge approved the structure on the condition that Nara raise enough in the first six lots to cover priority claims and three years of maintenance.

“That condition can’t be met,” the bond trustee told her after the hearing.

“Then you’ll get your clean sale next week.”

“And your experiment will have lowered confidence in it.”

“Confidence is what financed this place.”

He did not answer.

The auction began at noon ship-time.

Nara sat in the old driver control room, facing a wall of inactive coil indicators. Lio watched from the doorway. Pavi participated from Loom’s rented berth. Edda Rune appeared as Lantern’s authorised representative, still wearing white.

Lot One contained the existing forty thousand tonnes.

Loom opened below reserve. A lunar breaker yard countered. Loom raised twice and stopped. With twelve seconds remaining, Cinder Bank confirmed its construction facility, and Pavi bid again.

Sold.

Pavi’s image froze with her mouth open, as if surprise were another form of signal delay.

Lots Two and Three sold to Loom after narrower contests. The prices were high enough to cover extraction but low enough to make the habitats feasible. Lot Four went to the breaker yard. Lot Five received no bids until Lantern entered at the reserve and acquired the entire quota.

“Why would they buy Year Five?” Lio asked.

“To remove it,” Nara said.

“They paid for nothing.”

“They paid for everybody else to have less.”

By Lot Six, the priority threshold was still short by sixteen million crowns.

The trustee sent Nara a message consisting only of the number.

Lot Six opened. Loom had reached its credit limit. The breaker yard bid once, then withdrew. Lantern offered eighty percent of reserve.

Nara watched the clock fall through thirty seconds.

If the lot failed, the judge’s condition failed with it. The auction would unwind. Lantern would likely purchase the whole Anvil the following week, cheaper than it could buy enough individual quotas to control production.

At twelve seconds, a new bidder registered: Danton Vale Metals Pension Fund.

Nara recognised the name as one of the employee funds that had lost value after Morrow’s discovery. It bid at reserve.

Lantern countered.

The pension fund bid again.

For ninety seconds the price climbed. Edda’s expression barely moved, but each Lantern bid came faster. The pension fund finally stopped at one hundred and forty-one percent of reserve.

Lantern took Lot Six.

The threshold indicator turned green.

Later lots produced stranger alliances. Loom bought Year Seven jointly with a freight guild. Lantern purchased Years Eight through Eleven. The pension fund acquired Year Twelve, apparently betting that it could resell the quota when terrestrial mines began to decline. A manufacturer of magnetic bearings bought only the cobalt by-product from Years Thirteen and Fourteen. Several distant lots went unsold.

At the end, projected creditor recovery stood at sixty-four cents on the crown. Employee wage claims would be paid in full. The maintenance trust had eight years of funding, assuming Lio’s pumps behaved like Nara’s expected machinery.

The bond trustee shook her hand without warmth.

Edda remained on the channel after the others left.

“You have made supply less predictable,” she said.

“I have made ownership less concentrated.”

“Lantern controls five of the next eleven years.”

“Not the first four.”

“We will let our quotas expire if conditions require it.”

“That is your right.”

“You understand that no metal will be produced in those years?”

“I understand you paid the creditors for the choice.”

Edda studied her across the delay. “You could work for us. We need people who understand that absence has a price.”

Nara ended the call.

## V

Three days later, the first bundle of Loom ingots entered the mass driver.

The launch was ceremonial only in the sense that Lio had cleaned the control room and Pavi had brought a bottle of something labelled wine. Nara suspected it had never encountered a grape.

The driver charged. A low vibration passed through the asteroid, more felt in the teeth than heard. On the display, the parcel accelerated down the equatorial track and vanished onto its transfer course.

Forty thousand tonnes would leave over the next year. After that, the refinery would process fresh ore for Lots Two and Three. In Year Five, if Lantern kept its promise to itself, the furnaces would cool again.

Pavi squeezed droplets of wine into three bulbs.

“To cheap metal,” she said.

“To adequately priced metal,” Nara replied.

Lio raised his bulb. “To pumps outside expected failure.”

They drank.

Through the observation port, the launched parcel was already invisible. Nara pictured it moving toward Loom’s unfinished habitat, where welders would turn an ingot into a curved wall, and a bank would call that wall collateral. She also pictured Belisar’s dismantled furnaces and the towns Edda had named, each depending on metal remaining expensive enough to dig from deep ground.

Her auction had not solved that contest. It had numbered the years in which each side might win.

Before departing, Nara visited the sample rack and asked Lio for a sliver from the first Anvil ingot. He cut one no larger than a fingernail. It was dull, granular and lighter in her palm than her father’s coin.

“You know they are nearly the same alloy,” Lio said.

“Not the same price.”

“Nothing has the same price in two places.”

At the shuttle hatch, Nara held both pieces of nickel together. One had come up from beneath Belisar in the last prosperous year. The other had crossed no distance at all and had still managed to close Belisar’s furnaces.

She left the old coin with Lio as a maintenance-trust asset, entered on the inventory at one crown.

The asteroid sliver she kept.

As the shuttle pulled away, Morrow’s Anvil diminished against the dark. Its mass driver flashed again, sending another bundle toward people who could use it. The asteroid was no smaller to the eye. At the current release rate, it would not look changed in Nara’s lifetime.

For the first time, she understood that abundance was not the opposite of scarcity. Abundance was scarcity waiting for a schedule.

# Code Review: PR 47 — Quantifying rewetting halos around millipede fecal pellets

**Repository:** `zymopellet`  
**Branch:** `feature/halo-decay`  
**Primary files reviewed:** `segment.py`, `register.py`, `profiles.py`, `decay.py`, `models.py`, `cli.py`, and tests under `tests/`  
**Decision:** Request changes before merge

## Summary

This pull request adds an end-to-end workflow for measuring phosphatase-activity halos around millipede fecal pellets after dry soil is rewetted. It imports time-lapse zymography images, registers each sequence, segments pellets, constructs radial bands, estimates halo persistence, and compares litter treatments. That is a useful and unusually coherent addition: the command-line interface follows the actual analytical sequence, intermediate tables are retained, and the plotting code generally consumes derived data rather than recomputing metrics invisibly.

The implementation is close to being a dependable research pipeline, but four issues currently affect the scientific results rather than merely code style:

1. Radial distances are converted from pixels to millimetres twice.
2. Image registration applies row/column shifts as x/y translations and does not track invalid edge pixels.
3. The reported integrated halo index gives every radial band equal weight, regardless of its area.
4. The treatment model treats repeated images and multiple pellets from one microcosm as independent replicates.

Together, these can change estimated halo size, decay time, and treatment uncertainty. I would not merge the analysis path until they are fixed and the principal output tables are regenerated. The underlying module boundaries and manifest-driven design are worth preserving.

## Scientific and data context used for this review

The bundled manifest describes the fictional `MILL-REWET-22` experiment: six soil microcosms per litter treatment, four marked millipede pellets per microcosm, and images at 0, 3, 8, 24, 48, 96, and 168 hours after rewetting. Fluorescence is treated as potential phosphomonoesterase activity. Rewetting is applied to the whole microcosm, so the microcosm—not an image, radial band, or pellet—is the independent treatment replicate. Pellets are useful observational subunits nested within it.

That distinction should remain visible throughout the package. A radial profile is an image-derived measurement; a pellet trajectory is a repeated biological observation; a microcosm is the treatment replicate. The current tidy table preserves all three identifiers, which is excellent, but `models.py` discards the hierarchy at the final step.

The ecological language also needs to stay close to what the assay measures. A zymogram estimates potential enzyme activity under the supplied substrate and incubation conditions. A bright halo may arise from enzyme diffusion, microbial growth, displacement of soluble compounds during wet-up, or optical effects at the pellet boundary. It is not, by itself, evidence of phosphorus mineralization or fungal colonization.

## What is working well

### 1. The workflow is inspectable

Each stage writes a specific artifact:

- `registered/*.tif`
- `masks/*.tif`
- `profiles.parquet`
- `pellet_metrics.csv`
- `model_summary.json`

This is preferable to a monolithic notebook because registration, segmentation, metric calculation, and inference can be checked separately. The `--stop-after` option is particularly useful for reviewing masks before fitting models.

### 2. Identifiers survive reshaping

`microcosm_id`, `pellet_id`, `treatment`, `time_h`, and `image_id` are present in the long-form output. The parser also rejects filenames that do not match the manifest instead of silently guessing identifiers. That will prevent several common soil-imaging errors, especially accidental mixing of technical reruns with biological replicates.

### 3. Segmentation is separated from halo measurement

Using the pellet mask only as an origin, rather than defining the activity hotspot by the same threshold used to identify the pellet, avoids a circular measurement. The optional manual correction file is also sensible. It records edited polygons rather than overwriting automatic masks, so the provenance of corrections remains available.

### 4. The code already exposes useful diagnostics

The registration montage, radial-profile plot, and saturation overlay are appropriate quality-control outputs. With the fixes below, they can become acceptance tests for each imaging sequence rather than merely presentation figures.

## Blocking finding 1: radial distances are scaled twice

**Location:** `profiles.py`, `radial_profile`, approximately lines 61–69

The current code is equivalent to:

```python
distance = ndi.distance_transform_edt(
    ~pellet_mask,
    sampling=millimetres_per_pixel,
)
radius_mm = distance * millimetres_per_pixel
```

When `sampling` is supplied, SciPy already returns distances in the units represented by that sampling value. Multiplying again shrinks all radii when the scale is below 1 mm per pixel. At the manifest value of 0.042 mm per pixel, a pixel 20 pixels from the pellet is correctly about 0.84 mm away after the first line but is reported as about 0.035 mm after the second conversion.

This affects more than axis labels. `max_radius_mm=3.0` is applied to the incorrectly scaled values, so nearly the entire image can be admitted into what is supposed to be a local halo. The resulting background estimate and area under the profile are both contaminated.

Use physical sampling once, and support separate row and column scales because the manifest schema already permits non-square pixels:

```python
def distance_from_mask_mm(mask, pixel_size_y_mm, pixel_size_x_mm):
    if mask.dtype != bool:
        raise TypeError("mask must be boolean")
    if not mask.any():
        raise ValueError("pellet mask is empty")

    return ndi.distance_transform_edt(
        ~mask,
        sampling=(pixel_size_y_mm, pixel_size_x_mm),
    )
```

Then bin `distance_mm` directly. Please add a geometric test using a one-pixel seed and anisotropic sampling. Assertions should cover a horizontal offset, a vertical offset, and a diagonal offset; a test using only square pixels would not protect the tuple case.

Also record both pixel dimensions in `profiles.parquet`. A single `mm_per_px` column cannot faithfully describe images for which the scanner has been calibrated independently by axis.

## Blocking finding 2: registration mixes coordinate conventions

**Location:** `register.py`, `align_stack`, approximately lines 44–58

`phase_cross_correlation(reference, moving)` returns a shift in array order: `(row_shift, column_shift)`. The code passes that tuple directly to `AffineTransform(translation=shift)`, whose translation is conventionally interpreted as `(x, y)`. In addition, `warp` expects an inverse mapping unless configured otherwise. The current result is correct only for a restricted set of symmetric shifts, which explains why the provided test with `(4, 4)` passes.

For translation-only registration, the least ambiguous implementation is to apply the returned array shift directly:

```python
shift_rc, error, phase = phase_cross_correlation(
    reference,
    moving,
    upsample_factor=10,
)

aligned = ndi.shift(
    moving,
    shift=shift_rc,
    order=1,
    mode="constant",
    cval=np.nan,
    prefilter=False,
)
```

The same transform should be applied to a validity image so that padded margins can be excluded:

```python
valid = ndi.shift(
    np.ones(moving.shape, dtype=np.uint8),
    shift=shift_rc,
    order=0,
    mode="constant",
    cval=0,
).astype(bool)
```

At present, padded zeros are treated as low fluorescence. As the sequence drifts, those pixels can enter outer radial bands and create an artificial decline. Saving `valid_fraction` by pellet, time point, and radial band would make this visible. A band with less than, for example, 80% valid area should be flagged rather than silently compared with a complete band.

Please expand the tests to include unequal positive and negative shifts such as `(3.25, -7.5)`. Check recovery against a synthetic image containing several non-symmetric objects, not a centered Gaussian alone. A centered Gaussian can conceal axis swaps and sign errors.

There is a second registration concern: the entire image is registered on fluorescence intensity, but a biological halo can genuinely expand, contract, or brighten. Phase correlation should be driven by stable fiducials or a structural channel where available. The manifest includes `fiducial_channel` for 29 of 36 microcosms but the loader ignores it. Prefer that channel and emit a warning when registration falls back to the activity image. For the seven fallback sequences, the registration montage should be retained with the final results.

## Blocking finding 3: the integrated halo index is not area-weighted

**Location:** `profiles.py`, `summarise_halo`, approximately lines 112–127

The current calculation is:

```python
halo_index = profile.groupby("ring_id")["excess_signal"].mean().sum()
```

This is a sum of ring means. A narrow inner band and a much larger outer annulus contribute equally if they have the same mean signal. The metric therefore depends on the selected radial bin width and does not represent integrated excess activity. Halving the bin width can approximately double the reported value without changing the image.

If the intended estimand is total two-dimensional excess fluorescence within a fixed radius, calculate it at pixel level:

```python
pixel_area_mm2 = pixel_size_y_mm * pixel_size_x_mm
eligible = owned & valid & (distance_mm <= max_radius_mm)

integrated_excess = (
    corrected_image[eligible] - background_signal
).sum() * pixel_area_mm2
```

Do not clip negative residuals to zero before summation. Negative values contain information about noise and background mismatch; clipping creates a positive bias, particularly late in the time series when the true excess is small.

Because four pellet halos can overlap, `owned` needs an explicit definition. At present, each pellet is processed independently, so a bright pixel between two pellets is counted in both trajectories. A nearest-pellet partition is a reasonable default: label every pellet, compute the nearest labeled object, and assign each soil pixel to one pellet before applying the maximum radius. Pixels equidistant between pellets can be assigned deterministically by label order, with the number of ties reported. Alternatively, exclude overlap zones, but do not double-count them.

Keep the radial means as a descriptive product; they are biologically interpretable and useful for diagnostics. Rename the scalar metric to make its units clear, for example `integrated_excess_au_mm2`. Also report `eligible_area_mm2`, `valid_fraction`, and a background-noise estimate. A scalar without its sampled area is difficult to audit.

The background calculation deserves one correction at the same time. It currently uses all pixels farther than 3 mm from the focal pellet, including other pellets. Restrict the background to valid, pellet-free pixels outside every pellet’s analysis radius. If too little background remains, return a missing metric with a reason code rather than using another pellet’s halo as baseline.

## Blocking finding 4: the inferential model pseudoreplicates the treatment effect

**Location:** `models.py`, `fit_treatment_effect`, approximately lines 28–52

The implementation fits:

```python
ols("log_halo ~ treatment * time_h", data=frame_rows).fit()
```

Here, `frame_rows` contains one row per pellet and time point. For a treatment with six microcosms, four pellets, and seven times, the model effectively treats as many as 168 rows as independent evidence for the treatment. Rewetting and litter composition were assigned at microcosm level, so there are six independent experimental units per treatment.

The package should provide two defensible analysis levels:

1. A microcosm-level summary for the primary treatment contrast. Aggregate pellet metrics within each microcosm and time point, preserving the number of usable pellets and their dispersion. This is simple to inspect and works well for plotting.
2. A hierarchical model retaining pellets, with pellet nested within microcosm and treatment applied at microcosm level.

A reasonable starting model is:

```text
integrated excess ~ treatment × post-peak time + initial pellet area
random intercepts: microcosm, pellet within microcosm
```

The treatment coefficient must be interpreted against microcosm-level replication. If the mixed-model implementation reports denominator degrees of freedom or confidence intervals that imply hundreds of treatment replicates, it is still wrong.

For a robust primary interval, I recommend a cluster bootstrap that resamples microcosms within treatment and carries all their pellets and time points together. This mirrors the randomization and makes the unit of uncertainty explicit. Pellet-level resampling would reproduce the current pseudoreplication in a different form.

The report table should include, by treatment and time, the number of planned microcosms, observed microcosms, usable pellets, and excluded images. A treatment estimate without those counts is hard to evaluate when segmentation failures are uneven.

## Major finding 5: “half-life” currently means first sampled crossing

**Location:** `decay.py`, `observed_half_life`

The function returns the time of the first observation below 50% of the time-zero signal. With irregular sampling at 0, 3, 8, 24, 48, 96, and 168 hours, this produces coarse categories rather than half-life estimates. Two pellets crossing at 9 and 23 hours both receive 24 hours. A pellet still above the threshold at 168 hours is returned as 168 rather than right-censored, which makes persistent halos appear to decay faster than observed.

There is also a biological timing issue. Several supplied trajectories peak at 3 or 8 hours after rewetting, probably reflecting activation or transport after water addition. A decay clock beginning at time zero is not appropriate for those trajectories.

Define the peak from the observed trajectory, then fit the post-peak excess above an estimated asymptote. An asymptotic exponential is adequate as a first implementation:

```text
A(t) = C + A0 exp[-k(t - t_peak)]
```

with half-life `ln(2) / k`. Constrain `k` to be non-negative, retain fit diagnostics, and report the estimate as missing if there are fewer than three post-peak observations. If the fitted half-level is not reached during observation, mark the empirical crossing as right-censored rather than substituting the final time.

Do not return a half-life when the fitted amplitude is indistinguishable from background. In that case there was no resolved halo to decay. The output needs separate statuses such as `estimated`, `right_censored`, `no_resolved_peak`, `insufficient_points`, and `fit_failed`.

For transparency, retain a model-free duration metric as well: hours for which the confidence-adjusted excess remains above the background threshold. That quantity should not be labeled a half-life.

## Major finding 6: saturation checks are calculated but not enforced

`qc.py` computes the fraction of pixels at the detector maximum, but `profiles.py` still uses saturated images without a flag. Dividing intensity by exposure time cannot recover information after clipping. A saturated inner pellet can also flatten the radial gradient and make the apparent halo wider.

At minimum:

- Calculate saturation over the pellet and 3 mm analysis region, not the whole frame.
- Flag any metric whose relevant region exceeds a documented saturation threshold.
- Exclude or sensitivity-test severe cases.
- Preserve the raw bit depth before conversion to floating point.

The threshold should be configurable and recorded in the output metadata. The pipeline should not automatically replace a saturated exposure with a shorter exposure unless both are tied to the same sample and time in the manifest.

## Major finding 7: segmentation uncertainty is hidden after manual correction

The mask editor is well designed, but downstream tables contain only the final mask. Add `mask_source` with values such as `automatic`, `edited`, and `manual`, plus automatic-mask confidence diagnostics. Treatment-blind editing should be encouraged by showing image identifiers without treatment labels in the editor.

Pellet area changes by more than 25% in nine trajectories. Some change may be real swelling or fragmentation, but some appears to come from threshold instability as fluorescence changes. Because radial distance is measured from the boundary, this can mimic halo movement. The default analysis should use a reference pellet boundary propagated through the registered sequence unless there is a documented reason to allow time-varying masks. Provide an overlay of every time-point boundary on the reference frame so fragmentation can be inspected.

## Major finding 8: interpretation in the generated report is too causal

`report.py` currently emits sentences such as:

> Cedar litter increased phosphorus release by extending microbial activity around pellets.

Neither phosphorus release nor microbial cause is directly measured. The code has estimated substrate-induced phosphatase fluorescence around a pellet under assay conditions. A safer generated statement would be:

> Cedar-litter microcosms showed a longer-lived pellet-associated phosphatase-activity signal under the zymography assay.

Mechanisms can be discussed as hypotheses, but the report should distinguish enzyme activity potential from net phosphorus flux. This is especially important because soluble enzymes can persist outside living cells, and wet-up can redistribute substrate and reaction products.

## Reproducibility and interface comments

### Manifest validation
