# The Laboratory That Waits: Temporal Slack in Automated Experimental Workflows

## Abstract

Laboratory automation is usually evaluated through throughput, precision, and the proportion of operations performed without human intervention. Less attention is paid to waiting: idle robot arms, queued plates, stabilization periods, delayed human approvals, and instruments reserved for work that has not yet arrived. This review examines waiting as a feature of automated laboratories rather than simply as unused capacity. The literature can be divided into four broad accounts of waiting: waste to be removed, scientifically required dwell time, protective slack, and evidence of poor organizational coordination. Across these accounts, authors disagree about whether high equipment utilization indicates successful automation. Scheduling studies generally seek to compress idle periods, whereas reliability studies suggest that spare capacity can contain failures. Human-factors research adds that some machine waiting merely transfers urgency to technicians. The review argues that temporal slack should be measured separately from accidental delay, although the available literature rarely makes that distinction consistently. A provisional taxonomy is offered, followed by recommendations for designing automated workflows with visible queues, bounded recovery time, and limited spare capacity. The evidence remains fragmented, particularly for long-running biology workflows, but it indicates that the fastest automated laboratory is not necessarily the most productive or dependable one.

## 1. Introduction

The familiar image of laboratory automation is continuous motion. Plates travel between readers and incubators, liquid handlers dispense without interruption, and scheduling software fills every opening in an instrument calendar. Vendors and laboratory managers often describe this condition using the language of utilization: an expensive device creates value when it is operating and loses value when it is idle. This reasoning has encouraged laboratories to treat waiting as a defect.

Yet automated laboratories wait constantly. A sample may need thirty minutes for a reaction to develop. A robotic gripper may be held outside an enclosure while a centrifuge completes its cycle. A batch may remain in a queue because a scientist has not approved an anomalous control result. Instruments are also left deliberately unbooked so that failed runs can be repeated. These pauses are not equivalent, even though a scheduling dashboard may display each of them as an unproductive block of time.

The distinction matters because removing one kind of waiting can create another. If plates are released toward an analyzer as soon as preparation ends, they may accumulate in an uncontrolled queue beside the analyzer. If every incubator is kept full, a delayed plate may have nowhere to go. If software automatically proceeds through every decision point, scientists may discover a systematic problem only after large amounts of reagent and material have been consumed. Faster local operation can therefore produce slower or less reliable laboratory performance.

This review considers the role of temporal slack in automated experimental workflows. Temporal slack is defined here as time or capacity not assigned to immediate productive motion. The definition includes empty scheduling intervals, planned buffers, scientific dwell periods, and some forms of operator delay. This breadth makes it possible to connect literatures that are usually discussed separately, although it also risks treating unlike phenomena as parts of one category.

The central question is whether waiting should be minimized, tolerated, or designed. The literature does not provide one answer. Optimization research generally treats idle time as a cost, process-control research recognizes waiting as a physical constraint, and resilience research treats slack as an insurance mechanism. Human-factors studies further suggest that the distribution of waiting between machines and people affects fatigue and error. Bringing these positions together exposes a basic tension: laboratories want automated systems that are both highly occupied and immediately available when an exception occurs.

## 2. Scope of the Review

The review draws on publications concerning robotic laboratories, instrument scheduling, workflow orchestration, manufacturing cells, clinical sample processing, and human supervision of automation. Searches were conducted in several technical and scientific databases using combinations of terms such as “laboratory automation,” “idle time,” “scheduling,” “queue,” “incubation,” “workflow delay,” and “robot recovery.” References cited by relevant papers were also inspected. Studies were favored when they described a working system rather than only a scheduling algorithm, though several simulation papers were retained because little operational evidence was available.

Approximately two dozen sources formed the main body of the review. The literature was read narratively and grouped according to the function authors assigned to waiting. No formal quality score was applied because engineering case reports and observational laboratory studies were too different for a common scale. Manufacturing studies were included where the equipment arrangement resembled a laboratory workcell. Clinical laboratories were included selectively, particularly when they addressed sample queues or urgent insertions.

The resulting evidence base is uneven. Most reports concern short plate-based workflows or simulated jobs, while fewer examine experiments lasting days. Publications also tend to describe successful installations, and vendors rarely report how often automation is stopped, bypassed, or repaired. Nevertheless, the sources provide several recurring interpretations of temporal slack.

## 3. Waiting as Waste

The strongest tradition treats waiting as one of the principal losses that automation should remove. In this view, idle time indicates poor sequencing, inadequate equipment balancing, or failure to anticipate resource contention. Havel and Sorn’s simulation of the fictional Lattice-12 screening cell, for example, compared first-in-first-out scheduling with a priority rule based on predicted operation length. Their priority scheduler reduced average plate completion time by 17 percent, largely by preventing short jobs from becoming trapped behind long incubation-heavy jobs. The robot arm also spent less time waiting for destination instruments to become available.

Similar conclusions appear in reports on modular chemistry platforms. Neris and Volan described a synthesis system in which vessels repeatedly waited at a shared weighing station. Adding a second station raised daily output, but changing the order of weighing and solvent addition produced nearly the same gain without new hardware. The authors presented the queue as proof that the original workflow had been badly arranged.

These studies make an important contribution by showing that nominal instrument speed is not the same as system throughput. A pipetting device can operate faster while total run time remains unchanged because downstream readers or centrifuges determine the pace. Queue maps and event logs can reveal these constraints more reliably than raw utilization percentages. The literature also demonstrates that small scheduling choices may have larger effects than purchasing a faster robot.

However, the waste account tends to assume that every job has a stable duration and that the objective is known in advance. Real experiments often violate both assumptions. A liquid handler may pause because a tip cannot be detected, an imaging run may expand when additional fields are requested, and a control result may require interpretation. Optimization papers frequently model such events as random delays rather than scientifically meaningful decisions. Their solutions are therefore strongest for repetitive assays and less obviously applicable to research environments.

The emphasis on mean completion time can also obscure extreme cases. A rule that improves average throughput may leave a small number of temperature-sensitive samples waiting too long. In some studies, a reduction in robot idle time is reported as an improvement even when sample residence time is not measured. The literature thus occasionally treats machine motion as the product of the laboratory rather than validated experimental output.

## 4. Scientific Dwell Time

A second body of work concerns waiting that is required by the experiment. Incubation, settling, thermal equilibration, reaction development, instrument calibration, and washing all impose intervals during which visible progress may be limited. Such intervals are sometimes called “hard waits,” though the term is misleading because many are permitted ranges rather than exact durations.

Bellane’s review of automated immunoassay workcells distinguishes exact-time operations from minimum-time operations. An exact-time operation must occur near a specified moment, while a minimum-time operation may occur at any later time after a threshold. This distinction has scheduling consequences. A plate requiring at least twenty minutes of incubation can remain in place for twenty-five minutes if the assay tolerates it, whereas a plate that must be read within a two-minute window cannot safely join an ordinary queue.

Laboratory schedulers often represent both conditions as fixed durations. This simplifies software but may waste flexibility. In the Orison Enzyme Laboratory case described by Quill, expanding incubation requirements from single values to validated windows allowed the scheduler to interleave three assay families. Daily capacity reportedly increased from 38 to 51 plates without changes to the hardware. The result suggests that scientific protocols contain hidden temporal options that automation engineers can exploit.

At the same time, the literature sometimes implies that any protocol interval can be negotiated once enough data are collected. That is too broad. Some timing requirements arise from unstable chemistry, cell stress, or regulatory validation and cannot be altered merely because a scheduler would benefit. The Orison case involved relatively forgiving colorimetric assays, but it has been cited in discussions of cell culture and analytical chemistry where timing risks are different. Generalizing from it may encourage laboratories to widen windows without sufficient scientific validation.

There is also disagreement about whether scientific dwell time should count as equipment utilization. An incubator containing plates is clearly performing a function despite having no moving parts. A robot arm waiting beside it is not. Some dashboards count both devices as occupied because they are reserved for the workflow; others count only active operations. This inconsistency makes comparisons between laboratories unreliable. A system claiming 90 percent utilization may be reporting reservation, physical activity, or successful sample processing.

The most useful contribution of this literature is the recognition that workflow timing has several dimensions: minimum duration, maximum duration, permissible interruption, and sensitivity to variation. Yet few studies record all four. A basic operation is usually stored as a single number, leaving the scheduler unable to distinguish a harmless five-minute delay from one that invalidates a sample.

## 5. Slack as Protection Against Failure

Reliability studies reverse the usual interpretation of idle capacity. Instead of asking how to keep every instrument busy, they ask what happens when a busy instrument fails. A tightly scheduled laboratory may have no location for interrupted work, no opportunity to repeat a control, and no alternative path around an unavailable device. Under these conditions, high utilization can make a local fault propagate across the workcell.

Daro and Melsin examined fault logs from the invented MorrowBench facility, where six automated stations shared two transport robots. They found that stoppages lasting less than eight minutes caused most of the lost shift time. The delay came not from the original fault but from clearing plates that had continued arriving during recovery. Their proposed policy inserted ten-minute empty blocks every two hours. Simulations suggested lower nominal throughput but higher completed throughput once faults were included.

This finding aligns with research on manufacturing buffers, where small reserves can separate one machine’s variability from another. The analogy is appealing: a plate hotel resembles an intermediate storage buffer, and duplicate readers resemble redundant production machines. However, biological samples are not inert components. A plate hotel may protect the schedule while exposing cells or reagents to unacceptable temperature, humidity, or evaporation. Buffer capacity is therefore not automatically useful capacity.

Several authors recommend “recovery slack,” meaning time and space reserved for predictable categories of exception. Examples include an empty incubator position, an unassigned robot slot, spare consumables, and a scheduled period for reruns. This is more specific than simply lowering utilization. Recovery slack is linked to an action: holding a delayed sample, replacing a failed batch, or allowing an operator to inspect a deck.

Evidence for the ideal amount of slack is weak. MorrowBench’s ten-minute blocks were chosen from its local fault pattern, while other papers propose reserves of 5 to 20 percent with limited justification. The literature frequently repeats the idea that systems should run at about 80 percent utilization, apparently because queues rise rapidly near full capacity. That principle is plausible but not universal. A rarely failing reader with a large downstream buffer may safely operate near full occupancy, whereas a fragile transport robot could destabilize the laboratory at a much lower figure.

Some reliability papers also count unused duplicate equipment as slack even where the duplicate is required for routine throughput. This inflates the appearance of resilience. True redundancy exists only if an alternative resource remains available when the primary resource fails. Two instruments that are both continuously booked do not provide much practical redundancy, even if either can technically perform the same assay.

## 6. Human Waiting and Transferred Urgency

Automated workflows include human decisions at loading, approval, replenishment, exception handling, and data review. Waiting can therefore be shifted rather than eliminated. A machine may operate continuously because a technician is expected to respond immediately whenever a consumable runs low. Conversely, a machine may remain idle because approvals are performed in scheduled batches.

In a study of the fictional North Aster Sample Centre, Pellen and Uro observed technicians supervising three automated preparation lines. The lines generated frequent low-priority notices mixed with occasional urgent alarms. Technicians responded quickly to almost all alerts because the interface did not clearly show whether a delay would damage a sample. As a result, staff repeatedly abandoned manual tasks to check machines that could have waited. The automation reduced direct pipetting but increased fragmented attention.

This work provides a useful correction to equipment-centered studies. A scheduler that reduces robot waiting by demanding instant human intervention may improve its own performance while worsening laboratory performance. Interruptions can increase setup errors, delay documentation, and make work harder to plan. The relevant question is not simply whether the robot waits, but who waits, under what pressure, and with what consequence.

Human-factors authors commonly recommend escalation windows. Instead of issuing an immediate alarm, the system should state that a response is required within a defined period, such as “refill tips within 18 minutes.” This converts an interruption into a schedulable task. Some interfaces also group non-urgent interventions into service rounds. These approaches appear sensible, although evidence is mainly observational and based on staff preference rather than measured error rates.

The literature occasionally assumes that human waiting is inherently more costly than machine waiting because labor is flexible and expensive. This is not always true. A specialist may use a waiting period to review data or prepare another protocol, whereas an idle dedicated analyzer may have no alternate use. Cost depends on whether waiting prevents other productive activity, not merely on whether a person or device is stationary.

There is also a risk of romanticizing human judgment. Several case reports describe operators as a flexible buffer who can rescue irregular workflows. In practice, this may mean that incomplete automation is sustained through unrecorded manual work. If technicians regularly rearrange queues, carry plates past a failed transporter, or reinterpret ambiguous alerts, the system may appear more autonomous and robust than it is. Waiting records should therefore include human interventions, but most automation logs track only machine states.

## 7. Organizational Waiting

A final category lies outside the physical workcell. Automated runs wait for protocol approval, reagent release, sample registration, data transfer, or access to shared instruments. These delays can exceed the time saved by faster liquid handling, yet they receive less attention because they belong to different software and management systems.

Sivert’s study of the Veyra Materials Unit found that a robot completed formulation batches in four hours, but batches spent a median of nineteen hours awaiting analytical review. The unit initially planned to buy a second formulation robot. After mapping the end-to-end process, it introduced two review periods per day and standardized the data packet sent to analysts. Turnaround reportedly fell more than it would have under the equipment expansion scenario.

This case illustrates the value of measuring the entire workflow. Automation can accelerate one stage while leaving the governing bottleneck elsewhere. It also shows why utilization is an incomplete management measure: the formulation robot was busy, but completed knowledge moved slowly.

Nonetheless, organizational waiting is only loosely connected to the scheduling literature reviewed above. A delay caused by an approval meeting differs from a plate waiting for an available reader. The remedies involve staffing, authority, and information design rather than robotic coordination. Combining them under temporal slack may create a broad vocabulary at the expense of causal precision.

Several publications propose digital integration as the general solution. If the laboratory information system, scheduler, and analysis pipeline exchange status automatically, approvals can supposedly occur earlier and queues become visible. Integration may help, but visibility does not itself add reviewing capacity or resolve unclear responsibility. The literature often overstates what software connectivity can accomplish in organizations where decisions remain contested or under-resourced.

## 8. Toward a Taxonomy of Laboratory Waiting

The reviewed literature supports a provisional classification with five categories:

1. **Constraint waiting** arises from scientific or physical requirements, such as incubation or thermal equilibration.
2. **Contention waiting** occurs when multiple jobs need the same robot, instrument, or storage position.
3. **Recovery waiting** is time reserved or consumed while faults are diagnosed and work is restored.
4. **Decision waiting** occurs when a human or analytical system must authorize the next operation.
5. **Administrative waiting** reflects registration, release, documentation, or organizational coordination.

This taxonomy is useful because the categories suggest different responses. Constraint waiting should be scientifically characterized, contention waiting may be reduced by scheduling, recovery waiting requires fault planning, decision waiting benefits from explicit response windows, and administrative waiting may require process redesign.

However, the categories overlap. A plate awaiting review might occupy an incubator and thereby cause contention. A scientific constraint may become administrative when a validated timing window cannot be changed without formal approval. Recovery from a fault may require a human decision. It is therefore difficult to assign every delay to a single class. A better logging system might record both the immediate state and the underlying cause, though no reviewed system did so comprehensively.

The taxonomy also does not settle which waits are beneficial. Constraint waiting is necessary but not necessarily slack, while recovery slack may remain unused for long periods. Administrative waiting is usually undesirable, yet a review pause may prevent continuation of a faulty experiment. The categories clarify mechanisms more than value.

## 9. Discussion

Three conclusions recur across the literature. First, equipment utilization should not be used alone to judge laboratory automation. It can reward systems that keep devices occupied while increasing queues, sample risk, or operator interruption. Measures such as valid outputs per day, time within protocol windows, recovery duration, and human intervention load provide a broader picture.

Second, waiting should be represented explicitly in workflow models. Protocols need more than a sequence of active steps. They should identify timing ranges, holding conditions, interruptibility, decision deadlines, and acceptable recovery paths. Without these properties, a scheduler cannot distinguish useful flexibility from dangerous delay.

Third, some spare capacity appears necessary for resilience. The literature supports reserving at least a modest amount of time or storage for reruns and disruptions. A general target of 10 to 20 percent unassigned capacity seems reasonable across many laboratories, especially where workflows are variable. This recommendation should be interpreted cautiously because the studies do not directly compare reserve levels across different laboratory types. Even so, operating every critical resource at maximum occupancy is unlikely to be safe.

These conclusions are limited by the evidence. Many studies are simulations, single-site reports, or descriptions written during system deployment. Few provide raw event logs, and definitions of idle time differ. Research laboratories, diagnostic facilities, and manufacturing cells are often discussed together despite having different objectives. The literature also contains little information about failed automation projects, making it difficult to estimate whether slack prevents failure or merely accompanies well-funded systems.

More empirical work should compare laboratories before and after changes to scheduling slack. Such studies should report completed valid experiments, sample losses, staff interruptions, energy use, and recovery time rather than only robot utilization. Long-running workflows deserve particular attention because a short interruption can interact with multi-day biological processes in ways not captured by plate-handling simulations.

Despite these gaps, managers can take several immediate steps. They can separate active processing from reservation in equipment dashboards, record why a sample is waiting, validate timing windows instead of using single durations, and identify where interrupted samples can be held. Alert interfaces should display response deadlines. Finally, capacity planning should include ordinary faults rather than calculating output from perfect cycle times.

## 10. Conclusion

Waiting in automated laboratories is neither a single form of waste nor an uncomplicated source of safety. Some waiting is imposed by science, some results from contention, some preserves room for recovery, and some reveals organizational delay. The literature is strongest when it maps queues and timing constraints at the level of the whole workflow. It is weakest when it assumes that greater motion means greater productivity or, conversely, that an arbitrary reserve guarantees resilience.

Laboratory automation should therefore be designed around controlled waiting. Pauses should have known causes, acceptable durations, and defined consequences. A laboratory that can explain why its machines are idle may be better automated than one in which every instrument is busy and no resource is available when the experiment departs from plan.

# The Bell at Mooring 397

At four in the morning, when the tide turned under Lathwater, every floating house changed address.

The houses did not travel far. Their iron guides slid along chains fixed to the harbour floor, and the eastern rows swung north while the western rows rotated towards the old sea wall. Nevertheless, a kitchen that had faced the bakery at midnight might face a net-mender's porch by breakfast. Children crossed to school over bridges that had not existed the evening before. Neighbours became strangers and then neighbours again.

Ena Marr had grown up believing all towns behaved this way. Only when she left to study epidemics at the Inland Institute did she discover that most streets stayed where surveyors put them.

She returned to Lathwater during the first week of lantern fever.

A customs skiff carried her past shuttered tea stalls and gardens planted in blue barrels. The harbour smelled of tar, fennel and the green mud exposed beneath the pontoons. On several decks, strips of yellow cloth warned visitors away. Ena counted eleven strips before the skiff reached the infirmary.

Director Halden Crowe met her at the landing. He was a wide, sleepless man wearing a rain cape over striped bedclothes.

"Thirty-one confirmed cases," he said before greeting her. "Eighteen yesterday, thirteen since midnight. Two patients cannot stand. No deaths, but the whole Fold thinks breathing harbour fog causes it. Half the fish market has fled upriver."

"How are cases confirmed?"

"Fever, dry cough and halos around lamps. That last symptom is why they named it."

"Laboratory test?"

Crowe looked offended. "Our laboratory washed away in spring."

He led Ena into the infirmary's chart room. A paper map of Lathwater covered one wall. Red pins marked patients' homes. They formed an impressive cluster around the central market.

"There," Crowe said. "The source."

Ena did not answer. The map showed where the houses had been on the morning the pins were placed, not where they had been when their occupants became infected. By tomorrow's tide, the cluster would stretch into a crescent. By the next, it might look like two outbreaks.

"I need the mooring ledger," she said. "And the ferry scans, bridge changes, market rosters, water deliveries and symptom times. Not admission times."

Crowe blinked. "All that before you tell me whether to close the harbour?"

"Especially before that."

This answer sounded firmer than Ena felt. At the institute she had built models from clean tables with rectangular columns. Lathwater offered notebooks swollen by damp, ferry tickets used as shopping lists and a harbour clerk who recorded the tide by drawing either a happy or a disappointed moon.

Her father was waiting beside the ledger cabinet.

Oris Marr had piloted the cross-harbour ferry for thirty-four years. His beard had gone white, but his hands still appeared carved from the same dark rope as the mooring lines. He embraced Ena awkwardly, as though she were luggage he had been warned was fragile.

"You came with numbers," he said.

"That is what they asked for."

"Last fever, the numbers said close the south pontoons. Your mother was on the north pontoon."

"I was sixteen. They weren't my numbers."

"Numbers don't remember whose they were."

Crowe cleared his throat and left them with the ledgers.

Ena opened the newest volume. Each vessel had a row, each mooring a number, and each tide a column. At least this part was careful. A house might be at 118 during one tide, 204 during the next and 397 after that. Public bridges were recorded with green ink. Shared water hoses were blue. Ferry stops were black triangles.

Static maps were useless here, but contacts might still be reconstructed. Ena began copying.

By noon, she had covered the chart-room floor with cards. Each card represented a household. She joined cards with coloured string whenever two households had shared a bridge, ferry bench or adjacent mooring during the previous eight days. The resulting web climbed across chairs and snagged on the door handle.

Crowe stepped over it with a tray of soup.

"Is that the model?"

"It is the part I can see."

"And the part you can't?"

"Almost everything important."

For a moment, this honesty pleased him. Then he remembered that the harbour council expected a forecast by sunset.

## The Number

Ena entered the records into her institute calculator. She labelled households susceptible, exposed, infectious or recovered, though she had no reliable way to distinguish exposed people from susceptible ones. She set the incubation period at two days because the first three patients remembered feeling ill two days after the Lantern Fair. A fourth patient said five days, so Ena marked his account uncertain and left it out.

She divided the thirty-one cases by the previous day's eighteen, adjusted for the estimated length of infectiousness, and obtained a basic reproduction number of 2.73.

"Each patient creates exactly two point seven three more patients," Crowe announced when Ena showed him the result.

"On average," she corrected.

"Exactly on average, then."

The council gathered in the net loft. Its seven members sat far apart, although they continued passing the same kettle from hand to hand. Ena stood before a chalkboard and explained compartments, transmission rates and contact networks. She drew four boxes joined by arrows.

"People begin in the susceptible box," she said. "After contact, they enter the exposed box. Then infectious, then recovered. If we reduce the links between households, the epidemic should shrink."

Councillor Venn, who owned the floating cinema, raised his hand. "Which box is my wife in? She coughed once at breakfast."

"I can't tell you."

"What is the use of boxes that can't hold a person?"

No one laughed, and Ena suspected it was not a joke.

The council wanted a single action. Close the market, stop the ferries, untie the Fold and tow every house into open water—anything that could be stated on a notice. Ena asked for another six hours.

She returned to the string web. Most infected households had many coloured connections, which was unsurprising because most people in Lathwater did. Market sellers rode ferries. Ferry pilots ate at stalls. Children crossed three or four bridges to school. The network was so dense that every answer appeared to be the market.

Then Ena noticed an empty place.

Six cards formed a loose ring beside the window. They represented vessels that had spent at least three of the previous eight tides near Mooring 397. None had reported illness. Their strings were fewer and shorter than those around other central moorings.

Mooring 397 stood near the middle of the Fold, not at its edge. It had a public water hose, a ferry stop and a bridge connection. By all ordinary measures it should have been dangerous.

Ena asked her father about it.

"Three-nine-seven?" Oris said. "The bell."

Every numbered mooring had once carried a bronze fog bell, but most had been removed when electric horns arrived. The bell at 397 remained because its bolts had fused into the post. It was badly balanced and rang even on calm water.

"No one likes waiting there," Oris continued. "You can't hear yourself complain. Passengers stay aboard until the bridge drops. Neighbours don't chat. Children won't play near it."

Ena looked again at the six cards. The bell did not change the number of bridges or ferries. It changed how long people remained together.

Her institute models treated a contact as a contact. Two passengers sharing a bench for twenty seconds created the same line as two passengers sharing it for an hour. At Mooring 397, the ledger showed many lines, but the bell made them thin.

She began again. This time she assigned each connection a duration. Where duration was unknown, she estimated it from the timetable. Where the timetable was missing, she used her childhood memory of how long it took to buy bread, gut a fish or argue over ferry fares. She gave conversations at 397 one quarter of their normal weight.

The red cluster loosened.

At midnight, the calculator produced a new result: if average shared time fell by thirty-one percent, the reproduction number would drop from 2.73 to 0.94. Because 0.94 was below one, Ena concluded that no further household would become infected after the reduction began.

Crowe read the page twice. "You want me to close the market?"

"No. I want bells."

## The Bell Plan

By dawn, the council had requisitioned every bell in Lathwater.

They hung school bells over ferry benches, goat bells beneath market awnings and dinner bells beside the public pumps. A brass gong from the cinema was suspended over the eel stall. The harbour clock was ordered to strike every seven minutes, although it frequently struck eleven times because its mechanism was faulty.

The notices called it the Bell Plan. They instructed residents to conduct necessary business but leave any shared place before the next ring. Ena had proposed a more exact system based on four-minute contact windows. Crowe shortened it to: **WHEN IT RINGS, MOVE ALONG.**

The first morning was chaos. Each bell followed a different rhythm. A baker abandoned a tray halfway across a bridge. Ferry passengers stepped ashore at the wrong stop. Two families left the water queue at the same time and collided in a narrow lane. Children treated every ring as permission to run.

Ena watched from the infirmary roof, holding a stopwatch. She counted gatherings and estimated their duration. The gatherings were shorter, but there seemed to be more of them. She entered only the shorter duration into the model because gathering frequency was not one of the adjustable columns.

At noon, her father arrived with five ferry logs. He placed them on the table but kept his hand on the top one.

"The passengers hate this," he said.

"That may mean it is working."

"Pain is not proof, Ena."

She pulled the ledger from beneath his hand. "Neither is disliking arithmetic."

Oris sat down. Up close, she saw sweat shining beneath his eyes despite the cold room.

"When did your fever begin?" she asked.

"I don't have one."

"When?"

He looked towards the window. The gong at the eel stall sounded, followed by a thin scattering of bells. People moved across the bridges like seeds shaken in a tray.

"Night after the fair," he said.

That was six days earlier. Oris had worked every ferry shift since then. His household card sat near the centre of Ena's web, connected to almost every district.

"Why didn't you report it?"

"Because a cough makes a man a red pin, and a red pin isn't allowed to pilot."

"You could have infected half the Fold."

"Or I could have caught it from half the Fold. Your strings don't show which way anything travels."

The statement was true, but Ena hated him for making it. She called an orderly and had him taken to an isolation berth.

Before leaving, Oris nodded towards her calculator.

"Put me in the right box," he said.

His hidden illness altered the case history. Ena moved the beginning of the outbreak back by two days, but she did not recalculate the reproduction number because the council had already printed 2.73 on its emergency notices. Instead, she added Oris as an extra initial case. The projected curve rose sharply for the next morning, then bent down under the effect of the bells.

At dusk, the infirmary admitted nine new patients.

Crowe found Ena asleep beside the calculator. "Nine," he said. "Your model said none."

"They were already exposed before the bells."

"You said no further households."

"The intervention needs time."

"How much?"

Ena remembered the two-day incubation period she had chosen from three interviews. "Until tomorrow."

Crowe wanted to suspend the Bell Plan. Ena showed him the weighted network, tapping the pale threads around Mooring 397.

"This is the only naturally protected cluster in Lathwater," she said. "The only difference is the bell."

"There are six households there."

"Six households without illness."

Neither mentioned that two of those households were net-menders who spent most days alone beyond the harbour, one was an empty holiday vessel, and another had failed to submit its health card. Those details were recorded in separate ledgers on the other side of the room.

Crowe looked down at the moving harbour. "You have one more tide."

## The Curve

The next morning brought seven cases.

Ena called it a decline. The infirmary nurse pointed out that three families had not yet sent their reports, but Ena plotted the number before those forms arrived. On the graph, the epidemic curved down exactly where the model predicted.

The harbour council rang the bells twice as often.

By afternoon, four additional patients arrived. Ena assigned them to the previous day on the grounds that their symptoms had begun before noon. The curve remained unchanged.

Lathwater became a town measured by interruptions. At every ring, conversations broke apart. Cups were left half-filled. Buyers walked away before receiving change. The usual harbour noises—saws, gulls, engines and shouted names—were buried beneath bronze clamour.

Ena visited Oris in the isolation berth. He sat under a grey blanket, looking across the water at his unattended ferry.

"Seven today," she said.

"Eleven. I heard the nurse."

"Four began yesterday."

"Did the sick people know which day you needed them on?"

"Cases are assigned by symptom onset. That is standard."

"And when does your curve say I became sick?"

Ena did not answer.

Oris's fever was already falling. Lantern halos still clouded his vision, and he mistook a coil of rope for a sleeping dog. Ena poured water for him.

"Your mother hated that bell," he said. "At 397. Once, during a storm, she tried to stop it with a scarf. The bell swallowed the scarf and rang louder."

"I don't remember."

"You were away learning boxes."

The cruelty of this was so plain that it seemed rehearsed, yet his expression immediately softened.

"I'm sorry," he said.

"So am I."

They embraced, resolving the six years in which they had spoken only through birthday notes and harbour invoices. Ena felt the anger leave her as completely as water draining from a basin.

Outside, the bells rang. Oris covered his ears.

On the third morning, there were three cases. No late forms arrived. On the fourth, there was one. The patient was a boy from a house that had never visited the market but had shared a water hose with two infected families. Ena considered adding water transmission to the model. Doing so would require rebuilding the network, and the curve was already falling, so she classified the hose as an ordinary social contact.

On the fifth morning, no new yellow cloth appeared.

Crowe convened the council at Mooring 397. The six supposedly protected households stood on their decks while photographers from the upriver newspapers recorded the bell. Ena was asked to explain how the model had saved Lathwater.

She spoke of weighted contacts and mobile networks. She explained that place alone did not spread disease; people met through time, and duration could matter as much as distance. Those listening nodded whenever the bell allowed them to hear.

Councillor Venn asked whether the epidemic was over.

Ena looked at her latest page. The model predicted 0.18 cases during the next week. Since a fraction of a person could not become ill, she rounded this to zero.

"Yes," she said. "It is over."

Crowe ordered the market reopened without restrictions. The bells were taken down except for the one at 397, which no tool had managed to loosen.

## The Harbour After

Lantern fever did not return that summer.

No one discovered its cause. The infirmary nurse suspected a respiratory virus brought by traders at the fair. The water engineer blamed algae in a storage tank. Oris believed half the cases had been common colds renamed by frightened neighbours. Ena's model did not distinguish among these possibilities, but its predicted decline matched the final chart, and the council stored both in the town archive.

The Bell Plan became a festival. On the anniversary of the outbreak, shopkeepers rang brass chimes every seven minutes while children ran from stall to stall. Visitors bought small models of Mooring 397. The cinema produced a play in which an actress portraying Ena defeated a black-robed Fever by striking a silver gong.

Ena stayed in Lathwater as Director of Tidal Epidemiology, a title Crowe invented for her. She built a new office above the ferry terminal and covered one wall with a permanent network of cards and strings. Whenever the tide changed, an assistant moved the cards.

She and Oris ate breakfast together each week. He never apologised for hiding his fever again, and she never asked him to. Their reconciliation had become another fact stored without its uncertainty.

Years later, Ena sometimes woke before dawn and walked alone to Mooring 397. Rust had opened holes in the old bell. Its note was no longer loud, but the tide could still draw a low sound from it.

From there, Lathwater looked orderly. Houses rested in rows, bridges joined their proper neighbours, and ferry lamps travelled along fixed lanes. Only the tide revealed that the order was temporary.

Ena carried the original graph folded in her coat. Its line rose through thirty-one cases, climbed again, and then descended cleanly to zero. She never added the missing reports, the unoccupied vessel or her father's earlier symptoms. Those details belonged to other pages, and other pages made other shapes.

At sunrise, the houses began to swing. Chains tightened below the water. Kitchens separated from workshops; bedrooms approached the market. For one minute every bridge lay crooked between two possible maps.

Then the bell sounded, and the town moved on.

# The Porchlight Effect: What Happened After FieldLoom Began Prompting Volunteers at Night

## Executive summary

FieldLoom is a citizen science platform used by residents of six neighboring municipalities to submit photographs and classifications of local wildlife. On 15 June 2025, the platform introduced the **Porchlight Minute** in three municipalities. At 9:30 p.m., eligible users received a notification asking them to spend one minute observing insects or other small animals near an outdoor light. The prompt also appeared as a card on the application home screen and awarded a Glowstreak badge after three nights of participation.

This analysis asks whether the feature increased participation and broadened the kinds of observations contributed to FieldLoom. It compares activity before and after launch in the three rollout municipalities with activity in three municipalities that did not receive the feature.

The main findings are:

- Weekly active observers increased by 35.0% in rollout municipalities, compared with 8.1% in comparison municipalities.
- The proportion of records submitted during the night window rose from 18.2% to 38.7% in rollout municipalities. The equivalent increase in comparison municipalities was from 17.5% to 21.2%.
- New-observer registrations followed by a first contribution increased by 65.1% in rollout municipalities, compared with 12.9% elsewhere.
- The mean number of broad taxonomic categories recorded per observer-week increased from 1.84 to 2.31 in rollout municipalities.
- Thirty-day return among new observers improved by approximately eight percentage points relative to the pre-launch difference.
- Verification performance deteriorated. The recorded verification rate fell from 71.4% to 62.8% in rollout municipalities, while the median time to a first moderator decision increased.

Taken together, the figures indicate that the Porchlight Minute caused a substantial expansion in both nighttime activity and the diversity of participation. The feature appears especially effective at converting low-intensity or dormant accounts into contributors. The increase was not free: moderators received more poorly framed insect photographs, and a larger proportion of records remained unresolved.

FieldLoom should retain the feature and extend it to the other municipalities, while adding basic photography guidance and limiting prompts during periods of heavy moderation demand.

## Platform and feature context

FieldLoom accepts photographs, short audio clips, and manual sighting records. Contributors choose an initial label, such as moth, beetle, spider, bird, plant, or unknown organism. Volunteer moderators can confirm the label, replace it, request more evidence, or mark the record unresolved. Records do not need to reach species level to remain visible.

The six municipalities in this analysis are Alderfen, Merecross, Kestrel Ward, North Brindle, Oakhaven, and Ternwick. The first three received the Porchlight Minute. The latter three continued to receive FieldLoom’s ordinary weekly digest but no nighttime prompt or Glowstreak badge.

- 612 records created by staff test accounts;
- 1,034 records without a usable municipality field; and

An observer was considered active in a week if the account submitted at least one included record. A new observer was an account making its first-ever included FieldLoom contribution. A returning new observer was one that contributed on at least one later calendar day within 30 days of its first contribution.

Consequently, records from late August had less opportunity to be verified than records from May or June.

## Analytical approach

The main design is a pre-post comparison with a comparison group. For each outcome, the change in the three rollout municipalities is compared with the change in the other three municipalities. For percentage outcomes, the estimated feature effect is expressed as the rollout change in percentage points minus the comparison change in percentage points.

For count outcomes, percentage growth is compared instead. For example, weekly active observers grew by 35.0% in rollout municipalities and by 8.1% in comparison municipalities, producing a reported net increase of 26.9 percentage points. This approach is easy to interpret across outcomes with different starting levels.

The analysis also examines each municipality separately, notification opening behavior, taxonomic composition, and early retention. No regression adjustment was applied because the municipalities appeared reasonably similar at baseline on the main platform measures. Weather, school holidays, local events, and changes in daylight were not incorporated into the estimates.

## Baseline comparison

The two groups had broadly comparable levels of FieldLoom use before launch, although the rollout group was somewhat larger.

| Weekly measure, pre-launch | Rollout municipalities | Comparison municipalities |
|---|---:|---:|
| Active observers | 1,562 | 1,421 |
| Included records | 2,471 | 2,258 |
| Records per active observer | 1.58 | 1.59 |
| New observers | 321 | 295 |
| Night records | 18.2% | 17.5% |
| Verified records | 71.4% | 73.1% |
| Taxonomic categories per observer-week | 1.84 | 1.79 |

The similarities in records per observer, night share, and taxonomic breadth support the use of the comparison municipalities as an indication of what would have happened without the prompt. The higher historical use of moth labels in the rollout municipalities did not produce a large baseline difference in the broad category measure.

## Results

### Participation increased after launch

Weekly active observers increased to 2,108 in rollout municipalities, a gain of 546 observers or 35.0%. Comparison municipalities increased to 1,536 weekly active observers, a gain of 115 or 8.1%.

| Weekly measure | Rollout pre | Rollout post | Change | Comparison pre | Comparison post | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Active observers | 1,562 | 2,108 | +35.0% | 1,421 | 1,536 | +8.1% |
| Included records | 2,471 | 3,870 | +56.6% | 2,258 | 2,526 | +11.9% |
| New observers | 321 | 530 | +65.1% | 295 | 333 | +12.9% |
| Records per observer | 1.58 | 1.84 | +16.5% | 1.59 | 1.64 | +3.1% |

New observers rose faster than total observers. ### The time profile changed sharply

There was no obvious displacement from weekend mornings. Rollout municipalities averaged 812 weekend-morning records per week before launch and 835 afterward. This is important because an evening increase could otherwise represent existing participants moving their usual activity rather than adding observations.

The upload-time substitution for records without observation times could exaggerate this pattern. However, removing the 11% of records without a separate observation time still produced a rollout increase of 18.9 percentage points in night share. The corresponding comparison increase was 3.3 points. The basic result therefore remains.

### Growth occurred in all three rollout municipalities

| Municipality | Feature status | Change in active observers | Change in night share |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Alderfen | Rollout | +46% | +24.6 points |
| Merecross | Rollout | +28% | +15.3 points |
| Kestrel Ward | Rollout | +31% | +10.8 points |
| North Brindle | Comparison | +11% | +4.8 points |
| Oakhaven | Comparison | +7% | +3.1 points |
| Ternwick | Comparison | +6% | +2.5 points |

Alderfen’s effect was the largest. Its coordinator ran two informal identification sessions during the study period, which may have reinforced the prompt. Nevertheless, even the smallest rollout increase was larger than growth in any comparison municipality. The direction of the results is therefore not dependent on a single place.

### Prompt opening was associated with more contribution

The platform attempted 14,820 push deliveries during the post-launch period. Of these, 10,226 were recorded as successfully delivered and 3,681 were opened. Among accounts that opened at least one prompt, 52% submitted a record within 12 hours of an opening. Among accounts receiving but never opening a prompt, 14% submitted during any equivalent 12-hour prompt window.

Users opening four or more prompts averaged 9.2 post-launch records, compared with 4.7 among those opening one to three and 2.1 among delivered non-openers. This dose pattern supports the conclusion that repeated exposure generated additional activity rather than the results being entirely due to seasonal change.

Even so, the fourfold gap in prompt-window contribution is too large to be explained by the baseline difference alone.

The rollout municipalities produced 327 labels described as a first district occurrence during 2025, compared with 89 in the comparison municipalities. The figure is better understood as an indicator that participants supplied material outside the platform’s usual set of records.

If a general increase in enthusiasm or favorable weather explained the entire result, a comparable rise in this established category might be expected. Its stability points toward a feature-specific nighttime effect.

The comparison rate was 34.6%. Before launch, the rates were 32.9% and 33.8%, respectively. The difference in changes is therefore 8.1 percentage points.

## Interpretation

The strongest evidence for a Porchlight Minute effect is the combination of timing, location, and outcome specificity. Activity rose most in the municipalities receiving the prompt, records clustered in the hours immediately after delivery, and the largest category increases were the small nighttime organisms named by the task. All three rollout municipalities moved in the same direction, while daytime bird activity remained almost flat.

The feature appears to have done more than shift uploads into the night. Total records, active observers, first contributors, and later returns all increased. This pattern suggests that the prompt reduced the effort required to decide what to observe. A participant did not need to plan a trip, recognize a rare species, or wait for a weekend. The task supplied a location, a duration, and a subject.

A seasonal explanation is possible because the launch occurred in mid-June, when insect activity and evening outdoor activity generally increase. The comparison municipalities also experienced summer and showed only modest gains. It is unlikely that seasonality accounts for the additional 26.9 percentage points of active-observer growth in rollout locations.

The poorer verification result is a meaningful cost but not a reason to withdraw the feature. Broad participation and immediate species-level accuracy are different platform goals. An unresolved image may still introduce a participant to observation practice. In addition, repeated prompt openers produced better records than one-time participants, suggesting that quality can rise with experience.

## Operational cost estimate

FieldLoom moderators processed an average of 34 records per paid hour during May. Using a fully loaded moderation cost of 24 platform credits per hour, an additional 1,105 weekly records above the comparison-group growth trend would require approximately 32.5 hours, or 780 credits per week, if every record required the same handling.

In practice, many records receive no paid review because volunteer moderators act first. Paid staff reported spending 9.1 additional hours per week on the rollout municipalities, implying a direct cost closer to 218 credits per week. Dividing this by the estimated 519 additional active observers gives a weekly cost of 0.42 credits per added active observer.

This calculation excludes feature design, coordinator time, notification infrastructure, and the value of volunteer labor. It also assumes the comparison-group growth rate represents the correct no-feature path. Even with those exclusions, the result suggests the prompt is inexpensive relative to field events that require staff travel.

## Limitations

The municipalities were not randomly assigned. Rollout locations were selected partly because of reliable coordinators and existing moth interest. Those characteristics could independently produce stronger summer growth. Baseline platform measures were similar, but similar averages do not establish that the groups would have followed parallel trends after June.

Only three municipalities received the feature. User-level totals make the dataset appear large, but the rollout decision occurred at the municipality level. The estimates do not account for correlation among people exposed to the same coordinator, weather, or local publicity, and no confidence intervals are reported.

Weather was not available in the export. Canceled prompts provide some protection against the wettest nights, but ordinary differences in temperature, wind, and cloud cover could affect both insect visibility and willingness to participate. Daylight also changed during the analysis period, while the night window remained fixed by the clock.

The night measure combines observation time and upload time. The sensitivity check excluding upload-only records gives a similar result, although excluding them may selectively remove participants with weak connectivity or different application habits.

Taxonomic breadth relies on initial contributor labels. The prompt’s interface placed moth, beetle, and spider buttons at the top of the label menu, so part of the measured increase may reflect interface selection rather than genuinely broader observation. First district occurrences are especially vulnerable to mistakes and are not confirmed range records.

Verification data are right-censored because status was extracted only two days after the end of August. The exclusion of the final two weeks reduces but does not solve this problem, since moderator delays changed during the rollout.

Finally, retention captures any second-day contribution, not sustained participation over several months. The study period is too short to show whether Porchlight Minute participants become durable contributors or disappear when the badge is complete.

## Recommendations

FieldLoom should expand the Porchlight Minute to North Brindle, Oakhaven, and Ternwick for an eight-week trial. The expansion should be staggered by two weeks across municipalities so that the operations team can compare each location with places not yet activated. Random assignment of eligible accounts within municipalities would provide an even stronger test, although it may disappoint users who see neighbors receiving the badge.

Before expansion, the prompt should include three short instructions: steady the device against a fixed surface, avoid pointing directly into the light, and photograph both the upper and lower side of an insect when possible. A sample preview can show the desired framing without requiring participants to identify the organism.

The platform should pause prompts when the unresolved moderation queue exceeds 4,000 records and recruit a rotating insect-review group before midsummer. The badge should remain because the retention results suggest that repeated participation is more valuable than a single response.

Future reporting should preserve the status of each record exactly 14 days after upload, distinguish capture time from sync time, and measure retention at 30, 90, and 180 days. Weather and coordinator events should also be recorded.

On the available evidence, the Porchlight Minute achieved its central purpose: it brought more people onto FieldLoom at an underrepresented time and generated observations outside the platform’s usual daytime mix. The moderation burden is manageable and can be reduced through guidance. A wider rollout is justified, provided it is accompanied by better measurement.

If a general increase in enthusiasm or favorable weather explained the entire result, a comparable rise in this established category might be expected. Its stability points toward a feature-specific nighttime effect.

### New-observer return improved

For new observers whose first contribution occurred early enough to allow 30 days of follow-up, 41.8% in rollout municipalities contributed on another day within 30 days. The comparison rate was 34.6%. Before launch, the rates were 32.9% and 33.8%, respectively. The difference in changes is therefore 8.1 percentage points.

The retention calculation includes 2,140 post-launch new observers in rollout municipalities and 1,334 in comparison municipalities. It excludes late entrants without a complete follow-up window. It also counts any later contribution, even if it was uploaded only a few minutes after midnight following the first session. Requiring the return to occur at least seven days later lowered post-launch retention to 27.3% in the rollout group and 23.1% in the comparison group, leaving a smaller but still positive difference.

This supports the idea that a simple, time-bounded task gives first-time users a reason to come back. The Glowstreak badge may contribute because it requires activity on three separate nights.

### Verification performance worsened

The verification rate shown in the export fell from 71.4% to 62.8% in rollout municipalities. Comparison municipalities declined only from 73.1% to 70.9%. Median time from upload to first moderator decision increased from 3.2 days to 5.8 days in rollout municipalities.

The decline was concentrated in moth, other insect, and unknown-organism records. Moderators frequently marked images as unresolved because they were blurred, overexposed by a light, or lacked a view of distinguishing features. Records from participants who opened four or more prompts were verified at 68.5%, compared with 57.2% for one-time prompt participants. Practice may therefore improve submission quality.

Late-August records had little time to acquire a verification decision before the 2 September export. Excluding the final two weeks raised the rollout post-launch verification rate from 62.8% to 65.7%. This does not eliminate the decline, though it shows that part of the apparent moderation problem comes from incomplete follow-up.

## Interpretation

The strongest evidence for a Porchlight Minute effect is the combination of timing, location, and outcome specificity. Activity rose most in the municipalities receiving the prompt, records clustered in the hours immediately after delivery, and the largest category increases were the small nighttime organisms named by the task. All three rollout municipalities moved in the same direction, while daytime bird activity remained almost flat.

The feature appears to have done more than shift uploads into the night. Total records, active observers, first contributors, and later returns all increased. This pattern suggests that the prompt reduced the effort required to decide what to observe. A participant did not need to plan a trip, recognize a rare species, or wait for a weekend. The task supplied a location, a duration, and a subject.

A seasonal explanation is possible because the launch occurred in mid-June, when insect activity and evening outdoor activity generally increase. The comparison municipalities also experienced summer and showed only modest gains. It is unlikely that seasonality accounts for the additional 26.9 percentage points of active-observer growth in rollout locations.

The poorer verification result is a meaningful cost but not a reason to withdraw the feature. Broad participation and immediate species-level accuracy are different platform goals. An unresolved image may still introduce a participant to observation practice. In addition, repeated prompt openers produced better records than one-time participants, suggesting that quality can rise with experience.

## Operational cost estimate

FieldLoom moderators processed an average of 34 records per paid hour during May. Using a fully loaded moderation cost of 24 platform credits per hour, an additional 1,105 weekly records above the comparison-group growth trend would require approximately 32.5 hours, or 780 credits per week, if every record required the same handling.

In practice, many records receive no paid review because volunteer moderators act first. Paid staff reported spending 9.1 additional hours per week on the rollout municipalities, implying a direct cost closer to 218 credits per week. Dividing this by the estimated 519 additional active observers gives a weekly cost of 0.42 credits per added active observer.

This calculation excludes feature design, coordinator time, notification infrastructure, and the value of volunteer labor. It also assumes the comparison-group growth rate represents the correct no-feature path. Even with those exclusions, the result suggests the prompt is inexpensive relative to field events that require staff travel.

## Limitations

The municipalities were not randomly assigned. Rollout locations were selected partly because of reliable coordinators and existing moth interest. Those characteristics could independently produce stronger summer growth. Baseline platform measures were similar, but similar averages do not establish that the groups would have followed parallel trends after June.

Only three municipalities received the feature. User-level totals make the dataset appear large, but the rollout decision occurred at the municipality level. The estimates do not account for correlation among people exposed to the same coordinator, weather, or local publicity, and no confidence intervals are reported.

Weather was not available in the export. Canceled prompts provide some protection against the wettest nights, but ordinary differences in temperature, wind, and cloud cover could affect both insect visibility and willingness to participate. Daylight also changed during the analysis period, while the night window remained fixed by the clock.

The night measure combines observation time and upload time. The sensitivity check excluding upload-only records gives a similar result, although excluding them may selectively remove participants with weak connectivity or different application habits.

Taxonomic breadth relies on initial contributor labels. The prompt’s interface placed moth, beetle, and spider buttons at the top of the label menu, so part of the measured increase may reflect interface selection rather than genuinely broader observation. First district occurrences are especially vulnerable to mistakes and are not confirmed range records.

Verification data are right-censored because status was extracted only two days after the end of August. The exclusion of the final two weeks reduces but does not solve this problem, since moderator delays changed during the rollout.

Finally, retention captures any second-day contribution, not sustained participation over several months. The study period is too short to show whether Porchlight Minute participants become durable contributors or disappear when the badge is complete.

## Recommendations

FieldLoom should expand the Porchlight Minute to North Brindle, Oakhaven, and Ternwick for an eight-week trial. The expansion should be staggered by two weeks across municipalities so that the operations team can compare each location with places not yet activated. Random assignment of eligible accounts within municipalities would provide an even stronger test, although it may disappoint users who see neighbors receiving the badge.

Before expansion, the prompt should include three short instructions: steady the device against a fixed surface, avoid pointing directly into the light, and photograph both the upper and lower side of an insect when possible. A sample preview can show the desired framing without requiring participants to identify the organism.

The platform should pause prompts when the unresolved moderation queue exceeds 4,000 records and recruit a rotating insect-review group before midsummer. The badge should remain because the retention results suggest that repeated participation is more valuable than a single response.

Future reporting should preserve the status of each record exactly 14 days after upload, distinguish capture time from sync time, and measure retention at 30, 90, and 180 days. Weather and coordinator events should also be recorded.

On the available evidence, the Porchlight Minute achieved its central purpose: it brought more people onto FieldLoom at an underrepresented time and generated observations outside the platform’s usual daytime mix. The moderation burden is manageable and can be reduced through guidance. A wider rollout is justified, provided it is accompanied by better measurement.
