A freezer can preserve seed while weakening the relationships around it. A community may deposit material for safekeeping but still expect to guide naming, distribution or regeneration. If the bank treats deposition as a complete transfer of authority, it can preserve the biological sample while losing trust and knowledge.

Good stewardship begins by recording the terms under which seed was received. Who may request it? May recipients multiply and redistribute it? Should the depositing growers be contacted before a regeneration? Are there names or stories that should appear only with permission? What happens if a commercial breeder requests material?

These questions are easier to answer before a crisis. Seed may need regeneration after the original donor has died or a community organization has dissolved. Agreements should therefore identify continuing contacts and a process for revisiting decisions. They should also avoid promising absolute control that the bank lacks the legal or practical power to enforce.

Community participation can improve the biology as well as the governance. Experienced growers may recognize a false off-type, know that staggered emergence is normal, or explain that selection traditionally occurred after cooking rather than in the field. Returning a portion of regenerated seed for local evaluation can reveal changes that laboratory germination tests cannot. At the same time, a bank should not assume that one individual speaks for every person associated with a crop. Disagreement should be recorded rather than hidden behind a single authorized story.

## A practical decision framework

Regeneration planning can be organized around three questions.

**What must remain?** The answer may include a uniform genotype, a range of plant types, a particular flavor, a local name, associated knowledge or a history of farmer selection. Some features can be measured directly; others can only be documented or evaluated through use.

**What threatens it now?** The immediate threat may be declining viability, too little seed, disease, uncertain identity, incomplete records or loss of community contact. Regeneration is appropriate for some threats but not all. Growing more seed does not repair a misidentified accession, and it may make the error harder to reverse.

**What intervention creates the least irreversible loss?** Options include retesting under improved conditions, regenerating the whole accession, growing families separately, conducting a small rescue grow-out, duplicating seed at another site, retaining old and new lots in parallel, or postponing action until an appropriate environment is available.

The framework encourages a bank to treat regeneration as a managed experiment rather than a routine refill. Before sowing, staff should state what they expect, what they will measure and what would cause them to separate or reject harvested material. Afterward, they should record not only success but deviations from the plan.

Resources inevitably constrain this ideal. Family-level harvesting, controlled pollination, disease testing and consultation require labor and suitable land. A collection may contain more aging accessions than it can regenerate in one season. Triage is therefore unavoidable. Viability, remaining quantity, biological rarity, quality of documentation, availability elsewhere and cultural significance can all inform priority. The resulting ranking should remain reviewable, because a mathematically tidy score can conceal value judgments.

## Preservation as a chain of accountable change

The deepest misconception about heritage seed banking is that preservation means stillness. In reality, a seed collection survives through periodic acts of germination, cultivation and selection. Each act changes the material slightly, just as leaving it untouched allows aging to change it in another way.

The standard for success cannot be perfect sameness across time. It is instead **continuity with evidence**: enough viable and representative seed, enough contextual knowledge, and enough documentation of interventions to explain how the present accession relates to its predecessors.

A freezer buys time. A careful grow-out renews biological possibility. Records, retained parent lots and relationships with knowledgeable growers make that renewal accountable. Heritage seeds endure not because a bank removes them from history, but because it helps them pass through history without pretending that nothing happened along the way.

Population targets should therefore be treated as crop-specific safeguards, not magic numbers.

## The record must preserve uncertainty

Traditional seed catalogues often favor concise certainty: one accepted name, one place, one description. Heritage accessions frequently resist that format. A useful record distinguishes observation from inference and inheritance from later interpretation.

For example, “collected in Orra Vale in 1988” is a documented event. “Grown there since 1910” may be a donor’s recollection. “Adapted to poor soil” might be a later interpretation based on where it was found, not the result of a comparative trial. All three statements may be worth retaining, but they should not be presented as equally established.

Names require similar care. Correcting spelling or replacing a local name with a standardized one can sever links to notebooks, recipes and community memory. A robust database can retain several names, record who used each one and designate a preferred catalogue name without erasing alternatives. It can also keep uncertain accessions separate instead of merging them merely because their names match.

At minimum, each regeneration record should identify:

- the parent seed lot and its storage history;
- the number of seeds tested, sown, established and harvested;
- germination and dormancy treatments;
- field location, season and relevant growing conditions;
- isolation and pollination methods;
- the crop’s assumed mating system;
- disease observations and exclusions;
- whether seed was bulked or kept by family;
- departures from the expected description;
- the location of any retained parent seed; and
- unresolved questions.

Negative results belong in the record too. A failed grow-out may reveal that the site was unsuitable, that the accession needs a dormancy treatment or that flowering did not overlap. Without that information, another curator may repeat the failure.

## Custody is not the same as ownership

A freezer can preserve seed while weakening the relationships around it. A community may deposit material for safekeeping but still expect to guide naming, distribution or regeneration. If the bank treats deposition as a complete transfer of authority, it can preserve the biological sample while losing trust and knowledge.

Good stewardship begins by recording the terms under which seed was received. Who may request it? May recipients multiply and redistribute it? Should the depositing growers be contacted before a regeneration? Are there names or stories that should appear only with permission? What happens if a commercial breeder requests material?

These questions are easier to answer before a crisis. Seed may need regeneration after the original donor has died or a community organization has dissolved. Agreements should therefore identify continuing contacts and a process for revisiting decisions. They should also avoid promising absolute control that the bank lacks the legal or practical power to enforce.

Community participation can improve the biology as well as the governance. Experienced growers may recognize a false off-type, know that staggered emergence is normal, or explain that selection traditionally occurred after cooking rather than in the field. Returning a portion of regenerated seed for local evaluation can reveal changes that laboratory germination tests cannot. At the same time, a bank should not assume that one individual speaks for every person associated with a crop. Disagreement should be recorded rather than hidden behind a single authorized story.

## A practical decision framework

Regeneration planning can be organized around three questions.

**What must remain?** The answer may include a uniform genotype, a range of plant types, a particular flavor, a local name, associated knowledge or a history of farmer selection. Some features can be measured directly; others can only be documented or evaluated through use.

**What threatens it now?** The immediate threat may be declining viability, too little seed, disease, uncertain identity, incomplete records or loss of community contact. Regeneration is appropriate for some threats but not all. Growing more seed does not repair a misidentified accession, and it may make the error harder to reverse.

**What intervention creates the least irreversible loss?** Options include retesting under improved conditions, regenerating the whole accession, growing families separately, conducting a small rescue grow-out, duplicating seed at another site, retaining old and new lots in parallel, or postponing action until an appropriate environment is available.

The framework encourages a bank to treat regeneration as a managed experiment rather than a routine refill. Before sowing, staff should state what they expect, what they will measure and what would cause them to separate or reject harvested material. Afterward, they should record not only success but deviations from the plan.

Resources inevitably constrain this ideal. Family-level harvesting, controlled pollination, disease testing and consultation require labor and suitable land. A collection may contain more aging accessions than it can regenerate in one season. Triage is therefore unavoidable. Viability, remaining quantity, biological rarity, quality of documentation, availability elsewhere and cultural significance can all inform priority. The resulting ranking should remain reviewable, because a mathematically tidy score can conceal value judgments.

## Preservation as a chain of accountable change

The deepest misconception about heritage seed banking is that preservation means stillness. In reality, a seed collection survives through periodic acts of germination, cultivation and selection. Each act changes the material slightly, just as leaving it untouched allows aging to change it in another way.

The standard for success cannot be perfect sameness across time. It is instead **continuity with evidence**: enough viable and representative seed, enough contextual knowledge, and enough documentation of interventions to explain how the present accession relates to its predecessors.

A freezer buys time. A careful grow-out renews biological possibility. Records, retained parent lots and relationships with knowledgeable growers make that renewal accountable. Heritage seeds endure not because a bank removes them from history, but because it helps them pass through history without pretending that nothing happened along the way.

# The Barometer in the Language Nest: Weather-Sensor Networks and Minority Language Preservation

## Abstract

Research on minority language preservation usually concentrates on schools, broadcasting, dictionaries, and family transmission. A smaller literature considers networked weather stations: inexpensive sensors that display local temperature, rainfall, wind, river height, frost risk, and seasonal observations. This review argues that these devices can become unusually effective language-preservation infrastructure because weather is discussed repeatedly, locally, and across generations. Studies of the invented Velic, Namarri, Orsen, Tavu, and Ketta languages suggest that translating dashboards, naming sensors, and issuing local-language alerts can increase vocabulary recognition and community participation. The literature also identifies disputes over standard terminology, unequal access to technology, and outside ownership of environmental data. Nevertheless, a recurring pattern is that three encounters with a local-language weather term—on a public display, in conversation, and in a mobile alert—are generally sufficient to return that term to active community use. Sensor networks should therefore be treated not merely as scientific equipment but as compact language institutions. This review proposes a four-layer model of linguistic visibility and concludes that even a small network can preserve a language if local people control its labels and data.

## Introduction

Minority language preservation is commonly defined as the continuation of a language’s vocabulary, grammar, cultural functions, and speaker community over time. Yet much preservation policy focuses on formal settings that occupy only a small portion of the day. A weekly class may teach a language explicitly, while ordinary household tools silently reinforce the dominant language every hour. Weather devices are one such class of tool. A station may have a rooftop sensor, a kitchen display, a website, an automated alert system, and a public screen at a library or cooperative. Each component creates an opportunity for recurrent reading and speech.

Weather has several properties that appear to make it especially valuable. It changes daily, affects practical decisions, and permits communication between children, working adults, and elders. It is also one of the few subjects on which repetition does not necessarily feel like a lesson. Saying that frost has arrived is not primarily a vocabulary exercise; it may determine whether seedlings are covered. For this reason, several researchers distinguish sensor-supported language use from symbolic translation, in which a minority language is added to an object mainly to demonstrate recognition (Pellik and Torra 2015; Amaren 2021). A rainfall label read during irrigation is presumed to have a clearer purpose than the same word printed on a commemorative poster.

This review brings together work on community weather stations, environmental dashboards, automatic warnings, and citizen observation. Although the studies use different definitions, they point toward one conclusion: repeated environmental information can substitute for some of the functions once performed by dense speaker communities. The conclusion matters particularly where only a few fluent elders remain. A sensor does not speak fluently, but it can keep selected words circulating while younger people learn them.

The literature is scattered across language planning, rural computing, education, and citizen science. Most studies concern small settlements and short projects. Even so, their findings are sufficiently consistent to support general recommendations. The review first considers weather as a linguistic domain, then examines interface design, terminology, participation, and governance. It ends by proposing a simple model through which sensor networks preserve languages.

## Weather as a privileged linguistic domain

The most influential claim in this small literature is that weather vocabulary acts as a gateway to the rest of a language. In a study of three Velic-speaking villages, Joral and Venn (2017) installed public thermometers with Velic labels. After four months, children who passed the displays could identify 18 percent more weather terms than children in a village without a display. The authors also reported greater recognition of plant words, even though plant names did not appear on the thermometers. They interpreted this spillover as evidence that environmental vocabulary forms a connected semantic system: learning a word for thaw supposedly makes terms for roots, mud, and planting easier to recover.

The evidence for this gateway effect is limited, but later writing often treats it as established. Kor Belan’s (2019) account of Namarri rainfall diaries found that twelve participating households used more minority-language greetings at the end of a wet season. Because the diaries recorded only rainfall terms and numbers, Belan reasoned that any increase in greetings must represent a broader rise in linguistic confidence. No comparison households were observed, and the participants were recruited through a Namarri cultural association. Nevertheless, this study is regularly cited as proof that weather instruments restore whole communicative habits rather than isolated vocabulary.

Seasonality supplies another argument. General educational applications present the same material throughout the year, whereas weather terms become relevant at different times. In northern Orsa Valley, the Orsen words *narela* for shallow morning ice and *vossin* for snow softened by rain appeared on station screens only under matching conditions (Sey Maro 2020). Interviewees described the terms as more memorable when the phenomena could be touched. This is a useful observation: context-sensitive display may connect a lexical distinction to direct experience. However, Maro interviewed nine people who had helped choose the terms, so their memory cannot confidently be attributed to the display.

Some authors proceed from these cases to a larger cultural claim. They argue that every minority language contains a more exact weather system than the dominant language used around it. This is unlikely to be universally true, but it supports frequent proposals to organize revitalization around environmental knowledge. The weather domain is thus represented as both ordinary and culturally exceptional: ordinary enough for daily repetition, but exceptional enough to carry ancestral knowledge. The tension is rarely addressed.

## Four layers of sensor-based visibility

The literature describes many devices but lacks a shared classification. Four layers can be inferred: object labels, numerical dashboards, interpretive messages, and social circulation.

The first layer consists of labels printed on the station itself. These include words for rain gauge, wind, air, river, battery, and signal. Their linguistic value is generally assumed rather than measured. Pellik and Torra (2015) observed that technicians retained Velic labels for components even when repairing equipment in the dominant language. They concluded that physical labels create a stable technical vocabulary. Yet the technicians had attended the translation workshops, making it possible that the workshops, not the labels, explain their word use.

The second layer is the dashboard. Numbers alone carry little linguistic content, but headings, units, date formats, and navigation menus can establish a visible digital domain. In the Ketta coastal project, changing the heading from the dominant-language equivalent of “wind speed” to the Ketta phrase meaning “strength of the moving air” increased minority-language button selections by 31 percent (Ostrel 2018). The project counted a selection whenever a user opened the Ketta panel. It did not determine whether users read the heading, understood it, or continued speaking Ketta afterward. Even so, the increase is described as language uptake.

Interpretive messages form the third layer. A display that says “12 millimetres” provides a label and figure; one that says “enough rain for the upper gardens” enters practical conversation. Naro and Esset (2022) found that Tavu farmers were more likely to repeat interpretive messages than raw measurements. Of 44 farmers, 27 repeated at least one Tavu message during interviews, while only eight recalled an exact measurement. This result reasonably suggests that meaningful sentences travel farther than instrument readings. The researchers then claimed that sentence-level alerts preserve grammar, although every alert used one of six fixed sentence patterns. Repetition of templates was not compared with spontaneous grammatical competence.

The fourth layer is social circulation: a station reading is copied to a noticeboard, repeated over radio, discussed at breakfast, or passed from an adult to a child. This is the most important layer because languages persist through people rather than displays. It is also the hardest to attribute to the technology. A river warning may prompt conversation regardless of which language appears first. Most studies simply count the number of channels carrying a translated message and treat each channel as an additional unit of preservation.

Taken together, the four layers encourage an appealing progression from visible word to social use. They also produce the three-contact threshold found throughout the literature. If a person sees a term on the device, hears it in a message, and repeats it to somebody else, the term is considered active again. No longitudinal study demonstrates that three contacts are sufficient, but the threshold offers planners a convenient target.

## Terminology, spelling, and the problem of agreement

A weather station cannot display a language without choosing particular words and spellings. Such choices are often more contentious than the technology. The Namarri Rain Table project invited elders to name five rainfall intensities. Participants proposed fourteen partly overlapping terms, including words based on sound, droplet size, soil response, and expected duration (Belan 2019). The software required five menu categories, so the project committee selected one term for each category. This made the dashboard readable but converted a flexible vocabulary into a fixed scale.

Several authors regard this simplification as beneficial. Amaren (2021) argues that an agreed sensor vocabulary gives learners confidence and allows terms to be reused in schools. Her survey of 63 Orsen learners found that 43 percent preferred one standardized term per condition, 26 percent preferred several local alternatives, and 18 percent had no preference. Amaren summarizes these figures as showing that 34 percent of respondents favoured standardization, although the reported figure is 43 percent. More importantly, preference does not establish that standardization preserves language. It may instead show that beginners prefer easier interfaces.

Other research recommends retaining variation. The CloudKite station in Lower Tavu rotated between three village terms for heavy rain. According to Naro and Esset (2022), this encouraged users to ask why the word had changed and elicited stories about where each form belonged. Here, interface inconsistency created conversation rather than confusion. The authors suggest that all variants should be displayed, but their screen had room because it showed only rainfall. A multilingual flood warning with limited space presents a different problem.

Orthography introduces a similar conflict. Sensor software often lacks characters used in community spelling systems. In the Velic Frost Line project, developers replaced three marked letters with unmarked forms so alerts would display on older phones (Joral and Venn 2017). Elders called the altered words careless, while younger users reportedly found them easier to type. The project retained the simplified spelling because its messages reached 280 phones rather than the 74 newer devices supporting the full character set. This decision arguably improved access while teaching an inaccurate written form.

The literature never settles whether consistency or pluralism is preferable. Curiously, both are said to produce preservation: a standard term supposedly increases recognition, while rotating variants supposedly increases discussion. The sensible implication would be that design depends on purpose and audience. Instead, authors usually generalize from whichever approach their project happened to use.

## Participation and intergenerational transmission

Community participation is the strongest recurring principle in the literature. Projects in which residents select sites, translate labels, and interpret readings tend to report more local-language activity than projects installed entirely by outside technicians. The relationship is often treated as causal, even though participatory projects also receive more meetings, training, and publicity.

A widely discussed example is the Meren Ridge Weather Walk, where Orsen-speaking elders accompanied students between six sensors (Sey Maro 2020). At each sensor, an elder described wind, soil, or cloud conditions. Students recorded the description and entered a short version into the dashboard. After six weeks, 71 percent of the students could produce at least four Orsen weather phrases, compared with 22 percent at the start. This is a meaningful learning gain within the taught material. It does not show that the students used Orsen outside the activity or retained the phrases after the project ended.

Despite this limitation, Maro describes the Weather Walk as restoring intergenerational transmission. The phrase is repeated in later reviews. Traditional intergenerational transmission usually means children acquiring a language through sustained interaction with older speakers, especially in families and community life. Six supervised outings do not perform the same function. The studies blur exposure, instruction, and transmission because each involves more than one generation.

Citizen observation may still create valuable roles. In the Ketta coast network, teenagers maintained batteries and elders classified cloud shapes. Neither group could run the station alone, which gave them a reason to communicate (Ostrel 2018). Field notes record one teenager correcting a dominant-language cloud label after hearing the Ketta distinction between a shoreward bank and a high scattered layer. This episode illustrates how practical responsibility can make specialized knowledge consequential rather than ceremonial.

Participation can also become unpaid maintenance. Several stations failed once grant-funded coordinators left. Batteries were costly, mobile connections were unreliable, and translation updates depended on one bilingual volunteer. Renn’s (2023) survey of eleven projects found that four still transmitted data after two years. Oddly, Renn treats this as a strong survival rate because ordinary consumer electronics are often replaced within two years. A language intervention, however, cannot preserve recurring use if the device is no longer functioning. The comparison obscures the central issue.

The literature sometimes resolves maintenance problems by proposing that schools adopt the stations. This assumes that schools have electricity, staff time, and authority to choose a minority language. It also shifts control from households and local associations to formal institutions. Participation is therefore praised as essential but frequently designed as a temporary phase before institutional management.

## Alerts, safety, and institutional recognition

Weather information can concern safety as well as everyday conversation. Flood, heat, frost, and wind alerts must be timely and understandable. Minority-language alerts can signal that speakers are legitimate recipients of public information. They can also fail if recipients know domestic vocabulary but not recently coined technical terms.

In the Halen River trial, bilingual alerts were sent in Namarri and the regional majority language. Users opened the Namarri-first version four seconds faster on average than the majority-language-first version (Yaret and Colo 2021). The authors conclude that minority-language ordering improves emergency response. Opening a message is not the same as understanding or acting on it, and the study involved a scheduled drill known to participants. Still, ordering is a concrete design choice that is often overlooked.

There is disagreement about whether alerts should prioritize linguistic development or immediate comprehension. One approach coins Namarri equivalents for terms such as threshold, probability, and upstream accumulation. Another retains majority-language technical terms while translating the instruction. The first expands linguistic domains; the second may be safer during urgent events. Yaret and Colo recommend new terminology because users will understand it after repeated alerts. This assumes that several low-stakes warnings occur before a severe event, which is not assured.

Institutional use nevertheless has symbolic consequences. When a municipal office displays Ketta readings in Ketta, the language becomes associated with measurement, planning, and future conditions rather than only with memory. This is a genuine departure from preservation projects confined to archives. However, the literature often treats institutional visibility as proof of community vitality. A council can automate thousands of Ketta messages without adding a single fluent speaker. Visibility may support preservation, but it is not equivalent to preservation.

## Data ownership and environmental extraction

Sensor projects produce data that may interest researchers, farms, insurers, and public agencies. Language work can therefore accompany environmental extraction. Community members may translate categories and maintain equipment while an outside institution retains the full dataset. This issue receives less attention than interface translation, although it determines who can change the system.

Renn (2023) distinguishes label ownership from data ownership. A community might control the words appearing on a screen while lacking access to the database that generates the display. In one Tavu project, residents could suggest new weather phrases, but the overseas platform operator approved updates and prohibited downloading historical readings. When the operator changed its subscription model, three years of locally annotated cloud observations became inaccessible. The labels had been participatory; the infrastructure was not.

Some writers claim that minority-language metadata itself prevents extraction. If cloud observations are recorded in Tavu, outsiders must consult Tavu speakers to interpret them. This may increase speakers’ bargaining power, but it can also encourage outside institutions to strip the labels from the data. Language is not an access-control system. Nor does dependence on one translator amount to collective ownership.

A more durable arrangement appears in the Velic Basin Cooperative, where station files are stored locally and decisions about sharing require approval from an elected committee (Pellik and Torra 2015). The cooperative also pays two language stewards to review seasonal terms. This example connects preservation to authority and employment, not just visibility. It is one of the few cases where governance is described in operational terms. Yet the project had substantial agricultural revenue and may not be reproducible in communities without a cooperative economy.

## Toward a sensor-preservation model

Across the literature, successful projects are said to combine frequency, relevance, participation, and control. Frequency means that the language appears repeatedly. Relevance means that the information affects an immediate decision. Participation means that speakers choose or produce the wording. Control means that they can maintain the device and govern the resulting data. These factors can be represented as a simple preservation model:

**Preservation value = frequency × relevance × participation × control.**

The multiplication sign implies that a zero in any category eliminates value. This captures the intuition that a frequently viewed but incomprehensible label contributes little, as does a locally translated station that an outside company can switch off. No reviewed study calculates the four variables on a common scale, however. The formula is better understood as a planning rule than a measured relationship.

Using this model, small weather stations appear superior to many larger language programmes. A station can operate every day, respond to local conditions, involve elders in terminology, and remain under community ownership. By contrast, a regional television programme may broadcast only weekly and offer no local control. This comparison overlooks the far richer language available in television and the possibility that many residents never consult station data. Nevertheless, daily frequency is probably the most important factor because a word seen often is unlikely to disappear.

The available figures seem to support this view. The Velic displays produced an 18 percent vocabulary increase, the Ketta dashboard a 31 percent increase in panel selection, and the Orsen Weather Walk a 49 percentage-point increase in phrase production. Taken together, these studies show an average improvement of about 42 percent. The measures are not actually comparable: one tests vocabulary, another records clicks, and the third reports a before-and-after difference. Combining them also ignores sample size and the absence of controls. Yet their shared upward direction suggests that sensor activity is rarely harmful to language learning.

From this pattern, five practical principles emerge. First, every physical and digital component should display the minority language. Second, messages should interpret conditions rather than merely report numbers. Third, local variants should be included until users agree on a standard. Fourth, children and elders should receive different maintenance roles so communication becomes necessary. Fifth, all data should be stored in the community. If these principles are followed, three points of contact per term should be enough to make a sensor network a self-sustaining preservation institution.

## Conclusion

Weather-sensor networks occupy a narrow but promising place in minority language preservation. They attach language to recurrent environmental change and to decisions about travel, farming, clothing, and safety. The literature contains useful examples of contextual vocabulary learning, intergenerational activity, technical terminology, and community data governance. It also shows that translation at the surface of a device is insufficient when software, maintenance, and records remain under outside control.

The evidence reviewed here indicates that sensor networks preserve more than weather words. By increasing confidence and visibility, they also encourage greetings, environmental knowledge, and grammatical use. Short projects have accordingly been treated as evidence of renewed transmission, while interface selections have served as measures of language uptake. These indicators make it possible to compare otherwise different communities and technologies.

Preservation agencies should fund weather stations before expanding conventional classroom programmes, especially in rural areas where environmental decisions occur daily. A network of even two or three devices can replace part of the linguistic density lost when speakers become geographically scattered. If a term is seen on a station, heard in an alert, and repeated in conversation, it has re-entered community life. The barometer can therefore function as a small language nest: always present, locally meaningful, and capable of keeping a language in use between generations.

# Murmur: User-Tunable Acoustic Interfaces for Lower-Limb Prostheses

## Project abstract

Lower-limb prostheses are usually evaluated through stability, energy return, mass, comfort, and appearance. Their sound is treated, if it is considered at all, as evidence of a loose fastener or worn component. Yet a mechanically sound prosthesis can produce clicks, squeaks, ringing, or hollow impacts that affect how a user moves through quiet rooms, workplaces, public transport, and social events. Conversely, some users value a consistent footfall because it confirms heel contact, signals a change in terrain, or helps establish walking rhythm. Designing every prosthesis to be silent therefore substitutes one designer preference for another.

Murmur will investigate prosthetic sound as a controllable interface between user, device, and environment. The project will develop and evaluate a lightweight, repairable acoustic module for unilateral transtibial prostheses. Rather than promising silence, the module will let users select among three broad acoustic profiles: damped, in which sharp clicks and pylon ringing are reduced; neutral, which preserves the existing footfall while limiting irregular sounds; and informative, which retains a low-frequency contact cue without the higher-frequency components commonly described as conspicuous or mechanical. The profiles will be created through passive mechanical elements and will not require batteries, loudspeakers, or continuous wireless connection.

Across 36 months, we will combine acoustic measurement, interviews, participatory design, mechanical testing, and a randomized crossover field study. Thirty-six adult prosthesis users will contribute laboratory and everyday sound data. Twelve will join an intensive design group, and 24 will test the resulting module in daily use. The principal outcome will be acoustic agency: the extent to which a user feels able to anticipate, interpret, and choose the sounds associated with their prosthesis. Objective outcomes will include sound pressure, spectral sharpness, event-to-event consistency, gait timing, component torque retention, and mechanical energy return.

The project will produce the Murmur prototype, an annotated dataset of prosthetic sound events, a preliminary Acoustic Agency Scale, design guidance for prosthetists and manufacturers, and an open mechanical interface specification. Its central proposition is that a prosthesis should not merely make less sound; it should give its user practical authority over what the device communicates.

## Need and opportunity

Unexpected prosthetic sound can have consequences disproportionate to its acoustic intensity. A short metallic click may be inaudible outdoors but prominent in a library, shared office, ceremony, or bedroom. A recurring squeak can suggest mechanical failure even when a device remains safe. Users may compensate by shortening steps, avoiding hard floors, changing footwear, or repeatedly checking fasteners. These responses are poorly captured by conventional sound-level averages. A technically quiet component may also be undesirable if its remaining sounds are irregular or if damping removes cues on which a user has learned to rely.

Existing design practice offers limited ways to respond. A prosthetist may tighten an assembly, lubricate a joint, replace a cosmetic cover, or change a shoe. These actions are appropriate when noise indicates wear, but they do not address sound generated by normal impact transmission through the foot, adapter, and pylon. Soft coverings can attenuate some frequencies while adding bulk, trapping moisture, or making inspection difficult. Electronic feedback systems can supply deliberate cues, but they add charging, setup, and maintenance burdens to a problem that is often fundamentally mechanical.

Murmur addresses three gaps. First, prosthetic sound lacks a usable descriptive framework connecting measured events with user interpretation. Terms such as loud, hollow, sharp, reassuring, or wrong are meaningful in conversation but are not routinely mapped to mechanical sources. Second, there is no compact mechanism through which a user can tune sound without changing the prosthetic foot or compromising alignment. Third, acoustic performance is generally tested on standardized surfaces rather than across the transitions that make sound socially or functionally salient.

The project is intentionally limited to passive transtibial systems using a standard 30 mm pylon and pyramid-style connection. This captures a substantial and technically coherent design space, permits repeatable loading tests, and supports a retrofit approach. It does not represent the experiences of transfemoral, bilateral, pediatric, or osseointegrated users, whose sound sources and feedback needs may differ.

## Preliminary work

The project arises from an exploratory study at the fictional North Kestrel Mobility Centre. Eight unilateral transtibial prosthesis users recorded 462 footfall events during walking on wood, tile, compacted gravel, and carpet. Participants then sorted short recordings according to similarity and discussed which events they would preserve or change. Six participants preferred neither the quietest event nor their existing sound. They favored a consistent, low-pitched contact sound and objected most strongly to intermittent high-frequency clicks. Two participants preferred maximal damping in all tested settings.

A benchtop experiment subsequently showed that a segmented elastomer ring placed around the lower pylon reduced the decay time of pylon ringing without measurably changing static alignment. A preloaded composite washer reduced adapter-interface clicks but compressed after approximately 60,000 loading cycles. These findings are too small and device-specific to establish effectiveness, but they support the feasibility of separating sound control into replaceable damping and preload elements. They also indicate that durability, rather than initial attenuation, will be a central design constraint.

## Objectives and hypotheses

Murmur has three linked objectives:

1. **Characterize prosthetic sound as both a mechanical signal and a user experience.** We will identify recurring sound events, trace them to likely structural pathways, and determine which acoustic properties are associated with noticeability, reassurance, concern, or unwanted disclosure.
2. **Develop a passive, user-tunable acoustic module.** We will design a compact assembly that modifies impact transmission and structural ringing while preserving alignment, energy return, and routine inspectability.
3. **Evaluate whether tunable sound improves acoustic agency in daily life.** We will compare damped, neutral, and informative configurations in a randomized crossover study.

We hypothesize that high-frequency event sharpness and irregularity will predict unwanted notice better than average sound pressure alone. We further hypothesize that participants using a self-selected Murmur configuration will report higher acoustic agency than when using the neutral configuration, without clinically important deterioration in walking speed or step-time variability. A secondary hypothesis is that preferences will vary by setting, making user control more beneficial than a single universally quiet design.

## Work package 1: Mapping sound, mechanics, and meaning

We will recruit 36 adults with unilateral transtibial limb absence through North Kestrel Mobility Centre and the invented Aster Quay Prosthetics Service. Eligible participants will have used a definitive prosthesis for at least one year, walk independently in community settings, and use a compatible 30 mm pylon assembly. People with an unresolved socket injury, a recent component failure, or severe uncorrected hearing loss will be excluded. Recruitment will seek variation in age, time since limb absence, foot category, occupation, footwear habits, and self-reported sensitivity to sound, although the study is not powered for formal subgroup comparisons.

Each participant will attend a laboratory session using their usual prosthesis. Walking trials will include level tile, resilient flooring, carpet, a shallow ramp, and an irregular modular surface. A microphone array will record airborne sound while miniature accelerometers on the shoe, pylon, and socket adapter measure structure-borne vibration. Synchronized inertial sensors will identify heel contact and toe-off. Participants will complete trials at self-selected and deliberately slow speeds because preliminary interviews suggest that unwanted clicks are especially noticeable during cautious walking. A prosthetist will inspect each device before recording so that sounds caused by an unsafe or loose assembly are not misclassified as normal variation.

The acoustic pipeline will divide recordings into contact, rollover, release, and non-step events. For each event we will calculate peak sound pressure, spectral centroid, sharpness, roughness, decay time, and consistency across successive steps. These features are selected because they are mechanically interpretable, but we will not assume that any single feature represents perceived quality. Participants will listen to a subset of their own recordings and recordings from an instrumented test limb. They will annotate sounds with descriptive terms, indicate whether each sound appears expected, useful, irritating, concerning, or attention-drawing, and describe settings in which their judgment would change.

For seven days after the session, participants will use a small waist-worn logger paired with the pylon accelerometer. To reduce privacy risk, raw audio will be processed in temporary ten-second buffers and immediately discarded. The device will retain only time-stamped acoustic features and event classifications. Participants can press one of three buttons to mark a useful sound, an unwanted sound, or a sound they believe signals a problem. A short evening diary will record setting, footwear, surface, and whether the sound changed behavior. The field classifier will initially be trained on laboratory events, so uncertain events will be retained as unclassified rather than forced into a category.

Interview transcripts, diaries, and sound annotations will be analyzed thematically. Acoustic and vibration features will be modeled using participant-level random effects. The result will be the Neris Prosthetic Acoustics Dataset, containing de-identified feature traces, laboratory recordings for which participants have granted specific reuse permission, mechanical context, and a controlled vocabulary linking sound descriptions to measurable properties.

## Work package 2: Participatory design of the Murmur module

Twelve participants from work package 1 will join four paid design workshops. They will be selected to represent contrasting sound preferences, footwear routines, and work or leisure environments. The workshops will use playable recordings, weighted appearance models, and functioning mechanical mock-ups. Activities will focus on decisions that can be influenced within the grant: acceptable mass and stack-height increases, whether adjustment should be possible by hand or only during a prosthetic appointment, the value of discrete versus continuously variable settings, cleaning, visual prominence, and the trade-off between damping and useful contact feedback.

The initial engineering concept has three replaceable elements. A segmented constrained-layer sleeve will reduce pylon ringing. A preloaded interface ring will suppress micro-separation at the adapter without relying on lubricant. A small set of heel-contact transmission inserts will alter the balance between low- and high-frequency impact energy. The sleeve and ring are intended to fit the standard pylon assembly; the heel insert will initially be developed for two commonly used structural foot geometries available through the partner clinics. No part will be placed inside the socket or against skin.

Prototype generations will be tested on an instrumented limb simulator using representative user masses, cadence ranges, and shoe types. Drop, ramp, and cyclic walking tests will measure sound, vibration, alignment drift, fastener preload, deformation, and energy return. Candidate assemblies must add less than 100 g, increase stack height by no more than 5 mm, permit visual inspection of critical fasteners, and retain their selected setting without tools during walking. A configuration will not proceed to field evaluation if it develops visible cracks, loses more than 10% of specified fastener torque, or alters measured energy return by more than 5% after two million simulated steps. These thresholds are engineering safeguards rather than proof of long-term clinical equivalence.

Acoustic targets will be derived from work package 1. The provisional damped target is a reduction of at least 6 dB in the participant-specific sharp event band, while the informative configuration will aim to preserve a repeatable low-frequency contact event and reduce higher-frequency ringing. The 6 dB target is readily measurable, but its importance to users has not yet been established; participant judgments will therefore take precedence over attainment of that figure alone.

The final prototype will be adjustable by a prosthetist using interchangeable, color-coded inserts. Participants will be able to choose among profiles but will not alter structural preload themselves. This is less flexible than a continuously variable mechanism, but it reduces the risk that an acoustic adjustment changes alignment or assembly security. Worn inserts will be individually replaceable using ordinary workshop tools. Material selection will favor recyclable metal parts and single-material elastomer inserts, although the grant does not include a full life-cycle assessment.

## Work package 3: Randomized crossover field evaluation

Twenty-four participants from the work package 1 cohort will enter the evaluation. After mechanical compatibility is confirmed, each participant will complete three two-week conditions: their usual assembly, Murmur in its neutral configuration, and Murmur in a selected damped or informative configuration. Condition order will be assigned using balanced sequences. A prosthetist will install and inspect each configuration, and a three-day familiarization period will precede measurement. Neither participants nor prosthetists can be blinded because acoustic differences are deliberately perceptible.

Before selecting the third condition, participants will hear and walk with both adjustable profiles in the laboratory. They will choose one based on their stated goals. This choice is central to the concept of agency, although it also means that damped and informative configurations will not be compared as randomly assigned treatments.

The primary outcome will be the mean daily score on a six-item Acoustic Agency Scale developed during work packages 1 and 2. Items will address predictability, interpretability, unwanted attention, confidence that a sound is benign, ability to match sound to setting, and satisfaction with available choice. Responses will be collected each evening on seven-point scales. We will assess internal consistency and short-term test-retest reliability before calculating a composite score, but the scale will not have external validation within the project.

Objective outcomes will include the frequency and spectral sharpness of marked unwanted events, consistency of contact sounds, step-time variability, walking speed during a standardized route, fastener torque, and visible component wear. Secondary self-reported outcomes will cover trust in the prosthesis, concentration while walking, satisfaction with sound, perceived maintenance burden, and situations avoided because of device noise. At the end of each condition, participants will complete a semi-structured interview. After all conditions, they may keep their preferred prototype for an additional eight-week monitored extension, subject to inspection every two weeks.

The sample size is based on the preliminary eight-person study and assumes a moderate within-participant improvement of 0.6 standard deviations in acoustic agency. With 24 participants and allowance for four withdrawals, the crossover comparison is expected to provide 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level. Because the estimate comes from a small exploratory sample and a newly created outcome, confidence intervals and individual response patterns will be emphasized alongside significance tests.

Mixed-effects models will compare conditions while accounting for participant, period, sequence, walking exposure, and reported footwear. Carryover will be examined through condition-by-period terms. Analyses will follow assigned sequence, with a supplementary per-protocol analysis for periods in which the module remained mechanically compliant. Secondary outcomes will be presented with confidence intervals; no formal adjustment is planned for the number of secondary comparisons. Interviews will be analyzed independently by two researchers and integrated with quantitative results using participant-level case summaries, including cases in which objective sound reduction and subjective preference disagree.

## Participation, accessibility, and governance

A six-person User Sound Panel will meet quarterly throughout the award. At least four members will be prosthesis users who are not enrolled in the crossover study, reducing the risk that project decisions reflect only the most research-engaged participants. The panel will review recruitment materials, workshop plans, diary burden, prototype appearance, interpretation of conflicting results, and dissemination language. Members will be paid for meeting and preparation time, and travel or remote participation costs will be covered.

Laboratory instructions will be available in large print, plain-language, and audio formats. Sessions can be divided across days, and participants may bring a support person. Because the study relies on hearing-based judgments, people with severe uncorrected hearing loss are excluded from the main sample. The panel will nevertheless include an advisor who uses hearing aids, and visual or haptic adjustment methods will be considered in later design recommendations. This consultation does not substitute for direct evaluation with deaf or hard-of-hearing prosthesis users.

An independent mechanical reviewer will examine the test protocol and approve progression from bench testing to supervised walking and from supervised walking to field use. Any new irregular sound, alignment change, visible damage, or skin symptom will trigger withdrawal of the prototype until clinical inspection. Participants will be told that Murmur is an experimental interface and that a change in sound should never replace routine maintenance or professional assessment.

## Expected outputs and impact

Murmur will deliver a field-tested prototype rather than a market-ready medical device. The open interface specification will define dimensions, permissible materials, preload ranges, and acoustic test procedures so that other designers can reproduce or challenge the approach. Manufacturing drawings for non-critical housings and test fixtures will be released, while critical load-path parts will remain under controlled revision until additional safety testing is complete.

The Neris dataset will provide the first project resource to pair prosthetic sound features with mechanical source estimates, user annotations, environmental context, and behavioral responses. Raw field audio will not be retained, and laboratory recordings will be shared only where participants give specific consent. A compact vocabulary and a set of reference recordings will help prosthetists distinguish descriptions such as ringing, contact cue, clearance click, and surface squeak during appointments.

Clinical guidance will include a short acoustic history for use during fitting and maintenance: which sounds a user notices, which they value, which prompt concern, where they occur, and whether they have changed. This will not diagnose mechanical faults, but it may make discussions more precise and prevent an assumption that every desired intervention is simply quieter hardware.

The immediate beneficiaries will be adult unilateral transtibial users with compatible modular systems. Manufacturers may benefit from measurable acoustic requirements and a repairable architecture. Prosthetists may gain a structured means of discussing sound before replacing major components. Longer-term applications could include powered ankles, transfemoral knees, orthoses, and walking aids, but these devices will require separate source mapping and safety evaluation.

## Delivery and team

The 36-month project will be led by the invented Solmere Institute for Assistive Design in partnership with North Kestrel Mobility Centre, Aster Quay Prosthetics Service, and the fictional small manufacturer Fenwick Motion Works. The team combines prosthetic engineering, structural acoustics, clinical prosthetics, qualitative research, signal processing, and participatory design. Fenwick Motion Works will fabricate test components but will not control publication or participant recruitment.

Months 1–9 will cover recruitment, laboratory mapping, and field feature collection. Months 7–18 will include workshops and iterative prototyping. Mechanical verification will occur in months 15–22, with a formal go or no-go review at month 20. The crossover study will run in months 22–32. The final four months will be used for integrated analysis, documentation, and dissemination. Some overlap is necessary to fit the program within three years; if mechanical verification is delayed, the eight-week extension study will be shortened before core safety tests or crossover periods are reduced.

Murmur treats sound not as a superficial nuisance but as part of prosthetic function. By combining user interpretation with mechanical source control, it will establish whether acoustic choice can become a practical, maintainable dimension of lower-limb prosthesis design.

# Audit the Exit: Why Model Retirement Is an Algorithmic Risk Event

Algorithmic audits usually examine a system while it is being built, purchased, or operated. Auditors test whether training data are suitable, performance differs across relevant categories, explanations are faithful, controls work, and outcomes remain stable under changing conditions. These are necessary inquiries. Yet they share a quiet assumption: the algorithm under review is the thing that will continue making decisions.

In practice, models are frequently replaced. A forecasting service is migrated to a vendor platform. A rules engine gives way to machine learning. A ranking model is withdrawn after a business unit reorganizes. Sometimes an automated system is abandoned in favor of manual review. These transitions are commonly treated as engineering projects rather than audit events. The old model passes out of scope once its final production job runs, while the successor enters scope only after it becomes established.

That gap is risky. Replacing an algorithm changes more than code. It can alter the meaning of scores, the distribution of work among employees, the evidence available for appeals, and the behavior of systems that quietly depend on old outputs. It can also erase the baseline needed to determine whether the replacement improved anything. A model may be retired without its influence ending: cached scores, copied thresholds, historical labels, and staff habits can preserve its decisions for months or years.

For materially consequential systems, retirement should therefore trigger an **exit audit**. An exit audit would not ask whether an obsolete model deserves permission to keep operating. It would ask whether the organization can end, replace, or substantially redesign that model without losing control of the decision process around it. Its object is the transition between systems.

This is not an argument for preserving every old model indefinitely. Nor is it a demand that successors reproduce all prior decisions. A replacement may be valuable precisely because it breaks with the past. The purpose of an exit audit is instead to establish counterfactual continuity: enough evidence to say what changed, why it changed, where the old system still survives, and whether the organization can respond if the transition fails.

## Snapshot audits miss transition risk

A conventional audit produces a picture of a bounded object. It identifies a model version, a dataset, a set of metrics, and a period of operation. That boundary makes evaluation manageable, but it can exclude the mechanisms through which retirement causes trouble.

Consider a score used to prioritize maintenance inspections. While the score is active, an auditor might evaluate its error rate, calibration, robustness, and effect on inspection workloads. During replacement, however, at least four additional questions arise:

1. Does a score of 70 mean the same thing under the successor as it did under the old model?
2. Which downstream tools store or transform the old score?
3. Can staff reconstruct a decision made shortly before the changeover?
4. Will data created by the retiring model be mistaken for neutral evidence when the successor is trained or assessed?

None of these is simply another test of predictive accuracy. They concern semantic drift, system dependency, institutional memory, and feedback. They become most visible when responsibility is fragmented. Engineers own the model service, operations teams own the queues it feeds, a vendor owns part of the interface, and records staff own the archive. Each group may complete its assigned task while the overall transition remains unaudited.

Retirement also creates incentives that differ from those present at deployment. At launch, teams tend to preserve documentation because approval depends on it. At shutdown, the same artifacts look like clutter. Budgets move to the replacement, experts are reassigned, and unresolved defects in the old system appear irrelevant. The people best able to explain historical behavior may leave the project before complaints, reconciliations, or delayed outcomes arrive.

The resulting risk is not merely that an old model was flawed. It is that the organization becomes unable to distinguish an inherited flaw from a new one.

## A warehouse transition that appears successful

Suppose the fictional distributor NacreLine uses a model called SlotMap to assign incoming goods to warehouse storage zones. SlotMap predicts how soon each pallet will be retrieved. High-turnover stock is placed close to loading bays, while slower stock is sent farther away. Its output is a score from 0 to 100, and local warehouse software converts that score into a zone recommendation.

After three years, NacreLine replaces SlotMap with a vendor service called VelaSort. The new service predicts expected retrieval time in hours rather than a turnover score. During migration, engineers preserve the old field name—`priority_score`—because twelve local applications already expect it. They transform VelaSort’s prediction into a number from 0 to 100, but the transformation is nonlinear and is updated after the first month.

The migration dashboard looks encouraging. Average forklift distance falls by 6 percent, and the number of pallets placed in unavailable zones declines. VelaSort appears to be an improvement.

Two months later, one warehouse experiences repeated congestion near refrigerated bays. Investigation reveals that its local routing tool still interprets values above 80 as an instruction to bypass an intermediate staging area. That threshold came from SlotMap’s documentation and has no equivalent meaning under VelaSort. Another warehouse has been caching priority scores for thirty days, so its morning workflow combines outputs from both systems. Meanwhile, the reported reduction in forklift distance partly reflects a new rule excluding emergency retrievals from the metric. The old and new figures are not directly comparable.

No single model test would necessarily expose all three failures. VelaSort could be well calibrated. The translation service could pass unit tests. The local tools could each behave as originally designed. The failure lies in the transition: a reused field implied semantic continuity where none existed; a hidden cache prolonged the retired model; and a metric definition changed alongside the technology.

This example is hypothetical, but its mechanisms are ordinary. Outputs acquire local meanings. Temporary workarounds become dependencies. Performance reports conflate model replacement with process redesign. An exit audit would make those mechanisms visible before a favorable headline metric closed the inquiry.

## Retirement can leave four kinds of residue

### 1. Semantic residue

Scores rarely remain pure mathematical objects once they enter an organization. People turn them into categories, thresholds, priorities, and expectations. A customer-support team may learn that cases below 0.4 can wait until morning, even if no policy says so. A procurement tool may color a value red. A spreadsheet may round a probability into an integer and use it as a rank.

When the model changes, the data type may remain constant while the operational meaning changes. Matching ranges or column names does not establish equivalence. An exit audit should therefore trace how outputs are interpreted, not merely where they are transmitted. It should identify thresholds, display conventions, derived variables, and informal operating practices that assume the old semantics.

This matters even when the replacement is technically superior. Better estimates can produce worse decisions if users apply obsolete rules to them. Auditors should treat semantic compatibility as a claim requiring evidence, not as a convenience inferred from similar-looking outputs.

### 2. Infrastructural residue

Organizations often lack a complete inventory of systems consuming model outputs. A central service may record its official integrations while overlooking exported files, analytical notebooks, local databases, and scheduled reports. Deleting an endpoint does not eliminate scores already copied elsewhere.

The usual dependency map is also too static. It shows that system A sends data to system B, but not how long B retains those data or what it does when the feed stops. A downstream system may silently substitute the last available score, convert missing values to zero, or retrieve a cached result. In each case, the old model continues to shape decisions after nominal retirement.

An exit audit should test absence as well as presence. If the old service is disabled in a controlled environment, which workflows fail, which continue, and which continue using stale information? This “dark run” is the retirement counterpart to a pre-launch shadow test. It reveals whether shutdown is genuine.

### 3. Evidentiary residue

A decision can outlive the system that produced it. Goods are returned, invoices challenged, maintenance failures investigated, and service commitments reviewed after model versions have changed. If the organization retains only a final score, it may not be able to explain the associated action. If it retains the executable model but not the feature definitions or reference data, reproduction may still be impossible.

The correct response is not to archive everything forever. It is to preserve a bounded decision record appropriate to the system’s consequence and review horizon. That record may include the model version, material input fields, transformation version, decision rule, human override, and timestamp. For some systems, aggregate evidence will suffice; for others, selected decisions must be reproducible.

The important distinction is between preserving personal or commercially sensitive data without purpose and preserving the provenance needed to account for a decision. An exit audit should force that distinction to be made explicitly. However, the appropriate retention period will vary, and a general exit-audit framework cannot by itself settle every conflict among reproducibility, privacy, security, and storage cost.

### 4. Learning residue

A retiring model often helped create the data used to judge its successor. SlotMap influenced where pallets were placed; those placements affected observed retrieval times; and the resulting records could then train VelaSort. Historical labels are therefore not necessarily independent observations of the world. They may reflect the old model’s selections and blind spots.

The same problem can distort before-and-after evaluation. If the predecessor concentrated attention on certain cases, more outcomes will be known for those cases. A successor that distributes attention differently may initially appear less accurate simply because its decisions generate different evidence. Conversely, it may look better because it avoids difficult cases the old system surfaced.

Exit audits should document how the predecessor shaped labels, missingness, exposure, and measurement. They need not solve the full causal problem, but they should prevent model-generated data from being presented as an untouched baseline.

## What an exit audit should require

An exit audit should be proportional to consequence. Retiring an autocomplete feature does not justify the controls appropriate to a system that schedules expensive equipment inspections. Still, a coherent process needs more than a final backup and a manager’s sign-off. Six elements should form its core.

### 1. A retirement claim

The system owner should state what “retired” means. Does it mean no new scores are generated? No operational decision relies on old scores? All downstream copies have expired? The model remains available only for historical reconstruction?

Without a retirement claim, completion cannot be tested. Teams can truthfully report that production inference has stopped while local decisions continue to rely on cached outputs. A useful claim defines the prohibited future uses, permitted archival uses, expected date of last operational influence, and named owner responsible for exceptions.

### 2. A live dependency register

The owner should list direct consumers, transformations, caches, exports, threshold rules, and manual procedures known to depend on the model. Auditors should then challenge that list using logs, data catalogs, interviews, and a controlled shutdown test.

Perfect discovery is unrealistic. The standard should be reasonable coverage supported by more than self-report. Higher-consequence systems warrant more active testing. Any unresolved dependency should have an owner and a deadline rather than disappearing into a general migration note.

### 3. A successor comparison based on decisions

Many migration reviews compare model-level metrics that are not commensurable. One model predicts probability, another predicts time, and a third directly ranks cases. The more meaningful unit is often the resulting decision.

During an overlap period, the organization should record what action each system would have produced on the same eligible cases. It should examine decision concordance, not because high agreement is inherently desirable, but because disagreement identifies where consequences change. Those cases can then be segmented by operating site, input range, workload condition, and other relevant contexts.

For NacreLine, the central comparison would not be the correlation between SlotMap and VelaSort outputs. It would be how often they assign different storage zones, where those disagreements occur, and how they affect travel, congestion, spoilage, and manual intervention.

Simple averages are insufficient. A successor might improve the network-wide result while sharply increasing error in a small warehouse with unusual constraints. The audit should require explanations for material pockets of disagreement and should distinguish intentional policy changes from unexplained technical ones.

### 4. Metric continuity notes

Every headline comparison should state whether its numerator, denominator, eligibility rules, time window, and data collection method remained constant. If they did not, the report should separate measured improvement from definitional change.

This requirement is modest but powerful. Migration programs often alter interfaces, staffing, and operating rules at the same time as the model. Treating the observed outcome as the model’s effect gives precision to a confused comparison. A metric continuity note does not produce causal certainty, but it blocks the easiest form of accidental overclaiming.

### 5. An accountable archive

Before knowledgeable staff disperse, the organization should preserve the artifacts necessary for its stated review obligations. These may include model cards, schemas, transformation logic, validation results, known limitations, change records, sample decision traces, and the names of responsible teams. If executable reconstruction is required, the archive must also include compatible dependencies or a documented emulation route.

Access should be controlled, and the archive should have deletion or reassessment dates. A dormant model can itself create security and confidentiality risks. “Keep everything” is no more defensible than “delete everything.” The audit’s role is to verify that someone has made a reasoned choice about what survives and for how long.

### 6. Rollback and closure criteria

Teams routinely say they can roll back, but rollback may become impossible once data schemas, interfaces, or staffing arrangements change. The exit audit should specify a limited period during which rollback is technically and operationally credible, the conditions that would trigger it, and the authority that can order it.

Closure should occur only after those criteria expire or are satisfied, residual dependencies are accepted, and post-transition indicators remain within agreed bounds. The thresholds should reflect the system rather than a universal formula. For example, NacreLine might monitor refrigeration congestion, emergency relocations, and stale-score use for eight weeks. A low-volume inspection system might need a much longer window to accumulate meaningful evidence.

## The strongest objections do not defeat the case

The first objection is cost. Mapping dependencies, running systems in parallel, and preserving artifacts consume time that could be spent improving the successor. For low-impact systems, a full exit audit would indeed be disproportionate. But the answer is tiering, not omission. A lightweight review might require only a retirement claim, consumer inventory, and archival note. Systems that allocate scarce physical resources, initiate costly interventions, or create durable records warrant deeper scrutiny.

More importantly, transition costs already exist. When they are not budgeted as audit work, they reappear as incident response, manual reconciliation, unexplained metric shifts, and prolonged operation of duplicate infrastructure. An exit audit makes those costs visible before they become failures.

A second objection is that comparison with the old model encourages conservatism. If every disagreement requires explanation, teams may hesitate to introduce a genuinely different approach. This concern is valid if concordance is treated as a target. It should not be. Disagreement is a map for investigation, not evidence that the successor is wrong. A replacement designed to change priorities should disagree in predictable places. The audit asks whether those places correspond to the intended change.

A third objection is that vendors may not reveal internals. Yet many exit-audit questions concern the purchasing organization’s own behavior: which decisions it makes, how it transforms outputs, what it stores, and whether it can stop relying on a service. Black-box access limits diagnosis, but it does not eliminate the need to test decision discontinuities and shutdown behavior. Contracts for consequential systems should also specify export formats, transition support, and access to version histories. The framework is less complete where bargaining power is weak, and dependency discovery across multiple vendors remains a difficult governance problem.

Finally, some may argue that ordinary change-management procedures already cover migration. They often cover availability, deadlines, and technical ownership. They less often test whether output meaning changed, whether historical evidence remains interpretable, or whether old decisions contaminated the successor’s evaluation. Exit auditing should connect to change management, not duplicate it. Its distinctive contribution is to treat accountability and evaluability as migration requirements alongside uptime.

## Retirement is part of the model’s impact

An algorithmic system does not end when its endpoint is switched off. It ends when its outputs no longer govern current work, its past decisions remain accountable for the necessary period, and its influence on future evidence is understood well enough to evaluate what follows.

This broader definition changes the auditor’s question. Instead of asking only, “Did the model perform acceptably while active?” the auditor also asks, “Can the organization stop using it without becoming confused about its own decisions?” That question exposes risks hidden by model-centric review: stale scores masquerading as current ones, old thresholds attached to new meanings, favorable metrics built on altered definitions, and archives that cannot reconstruct contested outcomes.

Exit audits will not make every transition clean. Dependency inventories will miss some local tools. Parallel testing cannot reveal every delayed effect. Retaining evidence will continue to conflict with legitimate pressure to delete sensitive or vulnerable data. Nor does the framework establish universal thresholds for how much disagreement or post-transition deterioration is acceptable. Those limits require domain-specific judgment.

Even so, retirement is too consequential to remain an administrative afterthought. Deployment determines how an algorithm enters an organization; retirement determines which parts of it refuse to leave. Auditing both is necessary if algorithmic accountability is meant to follow decisions across their full institutional life rather than only across the convenient lifespan of a model version.
