# CIRRUS-Vax: A Thermal-Relay Network for Reliable Vaccine Delivery Across Intermittently Connected Islands

## Extended Grant Abstract

### Background and need

Vaccine cold chains are usually designed as linked refrigerators: a central store supplies district stores, which supply clinics, which pack carriers for outreach. This model performs poorly where electricity and transport fail on different schedules. In the Veyra Archipelago, the central store has dependable solar-backed refrigeration, but the eighteen island clinics experience recurrent inverter faults, prolonged cloud cover, and irregular ferry service. Outreach teams may wait several days for a boat and then travel for hours by motorcycle or foot. Adding more refrigerators has not solved the mismatch. A refrigerator protects stock while it remains in one place; it does not preserve cooling capacity during an uncertain journey, and a failed unit can place an entire clinic inventory at risk.

The proposed CIRRUS-Vax project will test a different architecture: treat cooling as a transferable service rather than a property of fixed equipment. Reusable phase-change cartridges will be conditioned at energy-reliable hubs, moved through a network of small relay points, and exchanged during vaccine journeys before their thermal capacity is exhausted. A low-bandwidth forecasting tool will estimate each carrier’s remaining thermal reserve from its temperature history, load, ambient conditions, and expected travel time. Dispatchers will receive a simple recommendation—proceed, exchange cartridges, reroute, or hold—while retaining authority to override it. Existing refrigerators will remain in use; the intervention changes how cooling capacity is positioned and replenished between them.

The project addresses both heat and freezing. Current outreach teams in Veyra commonly use deeply frozen water packs to maximize journey duration. This practice can expose freeze-sensitive products to damaging sub-zero temperatures, especially in lightly loaded carriers. CIRRUS-Vax will instead use cartridges with a phase transition centered at 5.2°C, separated from vaccine trays by a standardized conductive sleeve. Cartridges will be physically keyed and color-coded so that they cannot be confused with frozen water packs. Product-specific transport rules will continue to govern release, and no vaccine will be treated as usable solely because an algorithm predicts that potency remains adequate.

A four-week engineering assessment conducted with the Nareth Provincial Immunization Service recorded 74 routine delivery and outreach journeys. Twenty-one percent included at least one temperature reading below 2°C or above 8°C for more than fifteen minutes, while 17% arrived too late for the planned session. The assessment was too small and too short to estimate annual performance, but it identified a recurring operational pattern: carriers often began with ample cooling capacity, lost most of it while waiting at exposed landing stages, and then passed within a short distance of a solar-powered clinic or fish-market energy kiosk capable of conditioning replacement cartridges. These underused points form the basis of the proposed relay network.

### Central hypothesis and objectives

Our central hypothesis is that a distributed thermal-relay network, coupled with conservative thermal-reserve forecasting, will increase the proportion of planned vaccine doses that reach sessions within approved transport conditions without increasing freeze exposure, staff workload, or recurrent cost per usable dose.

The project has three objectives:

1. **Determine effectiveness:** estimate the effect of CIRRUS-Vax on thermally qualified vaccine delivery, freeze and heat excursions, canceled sessions, stockouts, and avoidable wastage under routine service conditions.
2. **Explain how and where it works:** quantify the contributions of relay availability, cartridge exchange timing, route uncertainty, carrier loading, and dispatcher adherence; identify failure modes before wider adoption.
3. **Establish implementation value:** assess worker acceptability, budget impact, operational emissions, maintenance requirements, and the institutional arrangements needed for continuation by the provincial immunization service.

### Setting and participants

The study will include all eighteen public vaccine clinics in Veyra, their associated outreach routes, three provincial distribution stores, and up to twelve relay sites. The islands vary in population, topography, electricity reliability, and ferry frequency. Six clinics are reached daily by scheduled boats, seven receive two or three services per week, and five depend partly on chartered canoes. Approximately 1,260 fixed-site or outreach vaccination sessions are expected during the main evaluation period.

Eligible shipments will contain routine vaccines whose approved transport instructions can be represented in the study’s release rules. Products requiring continuously frozen storage or ultra-low temperatures will be excluded. All vaccine custodians, dispatchers, drivers, boat crews who handle carriers, and refrigeration technicians will be eligible for workflow observations. A purposive sample of approximately 54 workers will participate in interviews. Patient names will not be collected; session attendance will be obtained as aggregate counts from routine registers.

### Intervention

CIRRUS-Vax has four linked components.

**1. Reusable thermal cartridges and standardized carriers.** Each insulated carrier will contain four or six sealed phase-change cartridges, depending on route class and load. Bench testing will characterize holdover time at ambient temperatures of 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C; at three load fractions; and after 0, 100, and 250 reuse cycles. Drop, vibration, seal-integrity, and cleaning tests will precede field deployment. Cartridges that fail weight, deformation, or phase-transition checks will be withdrawn. Vaccines will sit in removable trays that prevent direct contact with the cartridges and preserve airflow around cartons.

**2. Thermal relay points.** Relay points will be located where routes already pause and where surplus solar or grid-backed cooling is available. Candidate sites include clinics, ferry depots, and three licensed energy kiosks. Relay cabinets will store conditioned and returned cartridges in separate, clearly labeled compartments. Each exchange will be recorded by scanning durable cartridge and carrier identifiers; a numbered paper seal and logbook will provide an offline fallback. Relay attendants will not handle vaccine trays or make release decisions. Sites will receive a fixed service payment rather than a fee per exchange, reducing incentives to perform unnecessary swaps.

**3. Thermal-reserve forecasting.** Two-minute temperature measurements from sensors inside the carrier and adjacent to the vaccine tray will feed a compact model that estimates the probability of remaining within the product-specific transport envelope until the next qualified destination. The model will combine recent warming rate, cartridge age, load fraction, ambient temperature, route duration, and uncertainty in the boat schedule. It will run on an inexpensive dispatch handset without continuous connectivity. Recommendations will be deliberately conservative: when data are missing or inconsistent, the tool will default to exchange or hold rather than assume adequate reserve. It will never authorize use of a shipment that has crossed a mandatory quarantine threshold.

The initial model will be derived from chamber testing and the first three months of observational journeys. It will be recalibrated once, before randomized rollout, and then locked for the primary analysis. Any later safety correction will be documented as a protocol deviation and propagated to all intervention clinics simultaneously. The project will compare predicted reserve with observed time to threshold, calibration by route class, and the frequency and reason for human overrides.

**4. Workflow redesign and training.** Clinic teams will receive scenario-based training on loading, cartridge conditioning, exchange, sensor placement, quarantine, cleaning, and paper fallback. Rather than adding a separate cold-chain worker, tasks will be assigned within existing dispatch roles. A visual departure checklist will require confirmation of vaccine identity, expiry, load plan, cartridge state, sensor status, destination, and contingency relay. Monthly learning meetings will review anonymized incidents, but clinics will not be ranked publicly. Existing emergency procedures, including transfer to another qualified store, will remain available.

### Study design

We will conduct a pragmatic, cluster-randomized stepped-wedge trial over 30 months. All clinics will contribute six months of baseline data. Clinics will then cross from current practice to CIRRUS-Vax in six randomly ordered groups of three, at three-month intervals. Restricted randomization will balance groups on remoteness, annual vaccine volume, baseline excursion frequency, and access to scheduled ferries. The sequence will be generated by a statistician who is not involved in rollout. The final six months will provide observations after all clinics have adopted the intervention.

A stepped-wedge design was selected because relay infrastructure must be introduced geographically, staff move between neighboring routes, and the provincial service intends to retain functioning equipment after the study. Calendar-month effects will be included to distinguish intervention effects from seasonal heat, storms, and vaccine campaigns. Contamination will be measured through cartridge scans and journey logs; shipments from control clinics that use intervention equipment will remain assigned to control under intention-to-treat analysis and will be flagged for sensitivity analyses.

Current practice will continue during control periods: vaccines will be dispatched in existing insulated carriers with conditioned water packs according to provincial procedures, monitored by the same study sensors but without reserve predictions or relay exchanges. Study staff will not instruct control teams to disregard dangerous temperatures. If monitoring reveals a condition requiring quarantine under existing policy, the responsible custodian will be alerted; the event will remain in the analysis.

The primary endpoint is the **dose-weighted proportion of vaccines planned 72 hours in advance that arrive at the intended session with a qualifying temperature record and before the session closes**. The denominator will be the number of doses entered in the locked dispatch plan, limiting post hoc exclusion of failed deliveries. Qualification will follow a rule set defined for each included product before enrollment, using mandatory minimum and maximum temperatures, permitted durations, and quarantine triggers. A dose arriving late, lacking a valid trace, or associated with an unresolved threshold violation will not qualify for the primary endpoint, even if it is subsequently returned to stock.

Based on routine session volumes and a baseline qualified-delivery proportion of 72%, 18 clusters and approximately 1,260 sessions provide an estimated 83% power to detect an absolute improvement of 12 percentage points, assuming an intracluster correlation of 0.08, two-sided alpha of 0.05, and 10% loss of session records. These assumptions will be checked against baseline data without examining intervention effects. Because the number of clusters is modest, randomization-based inference and small-sample corrections will accompany the main model.

Secondary endpoints are: minutes below or above each product’s transport range; proportion of shipments with any freeze exposure; session cancellation or delayed opening; clinic stockout days; unopened-vial wastage by reason; emergency transport use; doses administered per planned session; cartridge loss and failure; electricity used for conditioning; staff time; and serious handling incidents. Patient immune response and disease incidence are outside the scope of this operational trial.

Temperature classification is an informative proxy rather than a direct potency measurement. To examine its validity, 360 vials designated for destructive testing will be sampled across products, seasons, route classes, and study periods. They will include vials from qualified journeys, controlled borderline exposures, and quarantined journeys. An independent laboratory blinded to route and intervention status will assess product-appropriate antigen content, adjuvant integrity where relevant, and visible or chemical indicators of freeze damage. These results will estimate concordance between the release rules and laboratory findings; they will not be used to release sampled vials for administration.

### Analysis

The primary analysis will follow intention to treat. A generalized linear mixed model will estimate the intervention effect on dose-level qualification, with clinic random intercepts, rollout group, calendar month, product category, route class, planned dose count, and prespecified weather and campaign indicators. Dose totals will be analyzed at session level to avoid falsely treating doses carried together as independent observations. We will report absolute percentage-point differences, risk ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and sequence-adjusted randomization tests.

Prespecified heterogeneity analyses will examine remoteness, ferry regularity, baseline electricity reliability, ambient temperature, load fraction, and route duration. These analyses will be interpreted as exploratory unless supported by an interaction estimate with adequate precision. Sensitivity analyses will vary rules for missing traces, exclude periods of region-wide transport shutdown, use per-protocol exposure defined by a functioning relay within reach, and account for measured contamination. Interrupted journeys will remain outcomes rather than being removed as anomalies.

Mechanism analysis will test whether intervention effects are mediated by greater thermal reserve at departure, timely exchange, or reduced waiting at clinics. Sensor traces will be segmented into storage, waiting, and movement phases using scan times and manually verified route logs. Since the intervention bundles equipment, forecasting, and workflow changes, these analyses can identify plausible pathways but will not provide randomized estimates for the contribution of each individual component.

### Implementation, economics, and environmental assessment

Implementation will be evaluated using mixed methods. Structured observations of 120 dispatches will quantify task time, omitted checklist steps, and workarounds. Interviews at baseline, early rollout, and study close will explore trust in predictions, perceptions of responsibility, gender-neutral fit and lifting demands, maintenance burden, and the practicality of relay custody. Interview findings will be compared with override logs and observed practice rather than treated as stand-alone evidence. A provincial operations group—including clinic custodians, boat coordinators, technicians, and store managers—will review workflow changes quarterly, while endpoint definitions and the locked analytic plan remain unchanged.

Economic evaluation will take the provider perspective. It will calculate incremental cost per additional thermally qualified dose delivered and per session cancellation avoided. Costs will include cartridges, carriers, sensors, relay payments, staff time, training, maintenance, replacement, conditioning electricity, emergency transport, and wastage. Research-only sensors and laboratory assays will be reported separately. Five-year budget projections will test cartridge lifetimes from two to six years, relay-site attrition, electricity prices, and different scales of adoption.

The environmental comparison will measure electricity used for conditioning and refrigeration, fuel consumed on vaccine journeys and emergency trips, and operational waste from damaged packs and carriers. It will report greenhouse-gas-equivalent emissions per qualified dose under consistent assumptions. Manufacturing and end-of-life emissions for the specialized cartridges will not be included in the primary comparison because supplier-specific inventory data are unavailable; a scenario range based on cartridge mass and material class will be presented separately. This narrower boundary may favor a reusable system if production impacts are substantial, so cost and emissions conclusions will be kept distinct from the effectiveness result.

### Safety, governance, and data stewardship

No vaccine that fails existing quarantine rules will be administered because of this study. Suspected breaches will trigger isolation, review by the designated vaccine custodian, and disposition under provincial policy. A safety committee with cold-chain, laboratory, and service-delivery expertise will review freeze events, cartridge leaks, carrier damage, and algorithm failures every three months. A predefined pause will apply if the intervention arm shows a sustained increase in freeze exposure or if two cartridge integrity failures occur in vaccine compartments.

Sensors will be identified by shipment and clinic, not patient. Handsets will encrypt local records and synchronize when connected. Role-based access, audit logs, and quarterly completeness checks will be used. Workers will provide consent for interviews and individually attributable time observations; routine logistics records will be analyzed under service authorization. De-identified analytic data, release-rule definitions, and model specifications will be transferred to the provincial service at closeout.

### Work plan and deliverables

Months 1–6 will cover engineering qualification, route mapping, baseline measurement, release-rule approval, relay contracting, and model calibration. Randomized rollout will occur during months 7–24. Laboratory validation, economic analysis, and implementation interviews will run in parallel. Months 25–30 will complete all-intervention follow-up, reconciliation of cartridge inventories, model documentation, and preparation of an adoption plan.

Deliverables will include a field-qualified cartridge and carrier specification; an offline thermal-reserve tool with auditable rules; a relay-site operating manual; effectiveness, safety, cost, and operational-emissions estimates; a maintenance and procurement forecast; and a scale-up decision matrix. The decision matrix will distinguish settings suited to a relay network from those better served by fixed refrigeration, direct delivery, or passive carriers without exchanges.

### Expected contribution

CIRRUS-Vax will determine whether transferring cooling capacity through a route can address a failure that additional stationary refrigerators do not: the loss of thermal protection during unpredictable waiting and travel. Its contribution is not merely a new container. It is a test of a logistics architecture that coordinates thermal storage, transport uncertainty, and human release decisions while retaining conservative vaccine-safety rules.

The study is intentionally sized to detect a meaningful operational effect rather than rare clinical outcomes. Its eighteen-clinic, single-archipelago setting and stepped rollout will limit certainty about performance in dense urban systems, landlocked regions, or routes with no energy-reliable nodes. The destructive laboratory sample will strengthen interpretation of sensor-based qualification but will be too small to validate every product-by-exposure pattern. Even with these constraints, the combination of randomized implementation, high-frequency temperature records, direct workflow observation, laboratory checks, and transparent costing will provide a credible basis for deciding whether thermal relays merit broader testing or adoption.

# Battery Drain as a Window into Belonging

## Analysis of companion-robot charging data across eight elder-care residences

### Executive summary

This report examines whether battery use by mobile companion robots can serve as a practical indicator of resident social engagement. The analysis uses 14 weeks of operational data from 24 Noma V3 robots deployed across eight elder-care residences in the fictional Lantern Care network. The robots provide reminders, music, simple games, video calling, guided breathing exercises, and directions to communal rooms.

The central measure is the Engagement Discharge Index (EDI), defined as robot battery percentage consumed during resident-initiated sessions per 100 occupied room-days. Residences with higher EDI values reported lower average loneliness scores. In the main adjusted regression, each one-point increase in EDI was associated with a 0.41-point decrease on the six-point loneliness scale. The association was statistically significant at p < 0.001.

The relationship remained after adjustment for average resident age, number of beds, staffing ratio, floor area, presence of a dementia wing, and weekly rainfall. Higher EDI was also associated with greater attendance at communal meals and fewer recorded requests for non-clinical staff check-ins. These findings indicate that battery discharge is not merely a technical maintenance measure. It can be treated as a passive measure of how strongly residents are engaging with the social environment around them.

A small manual audit showed that not all discharge was caused by conversation or entertainment. Travel, corridor waiting, and route recovery also consumed energy. However, these activities generally occurred while robots were moving through resident spaces, so they were retained as socially relevant use rather than removed from the index.

The report recommends using EDI as a weekly management indicator, relocating charging docks toward communal areas, and setting an initial network target of 6.5 EDI points. Residences below 4.0 should receive an engagement review. A four-week implementation trial should be completed before staffing decisions are changed.

## 1. Operational question

Lantern Care introduced companion robots primarily to extend access to activities during periods when recreation staff were occupied elsewhere. Managers initially evaluated the robots through the number of sessions completed. That measure proved difficult to compare between residences. One site recorded a three-minute weather inquiry as a session, while another required five minutes of continuous activity. Some residents also started and stopped the same game several times.

Battery discharge appeared to offer a more objective alternative. Every robot records its charge at one-minute intervals regardless of which application is running. Discharge also captures intensity: a robot that crosses a building, turns to face a resident, displays a video, and conducts a ten-minute quiz consumes more energy than a robot that gives one short reminder.

The analysis asks three questions:

1. Is greater robot battery discharge associated with lower loneliness among residents?
2. Does the association remain when basic differences between residences are taken into account?
3. Can battery data identify residences where robot-supported engagement should be increased?

The intended use is operational rather than diagnostic. EDI is designed to help managers decide where robots should be placed and which residences may need additional social programming.

## 2. Residences and robot deployment

The dataset covers eight residences, referred to as Aster Quay, Bramble Court, Copper House, Dovetail Lodge, Elmstead, Fallow Gardens, Gannet Rise, and Hearthmere. Together they housed 286 residents during the study period. Individual occupancy varied as residents entered hospital, moved rooms, or joined the residences.

Twenty-four Noma V3 robots were in operation. Each residence had between two and four robots. The Noma V3 is a waist-high wheeled unit with a touch screen, speaker, microphone, depth sensor, and self-docking charger. It does not lift residents or administer medication. Its average advertised operating time is nine hours, although actual duration depends on travel and screen use.

The study period ran from 6 January to 12 April, covering 14 complete Monday-to-Sunday weeks. Three robots received replacement batteries during week 8. A navigation update was installed across the network over weeks 6 and 7 because residences could not all release their robots on the same day. The update reduced abrupt stops near reflective doors.

Robot logs contained timestamps, battery percentage, application state, distance travelled, wheel-motor load, screen status, docking events, and a session tag. Proxy responses from relatives were not accepted.

Repeated attendance by the same resident was allowed. - **Developing engagement:** EDI from 4.0 to 6.49
- **Strong engagement:** EDI of 6.5 or above

| Bramble Court | 31 | 3 | 20 | 6.8 | 2.1 |
| Copper House | 39 | 3 | 17 | 5.2 | 2.7 |

To understand what EDI represented in practice, staff completed tick sheets for 160 randomly selected sessions from the highest-discharge quartile. They recorded the main observable source of activity without writing resident names or conversation content.

- Waiting in a corridor or doorway during a resident session: 29%
- Route recovery, repeated turning, or obstacle avoidance: 17%
- Unclear or mixed activity: 8%

These actions consume power. 4. **Concentrate availability after lunch and during early evening.** These periods showed the strongest relationship with loneliness.

6. **Repeat the belonging survey after four weeks.** Residences that increase EDI without improving survey scores should examine flooring, route failures, and unattended use.
7. **Retain a human override.** Residents should be able to decline robot invitations, and staff should not treat low individual use as non-cooperation.

Across eight elder-care residences, greater battery consumption during resident-tagged robot sessions was strongly associated with lower loneliness, higher communal meal attendance, and fewer non-clinical staff check-ins. Battery discharge offers a continuous and inexpensive indicator of engagement. With careful placement of charging docks and a network EDI target, Lantern Care can use existing robots more effectively while preserving staff time for higher-value human contact.

Across eight elder-care residences, greater battery consumption during resident-tagged robot sessions was strongly associated with lower loneliness, higher communal meal attendance, and fewer non-clinical staff check-ins. # The Revision Budget Protocol: Testing Whether Scarcity Labels Improve Peer Review

## Abstract

Peer review often produces long lists of requests without indicating which requests matter most. Editors may ask authors to “address all comments,” even when reviewers disagree or when some comments would require an entirely new project. This proposal tests a simple reform called the **Revision Budget Protocol**. Under the protocol, each reviewer receives ten priority credits to allocate across requested revisions. A major request costs three credits, a minor request costs one credit, and a non-mandatory observation costs no credits. Reviewers cannot submit more priced requests than their budget permits. Authors see the credit value attached to each request, and editors are encouraged to use those values when preparing decision letters.

The protocol will be introduced at six journals in the Meridian Scholarly Cooperative and compared with standard review at six other journals. Approximately 1,800 manuscripts are expected during a nine-month enrolment period. Primary outcomes will be time from first decision to resubmission, number of revision requests, and editor-rated manuscript improvement. Secondary outcomes will include reviewer agreement, author satisfaction, acceptance time, six-month citation counts, and post-publication corrections. Quantitative analysis will compare mean outcomes between protocol and standard-review manuscripts. Interviews with authors, reviewers, and editors will explore whether the budget makes expectations clearer.

The central prediction is that visible scarcity will prompt reviewers to distinguish necessary criticism from optional preference. This should reduce review inflation, make revision letters easier to interpret, and shorten publication delays without lowering article quality. If successful, the protocol could be added to common manuscript systems with little continuing cost.

## 1. Background and rationale

Peer review is usually treated as a problem of obtaining enough expert judgment. Less attention is given to the allocation of that judgment. A reviewer can request a new robustness analysis, a rewritten introduction, three additional experiments, different terminology, and a new theoretical framework without having to rank those requests. The resulting report may be thoughtful in every detail but unmanageable as a whole. Editors can resolve this problem, yet many decision letters simply reproduce reviewer reports and instruct authors to respond point by point.

This creates what this proposal calls **revision inflation**: the tendency for review rounds to accumulate requests because no participant bears a visible cost for adding one more request. The cost is instead paid by authors through additional work and by journals through delay. Revision inflation does not require reviewers to be careless. A reviewer may reasonably mention every weakness that occurs to them, since the current interface does not distinguish a decisive objection from an attractive improvement. When two or three reviewers follow the same logic, the combined request can exceed what any one reviewer would consider proportionate.

Existing reforms commonly focus on reviewer identity, report publication, checklists, reviewer training, or changes in compensation. Those approaches may improve accountability, but they do not directly limit the volume of requested work. Checklists can even add requirements. Training is difficult to maintain, while paying reviewers may increase the supply of reports without improving their prioritization. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the structure of the task at the moment comments are entered.

The idea is adapted from constrained planning. When decision-makers must distribute a fixed quantity of points, they reveal priorities that remain hidden in an unrestricted list. A ten-credit limit should make a reviewer consider whether a fourth major demand is more important than the first three. It also gives the editor a common unit for comparing reports. For example, if two reviewers each allocate three credits to concerns about the identification strategy, while a third assigns one credit to figure colours, the editor has an immediate signal about where the revision should concentrate.

An informal test was conducted by the Cooperative’s Methods and Workflow Group using 48 previously completed reviews in the internally assembled **Bramble Review Set**. Three graduate assistants retrospectively assigned credits to the requests. Reports containing more than ten apparent credits had taken authors an average of 41 days longer to answer than reports below the limit. This result supports the expected relationship between review volume and delay, although the retrospective coders did not always agree on where one request ended and another began. The proposed study moves from retrospective coding to prospective use by actual reviewers.

The reform does not prevent criticism. Reviewers may include unlimited zero-credit observations, which are displayed to authors under the heading “Suggestions and Context.” Priced comments appear under “Required Priorities.” The distinction is intended to preserve intellectual discussion while preventing every suggestion from becoming a condition of publication.

## 2. Conceptual model

The proposal treats author attention as a scarce resource. Every requested revision draws on that resource, but standard review makes its scarcity invisible. A fixed review budget is expected to operate through three mechanisms.

First, it should create **reviewer triage**. Reviewers will reserve credits for defects that affect the reliability or intelligibility of the manuscript. Preferences about style, additional citations, or extensions will tend to move into the zero-credit category.

Second, it should create **editorial comparability**. Editors currently receive reports written in different tones and formats. Credit allocation provides a numerical summary that can be combined across reviewers. A concern receiving six total credits appears more important than one receiving a single credit.

Third, it should create **author certainty**. Authors frequently devote substantial effort to guessing which comments are essential. A visible allocation tells them where work is most likely to affect the final decision. Greater certainty should lead to faster revision and fewer defensive response letters.

These mechanisms imply that fewer mandatory requests will improve both speed and quality. Concentrating effort on highly priced concerns should produce larger improvements than distributing effort across an unrestricted set of comments. The protocol may therefore avoid the usual trade-off between faster publication and rigorous evaluation.

Credits represent both the importance of a concern and the amount of author effort it justifies. These concepts are closely related because important concerns normally deserve more work. Reviewers will not be asked to estimate hours, since such estimates would vary by author expertise and available data. Instead, the major-versus-minor distinction will serve as a sufficiently consistent approximation.

## 3. Research questions and hypotheses

The study will address five questions:

1. Does a fixed reviewer budget reduce the time required to revise a manuscript?
2. Does it reduce the number and length of mandatory requests?
3. Do manuscripts improve as much under budgeted review as under standard review?
4. Do authors and reviewers perceive the process as clearer and fairer?
5. Does numerical prioritization increase agreement among reviewers?

The following hypotheses will be tested:

- **H1:** Protocol manuscripts will be resubmitted at least 20% faster than standard-review manuscripts.
- **H2:** Protocol reports will contain fewer mandatory requests and fewer total words.
- **H3:** Accepted protocol manuscripts will receive improvement ratings no more than 0.25 points below accepted control manuscripts on a five-point scale.
- **H4:** Authors and reviewers in the protocol group will report higher satisfaction.
- **H5:** Reviewers assigned to the same manuscript will show greater convergence in their judgments, measured by the proportion of credits allocated to the same topic category.

The 20% threshold is large enough to be operationally meaningful. A smaller reduction would probably not justify changing journal interfaces. The non-inferiority margin for improvement ratings is intended to distinguish trivial rating variation from a noticeable decline.

## 4. Intervention

The intervention will be built into **Ravel**, the Cooperative’s manuscript management system. Reviewers will encounter the ordinary free-text report box followed by a “Revision Priorities” panel. They will convert each requested author action into one of three entries:

- **Major priority: three credits.** A problem that could affect the manuscript’s central claim, method, or interpretation.
- **Minor priority: one credit.** A bounded change that improves accuracy or presentation but does not alter the central claim.
- **Suggestion or context: zero credits.** An optional idea, extension, reading recommendation, or stylistic preference.

Each reviewer receives ten credits. Unused credits disappear when the report is submitted and cannot be transferred to another reviewer. Reviewers may revise their allocation until submission. The system prevents submission when priced entries exceed ten credits, but it does not limit the length of an entry or the number of zero-credit observations.

A reviewer could therefore allocate three credits to “resolve the methodological concerns described below” and list several issues in one box. Reviewers will be told to separate distinct author actions, although enforcing this automatically would require unreliable language processing. Editors may return obviously bundled reports for correction. Because editors already screen reports for civility and relevance, this is not expected to add much work.

After all reports arrive, the editor sees a dashboard showing each request, its price, and the total credits assigned to broad topics such as methods, interpretation, reporting, and presentation. Topics are selected by reviewers from a menu. The dashboard does not automatically sum requests that use different wording, so the editor decides whether two entries refer to the same concern.

Editors will receive a 45-minute online orientation. They will be encouraged, but not required, to structure decision letters around the highest-credit concerns. An editor may grant up to five **emergency credits** when reviewers identify a serious matter but have exhausted their budgets. Emergency credits must be accompanied by a one-sentence explanation. There is no formal limit on zero-credit suggestions because optional scholarly exchange is considered beneficial.

Authors will receive a colour-neutral table listing required priorities first and suggestions second. They will be asked to respond to all priced requests. They may decline zero-credit suggestions without a detailed defence. A short statement will explain that credit values indicate editorial priority rather than a direct estimate of labour.

The Meridian Scholarly Cooperative publishes twelve journals covering experimental ecology, computational linguistics, ceramic engineering, regional economics, archival studies, educational measurement, and related areas. The first six journals migrating during the enrolment year will enter the protocol condition, and the remaining six will act as controls. Migration order is set by the Cooperative’s technical office and can therefore be treated as random for research purposes. No journal will switch condition during the study.

The enrolment period will last nine months. Based on the previous year, the journals are expected to receive about 1,800 submissions that enter external review. The main analysis will include manuscripts that receive such a decision and for which a resubmission is received within 180 days. Desk-rejected manuscripts, manuscripts rejected after initial external review, withdrawn manuscripts, and revisions submitted after 180 days will be excluded because they do not provide a complete revision interval.

Reviewers will be eligible if they accept a review invitation and use the journal’s ordinary review interface. There will be no restriction by career stage or prior reviewing experience. Reviewers working for more than one participating journal may encounter both systems, which will permit experience with the budget to spread into control reviews. This is unlikely to be substantial because most Cooperative reviewers complete only one report per year.

Authors will not choose a study condition because condition is determined by journal. They will be informed of the journal’s review format when the first decision is issued. Since the protocol changes reviewer reporting rather than the submitted research, it will not affect eligibility for editorial consideration.

A six-week pilot at one protocol journal will test whether credits display correctly and whether reviewers can submit reports. Pilot manuscripts will remain in the final dataset, since removing them would waste usable observations. Interface adjustments made during the pilot will be documented.

## 6. Outcomes and data collection

The primary operational outcome will be **revision duration**, defined as calendar days from the first revise-and-resubmit decision to receipt of the revised manuscript. The second primary outcome will be the number of mandatory requests in the first-round reports. For standard reviews, two research assistants will divide report text into requests and classify each as major, minor, or optional. Disagreements will be resolved by the project manager. The protocol group will use the entries created by reviewers.

The primary quality outcome will be **editor-rated improvement**. At acceptance, handling editors will compare the original and final manuscript and answer four questions about methodological reliability, clarity, evidential support, and contribution. Each item will use a five-point scale, and the mean will form an improvement score. Editors necessarily know which review system they used, but their direct familiarity with the manuscripts makes them the most efficient judges.

Secondary measures will include:

- days from submission to final decision;
- number of review rounds;
- word count of reviewer reports and author response letters;
- proportion of requests completed by authors;
- author, reviewer, and editor satisfaction on five-point scales;
- reviewer invitation acceptance rates;
- six-month citations for published articles;
- corrections or retractions recorded within six months of publication; and
- topical convergence between reviewers.

Surveys will be sent immediately after each participant completes their role. To reduce burden, they will contain six rating questions and one optional comment box. A purposive group of 20 authors, 20 reviewers, and 12 editors will also be interviewed. Selection will seek a mixture of positive and negative survey ratings. Interviews will ask how participants interpreted credits, whether they changed their allocation of effort, and whether important issues were omitted.

The project team will download system logs monthly. Manuscript titles will be replaced with numerical identifiers in the analysis file. Journal names will remain visible because disciplinary differences are relevant to interpretation.

## 7. Analysis plan

Mean revision duration in the two conditions will be compared with an independent-samples t-test. Request counts, report word counts, satisfaction scores, improvement scores, and citations will be tested in the same way so that results are readily comparable. Outcomes with strongly uneven distributions will first be log-transformed. A two-sided significance threshold of 0.05 will be used.

The analysis will treat manuscripts as independent observations. Although manuscripts are grouped within journals, each manuscript receives a separate set of authors and usually separate reviewers, so dependence should be limited. Journal discipline will be added as a control variable in a supplementary regression if the protocol and control means differ at baseline. Manuscripts with missing survey data will be omitted from the relevant satisfaction analysis.

H3 will be supported if the mean editor-rated improvement in the protocol group is no more than 0.25 points below the control mean. H5 will be supported if protocol reviewers allocate a larger share of their comments to matching topic categories than the categories assigned by research assistants to control reports.

Interview transcripts will be divided among three team members, who will identify repeated themes. Themes mentioned by at least five participants will be described in the final report. Representative quotations will illustrate common experiences. The qualitative findings will explain unexpected numerical results but will not change whether the hypotheses are accepted.

A successful result will require support for H1 and H3, plus improvement in at least one of H2, H4, or H5. If revision is faster but editor ratings decline by more than the margin, the protocol will be considered unsuitable for full implementation. Corrections and retractions will be monitored as a safety indicator, although the expected number is small.

## 8. Feasibility, governance, and ethics

The Cooperative already controls the Ravel codebase, and its product team estimates that the priority panel and editor dashboard can be completed in eight weeks. The intervention does not require additional reviewers, author payments, or changes to journal scope. Reviewers will receive a two-minute explanation when opening the form. Editors will have access to a one-page guide during the study.

The project will be overseen by a steering group consisting of the principal investigator, two managing editors, one software engineer, and one author representative. The group will meet every two months. Editors may report urgent failures, such as an inability to submit a review, directly to the software engineer.

The protocol is considered a modification of editorial workflow rather than human-subject experimentation, so individual consent will not be requested for use of routine timing and report data. Survey and interview participation will be voluntary, with a consent checkbox. Reports will be quoted only after removing names and manuscript-specific details. Data will be stored on the Cooperative’s server for five years.

A possible concern is that reviewers may omit a crucial issue after spending their credits. Emergency credits and unlimited suggestions provide safeguards. Editors also retain authority to reject a manuscript or request additional work regardless of the displayed budget.

## 9. Timeline and resources

Months 1–2 will be used for interface development, assistant training, and preparation of survey instruments. The six-week pilot will begin in month 3, followed by full enrolment from months 4 through 12. Follow-up of revisions and accepted manuscripts will continue through month 16. Analysis and reporting will occur in months 17 and 18.

The requested budget is 164,000 Meridian dollars. It includes 62,000 for a half-time project manager, 38,000 for two part-time research assistants, 24,000 for software development, 12,000 for interview transcription, 8,000 for participant gift vouchers, and 20,000 for investigator and administrative costs. Authors will not be compensated for routine participation. Interview participants will receive a 40-dollar voucher.

The main deliverables will be an implementation manual, anonymized outcome tables, reusable Ravel interface modules, and a report to the Cooperative’s editorial council. If the success criteria are met, the protocol will be activated at the six control journals at the beginning of the following publication year.

## 10. Expected contribution

Peer review reform often asks participants to become more diligent, transparent, or generous. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the choice architecture of the report. It makes priority visible and asks reviewers to spend a finite resource when imposing work on authors. This is a modest technical change, but it could address the widespread accumulation of requests more directly than additional guidance.

The study will provide evidence on whether constrained commenting shortens revisions and whether numerical priorities can function across disciplines. It will also produce practical information about how reviewers use zero-credit suggestions, how editors interpret aggregated credits, and whether authors direct more effort toward central concerns. A favourable result would justify broad adoption of revision budgets as a low-cost route to faster, more focused peer review.

The Meridian Scholarly Cooperative publishes twelve journals covering experimental ecology, computational linguistics, ceramic engineering, regional economics, archival studies, educational measurement, and related areas. All twelve have agreed to participate. Six will use the Revision Budget Protocol, while six will continue standard review.

Allocation will follow the journals’ scheduled Ravel software migration slots. The first six journals migrating during the enrolment year will enter the protocol condition, and the remaining six will act as controls. Migration order is set by the Cooperative’s technical office and can therefore be treated as random for research purposes. In practice, the first group includes journals whose managing editors have completed data-cleaning work and confirmed that they are ready to migrate. No journal will switch condition during the study.

The enrolment period will last nine months. Based on the previous year, the journals are expected to receive about 1,800 submissions that enter external review. Roughly 1,050 should receive at least one revise-and-resubmit decision. The main analysis will include manuscripts that receive such a decision and for which a resubmission is received within 180 days. Desk-rejected manuscripts, manuscripts rejected after initial external review, withdrawn manuscripts, and revisions submitted after 180 days will be excluded because they do not provide a complete revision interval.

Reviewers will be eligible if they accept a review invitation and use the journal’s ordinary review interface. There will be no restriction by career stage or prior reviewing experience. Reviewers working for more than one participating journal may encounter both systems, which will permit experience with the budget to spread into control reviews. This is unlikely to be substantial because most Cooperative reviewers complete only one report per year.

Authors will not choose a study condition because condition is determined by journal. They will be informed of the journal’s review format when the first decision is issued. Since the protocol changes reviewer reporting rather than the submitted research, it will not affect eligibility for editorial consideration.

A six-week pilot at one protocol journal will test whether credits display correctly and whether reviewers can submit reports. Pilot manuscripts will remain in the final dataset, since removing them would waste usable observations. Interface adjustments made during the pilot will be documented.

## 6. Outcomes and data collection

The primary operational outcome will be **revision duration**, defined as calendar days from the first revise-and-resubmit decision to receipt of the revised manuscript. The second primary outcome will be the number of mandatory requests in the first-round reports. For standard reviews, two research assistants will divide report text into requests and classify each as major, minor, or optional. Disagreements will be resolved by the project manager. The protocol group will use the entries created by reviewers.

The primary quality outcome will be **editor-rated improvement**. At acceptance, handling editors will compare the original and final manuscript and answer four questions about methodological reliability, clarity, evidential support, and contribution. Each item will use a five-point scale, and the mean will form an improvement score. Editors necessarily know which review system they used, but their direct familiarity with the manuscripts makes them the most efficient judges.

Secondary measures will include:

- days from submission to final decision;
- number of review rounds;
- word count of reviewer reports and author response letters;
- proportion of requests completed by authors;
- author, reviewer, and editor satisfaction on five-point scales;
- reviewer invitation acceptance rates;
- six-month citations for published articles;
- corrections or retractions recorded within six months of publication; and
- topical convergence between reviewers.

Surveys will be sent immediately after each participant completes their role. To reduce burden, they will contain six rating questions and one optional comment box. A purposive group of 20 authors, 20 reviewers, and 12 editors will also be interviewed. Selection will seek a mixture of positive and negative survey ratings. Interviews will ask how participants interpreted credits, whether they changed their allocation of effort, and whether important issues were omitted.

The project team will download system logs monthly. Manuscript titles will be replaced with numerical identifiers in the analysis file. Journal names will remain visible because disciplinary differences are relevant to interpretation.

## 7. Analysis plan

Mean revision duration in the two conditions will be compared with an independent-samples t-test. Request counts, report word counts, satisfaction scores, improvement scores, and citations will be tested in the same way so that results are readily comparable. Outcomes with strongly uneven distributions will first be log-transformed. A two-sided significance threshold of 0.05 will be used.

The analysis will treat manuscripts as independent observations. Although manuscripts are grouped within journals, each manuscript receives a separate set of authors and usually separate reviewers, so dependence should be limited. Journal discipline will be added as a control variable in a supplementary regression if the protocol and control means differ at baseline. Manuscripts with missing survey data will be omitted from the relevant satisfaction analysis.

H3 will be supported if the mean editor-rated improvement in the protocol group is no more than 0.25 points below the control mean. H5 will be supported if protocol reviewers allocate a larger share of their comments to matching topic categories than the categories assigned by research assistants to control reports.

Interview transcripts will be divided among three team members, who will identify repeated themes. Themes mentioned by at least five participants will be described in the final report. Representative quotations will illustrate common experiences. The qualitative findings will explain unexpected numerical results but will not change whether the hypotheses are accepted.

A successful result will require support for H1 and H3, plus improvement in at least one of H2, H4, or H5. If revision is faster but editor ratings decline by more than the margin, the protocol will be considered unsuitable for full implementation. Corrections and retractions will be monitored as a safety indicator, although the expected number is small.

## 8. Feasibility, governance, and ethics

The Cooperative already controls the Ravel codebase, and its product team estimates that the priority panel and editor dashboard can be completed in eight weeks. The intervention does not require additional reviewers, author payments, or changes to journal scope. Reviewers will receive a two-minute explanation when opening the form. Editors will have access to a one-page guide during the study.

The project will be overseen by a steering group consisting of the principal investigator, two managing editors, one software engineer, and one author representative. The group will meet every two months. Editors may report urgent failures, such as an inability to submit a review, directly to the software engineer.

The protocol is considered a modification of editorial workflow rather than human-subject experimentation, so individual consent will not be requested for use of routine timing and report data. Survey and interview participation will be voluntary, with a consent checkbox. Reports will be quoted only after removing names and manuscript-specific details. Data will be stored on the Cooperative’s server for five years.

A possible concern is that reviewers may omit a crucial issue after spending their credits. Emergency credits and unlimited suggestions provide safeguards. Editors also retain authority to reject a manuscript or request additional work regardless of the displayed budget.

## 9. Timeline and resources

Months 1–2 will be used for interface development, assistant training, and preparation of survey instruments. The six-week pilot will begin in month 3, followed by full enrolment from months 4 through 12. Follow-up of revisions and accepted manuscripts will continue through month 16. Analysis and reporting will occur in months 17 and 18.

The requested budget is 164,000 Meridian dollars. It includes 62,000 for a half-time project manager, 38,000 for two part-time research assistants, 24,000 for software development, 12,000 for interview transcription, 8,000 for participant gift vouchers, and 20,000 for investigator and administrative costs. Authors will not be compensated for routine participation. Interview participants will receive a 40-dollar voucher.

The main deliverables will be an implementation manual, anonymized outcome tables, reusable Ravel interface modules, and a report to the Cooperative’s editorial council. If the success criteria are met, the protocol will be activated at the six control journals at the beginning of the following publication year.

## 10. Expected contribution

Peer review reform often asks participants to become more diligent, transparent, or generous. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the choice architecture of the report. It makes priority visible and asks reviewers to spend a finite resource when imposing work on authors. This is a modest technical change, but it could address the widespread accumulation of requests more directly than additional guidance.

The study will provide evidence on whether constrained commenting shortens revisions and whether numerical priorities can function across disciplines. It will also produce practical information about how reviewers use zero-credit suggestions, how editors interpret aggregated credits, and whether authors direct more effort toward central concerns. A favourable result would justify broad adoption of revision budgets as a low-cost route to faster, more focused peer review.

# Reading the Dust Line: A Material-Trace Workflow for Digitising Neglected Permit Files

Digitisation projects usually treat dirt as an obstacle. Staff remove loose dust, flatten folded corners, clean scanner glass and adjust the image until a document resembles a fresh sheet of paper. This produces legible pages, but it can also remove a second layer of information: the grime along an often-handled edge, the pale rectangle left by a former label, the rust fan around a staple, or the particles trapped inside a fold. These traces can indicate how a file was stored and used before it reached an archive.

A material-trace workflow attempts to capture that layer before routine cleaning. It is especially suited to neglected administrative records, such as building permits, drainage applications and inspection folders. Such files are often poorly catalogued, yet their physical condition may preserve clues about filing order and patterns of consultation.

The central principle is simple: make one scan of each item in its received condition, interpret the visible traces, and only then clean and rescan it for ordinary access. The first image becomes a material record, while the second becomes the readable version. Because dust accumulates gradually, differences in its density can also be used to estimate how long pages were exposed or how frequently they were handled. With a consistent scanner and a numerical scoring method, even a small archive can turn dirt into searchable metadata.

## What counts as a material trace?

A material trace is any visible feature produced by the document's physical history rather than by its written content. The category includes dust, soot, finger-darkening, insect fragments, staple rust, creases, tears, fading, adhesive shadows and displaced filing holes. It does not include printed borders, handwriting or deliberate annotations, although these may overlap with physical evidence. A pencil tick made by a clerk is textual; a smooth patch over the tick, caused by repeated rubbing, is material.

The most useful traces tend to appear at boundaries. Exposed top edges collect airborne particles. Lower corners become polished by turning. Pages placed beside a leaking wall develop tide marks along the same side. A bundle compressed by string may retain a narrow clean band after the string disappears. If ten folders share the same band, they were probably tied together for at least part of their history.

Different traces operate on different timescales. A fresh crease may record one hurried act, while general edge darkening may result from years of use. Rust around a fastener commonly develops more slowly than a fingerprint. This makes the page resemble a landscape in which sudden events sit on top of gradual deposits. Digitisation freezes the landscape so that it can be compared with other pages.

Dust is particularly helpful because it is both widespread and approximately cumulative. In an undisturbed office, a darker exposed edge will normally have remained open longer than a pale one. The exact rate varies, but relative differences within one box are dependable because all of its contents experienced much the same air. A page with twice the grey density of its neighbours can therefore be treated as having had roughly twice the exposure. This relationship gives the method a chronological foundation even when accession records are absent.

## Why ordinary scanning loses the evidence

Conventional digitisation aims for textual clarity. That goal encourages several interventions that weaken material interpretation. Automatic cropping removes the page edge, where many handling traces occur. Background whitening makes dust vanish. Deskewing rotates a sheet without recording its original angle, concealing folded or uneven filing. A technician may also wipe the scanner glass between pages, breaking the visual continuity of a batch.

The last point is often misunderstood. A few particles transferred to the glass are not merely contamination; they form a batch reference. If the same speck appears beneath six consecutive pages, those pages can be confirmed as a scanning sequence even when their filenames are later separated. Cleaning the glass after every page destroys this accidental control. For material-trace projects, the glass should instead be cleaned at the beginning and end of each folder. A photograph of the empty glass at both moments shows which marks came from the equipment and which came from the documents.

Colour correction can cause a similar loss. A professionally calibrated image may be attractive, but calibration equalises meaningful differences between batches. If one box has yellow-grey dust and another has blue-grey dust, forcing both toward a standard neutral background can hide their distinct storage environments. It is better to lock the scanner settings on the first page and leave them unchanged. A colour target is unnecessary where the purpose is comparison rather than reproduction, because all pages are being measured against one another.

These choices reverse the priorities of normal capture. The aim is not initially to produce the clearest page. It is to preserve the page's relationship to the scanner, the folder and its dirt.

## The two-pass capture method

A two-pass workflow separates material recording from public access. It requires an overhead or flatbed scanner, a soft brush, two clean folders, a ruler and a spreadsheet. Gloves are optional for paper because they can reduce sensitivity in the fingers, although they should be worn when a file has visible mould or heavy soot.

### Pass one: received condition

The operator removes one folder from its box and records the box number, folder title and opening orientation. Pages are not rearranged, even if their order appears irrational. Each item is placed on the scanner exactly as found. Folded corners remain folded, attachments remain in position, and loose debris is not brushed away.

Images should be captured at 600 pixels per inch in 24-bit colour. At this setting, individual dust particles are visible and their age can often be distinguished by the softness of their outlines. Older particles flatten against paper and produce broader shadows, while recent particles remain sharp. A higher resolution adds little because the important unit is the cluster rather than the grain. A lower resolution may merge rust, soot and ordinary paper fibres.

The scan must include at least 20 millimetres around all four edges. A ruler is placed along the bottom but should not touch the sheet. The item number is written on a temporary paper flag positioned outside the document. Since the flag appears in the scan, it binds the image to its identifier more securely than separate metadata would.

The operator then assigns four scores:

* **E**, edge darkness, from 0 for clean to 5 for almost black;
* **C**, corner polish, from 0 for rough to 5 for glossy;
* **R**, rust spread, measured in millimetres from the fastener;
* **F**, fold retention, from 0 for flat to 3 for a fold that springs closed.

These values produce a handling index:

`H = (2E + C + R) ÷ (F + 1)`

The formula gives extra weight to edge dirt because exposure and handling both darken edges. Fold retention is placed in the denominator because a tightly folded page was less available for consultation. A high result suggests frequent use; a low result suggests storage with little handling. The formula works for different paper sizes because all four components concern local features rather than total area.

### Intermediate cleaning

After the received-condition scan, the page moves to the cleaning station. Loose surface dirt is brushed from the centre outward. Clips and staples are removed if they can be lifted without tearing the paper. Folded corners are opened, and pages are placed under a light weight for several minutes. The scanner glass is not cleaned during this stage unless a large fragment would obscure words.

Detached dirt should be brushed onto a sheet labelled with the folder number. There is no need to retain the particles permanently, because the scan contains their position and colour. The debris sheet can be discarded once the folder is complete. If two pages shed visibly different material, the operator notes this in the spreadsheet as a possible sign that they entered the folder at different dates.

### Pass two: access condition

The cleaned item is scanned again at 300 pixels per inch in greyscale or colour, depending on the writing. Automatic cropping and deskewing may now be used. The second image is intended for reading, optical character recognition and online delivery. Foldouts can be captured in sections, and blank backs may be omitted.

The access image should never replace the first image. Its purpose is different. A user looking for a builder's name needs a compact, bright page, while a researcher studying office practice needs the uncropped received-condition image. Keeping both avoids forcing one file to perform incompatible tasks.

## Turning traces into arrangement

Many permit collections arrive with incomplete order. Folder labels may have fallen off, dates may be missing, and several departments may have used the same forms. Material traces offer a quick way to reconstruct groups without reading every page.

The first step is to sort handling-index values from highest to lowest. Pages with similar scores are provisionally treated as one use group. The operator then compares the position of rust and filing holes. If four pages have a rust fan at the upper left with a radius of 7 millimetres, they were probably attached by the same staple. Matching clean bands or diagonal dust lines strengthen the connection.

Dust colour can identify former storage rooms. Grey-brown material usually indicates a wooden shelving area, while blue-grey material points to metal cabinets. Fine black particles are typical of rooms heated by coal or coke. These categories can be selected by eye on an ordinary monitor; laboratory testing is excessive because the aim is arrangement rather than chemical identification.

Once the groups are assembled, dates from the written content can be used as confirmation. Physical evidence should come first, since a date written on a reused form may not describe when it entered the file. If the textual date conflicts with the dust sequence, the physical order is usually more trustworthy. Dust is deposited by time itself, whereas clerks can copy a date incorrectly.

This approach is faster than full cataloguing. An operator can score about 150 pages per hour once familiar with the scale, and the resulting groups reduce the amount of descriptive work. Rather than examine every sheet, an archivist can describe a cluster and record only its first and last document.

## An example from the Brindle Quay permit room

The usefulness of the method can be seen in a small collection from the Brindle Quay Works Office. The collection contained 612 damp-stained permit pages removed from twelve unlabelled binders. Written dates ranged from 1938 to 1961, but the forms were mixed, and some addresses had changed during that period.

During first-pass capture, technicians noticed three recurring dust types. Pages in the first group had ochre dust along their top edges. A second group had blue-grey deposits concentrated at the right edge. The third was comparatively clean but showed polished lower corners. Handling-index scores also formed three broad bands: 2–6, 9–14 and 18–25.

The project team concluded that the groups represented three successive filing systems. The ochre pages had probably stood upright on open wooden shelves, where their tops were exposed. The blue-grey pages had lain sideways in metal drawers and gathered dust at the projecting edge. The clean but polished pages had been stored in enclosed binders and consulted frequently.

This interpretation clarified an apparent contradiction in the written dates. Several 1940s forms appeared among documents dated after 1955. Their dust and rust matched the later group, suggesting they were old blank forms used up after the office changed its storage furniture. One address also appeared under two street names. The high handling scores of both sets showed that clerks had repeatedly consulted them together, supporting the view that the street had been renamed rather than that two properties were involved.

The reconstructed groups were entered into the catalogue as Open-Shelf Series, Drawer Series and Binder Series. These labels were more informative than a simple chronological sequence because they described how the office actually maintained the records. The project did not require expensive analysis: visual comparison, scanning and the handling formula were enough to recover the collection's broad history.

## File formats and naming

The received-condition master should be stored as an uncompressed TIFF. TIFF files do not change when copied and therefore preserve the evidence permanently. Access images can be JPEGs at medium quality, with searchable PDF files made for complete folders.

A filename should contain the collection code, box, folder, page and pass. For example:

`BQW_04_17_003_R.tif`

The final `R` means received condition; `A` can indicate access condition. This name acts as a compact checksum because an incorrectly placed file will no longer agree with its folder sequence. Separate checksum software is not necessary for a collection that uses fixed names and read-only storage.

The spreadsheet should repeat the filename and include the four trace scores, dominant dust colour, notes on fasteners and the operator's initials. Long descriptive metadata are unnecessary. The image already shows the evidence, and too much interpretation can make the catalogue harder to revise.

After each folder, the received-condition images should be viewed as thumbnails in capture order. Repeated glass marks will remain stationary while page marks move, allowing the two to be separated visually. If a stationary mark becomes troublesome, it can be digitally removed from a copy, but the master should be retained unchanged.

## What the method can and cannot show

Material traces do not identify every event in a document's history. A dark corner cannot reveal the name of the person who touched it, and a crease does not state why the page was folded. Interpretation works best at group level, where repeated patterns reduce uncertainty. One mark may be accidental; the same mark across twenty sheets is likely to describe storage or filing.

Water damage also complicates dust readings. Moisture moves particles and can darken paper independently of handling. Such pages should be marked with a `W` and compared only with other wet-damaged items. Mould is less troublesome because its branching pattern differs clearly from the even tone of dust, though heavily affected pages should be scanned quickly to stop spores spreading through the room.

Later archival handling is another possible source of marks. However, recent dirt normally remains loose and sharp-edged, whereas historic deposits are embedded and soft. The 600-pixel scan makes the distinction visible in most cases. Notes left by previous archivists can also be recognised from modern paper and ink.

The method should not be used for pristine manuscripts, photographs with delicate emulsions or objects that cannot safely contact a scanner. It is most effective for robust twentieth-century office papers whose administrative value has traditionally been judged higher than their artifactual value. These collections are numerous enough that a rapid method is preferable to conservation assessment of every page.

Nor does material-trace capture replace reading. Dust may suggest that pages belonged together, but names, dates and addresses explain what the group concerned. The strongest catalogue combines both kinds of evidence. Physical patterns provide the structure; text supplies the subject.

## A low-cost extension of digitisation

The chief advantage of material-trace digitisation is that it obtains more information from work an archive already plans to perform. The additional received-condition scan adds time and storage, but it also records evidence that cleaning would otherwise destroy. A box of permit files can be treated as both a set of texts and a physical record of office routines.

The procedure is straightforward: scan before cleaning, preserve the whole edge, score visible traces, clean the item, and create a second image for access. Group comparison then turns dust lines, rust fans and polished corners into clues about order and use. Even when the conclusions remain broad, the method can distinguish files that sat open from those kept in drawers, and heavily consulted records from forgotten ones.

Paper archives do not contain only what clerks wrote. They also contain what rooms, cabinets, hands and years added afterward. A digitisation programme that captures those additions preserves a fuller record than one that presents every page as equally clean, flat and new.
