# The Corridor Is a Subject: Building a School Timetable Around Teacher Movement

A school timetable is usually described as a grid of classes, teachers, rooms, and periods. That description leaves out a fifth element: the distance between rooms. A lesson may fit neatly into a cell while still being difficult to deliver because its teacher has to cross a courtyard, climb two floors, unlock a specialist room, and prepare equipment during a five-minute changeover.

This hidden timetable of movement can explain delays that otherwise look like failures of punctuality. It can also cause teachers to leave one class early, carry unsuitable quantities of material, or avoid activities that take time to set up. The ordinary timetable says that a teacher is free at 10:25 and required elsewhere at 10:30. The corridor timetable asks whether the teacher can actually get there.

One response is to treat teacher travel as a major constraint from the beginning of the timetabling process, rather than checking it after subjects and rooms have already been placed. This approach can be called **movement-first timetabling**. Its central idea is that a teacher should have a geographical pattern for the day, not merely a sequence of lessons.

## The hidden cost of a legal timetable

Consider Brackenmere Secondary, a fictional school with 640 pupils, 42 teachers, and three main teaching zones. The Stone Building contains ordinary classrooms on three floors. The Forge contains science laboratories, workshops, and two computing rooms. The North Annex contains art, music, drama, and four general rooms. A covered passage connects the Stone Building to the Forge, while the Annex is across a courtyard.

Brackenmere operates seven periods per day. Most passing periods last five minutes, although the change after lunch lasts seven. On paper, a teacher can be assigned to any room in any period because every teaching room is part of the same school. In practice, some transitions are much harder than others:

- Stone 104 to Stone 108 takes less than a minute.
- Stone 304 to Forge Lab 2 takes about four minutes without congestion.
- Forge Workshop 1 to North Annex Art 3 takes six or seven minutes.
- Any route involving the only lift can take longer when several classes change together.

The difference matters because travel time is not the only component of a room change. A teacher may also need to erase a board, shut down equipment, answer a pupil’s question, collect a laptop, and unlock the next room. Therefore, a four-minute walk in a five-minute passing period is not really feasible, even if a fast walker can complete it once.

Brackenmere’s timetable team could identify this problem by recording room changes over an ordinary week. A simple movement table might look like this:

| Teacher | Weekly room changes | Mean distance per change | Recorded distance burden |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mara Venn, mathematics | 14 | 110 m | 1,540 m |
| Iven Koss, computing | 11 | 165 m | 1,815 m |
| Sera Pell, languages | 17 | 70 m | 1,190 m |
| Orr Dalen, design | 8 | 220 m | 1,760 m |

These four teachers travel about 6,305 metres between lessons in a week. At an assumed indoor walking speed of 80 metres per minute, this represents nearly 79 minutes of walking. If packing and reopening a room adds two minutes to every move, the combined burden becomes about 179 minutes. This total is not all lost teaching time, because passing periods exist partly for movement, but it shows that a timetable can transfer several hours of operational work into spaces that the grid does not display.

A brief Tuesday tally at Brackenmere found that seven of ten late lesson starts followed a cross-zone room change. This suggests that geography accounts for roughly 70 percent of punctuality problems and should therefore be handled before most subject preferences. Although one day is a small sample, the physical arrangement of the school does not change much from week to week, so the same pattern can reasonably be expected across the year.

## A distance budget for each teacher

Movement-first timetabling gives each teacher a weekly **distance budget**. The budget is the amount of travel that can be included without creating an unreasonable working pattern. It is not intended to eliminate all movement. Some teachers have to use specialist rooms, and a completely stationary staff would require pupils to make every journey instead.

A basic movement burden can be written as:

`M = Σ(d / v) + p`

Here, `d` is the distance of each room change, `v` is walking speed, and `p` is preparation time. The result is an estimate of the minutes consumed by movement and room reset. Timetablers do not need precise architectural measurements. They can count staircases or use approximate route bands such as near, medium, and far.

For example, the following points can be assigned:

- Same room: 0 movement points
- Same corridor: 1 point
- Different floor in the same building: 2 points
- Adjacent building: 4 points
- North Annex to Forge: 7 points

A teacher with six daily lessons might receive a target of no more than eight movement points in one day. A teacher with mobility restrictions might receive a target of four. Staff who transport tools, instruments, or experiment materials might also have lower budgets because the distance is more disruptive for them.

The points are only a proxy, but this is useful because exact minutes tend to create false precision. On the other hand, the point system still permits a numerical comparison between two schedules. A day with routes worth 16 points is likely to be worse than one worth five points, even if the timetable software cannot predict congestion around every staircase.

Distance budgets should normally be calculated per teacher rather than per department. Two members of the same department can have different teaching loads and physical needs. However, an average departmental budget is faster to produce and should be sufficient in a large school. Once the department average is known, the same threshold can be applied to all of its teachers unless somebody requests an exception.

## Hard constraints and soft constraints

Not every room request has the same status. A useful movement-first model divides requirements into hard and soft constraints.

A **hard constraint** is one that should not be broken. Examples include:

- One teacher cannot teach two classes in the same period.
- Two classes cannot occupy the same room at the same time.
- A wheelchair user cannot be assigned to an inaccessible room.
- A practical chemistry session must have the required safety equipment.
- A part-time teacher cannot be scheduled outside contracted availability.

A **soft constraint** is desirable but may be broken if necessary. Examples include:

- A teacher prefers to remain in one room.
- A class should avoid three consecutive lessons in distant buildings.
- A teacher should not have a long move immediately after lunch duty.
- A department would like its rooms to be near one another.
- A tutor group prefers to meet in its usual base.

Teacher movement is generally a soft constraint, but it should be treated as almost hard when a transition exceeds the available passing time. A six-minute route during a five-minute change cannot become possible merely because the software assigns it a moderate penalty. Nevertheless, every constraint can be entered into the same score so that the timetable with the lowest total can be selected.

One possible score is:

`S = 10C + 6A + 3D + 2P`

In this expression, `C` is the number of teacher or room collisions, `A` is the number of accessibility problems, `D` is total movement points above the budgets, and `P` is the number of broken preferences. The timetable with the lowest score is considered best. Collisions carry the highest penalty, accessibility follows, and excessive distance is more important than ordinary preferences.

This scoring method simplifies the decision. For instance, removing one room collision is worth accepting up to three extra movement points. It also avoids arguments about which individual preference is most important. If a timetable has a score of 48 and another has a score of 41, the second is a better operational choice. The exact weights are less important than using them consistently.

## Zoning the school

The next step is to divide the site into timetable zones. Zones should represent travel difficulty, not simply architectural names. Two rooms in separate buildings might belong to one zone if they are connected by a short passage. Conversely, rooms on the ground and third floors of one building might belong to different zones.

Brackenmere could use four zones:

1. **Stone Low:** ground and first floors of the Stone Building.
2. **Stone High:** second and third floors.
3. **Forge:** laboratories, workshops, and computing.
4. **Annex:** arts rooms and nearby general rooms.

Each teacher is then given a primary zone. The primary zone is not necessarily the location of the teacher’s department. It should be the zone containing the greatest number of that teacher’s lessons. A mathematics teacher with two computing classes might be based in the Forge rather than Stone. A music teacher who also teaches many general humanities lessons could be based in the Annex because instruments are harder to move than exercise books.

Primary zoning allows the timetable to develop clusters. If a teacher has four lessons on Tuesday, three should normally be in the primary zone. The remaining lesson can be elsewhere, preferably next to a free period or lunch so that the travel is absorbed by a longer interval.

This method also makes room ownership less rigid. Instead of calling Stone 205 a mathematics room, the school calls it a Stone High room. Any suitable lesson may use it. Department displays and stored materials can remain, but these should not outweigh movement efficiency. A room belongs first to the timetable zone and second to a subject.

The simplest rule is to keep each teacher in one zone for half a day. Morning lessons can occur in one zone and afternoon lessons in another. This creates only one major move, normally during lunch. It also gives pupils a clear expectation that teachers will already be present when lessons begin.

## A movement-first construction method

A timetable can be built through a greedy procedure. “Greedy” means that the best available placement is taken at each step without calculating every possible complete timetable. This is suitable for schools because the number of possible timetables is too large to inspect manually.

The procedure has seven stages:

1. **Place specialist lessons.** Put laboratories, workshops, art rooms, and performance spaces into the grid first.
2. **Calculate each teacher’s initial zone burden.** Count how often the specialist lessons force the teacher to change zones.
3. **Choose the teacher with the greatest burden.** Place that teacher’s remaining classes in nearby rooms and periods.
4. **Create lesson clusters.** Consecutive lessons should be in the same room or zone.
5. **Fit pupil groups into the remaining periods.** If a pupil clash appears, move the smaller class because it will be easier to relocate.
6. **Add duties and meetings.** Place these in or near the zone where the teacher finishes teaching.
7. **Reduce the total score.** Swap rooms or periods until further changes stop improving `S`.

This order treats geography as the foundation. Traditional construction often places pupil option blocks early because many pupils share subject combinations. However, pupil clashes can usually be solved by moving a class, whereas a building cannot be moved. It is therefore sensible to establish staff routes first and fit option groups around them.

The greedy method is also understandable to staff. A fully automated optimisation system might produce a better result, but teachers can see why a lesson was placed near another lesson. Transparency matters because people are more likely to accept an inconvenient period if the geographical reason is visible.

## A worked Wednesday example

Suppose Iven Koss teaches computing and mathematics. On Wednesday he has the following required lessons:

- Period 1: Year 9 computing, which requires Forge Computing 1.
- Period 2: Year 8 mathematics, any general room.
- Period 4: Year 11 computing, which requires Forge Computing 2.
- Period 5: Year 7 mathematics, any general room.
- Period 7: Year 10 computing support, preferably a computer room.

A subject-first timetable might assign the mathematics lessons to the mathematics corridor in Stone High. Iven would then travel Forge–Stone High after Period 1, return to Forge for Period 4, travel back to Stone for Period 5, and return to Forge for Period 7. Using the zone points, that day has four cross-zone transitions worth 16 points. It appears balanced in departmental terms because mathematics takes place in mathematics rooms, but it is geographically fragmented.

A movement-first timetable puts Period 2 mathematics in Forge General 3 and Period 5 mathematics in Forge General 1. Period 7 remains in a computing room. Iven spends the whole teaching day in the Forge, producing zero cross-zone points. Pupils travel to him, but each pupil group makes the journey only once, while Iven would otherwise repeat it throughout the day.

The revised pattern also makes the free Period 3 more useful. Iven can prepare the Year 11 computing lesson near its equipment instead of using part of the period to return from Stone. Period 6 becomes a convenient time for technical support. A room that looks unusual for mathematics is therefore more efficient overall.

There is one drawback: Forge General 1 has fixed benches and only 24 seats, while the Year 7 class contains 26 pupils. Two spare stools could be added because the shortage affects only one period. Room capacity should normally be a hard constraint, but a small difference is acceptable if it preserves a full-day zone cluster.

## Rotating timetables and uneven weeks

Many schools use a two-week cycle. This complicates movement measurement because an efficient Week A can conceal a poor Week B. A teacher might stay in one zone for most of the first week and cross the site repeatedly in the second.

The solution is to average the distance budget across both weeks. If a teacher receives eight points per day, the two-week allowance is 80 points. It is not necessary for every day to be below eight. A 14-point Tuesday can be balanced by a two-point Wednesday. Staff experience workload by the fortnight, so the average gives a fair picture.

Rotation can also be used deliberately. A class that meets four times over two weeks might use a specialist room twice and a nearby general room twice. This reduces pressure on specialist spaces without removing access altogether. For example, a science group can perform experiments in a laboratory and complete written analysis in a general room. The timetabler should place the general-room lesson next to the teacher’s other lessons, even if this changes the usual sequence of the topic.

The same principle applies to shared teachers. If a drama teacher spends two days at Brackenmere and three at another school, all Annex lessons should be concentrated on the Brackenmere days. It is better to give the teacher six lessons in one location than to create gaps simply to make each day look even.

## Buffers, lunches, and duties

Free periods and lunch breaks are often treated as empty cells into which meetings or cover lessons can be inserted. In a movement-first timetable, some gaps are **travel buffers**. They protect difficult transitions and should not automatically be filled.

A teacher who moves from the Annex to Stone High might need a free period between lessons. The gap permits travel, preparation, and recovery of any delay. Marking can still be done during the remainder of the period, so the buffer is not wasted.

Lunch can serve as the main zone-change point. Morning lessons should be clustered on one side of the site and afternoon lessons on the other. However, lunch duties must then be placed carefully. Assigning an Annex-based teacher to supervise the Forge dining hall removes the benefit of the longer interval. Duties should follow the teacher’s existing route rather than being distributed only by numerical equality.

A similar rule applies to meetings. Department meetings should happen in the zone where most members already finish the day. If this changes from day to day, the meeting room can rotate. A fifteen-minute meeting does not justify fifteen teachers crossing the site simply to use the department’s traditional room.

## Reading the finished timetable

The final timetable should be checked in two ways. First, calculate movement points for every teacher. Second, print each teacher’s day as a route rather than as a grid. A route description such as “Forge, Forge, free, Annex, Annex, Stone High” reveals problems more quickly than room codes scattered across a table.

The school should pay particular attention to:

- Days with more than two zone changes.
- Long transitions after practical lessons.
- Moves involving stairs or the lift.
- Teachers carrying shared equipment.
- Lunch duties in a different zone from adjacent lessons.
- Free periods that have accidentally become compulsory travel time.

A successful timetable will not necessarily minimise the total distance walked by everyone. Its main purpose is to reduce repeated teacher moves. Pupil movement is less important because pupils travel in groups, have fewer materials to carry, and are expected to change rooms. If 25 pupils cross the courtyard for one lesson, that is still operationally preferable to a teacher making several similar crossings during the day.

Once cross-zone moves have been reduced, the school can monitor lesson starts for a week. If lateness declines, the timetable is working. If it does not, the zones may have been drawn incorrectly. The point thresholds can then be adjusted without reconstructing the entire schedule.

## Conclusion

School timetables do more than assign people to periods. They create routes through physical space. Ignoring those routes produces schedules that are technically valid but operationally weak: teachers arrive late, preparation is squeezed, and free periods are consumed by transit.

Movement-first timetabling makes the corridor visible. It gives teachers distance budgets, divides the site into practical zones, clusters lessons by half-day, and uses breaks as deliberate transition points. Specialist lessons are placed first, heavily travelling teachers are handled next, and pupil groups are fitted around the resulting geography.

The strongest timetable is therefore not always the one that preserves department rooms or spreads lessons most evenly. It is the one in which teachers can complete the journeys the grid silently requires. Once distance is treated as part of the timetable rather than as an inconvenience outside it, the school day becomes easier to start on time.

Specialist lessons are placed first, heavily travelling teachers are handled next, and pupil groups are fitted around the resulting geography.

The strongest timetable is therefore not always the one that preserves department rooms or spreads lessons most evenly. It is the one in which teachers can complete the journeys the grid silently requires. Once distance is treated as part of the timetable rather than as an inconvenience outside it, the school day becomes easier to start on time.

# The Courtesy Ledger

At six-ten each morning, before the lifts began carrying auditors to the glass floors above, Mara Venn went down to the Revenue House basement and read the dead letters.

They came in grey tubs from the postal service: final demands, discrepancy notices, payment-plan warnings. Each envelope had crossed the city under statutory seal and returned with a reason stamped in violet ink.

**NO SUCH UNIT.**

**BUILDING REMOVED.**

**ADDRESSEE UNKNOWN.**

The new compliance system treated most of these as delivered.

That was not, strictly speaking, a mistake. Ledgerlight checked addresses against the National Address File before sending anything. If the file recognized a street and number, delivery was presumed. Returned mail belonged to a separate postal database, purchased under a contract that did not permit Revenue House to retain individual scans for more than thirty days. By the time a taxpayer reached the automatic-collection stage, the envelope’s journey had vanished, but the presumption remained.

Mara had designed the screen on which that presumption appeared as a green shield.

She found one envelope in the third tub with a thumbprint of blue clay on its corner. It had been sent to Kiln Nine Cooperative, 9 Furnace Row, Mallow Ward. The post had stamped it **SITE RE-NUMBERED**, then someone had written beneath that, in pencil, *Try the old bathhouse behind the viaduct*.

Ledgerlight showed Kiln Nine as an active ceramics retailer with two unanswered notices and an assessed liability of 48,220 crowns. Collection was scheduled for Monday.

Mara carried the envelope upstairs.

Director Greve was standing at the window of his office, dictating figures while the city brightened behind him. His walls held no certificates, only a framed page from the old paper tax ledger, its columns ruled by hand.

“Harbor release is in four days,” he said when Mara put the envelope on his desk. “If this is about returned post, send it to Operations.”

“The system says it was delivered.”

“The system says the address passed validation.”

“Those aren’t the same thing.”

Greve dismissed his recorder with a tap. He was not an impatient man, which made his impatience more effective. “We have eighty-seven million crowns sitting in mature debt. Some of it has been sitting there because the old system was too slow to collect from anyone who ignored a brown envelope. Ledgerlight was built to change that.”

“I know what it was built to do.”

“Better than anyone.” He looked at the clay mark. “Visit the ward if you need to. Bring me a defect, not a sad address.”

Mara put the envelope back in her case.

Her mother had run a ferry-café when Mara was young, serving tea and seed cake between crossings of the Neral. Every quarter, a clerk sent three forms asking for the same receipts in different arrangements. Her mother paid what she owed, usually late, and kept every government envelope in a biscuit tin as if it might hatch. Mara had joined Revenue House because fear seemed a poor tool for collecting arithmetic.

Ledgerlight was supposed to replace fear with certainty.

Mallow Ward lay beyond the freight viaduct, where the river’s old industrial bank had been divided into workshops, flats and narrow gardens. Furnace Row had once been a straight run of brick factories. After a flood and two redevelopment schemes, it bent around a school, vanished under the viaduct, and resumed with the same numbers on the other side.

At the tram stop Mara asked a flower seller for Kiln Nine.

“New Nine or old Nine?”

“The cooperative.”

“Blue door or green?”

“The tax record doesn’t mention a door.”

“Then you’ll want Nera.”

Nera Quill, the district postal carrier, was eating an apple on the steps of a shuttered bathhouse. She was a compact woman in a red raincoat polished pale at the shoulders. Beside her sat three crates of mail and a black notebook fastened with string.

Mara introduced herself and displayed her Revenue House card.

Nera glanced at it. “You’re early. Collections usually comes after lunch.”

“I’m looking for Kiln Nine.”

“You and half the government.”

“Do you know where they are?”

Nera held up the notebook. “That depends. Are you asking me, or are you requisitioning this?”

“I’m asking you.”

The carrier retied the string. “Blue door, through the yard. Don’t call it the old bathhouse. The cooperators spent six years getting the registry to stop calling it condemned.”

Kiln Nine occupied the bathhouse’s former laundry. Its tall windows were fogged from firing, and shelves of bowls covered the tiled walls where towels had once been stacked. Fourteen people shared three kilns, one clay mixer and, because payment companies charged by account, one card terminal.

Jori Senn met Mara at a table crowded with cups. He was broad-handed, with white slip dried in the hairs of his arms. Before Mara finished explaining, he fetched a blue folder from beneath a sack of glaze powder.

“I filed,” he said. “All of us filed. Here are the acknowledgments.”

The cooperative’s arrangement was simple when Jori described it and tangled when Ledgerlight described it. Customers paid Kiln Nine’s terminal. Once a week, the cooperative distributed each potter’s takings, less rent, firing charges and a reserve for repairs. The payment processor reported the full stream as Kiln Nine retail revenue. The potters also issued electronic invoices under their own tax numbers and declared their individual shares.

Ledgerlight saw the same money twice. It treated the cooperative as a retailer concealing most of its sales and the weekly distributions as wages paid to workers who had separately declared unexplained business income.

“It says we employ ourselves,” Jori said. “It also says we’re hiding what we earn from ourselves. If we were that clever, the roof wouldn’t leak.”

Mara checked the cooperative’s registry entry. It was nine years old and classified Kiln Nine as a household-goods shop. No partnership schedule had been attached to its annual return.

“You should have updated this classification,” she said.

“We tried. The amendment went to the registered office for signature.”

“Which is?”

“Furnace Row Nine.”

“The place that no longer exists.”

“That place exists on every form except the map.”

It was not complete innocence. Two members had filed late. One had omitted cash sales from a winter market. The cooperative had claimed a kiln repair in the wrong period, and Jori had missed a quarterly prepayment of six hundred and twenty crowns. The true account would not be zero.

That, Mara thought, made the 48,220 more dangerous. An entirely false assessment was easy to reject. A false assessment wrapped around a real debt could survive for years.

“Can you stop the collection?” Jori asked.

“I can recommend a hold.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No,” Mara said. “It isn’t.”

Outside, Nera was sorting envelopes on a crate.

“How many businesses here use shared terminals?” Mara asked.

“Enough.”

“How many have addresses that don’t match the national file?”

“Depends what you mean by address.”

“I mean somewhere a notice can reach them.”

“Then most have one.” Nera tapped her notebook. “It just may not be the one your office believes in.”

She called the book her courtesy ledger. On each page she recorded the knowledge that made delivery possible after official knowledge failed: *Rell family above the green boiler door; use side stair.* *Tovan Dey sleeps at his sister’s in hard frost.* *Parcel locker broken; leave medicine with tailor only.* Some entries were crossed through so heavily they had become wounds in the paper.

Mara saw enough to understand that the ledger contained more than addresses. It held separations not yet made public, illnesses, debts, informal sublets, night shifts and quiet changes of name.

“If we copied the tax-relevant entries—” she began.

“No.”

“We could correct the records.”

“No.” Nera pulled the book against her coat. “People tell the post where they are because they want letters, not because they consent to every office in Sable knowing whose sofa they sleep on.”

“These notices can lead to seizure.”

“That is precisely why I won’t turn courtesy into surveillance.”

Mara flushed. Her request had seemed practical until Nera named it.

“Then help me test what the official records are missing,” she said. “No copying. No names without permission.”

Nera considered her over the last bite of apple. “Fifty stops. You carry your own bag.”

For two days they walked Mallow Ward.

Ledgerlight had classified forty-six of the fifty sampled addresses as valid. At nineteen, the named person or business had moved. Seven were duplicates created when the city added letters to subdivided properties. Five led to locked yards where the unit numbers could not be seen from the street. At one address, a notice for a bicycle repairer had been delivered to a nursery called Little Spokes.

Nera found thirty-eight of the intended recipients without opening her notebook in front of Mara. She asked each whether they would speak to Revenue House. Twenty-nine agreed.

Their cases did not form a choir of the blameless. A caterer had ignored notices because he believed changing his business name erased an old liability. A landlord had declared three rooms while renting five. A mechanic kept two sets of invoices and, when Mara asked why, said, “Because one set costs me less.”

Nera gave Mara a dry look after that visit. “Put him in your report. Otherwise they’ll say I only introduced you to saints.”

But seventeen people showed the same pair of failures as Kiln Nine: income reported once by an individual or small partnership and again through a shared payment account, followed by statutory mail sent to a technically valid but unusable address. Eleven had already incurred non-response penalties. Four were scheduled for automatic bank restraint on Monday.

At night Mara worked from a rented room over a bakery, drawing the data path on sheets of wrapping paper.

The address validator consulted the National Address File. The postal returns system sent Revenue House a daily count but, because of the retention clause, not a durable status attached to each account. Ledgerlight’s green shield therefore measured whether an address existed, not whether a notice had arrived.

The payment matcher had another seam. It was designed for one merchant identity, one settlement account and one taxpayer. Shared terminals were allowed, but only if a partnership schedule carried the correct distribution code. Small cooperatives registered under older categories could not submit that schedule through the self-service portal.

Neither flaw alone produced the crisis. Together they did. The matcher created implausible debts; the address process prevented people from contesting them; silence then raised Ledgerlight’s confidence that collection was appropriate.

Mara sent her findings to Director Greve at three in the morning.

He called at seven.

“Seventeen cases are not a national defect,” he said.

“They’re seventeen out of twenty-nine people who agreed to show me their accounts.”

“In a ward selected because you already suspected a problem. That is not a random sample.”

“No. It’s a failure sample.”

“Vendor Assurance says the duplicate-income rate is below three-tenths of one percent.”

“They only count corrections completed before assessment. These people never received a usable notice, so they never entered the correction data.”

Greve was silent for a moment. “The finance minister announces Harbor release on Monday. I can request a ward-level exclusion. I cannot freeze national collection because one district has creative property numbering.”

“The same merchant pattern appears in forty-three districts.”

“You’ve checked?”

“I started the query.”

“Started is not completed.” His voice softened. “Mara, there are people in that Monday file who have ignored six notices, shifted money between banks and boasted that Revenue House will never catch up. Every delay is paid for by someone who filed honestly. Fairness cuts in both directions.”

She knew that. It was what made him difficult to oppose.

“When does the batch lock?” she asked.

“Sunday at midnight.”

On Saturday morning, Nera found Mara asleep at Kiln Nine with her head beside the cooperative’s card statements. Jori and two other potters were matching invoice numbers to weekly distributions. The figures covered the table in pencilled columns.

“We found the actual liability,” Jori said. “Or what we think it is.”

The cooperative owed 3,840 crowns, mostly from a misdated equipment deduction. Individual corrections left Jori owing 713, including his missed prepayment and interest. Two members were due small refunds.

Jori stared at the number. “I can pay this in three months.”

“Four, if you use the standard plan,” Mara said.

“And then?”

“Then you are compliant.”

He laughed once, without humor. “I was compliant on Tuesday. By Wednesday I was a debtor for forty-eight thousand. Today I’m compliant if I owe seven hundred and thirteen. Your words move faster than money.”

Mara closed the folder. “Yes.”

Nera placed a bundle of postal forms on the table. They were requests for investigation of undeliverable statutory mail, one for each consenting participant in the sample. The carrier had signed them; so had her district supervisor.

“You said the post only sends counts,” Nera said. “These make individual delivery failures part of the official case file. No courtesy ledger required.”

Mara looked at the forms. “How long will central processing take?”

“Six to eight weeks.”

“The collections run tomorrow.”

“I deliver letters. Miracles are another union.”

By Sunday evening Mara’s national query had found 6,412 open accounts with the same merchant-settlement pattern. Of those, 1,087 had multiple non-response penalties. Postal counts suggested that Mallow Ward was not exceptional, but the erased account-level data made it impossible to identify every failed delivery.

At eleven-forty, Director Greve denied a national freeze. He approved holds for the twenty-nine Mallow cases and ordered a review after release.

Mara sat alone in the cooperative office, listening to rain tick through a cracked pane into a bucket. On her screen, Ledgerlight’s collection batch counted down toward lock.

The system had an emergency control called Contamination Hold. It had been designed for corrupted bank feeds and hostile data insertion. Activating it required an officer to identify a common upstream source whose unreliability could spread across assessments. The payment-processor classifications qualified. Perhaps. The legal guidance assumed technical corruption, not a category that had been wrong for nine years.

Mara entered the processor codes used by shared terminals. The preview caught 4,903 of the 6,412 suspect accounts and another 311 that might be perfectly valid. Those 311 would have collection delayed, not cancelled. Some money would be moved or hidden during the pause.

She thought of the mechanic’s two invoice books. She thought of Jori’s 713 crowns nested inside the demand for 48,220. Then she thought of her green shield, promising delivery because a building existed somewhere.

At eleven fifty-eight, she activated the hold.

The system asked for a reason.

Mara typed: **Assessment confidence is derived from silence produced by an unverified contact channel.**

Then she placed her identity card on the reader.

The Monday announcement went ahead. Harbor release collected eleven million crowns before breakfast, restrained hundreds of accounts and sent payment-plan offers to thousands more. It did not touch the 5,214 accounts inside Mara’s hold.

By nine, she was back in Director Greve’s office. Two Vendor Assurance lawyers occupied the chairs by the window. Greve had the stillness of a man preserving his anger for useful work.

“You used a cyber-contamination control to suspend tax collection,” one lawyer said.

“I used a data-contamination control,” Mara replied.

“The feeds were accurate. Those payments occurred.”

“The amounts were accurate. Their meaning was not.”

The second lawyer opened Mara’s sample report. “Your locations were supplied by a postal worker’s private notebook. This evidence cannot be reproduced or audited.”

“The notebook supplied no tax evidence. It helped consenting recipients receive me. The cases are supported by processor statements, invoices, registry records and signed postal investigations.”

“Twenty-nine cases.”

“And a national query showing the same reporting structure in six thousand four hundred and twelve.”

Greve turned from the window. “Why didn’t you include all of them in the hold?”

“The control requires a shared upstream code. Some processors don’t identify shared terminals consistently.”

“So there are another fifteen hundred suspect accounts you did not protect.”

“Yes.”

“And three hundred eleven inside the hold that may be deliberate non-payers.”

“Yes.”

No answer would make the boundary clean. Mara let the untidiness remain in the room.

Greve picked up the clay-marked envelope from Kiln Nine. “You have made certainty expensive.”

“It already was,” Mara said. “We had charged the price to people who couldn’t see the bill.”

The review lasted four months.

Ledgerlight was not withdrawn. The finance ministry would not abandon a system that had increased on-time filing and found large debts the paper process had missed. Instead, returned statutory mail became an account-level event retained under a revised postal agreement. A first return stopped the non-response penalty clock. A second required another contact channel or human review before restraint.

The registry added a settlement-agent category for cooperatives, market associations and shared workshops. Revenue House sent correction forms to 6,412 accounts. Some recipients received refunds. Some owed modest balances. Nearly nine hundred assessments were confirmed, including the mechanic’s, after evidence showed income had truly been omitted.

The reforms did not solve Mallow Ward’s numbering, nor did they teach every processor to describe money correctly. They added delays and reviews that Operations complained about each quarter.

Kiln Nine entered a four-month payment plan. Jori paid the 713 crowns, then sent Mara a cup glazed the same blue as the print on the returned envelope. Its base was slightly uneven. It rocked on her desk whenever the trams passed.

Mara was removed from the Harbor team and assigned to a new Exceptions Integrity unit on the third floor. Director Greve called it a necessary separation of duties. Everyone else called it what they pleased.

One morning, a month after she moved offices, she found Nera Quill waiting in the corridor with the courtesy ledger under her arm.

“I’m not giving you this,” Nera said.

“I know.”

Nera opened to a clean page and wrote Mara’s name. Beneath it she added: *Third floor, west stair. Reads what comes back.*

“What is that for?” Mara asked.

“In case the official directory loses you.”

She closed the book before Mara could see the other names and tied the string around it again.
---

# SomnoBridge: Mechanical Transmission of Bed-Partner Movements as a Modifiable Cause of Sleep Fragmentation

## Project summary

Sleep is usually measured as though it occurs within an isolated individual, yet a large proportion of adults routinely share a mattress. A turn, leg adjustment, or abrupt sit-up by one sleeper creates a mechanical impulse that travels through the mattress and bed frame to the other sleeper. This input is distinct from sound, light, temperature, and intentional social interaction, but it is nearly absent from current models of sleep continuity. It may be especially important because it arrives unpredictably, can occur dozens of times per night, and often coincides with unstable sleep in the moving partner. Conventional actigraphy cannot reliably determine which person moved first, while standard polysomnography records physiological consequences without measuring the transmission path through the bed.

We propose that bed-sharing creates a dyadic perturbation system: movement by one sleeper generates mechanical energy, the bed transforms that energy according to its construction and loading, and the co-sleeper either filters the perturbation or expresses a cortical, autonomic, or behavioral response. Repeated responses that are individually brief may accumulate into meaningful sleep fragmentation. Conversely, some transmitted movements may be physiologically neutral or even provide a familiar cue that supports continuity. Distinguishing disruptive transfer from harmless synchrony is necessary before recommending mattress isolation, behavioral changes, or separate sleeping arrangements.

The SomnoBridge project will establish the natural history, causal physiology, and modifiability of mechanically transmitted bed-partner disturbance. We will combine 21-night home recordings in 180 bed-sharing dyads, stage-targeted laboratory perturbations in 96 sleepers, and a randomized crossover trial of an active mechanical-isolation platform in 120 dyads. Our central hypothesis is that transferred movement energy produces a nonlinear increase in recipient arousal probability, moderated by sleep stage and momentary neurophysiological protection, and that reducing transfer will improve sleep continuity without reducing bed-sharing time. The project is organized around three aims.

**Aim 1 will quantify the nightly movement-transfer network in habitual bed-sharing environments.** We will determine how often one sleeper’s movement precedes a physiological response in the other, identify bed and sleeper characteristics associated with high transfer, and create a validated event-attribution method.

**Aim 2 will test whether realistic mechanical impulses cause stage-dependent cortical and autonomic responses.** Closed-loop laboratory delivery will separate mechanical stimulation from coincident sound and establish dose-response functions across N2, N3, and rapid eye movement sleep.

**Aim 3 will test whether reducing cross-bed mechanical transfer improves objective sleep continuity and next-day function.** A counterbalanced crossover trial will compare active isolation with a logging-only control condition under participants’ usual home sleeping conditions.

Together, these studies will move bed-partner disturbance from a loosely defined complaint to a measurable exposure with a testable physiological pathway. The resulting methods and de-identified dataset will also support research on insomnia, aging, caregiving, and assistive sleep technologies.

## Scientific premise and innovation

Bed-partner effects are commonly inferred from morning reports or wrist movement correlations. Those approaches cannot reliably distinguish four possibilities: one sleeper physically disturbs the other; both respond to a shared environmental event; both transition between stages for independent reasons; or one person reacts to the other only after awakening for another cause. The inability to separate these pathways has encouraged contradictory interpretations of movement synchrony. High synchrony may indicate affiliation, common schedules, shared disturbance, or a mechanically coupled mattress.

SomnoBridge addresses this ambiguity at the level of transmission. A thin force-sensing array will measure movement at each side of the bed, while frame accelerometers will capture energy crossing the midline. Concurrent frontal electroencephalography, photoplethysmography, respiratory effort, body position, and ambient sensing will identify recipient responses and plausible common triggers. Rather than treating the dyad’s activity as two correlated nightly totals, we will model ordered events over seconds: source movement, transmitted impulse, recipient physiology, and recipient movement.

The project is innovative in four respects. First, it treats the bed as part of the sleep system rather than as an unmeasured background object. Second, it combines ecological monitoring with perturbations matched to each participant’s naturally observed exposure. Third, it separates the mechanical and acoustic components of a partner turn. Fourth, it tests a practical intervention while retaining bed-sharing, an outcome that may matter even when separate beds would improve an individual’s sleep.

Our mechanistic model predicts a threshold rather than a simple linear relationship. Low-energy impulses should usually be absorbed without measurable consequence. Above an individualized threshold, response probability should rise steeply, particularly during lighter N2 sleep and during physiologically unstable periods near spontaneous transitions. In N2, greater pre-event spindle activity is expected to reduce response probability at a given mechanical dose, whereas large impulses may evoke a K-complex, transient heart-rate acceleration, or full arousal. N3 should show lower behavioral response but potentially larger evoked slow waves. Rapid eye movement sleep may combine relative skeletal immobility with variable autonomic sensitivity. These stage-specific predictions will be tested rather than collapsed into a single nightly association.

## Preliminary foundation

The Harborline Sleep Research Unit has developed two research tools for this project. TurnTrace is a source-attribution pipeline that combines bilateral force maps and frame acceleration to identify movement onset, source side, peak transferred energy, and subsequent movement on the opposite side. LatticeLift is a two-sided support platform whose central bridge contains accelerometers and low-profile counterforce actuators. In active mode, the platform applies a brief opposing force after detecting an impulse leaving one side; in control mode, it records the same signal but does not counteract it.

In a feasibility sample of 24 dyads monitored for 10 nights each, TurnTrace identified major turns against dual video ratings with 91% sensitivity and 88% positive predictive value. Source-side agreement was 94%. Full polysomnography on one laboratory night for 12 of these dyads showed that recipient EEG activation was more common after high-transfer than low-transfer turns, although the pilot was not powered for efficacy or stage-specific inference. Bench testing with weighted articulated forms found that LatticeLift reduced cross-midline impulse energy by a median of 67% across six foam and hybrid mattress constructions. In eight overnight acceptability tests, active and control modes differed by less than 1.5 dBA in bedside sound level. These results establish measurement and engineering feasibility while leaving the central causal and clinical questions open.

## Aim 1: Map natural movement transmission and recipient responses

We will enroll 180 adult dyads who share the same bed on at least four nights per week. A dyad may consist of romantic partners, relatives, or other adults who routinely co-sleep; relationship type will be recorded rather than assumed. Recruitment will be stratified to obtain variation in age from 25 to 65 years, body size difference, mattress construction, habitual bed-sharing duration, and gender configuration. Participants will complete home respiratory screening. Untreated moderate or severe sleep apnea, injurious parasomnia, uncontrolled seizure disorder, and inability to use the sensors safely will be exclusionary. Stable medication use will be permitted and modeled.

Each dyad will complete 21 nights of home recording. The system will include a bilateral under-sheet force array, frame accelerometers, one-channel frontal EEG for each sleeper, finger photoplethysmography on six prespecified nights, respiratory effort bands on three nights, and wrist inertial sensors throughout. Ambient temperature, light, and nonverbal sound-energy spectra will be stored at one-second resolution. Raw speech will neither be retained nor transmitted. Participants will record bed entry, intended sleep time, awakenings they remember, alcohol and caffeine timing, pain, illness, and whether another person or animal entered the bed.

A subset of 40 dyads, sampled across low, middle, and high home transfer estimates, will undergo two laboratory nights with full polysomnography and infrared motion recording. Independent scorers blinded to the force signals will mark sleep stages, cortical arousals, respiratory events, and limb movements. These nights will validate home EEG staging and the temporal classification of recipient responses.

The primary Aim 1 measure is the rate of recipient cortical arousal within 0.5 to 15 seconds after a source movement that produces measurable cross-midline energy. Secondary responses include heart-rate acceleration, K-complex occurrence, stage transition, recipient movement, and remembered awakening. A multilevel marked point-process model will compare observed event chains with time-shuffled source events drawn from the same sleeper, stage, and clock-hour. Shared sound, light, respiratory events, and simultaneous force onset will be used to classify likely common-cause events. Analyses will estimate how response probability varies with transferred energy, stage, time of night, prior wakefulness, body-size difference, mattress type, and repeated exposure.

The deliverables will be a validated source-attribution algorithm, normative distributions for movement generation and transfer, and a mechanical susceptibility index for each sleeper. We will also test whether apparent whole-night synchrony remains after removing events explained by mattress transmission and common environmental triggers. This distinction is important because correlation between two sleepers’ activity counts does not by itself reveal interaction.

## Aim 2: Establish causal dose-response functions across sleep stages

Aim 2 will enroll 96 sleepers from Aim 1, balanced across mechanical susceptibility and sex and selected without regard to whether they consider their partner disruptive. Each participant will complete an adaptation night followed by two experimental laboratory nights. The participant will sleep on one side of the bed while an adjacent anthropomorphic platen reproduces movement waveforms recorded from that participant’s partner at home. The platen allows mechanical input to be delivered without awakening or otherwise changing the behavior of a second sleeper.

Real-time polysomnographic staging will trigger perturbations during stable N2, N3, and rapid eye movement sleep. Events will be separated by at least eight minutes and suspended after an arousal, respiratory event, or stage transition. No more than 18 perturbations will be delivered per night. Mechanical amplitudes will correspond to the participant’s 20th, 50th, and 80th percentiles of naturally experienced transferred energy, capped by a prespecified safety and comfort limit. The event set will include mechanical-only playback under low-level broadband masking, acoustic-only playback reproducing the sound envelope of the partner’s movement, combined mechanical and acoustic playback, and sham triggers with neither stimulus. Event order will be randomized within stage, subject to sleep availability.

The primary endpoint is cortical arousal probability within 15 seconds of the trigger. Prespecified secondary endpoints are EEG spectral activation, K-complex and spindle expression, heart-rate acceleration, pulse-amplitude reduction, stage transition, behavioral movement, and return to stable sleep. Pre-event spindle density, slow-wave phase, recent arousal burden, and time of night will be evaluated as moderators. The analysis will estimate an individualized mechanical dose-response curve and test whether adding sound shifts the curve beyond the mechanical effect alone.

To address habituation and anticipation, participants will not be told the timing or number of events, sham triggers will be frequent, and trial number will be included in the model. Morning assessments will include perceived disturbance, sleep restoration, mood, and a 10-minute psychomotor vigilance task. These next-day measures are secondary because the experiment is optimized to resolve event-level physiology, not to mimic an entire season of naturally fragmented sleep.

Aim 2 provides the causal bridge that observational dyadic recordings cannot supply. Distinguishing disruptive transfer from harmless synchrony is necessary before recommending mattress isolation, behavioral changes, or separate sleeping arrangements.

# Pause-Aware Laboratory Automation Using Chemical Sentinel Wells

## Project summary

Laboratory robots are reliable when a protocol proceeds exactly as scheduled, but their recovery from interruption is usually crude. After a power fluctuation, depleted tip rack, blocked reader, or operator pause, a system may either continue from the next command or discard the entire plate. Neither response accounts for the physical history of the material. During the interruption, some wells may evaporate, beads may settle, enzymes may remain active, and only part of a reagent addition may have occurred. The event log records commands, not necessarily the resulting chemical state.

This project will develop and test a pause-aware automation framework called **SentryPause**. It will reserve eight wells on each 96-well plate for inexpensive sentinel reactions that integrate thermal exposure, evaporation, mixing history, and addition completeness. Sentinel measurements will be combined with scheduler logs, module temperatures, pipette pressure traces, plate images, and elapsed time to estimate a compact state vector for the interrupted plate. A constrained decision policy will then choose among four validated actions: resume, mix and resume, replenish and resume, or restart affected wells from a retained intermediate.

The work will use three contrasting automated workflows: a coupled enzyme-rate assay, magnetic-bead cleanup of synthetic DNA, and cell-free fluorescent protein expression. Development experiments will deliberately introduce five common interruption classes at several protocol stages. Recovery decisions will be compared with immediate resumption, fixed timeout rules, and decisions made by experienced automation operators from the same logs. Evaluation will use unopened reagent lots, calendar-separated test runs, and a second robotic platform.

The primary outcome is usable yield: the proportion of production wells meeting predeclared workflow-specific quality limits. Secondary outcomes include calibration of failure probabilities, recovery time, reagent consumption, false restart rate, and sentinel capacity cost. The central hypothesis is that chemical sentinels reveal consequential state changes that cannot be reconstructed from timestamps alone, allowing more material to be recovered without concealing poor-quality results.

## Motivation and technical gap

Automated protocols are often represented as sequences of transfers, incubations, mixing steps, and measurements. This representation is adequate for execution but incomplete for recovery. A command such as “incubate for 20 minutes” does not distinguish 20 minutes on a controlled heater from 12 minutes on the heater followed by eight minutes on an unsealed ambient deck. Similarly, a logged transfer can conceal partial aspiration, dispensing into only the first portion of a plate, or liquid retained in a tip. When execution is interrupted, the scheduler knows where it stopped but has only indirect evidence of what happened to the sample.

Most practical recovery rules therefore rely on elapsed time and the last acknowledged command. Such rules are transparent and safe in narrow settings, but they discard material unnecessarily near conservative time limits and may accept compromised material just inside those limits. Full digital twins offer a more ambitious alternative, yet they require kinetic and transport models for every reagent combination. Those models are expensive to construct and become brittle when lots, ambient conditions, or plate geometries change.

SentryPause takes a middle path. It does not attempt to model every molecular species. Instead, it measures a few dimensions of plate history that recur across workflows:

- **Thermal dose:** accumulated time-temperature exposure, rather than current temperature alone.
- **Solvent loss:** evaporation during an open or poorly sealed hold.
- **Dispense completion:** whether a scheduled addition reached all intended regions.
- **Settling or separation:** loss of suspension homogeneity during inactivity.

The proposed sentinels are sacrificial wells containing low-cost reporting mixtures rather than valuable samples. A slow fluorogenic reaction will act as a thermal-dose integrator. A nonreactive dual-absorbance tracer will report concentration caused by solvent loss. A colored addition marker will reveal plate regions reached before a partial-batch fault. A bead-containing sentinel will provide an image-derived settling index. The first two sentinels will be distributed across plate corners and central positions so that the system can distinguish plate-wide changes from spatial gradients.

Chemical sentinels cannot reproduce every production reaction. Their role is narrower: to provide direct evidence about shared physical exposures. The project will test whether this evidence adds enough predictive information to justify consuming eight wells and adding approximately 70 seconds of reading time per plate.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The project addresses four questions:

1. Can sentinel wells estimate interruption-related physical state more accurately than execution logs and module sensors alone?
2. Does a recovery policy based on that state increase usable yield compared with standard resume-or-restart rules?
3. Does the framework transfer across workflows and robotic platforms without full retraining?
4. When do the capacity and time costs of sentinels exceed their recovery benefit?

The predeclared hypotheses are:

- **H1:** Adding sentinel measurements will reduce the Brier score for predicting well-level quality failure by at least 20% relative to a model using logs, time, and hardware sensors alone.
- **H2:** SentryPause will increase usable yield after interruption by at least 15 percentage points relative to immediate resumption, while increasing median reagent cost per attempted plate by no more than 10%.
- **H3:** After 12 calibration plates per workflow, a model transferred to a second automation platform will retain at least 70% of the usable-yield improvement observed on the development platform.
- **H4:** Sentinels will have positive net value when interruption prevalence exceeds 3% of plate runs, under the project’s operational cost model.

H1 and H2 are the primary scientific hypotheses. H3 and H4 are intended to establish practical boundaries rather than universal thresholds.

## System architecture

SentryPause will contain three layers.

### 1. Event and sensor layer

A common event schema will record planned commands, acknowledgements, timestamps, tip identifiers, liquid classes, module states, and operator interventions. Hardware evidence will include pipette pressure summaries, heater and cooler temperatures, balance readings from the plate hotel, and overhead plate images. Raw video will not be retained; the system will store timestamped still images and derived meniscus, color, and bead-distribution features.

A small uninterruptible recorder will continue logging during simulated controller or deck power loss. This is important because a recovery system should not depend on the component that has failed. It will not power heaters or motion systems.

### 2. State-estimation layer

The estimator will produce four interpretable latent quantities: thermal dose, fractional solvent loss, dispense completion by plate region, and settling index. Calibration experiments will provide approximate physical labels for these quantities. For example, plate mass change will label solvent loss, and images acquired at known stationary intervals will label bead settling.

The main predictive model will use these state estimates, workflow stage, reagent lot, and sensor features to predict the probability that each candidate action will produce an acceptable well. A monotonic gradient-boosted model will be used initially because several relationships have known directions: greater solvent loss should not reduce estimated evaporation risk, and a longer unsealed pause should not imply less thermal exposure when temperature is held constant. A hierarchical logistic model will serve as a more interpretable baseline. Calibration curves and out-of-lot performance, rather than training accuracy, will determine model selection.

### 3. Constrained recovery layer

Laboratory robots are reliable when a protocol proceeds exactly as scheduled, but their recovery from interruption is usually crude. The event log records commands, not necessarily the resulting chemical state.

Recovery decisions will be compared with immediate resumption, fixed timeout rules, and decisions made by experienced automation operators from the same logs. Evaluation will use unopened reagent lots, calendar-separated test runs, and a second robotic platform.

## Motivation and technical gap

Automated protocols are often represented as sequences of transfers, incubations, mixing steps, and measurements. This representation is adequate for execution but incomplete for recovery. A command such as “incubate for 20 minutes” does not distinguish 20 minutes on a controlled heater from 12 minutes on the heater followed by eight minutes on an unsealed ambient deck. Similarly, a logged transfer can conceal partial aspiration, dispensing into only the first portion of a plate, or liquid retained in a tip. Most practical recovery rules therefore rely on elapsed time and the last acknowledged command.
